# Chapter 7 

## AN EXISTENCE THEOREM FOR CONCAVE CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS

In this chapter some facts about the existence of concave central configurations are proved. While they have some interest in their own right, they are also necessary ingredients for later results.

With the conventions of the preceding chapter, we begin by studying points in the region $Q$, which gives us the inequalities $r_{12}=1 \leq r_{23} \leq r_{13}<2$ and $\theta_{123}<90^{\circ}, \theta_{132}>30^{\circ}$. These conditions on $\theta_{123}$ and $\theta_{132}$, when combined with the condition that $r_{23} \leq r_{13}$, are equivalent to:

$$
1<r_{13}<2 \text { and }
$$

$$
\begin{cases}1 \leq r_{23} \leq r_{13} & \text { if } 1<r_{13} \leq \sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{r_{13}^{2}-1}<r_{23} \leq r_{13} & \text { if } \sqrt{2} \leq r_{13} \leq \sqrt{2+\sqrt{3}} \\ \sqrt{r_{13}^{2}-1}<r_{23}<\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} r_{13}+\sqrt{4-r_{13}^{2}} / 2 & \text { if } \sqrt{2+\sqrt{3}} \leq r_{13}<2\end{cases}
$$

Definition 2. Labeled triangles with the third point in $Q$ will be called strictly admissible triangles, and those with the third point in $\bar{Q}$ will be called admissible.

In particular, the side lengths of any admissible triangle satisfy the inequalities in (7.1). For such configurations we have an existence theorem. For convenience let us use the notation $R_{C}=r_{C}^{-3}$ for the inverse cube of the circumradius. For admissible triangles the circumradius is in the range $[1 / \sqrt{3}, 1]$.

The following theorem gives us much of the existence result we desire, although it sidesteps the thorny issue of concavity.

Theorem 7. For a strictly admissible triangle, and any $R_{0}$ satisfying $1<R_{0}<R_{C}$, there exists a fourth point for which $r_{34} \leq r_{14} \leq r_{24}<r_{0}$ and such that the four points satisfy the consistency equations (4.2).

Proof. The strategy of the proof is to first show that there are positive numbers $\left\{r_{12}, r_{23}, z_{34}\right.$, $\left.z_{14}, r_{13}, z_{24}\right\}$ satisfying the consistency equations and the planarity condition $P=0$. Then these numbers will be shown to be interparticle distances of a planar configuration of four points.

First we pick the points of the outer triangle (points 1,2 , and 3 ) so that (7.1) are satisfied, and we pick a value of the parameter $R_{0}$ satisfying $1<R_{0}<R_{C}$.

Note that the consistency equations (4.2) are equivalent to

$$
R_{14}=F_{14}\left(r_{24}, r_{0}\right)
$$

and

$$
R_{34}=F_{34}\left(r_{24}, r_{0}\right)
$$

where

$$
F_{14}\left(r_{24}, r_{0}\right) \equiv R_{0}+\frac{S_{13}}{S_{23}}\left(R_{24}-R_{0}\right)
$$

and

$$
F_{34}\left(r_{24}, r_{0}\right) \equiv R_{0}+\frac{S_{13}}{S_{12}}\left(R_{24}-R_{0}\right)
$$

In defining the above functions $F_{14}\left(r_{24}, r_{0}\right)$ and $F_{34}\left(r_{24}, r_{0}\right)$ we are suppressing their dependence on $r_{13}$ and $r_{23}$ since these are fixed parameters throughout the argument. We will also use the notation $f_{34}=F_{34}^{-\frac{1}{4}}$ and $f_{14}=F_{14}^{-\frac{1}{4}}$.

A little algebra together with our assumed inequalities shows that $1 \leq \frac{S_{13}}{S_{23}} \leq \frac{S_{13}}{S_{12}}$; at least one of these inequalities must be strict. We will consider the the interval of $R_{24}$ values $R_{0} \leq R_{24} \leq R_{C}$. In this interval, $F_{34} \geq F_{14} \geq R_{24}$ by definition, with both equalities holding only at the endpoint $R_{24}=R_{0}$.

We will first show that $P\left(1, r_{23}, f_{34}, f_{14}, r_{13}, r_{24}\right)=0$ for a value of $R_{24} \in\left(R_{0}, R_{C}\right)$. At one endpoint of the interval, $R_{24}=F_{34}=F_{14}=R_{0}<R_{C}$. For these values the function

$P\left(1, r_{23}, r_{0}, r_{0}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$ can be simplified to:

$$
2 r_{0}^{2}\left(2 r_{23}^{2}+2 r_{13}^{2}+2 r_{23}^{2} r_{13}^{2}-1-r_{13}^{4}-r_{23}^{4}\right)-2 r_{23}^{2} r_{13}^{2}=32 r_{0}^{2} D_{4}^{2}-2 r_{23}^{2} r_{13}^{2}
$$

Recall that $D_{4}$ is the area of the triangle not containing the fourth point, and that the circumradius $r_{C}$ of this triangle is $\frac{r_{23} r_{13}}{4 D_{4}}$. Then it is easy to see that $P\left(1, r_{23}, r_{C}, r_{C}, r_{13}, r_{C}\right)=$ 0 . Furthermore, since $D_{4}^{2}>0$ we see that for $r_{0}>r_{C}$ the value of $P$ must increase, i.e. $P\left(1, r_{23}, r_{0}, r_{0}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)>0$ for $r_{0}>r_{C}$.

So $P>0$ at one endpoint, and we must show it is negative at the other endpoint, where $F_{34} \geq F_{14} \geq R_{24}=R_{C}$ (with at least one strict inequality). For this we need the following lemma:

Lemma 1. For $r_{34} \leq r_{14} \leq r_{24} \leq r_{12}=1 \leq r_{23} \leq r_{13}, \partial P / \partial r_{14}>0$ and $\partial P / \partial r_{34}>0$.

Proof. We simply explicitly compute the derivatives and regroup the terms as below:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \partial P / \partial r_{14}=4 r_{14}\left(\left(r_{13}^{2}-1\right)\left(r_{24}^{2}-r_{34}^{2}\right)+r_{23}^{2}\left(r_{34}^{2}+r_{13}^{2}-r_{23}^{2}+r_{24}^{2}+1-2 r_{14}^{2}\right)\right) \\
& \partial P / \partial r_{34}=4 r_{34}\left(\left(r_{13}^{2}-r_{23}^{2}\right)\left(r_{24}^{2}-r_{14}^{2}\right)+\left(r_{14}^{2}+r_{13}^{2}-1+r_{24}^{2}+r_{23}^{2}-2 r_{34}^{2}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Our assumptions imply that every expression in parentheses in the above formulae is nonnegative, and at least one term must be positive, so the partial derivatives are positive.

At the endpoint we are considering, only the third and fourth arguments could have changed from the arguments in the equation $P\left(1, r_{23}, r_{C}, r_{C}, r_{13}, r_{C}\right)=0$, and at least one of them decreased, so $P\left(1, r_{23}, f_{34}, f_{14}, r_{13}, r_{C}\right)<0$ at this endpoint.

Since $P\left(1, r_{23}, f_{34}, f_{14}, r_{13}, r_{24}\right)$ is a smooth function of $r_{24}$ for fixed $r_{0}$, the intermediate value theorem ensures that there is at least one zero of $P\left(1, r_{23}, f_{34}, f_{14}, r_{13}, r_{24}\right)$ for some $r_{24}$ in the interior of the desired interval. Let us call the arguments of the zero with smallest $r_{24}, z_{i j}$, so that $z_{34}=f_{34}\left(z_{24}, r_{0}\right), z_{14}=f_{14}\left(z_{24}, r_{0}\right)$, and $z_{24}=r_{24}$.

Note that the $z_{i j}$ values are all positive and real by construction. If we solve the equation

$P\left(1, r_{23}, z_{34}, z_{14}, r_{13}, z_{24}\right)=0$ for $z_{34}$ we find that

$$
\begin{gathered}
z_{34}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(r_{23}^{2}+r_{13}^{2}-1+z_{24}^{2}+z_{14}^{2}+\left(r_{13}^{2}-r_{23}^{2}\right)\left(z_{24}^{2}-z_{14}^{2}\right)\right. \\
\pm 4 D_{4} \sqrt{\left(1+z_{24}+z_{14}\right)\left(1-z_{24}+z_{14}\right)\left(1+z_{24}-z_{14}\right)\left(-1+z_{24}+z_{14}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

The right hand side of this equation must also be real and positive. Within the square root, our assumptions guarantee that every term in parentheses is positive except the last term, $\left(-1+z_{24}+z_{14}\right)$. So this term must be non-negative. Also note that since $z_{34}<z_{24}$ by construction, the smaller root in (7.6) is the correct one, since the sum of the first four terms are already greater than $z_{24}^{2}$.

To see that the $z_{i j}$ actually arise from a configuration of points in the plane, we consider a construction of such a configuration. The outer triangle is given. The circles of radius $z_{14}$ and $z_{24}$ around points 1 and 2 , respectively, intersect in one or two points since we know that $z_{24}+z_{14} \geq 1$. Since the possible $r_{34}$ must equal one of the values in (7.6), $z_{34}$ must be one of these possible $r_{34}$. Figure 7.1 shows a typical case; the length of the dashed lines in the figure would be the two possible $r_{34}$ values, of which $z_{34}$ is the smaller as noted above.
![img-4.jpeg](img-4.jpeg)

Figure 7.1: Example of possible $r_{34}$ values

This concludes the proof of Theorem 7.

The rest of this chapter consists of ingredients for the following theorem.

Theorem 8. For a strictly admissible triangle with $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$ and for $r_{0} \in\left(r_{C}, 1\right)$, there is a unique concave central configuration for which the triangle is the outer triangle with parameter $r_{0}$. As the parameter $r_{0}$ is varied from $r_{C}$ to 1 , the fourth point traces out a simple curve from the circumcenter to the equilateral point $\left(r_{14}=1, r_{24}=1\right)$.

For a strictly admissible triangle with $r_{23}^{2}<r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$ there exists an $r_{I} \in\left(r_{C}, 1\right)$ such that for each $r_{0} \in\left(r_{C}, r_{I}\right)$ there is a unique concave central configuration for which the triangle is the outer triangle with parameter $r_{0}$. Furthermore, in the limit $r_{0} \rightarrow r_{I}$ the fourth point of the configuration is collinear with the first and third points. As the parameter $r_{0}$ is varied from $r_{C}$ to $r_{I}$, the fourth point traces out a simple curve.

In both cases the position of the fourth point is a smooth function of $r_{0}, r_{23}$, and $r_{13}$ for $r_{23}$ and $r_{13}$ satisfying (7.1) and $r_{0} \in\left(r_{C}, 1\right)$ or $r_{0} \in\left(r_{C}, r_{I}\right)$.

The proof of this theorem will be deferred until the end of the chapter, after all the necessary tools have been assembled.

Lemma 2. For a given strictly admissible triangle and parameter $r_{0}$ such that $r_{C}<r_{0}<1$, there is at most one concave planar central configuration.

Proof. Recall from the proof in Theorem 7 that we can find such central configurations by varying $r_{24}$ in the interval $\left(r_{C}, r_{0}\right)$ and finding zeros of $P\left(1, r_{23}, f_{34}, f_{14}, r_{13}, r_{24}\right)$. Since $f_{14}$ and $f_{34}$ are monotonically increasing as functions of $r_{24}$, if there were two solutions corresponding to concave configurations one of them would have larger values of $r_{24}, r_{14}$, and $r_{34}$ than the other. This in turn would imply that the values of $D_{1}, D_{2}$, and $D_{3}$ would all be larger in one of the solutions, since $\partial D_{i} / \partial r_{j 4}=\left(r_{k 4}^{2}+r_{j k}^{2}-r_{j 4}^{2}\right) /\left(8 D_{i} r_{j 4}\right),(i \neq j \neq k)$, which is greater than zero for a concave configuration in which $r_{j 4}<r_{j k}$. But since the outer triangle is fixed, we must have $D_{1}+D_{2}+D_{3}=D_{4}$ be constant, which is a contradiction, so there could not be two concave central configurations with the same outer triangle and value of $r_{0}$.

The following simple lemma will be used several times:

Lemma 3. For an admissible triangle with $r_{23} \neq 1$,

$$
\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow 1} z_{24}=\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow 1} z_{14}=1
$$

Proof. This can be seen in many ways, but perhaps the simplest is to examine the original consistency equations (4.2). With our conventions it is immediate that $\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow 1} S_{12}=0$. Since $z_{34}$ is bounded away from 0 for a fixed third point in the interior of $Q$, all the terms in (4.2) must have zero as their limit. Furthermore, $S_{13}$ and $S_{23}$ are bounded away from zero (since $r_{23}>1$ ), so $\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow 1} S_{24}=\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow 1} S_{14}=0$, which is equivalent to the conclusion of the lemma.

There is a corresponding lemma for the other endpoint of $r_{0}$ values:
Lemma 4. For an admissible triangle

$$
\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow r_{C}} z_{24}=\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow r_{C}} z_{14}=r_{C}
$$

Proof. From the construction in the proof of Theorem 7 it is clear that $\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow r_{C}} z_{24}=$ $r_{C}$. Examining the equations (4.2) we see that $\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow r_{C}} S_{34}=\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow r_{C}} S_{14}=0$ since $\lim _{r_{0} \rightarrow r_{C}} S_{24}=0$ and the terms $S_{12}$ and $S_{23}$ are bounded away from zero for a fixed outer triangle.

The configurations constructed in Theorem 6 are central configurations if their masses are positive. As described previously, a concave configuration which satisfies the consistency equations and our conventions will have positive masses if and only if the inequalities (6.1) are satisfied. These results simply follow from careful examination of (4.3). The last three relations of (6.1) hold by assumption, and the first three follow immediately by the previous construction. However, we must ensure that the configurations obtained are concave. In fact, the configurations will not always be concave if $r_{23}^{2}<r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$; the lemmas below will elucidate this point in more detail.

We also need to know something about the regularity of the functions $z_{i j}$.
Lemma 5. For a planar solution to the consistency equations satisfying the conditions in Theorem 7 which is sufficiently close to concave,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{24}}\left(P\left(1, r_{23}, f_{34}, f_{14}, r_{13}, r_{24}\right)\right)>0
$$

and so $z_{24}\left(r_{13}, r_{23}, r_{0}\right)$ is a smooth function.

Proof. For $i=1,2,3$ we have

$$
\left.\frac{\partial P}{\partial r_{i 4}}\right|_{P=0}=-64 r_{i 4} \Delta_{i} \Delta_{4}
$$

from the investigations of Dziobek [D]. If the solution corresponds to a concave configuration, $\Delta_{i}<0$, and we can compute

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{24}}\left(P\left(1, r_{23}, f_{34}, f_{14}, r_{13}, r_{24}\right)\right)= \\
\frac{\partial P}{\partial r_{24}}\left(1, r_{23}, f_{34}, f_{14}, r_{13}, r_{24}\right)+\frac{\partial P}{\partial r_{34}} \frac{\partial f_{34}}{\partial r_{24}}+\frac{\partial P}{\partial r_{14}} \frac{\partial f_{14}}{\partial r_{24}}= \\
64 D_{4}\left(r_{24} D_{2}+r_{34} D_{3} \frac{S_{13} r_{34}^{4}}{S_{12} r_{24}^{4}}+r_{14} D_{1} \frac{S_{13} r_{14}^{4}}{S_{23} r_{24}^{4}}\right)>0
\end{gathered}
$$

Otherwise, the only $\Delta_{i}$ which could be positive is $\Delta_{2}$, and it is zero for a configuration on the border of concavity. This means that if the configuration is sufficiently close to concave, the terms in the above expression will dominate and $\left.\frac{\partial P}{\partial r_{i 4}}\right|_{P=0}>0$.

When the distances of the third point satisfy $r_{23}^{2}<r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$, which corresponds to the third point being below the diagonal in Figure 6.2, the configuration must cease to be concave before $r_{0}=1$. This follows from Lemma 3 ; the fourth point lies outside the convex hull of the first three points for $r_{0}$ sufficiently close to 1 . But when $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$ we must examine the curve of solutions in more detail.

Lemma 6. For admissible outer triangles with $r_{12}=1, r_{13}>1$, and $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$, the planar solutions of the consistency equations sufficiently close to $R_{0}=R_{14}=R_{24}=1$ with $R_{0}<1$ have $\theta_{214}<60^{\circ}$.

Proof. The distances $r_{23}$ and $r_{13}$ of the outer triangle can be considered as parameters for the following argument ( $r_{12}$ is always equal to 1 ). The independent variables are $R_{0}, R_{24}$, and $R_{14}$. The last distance $r_{34}$ could then be determined by choosing the root of the planarity condition $P=0$ with the smallest value of $r_{34}$. It is easy to check that $r_{34}$ is a $C^{1}$ function on the relevant domains. The consistency equations can be written as

$$
g_{1}\left(R_{0}, R_{14}, R_{24}\right)=0, \quad g_{2}\left(R_{0}, R_{14}, R_{24}\right)=0
$$

where

$$
g_{1}\left(R_{0}, R_{14}, R_{24}\right)=S_{23} S_{14}-S_{12} S_{34}
$$

and

$$
g_{2}\left(R_{0}, R_{14}, R_{24}\right)=S_{23} S_{14}-S_{13} S_{24}
$$

The Jacobian of the functions $g_{1}$ and $g_{2}$ is easily calculated:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& D\left(g_{1}, g_{2}\right)= \\
& {\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
\left(1-R_{23}+R_{34}-R_{14}\right) & -\left(R_{0}-R_{23}-\left(R_{0}-1\right) \frac{\partial R_{34}}{\partial R_{14}}\right) & \left(R_{0}-1\right) \frac{\partial R_{34}}{\partial R_{24}} \\
-\left(R_{23}-R_{13}+R_{14}-R_{24}\right) & -\left(R_{0}-R_{23}\right) & \left(R_{0}-R_{13}\right)
\end{array}\right] .} \\
& \text { At the solution } R_{0}=R_{14}=R_{24}=1 \text { this reduces to }
\end{aligned}
$$

Let us denote this Jacobian by $J_{(1,1,1)}$.
It is easy to see that $D\left(g_{1}, g_{2}\right)$ has rank 2 for any relevant values of the arguments; for instance, the fact that $R_{34}>R_{23}$ and $1>R_{13}$ is sufficient. Thus there is a smooth curve $\mathcal{L}$ of solutions near $(1,1,1)$. The tangent of $\mathcal{L}$ at $(1,1,1)$ is simply the kernel of $J_{(1,1,1)}$. A little linear algebra yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{ker}\left(J_{(1,1,1)}\right)= \\
& \operatorname{span}\left(\left(1-R_{23}\right)\left(1-R_{13}\right),\left(R_{34}-R_{23}\right)\left(1-R_{13}\right),\left(1-R_{23}\right)\left(R_{34}-R_{13}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since none of the components of a kernel vector are zero, any of the quantities $R_{0}, R_{14}$, or $R_{24}$ could be chosen as a parameter for $\mathcal{L}$. We will use $R_{14}$ as the parameter, and let $Z_{24}\left(R_{14}\right)$ denote the value of $R_{24}$ along the curve $\mathcal{L}$. The explicit dependence on $R_{14}$ will often be dropped. In order for nearby solutions to have $\theta_{214}<60^{\circ}$, they must satisfy the inequality $z_{24}^{2}<z_{14}^{2}-z_{14}+1$. That inequality is equivalent to $d Z_{24} / d R_{14}>1 / 2$ for solutions sufficiently close to $R_{0}=R_{14}=R_{24}=1$.

It is easy to compute from the above information that

$$
\frac{d Z_{24}}{d R_{14}}=\left(\frac{1-R_{23}}{1-R_{13}}\right)\left(\frac{R_{34}-R_{13}}{R_{34}-R_{23}}\right)
$$

at the solution $R_{0}=R_{14}=R_{24}=1$.
Note that

$$
\left(\frac{Z_{34}-R_{13}}{Z_{34}-R_{23}}\right) \geq 1
$$

where $Z_{34}$ is the value of $R_{34}$ on $\mathcal{L}$ determined by $R_{14}$ and $Z_{24}$. The inequality (7.14) follows from $r_{23} \leq r_{13}$, so

$$
\frac{d Z_{24}}{d R_{14}}\left(\left(R_{0}=R_{14}=Z_{24}=1\right) \geq\left(\frac{1-R_{23}}{1-R_{13}}\right)\right.
$$

It will be shown that $\left(\frac{1-R_{23}}{1-R_{13}}\right)>1 / 2$. First the case in which $r_{23}^{2}=r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$ will be proved. We consider $r_{13}$ as a parameter. It is easy to see that $\lim _{r_{13} \rightarrow 1}\left(\frac{1-R_{23}}{1-R_{13}}\right)=\frac{1}{2}$. In fact that is the infimum of $\left(\frac{1-R_{23}}{1-R_{13}}\right)$ for $r_{13}$ in the interval $(1,2)$. To see this first observe that the inequality $\left(\frac{1-R_{23}}{1-R_{13}}\right)>\frac{1}{2}$ is equivalent to $0<1+R_{13}-2 R_{23}$. Since this equality will be used in later chapters as well we will isolate it as a lemma:

Lemma 7. For points in $Q$ with $r_{23}^{2}=r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1,1+R_{13}-2 R_{23}>0$.
Proof. Substituting the expression for $r_{23}$ into the right hand side of the inequality and taking the derivative with respect to the parameter $r_{13}$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 3\left(-r_{13}^{-4}+\left(2 r_{13}-1\right)\left(r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1\right)^{-5 / 2}\right) \\
> & 3\left(-r_{13}^{-4}+\left(2 r_{13}-1\right) r_{13}^{-5}\right) \\
= & 3 r_{13}^{-5}\left(r_{13}-1\right) \\
> & 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The first inequality follows from the assumption that $r_{23}<r_{13}$ and the last inequality from the assumption that $r_{13}>1$. Since the function $2 R_{23}\left(r_{13}\right)-R_{13}$ is decreasing in the range we are considering, and equal to 1 in the limit $r_{13} \rightarrow 1$, it satisfies the desired inequality.

To obtain the result for $r_{23}^{2}>r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$, we can simply note that $\left(\frac{1-R_{23}}{1-R_{13}}\right)$ is a monotonically increasing function of $r_{23}$ and a decreasing function of $r_{13}$.

This completes the proof of the lemma.

Now it will be shown that the configurations obtained in the proof of Theorem 7 are always concave if $r_{23} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$. Lemma 6 ensures that the curve of solutions parameterized by $R_{0}$ starts from $R_{0}=R_{14}=R_{24}=1$ with the angle of its tangent line greater than 60 degrees relative to the segment $\overline{12}$. The next lemma shows that the angle of the tangent line never becomes exactly 60 degrees, which means that $\theta_{214} \leq 60^{\circ}$. This implies that the configurations stay concave since $\theta_{213} \geq 60^{\circ}$ for configurations with $r_{23} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$.

Lemma 8. For a strictly admissible triangle in which the third point is above the diagonal, i.e. $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$, there is a curve defined by the fourth point of the planar solutions of the consistency equations as the parameter $R_{0}$ is varied. The angle of the tangent line relative to the segment $\overline{12}$ is never equal to 60 degrees at any concave solution.

Proof. The condition on the angle of the tangent is equivalent to

$$
\frac{d r_{14} / d r_{0}}{d r_{24} / d r_{0}} \neq \frac{r_{24}\left(\sqrt{3\left(r_{24}^{2}-\left(1+r_{24}^{2}-r_{14}^{2}\right)^{2} / 4\right)}+\frac{1}{2}\left(1-r_{24}^{2}+r_{14}^{2}\right)\right)}{r_{14}\left(\sqrt{3\left(r_{24}^{2}-\left(1+r_{24}^{2}-r_{14}^{2}\right)^{2} / 4\right)}-\frac{1}{2}\left(1+r_{24}^{2}-r_{14}^{2}\right)\right)}
$$

This inequality is obtained by briefly reintroducing coordinates and substituting the interparticle distances into the condition on the angle of the tangent in these coordinates. We define coordinates by setting the coordinates of the first point equal to $(-.5,0)$, the coordinates of the second point to $(.5,0)$, and requiring that the $y$-coordinates of the third and fourth points are positive. Then $r_{14}^{2}=(x+.5)^{2}+y^{2}$ and $r_{24}^{2}=(x-.5)^{2}+y^{2}$, where $(x, y)$ are the coordinates of the fourth point. The desired condition on the tangent angle is equivalent to $\frac{d x}{d y} \neq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. Converting this back into the $r_{i j}$ variables gives the condition

$$
\frac{d x}{d y}=\frac{\left(\frac{d r_{14}}{d r_{24}} r_{14}-r_{24}\right)\left(\sqrt{r_{24}^{2}-\left(1+r_{24}^{2}-r_{14}^{2}\right)^{2} / 4}\right)}{r_{24}-\left(1+r_{24}^{2}-r_{14}^{2}\right)\left(2 r_{24}-2 \frac{d r_{14}}{d r_{24}} r_{14}\right) / 4} \neq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

This is equivalent to (7.17) when the denominator is not zero. If the denominator is zero, that is still okay since then $\frac{d y}{d x}=0 \neq \sqrt{3}$. The denominator and numerator cannot be zero simultaneously. If the numerator is equal to zero, then $\frac{d r_{14}}{d r_{24}}=r_{24} / r_{14}$ since the second factor in the numerator is actually equal to $y$, which is always positive. But in that case, the denominator would equal $r_{24}$, which cannot be zero.

We will show that the right hand side of (7.17) has a range contained in $(-\infty,-1) \cup(2, \infty)$ while the left hand side is always in $(-1,2)$.

If the complicated expression on the right hand side of (7.17) is positive then it is always greater than $\frac{2 r_{24}}{r_{14}}$ for $1 / 2<r_{14} \leq r_{24}<1$. To prove that, note that the denominator must be positive so we can cross-multiply to obtain the equivalent inequality

$$
\left(r_{14}^{2}-r_{24}^{2}\right)+(2 \sqrt{3} y-3)<0
$$

since $y<\sqrt{3} / 2$ the last term in parentheses in (7.19) is negative and the first term is non-positive. Here we have again used the fact that $y=\sqrt{r_{24}^{2}-\left(1+r_{24}^{2}-r_{14}^{2}\right)^{2} / 4}$.

If the right hand side of (7.17) is negative, then it will be less than $-r_{24} / r_{14}$ (which in turn is less than or equal to -1 ) if

$$
r_{14}^{2}-r_{24}^{2}+2 \sqrt{3} y>0
$$

Let us denote the left hand side of (7.20) by $h\left(r_{14}, r_{24}\right)$. Since $\partial h / \partial r_{14}=r_{14}(2+\sqrt{3}\left(1+r_{24}^{2}-\right.$ $\left.r_{14}^{2}\right) / y$ ) is positive for the relevant values of $r_{14}$ and $r_{24}$ we can check the boundary of the set of possible $r_{14}$ and $r_{24}$ to find the minimum of $h$. The lines $r_{14}=r_{24}, r_{24}^{2}=r_{14}^{2}-r_{14}+1$, and $r_{14}=1+r_{24}^{2}-\sqrt{3} r_{24}$ suffice for this computation; note that the last two correspond to $\theta_{214}=60$ degrees and $\theta_{124}=30$ degrees respectively. It is easy to compute that $h>0$ on all of those lines; in fact the minimum of $h$ is 1 .

We need to show that $\frac{d r_{14}}{d r_{24}}<2$, or $\frac{d R_{14}}{d R_{24}}<2\left(\frac{r_{24}}{r_{14}}\right)^{4}$. Throwing out the factor $\left(\frac{r_{24}}{r_{14}}\right)^{4}$, the stronger inequality $\frac{d R_{14}}{d R_{24}}<2$ will be proved. We will also see that $\frac{d R_{14}}{d R_{24}}>-1$ shortly.

To be in the kernel of $D\left(g_{1}, g_{2}\right)$ the ratio of the differentials $d R_{14}$ and $d R_{24}$ must satisfy:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{d R_{14} / d R_{0}}{d R_{24} / d R_{0}}= \\
& \frac{\left(\left(1-R_{23}+R_{34}-R_{14}\right)\left(R_{0}-R_{13}\right)+\frac{\partial R_{24}}{\partial R_{24}}\left(R_{23}-R_{13}+R_{14}-R_{24}\right)\left(R_{0}-1\right)\right)}{\left(\left(1+R_{34}-R_{13}-R_{24}\right)\left(R_{0}-R_{23}\right)-\frac{\partial R_{24}}{\partial R_{14}}\left(R_{23}-R_{13}+R_{14}-R_{24}\right)\left(R_{0}-1\right)\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The partial derivatives of $R_{34}$ will be obtained from the planarity condition. It will be shown below that $\frac{\partial R_{24}}{\partial R_{14}}<0$ and $\frac{\partial R_{24}}{\partial R_{24}}<0$. This makes it easy to see that $\frac{d R_{14}}{d R_{24}}>-1$ since if the right hand side of (7.21) is negative, it must be of the form $\frac{A-B}{C+B}$ with $A, B, C>0$ and $B>A$.

The denominator of the right hand side of (7.21) is always positive in our domain so we can cross-multiply the desired inequality $\frac{d R_{14}}{d R_{24}}<2$ to get the equivalent condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 0<\left(R_{23}+R_{14}-R_{13}-R_{24}\right)\left(R_{0}-1\right)\left(-2 \frac{\partial R_{34}}{\partial R_{14}}-\frac{\partial R_{34}}{\partial R_{24}}\right)+ \\
& 2\left(R_{0}-R_{23}\right)\left(1+R_{34}-R_{13}-R_{24}\right)-\left(R_{0}-R_{13}\right)\left(1+R_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

To prove (7.22) we will show the first line of the left hand side is non-negative and the second line is positive. In the first term, everything is positive by assumption except the partial derivatives. Since $\frac{d R_{34}}{\partial R_{24}}=\frac{d r_{34}}{d r_{24}}\left(\frac{r_{24}}{r_{34}}\right)^{4}$ and $\frac{d R_{34}}{\partial R_{14}}=\frac{d r_{34}}{\partial r_{14}}\left(\frac{r_{14}}{r_{34}}\right)^{4}$, we can compute the sign of these derivatives for concave configurations by simplifying the expression obtained from solving $P=0$ for $r_{34}$ and then taking a derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial r_{34}}{\partial r_{24}} & =\frac{r_{24}}{2 r_{34}}\left(1+r_{13}^{2}-r_{23}^{2}-D_{4} / D_{3}\left(1+r_{14}^{2}-r_{24}^{2}\right)\right) \\
& =\frac{r_{24}}{r_{34}}\left(r_{13} \cos \theta_{213}-D_{4} / D_{3} r_{14} \cos \theta_{214}\right) \\
& =\frac{r_{24} r_{13}}{r_{34} \sin \theta_{214}}\left(\sin \theta_{214} \cos \theta_{213}-\sin \theta_{213} \cos \theta_{214}\right) \\
& =-\frac{r_{24} r_{13}}{r_{34} \sin \theta_{214}}\left(\sin \theta_{213}-\theta_{214}\right) \\
& =-D_{2} / D_{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

To obtain the above result the law of cosines, Heron's formula, and the formulae $D_{4}=$ $r_{13} \sin \theta_{213} / 2$ and $D_{3}=r_{14} \sin \theta_{214} / 2$ are used along with some trigonometric identities.

A very similar calculation yields

$$
\frac{\partial r_{34}}{\partial r_{14}}=-D_{1} / D_{3}
$$

The second line in (7.22) can be rearranged as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 2\left(R_{0}-R_{23}\right)\left(1+R_{34}-R_{13}-R_{24}\right)-\left(R_{0}-R_{13}\right)\left(1+R_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right) \\
= & \left(R_{0}-R_{23}\right)\left(1+R_{34}-2 R_{13}-2 R_{24}+R_{23}+R_{14}\right)- \\
& \left(R_{23}-R_{13}\right)\left(1+R_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right) \\
\geq & \left(R_{0}-R_{23}\right)\left(1+R_{34}-2 R_{13}+R_{23}-R_{14}\right)- \\
& \left(R_{23}-R_{13}\right)\left(1+R_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right) \\
= & \left(R_{0}-R_{23}\right)\left(1-R_{13}\right)+\left(R_{23}-R_{13}\right)\left(R_{0}-1\right)+ \\
& \left(R_{34}-R_{14}\right)\left(R_{0}+R_{13}-2 R_{23}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The inequality follows from $-2 R_{24}+R_{14} \geq-R_{14}$. Only the last term in parentheses could be negative. However, simply note that $R_{0}+R_{13}-2 R_{23}>1+R_{13}-2 R_{23}$. From Lemma 7 we

already know that the latter function is positive on the diagonal, and since $1+R_{13}-2 R_{23}$ is monotonically increasing as a function of $r_{23}$ it is positive everywhere in $Q$ above the diagonal as well, which completes the proof of Lemma 8.

Proof of Theorem 8. This theorem is basically a consequence of the earlier Lemmas in this chapter.

For the outer triangles with $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$, we know from the analysis near the equilateral point with $r_{14}=1$ and $r_{24}=1$ that the fourth points of the solutions form a smooth curve $\mathcal{L}$ whose tangent angle is always greater than 60 degrees relative to the segment $\overline{12}$. Lemma 8 ensures that this tangent angle remains greater than 60 degrees. This in turn implies that the solution curve cannot become non-concave by leaving the region V on the line $\overline{13}$ or the boundary $r_{24}=1$ since $\theta_{214}<60^{\circ}$ (c.f. Figure 6.2). Since $\mathcal{L}$ is both closed and open in V it must end somewhere on the boundary of V . Note that it is impossible for $z_{24}=z_{14}$ for $r_{13} \neq r_{23}$ except for $z_{24}=z_{14}=z_{34}=r_{0}=r_{C}$, by inspection of the consistency equations. Likewise the curve cannot hit the boundary where $r_{14}=r_{34}$ except at the circumcenter. So the curve must end at the circumcenter.

The situation is a little different when $r_{23}^{2}<r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$. There are concave solutions near the circumcenter where $r_{14}=r_{C}$ and $r_{24}=r_{C}$, and we know that the solutions obtained in Theorem 7 leave the region V at some parameter value $r_{0}=r_{I}$. It is shown in Chapter 8 that this parameter value is continuous as a function of $r_{23}$ and $r_{13}$. That proof also guarantees that the curve of solutions cannot re-enter the region V. Note that again it is impossible for the curve to hit the lines defined by $r_{24}=r_{14}$ or $r_{14}=r_{34}$ except at the circumcenter, so at $r_{0}=r_{I}$ the fourth point is collinear with points 1 and 3 .

In either case it is easy to see that $\mathcal{L}$ is a simple curve since at a self intersection point there would be two values of $r_{0}$ for the same configuration, which is impossible away from the equilateral point.

# Chapter 8 

## BORDER CONFIGURATIONS

In this chapter the continuity of $R_{I}$ is proved on the relevant domains. Recall that this is the value of the parameter $R_{0}$ at which points 1,4 , and 3 are collinear.

Definition 3. Let $w_{24}\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{14}\right)=\sqrt{1+r_{14}^{2}-2 r_{14}\left(\frac{1+r_{14}^{2}-r_{23}^{2}}{2 r_{13}}\right)}$.

Definition 4. Let $w_{34}\left(r_{13}, r_{14}\right)=r_{13}-r_{14}$.
As before we will use the notation $W_{24}=w_{24}^{-3}$ and $W_{34}=w_{34}^{-3}$. Note that $\left(\frac{1+r_{14}^{2}-r_{23}^{2}}{2 r_{13}}\right)=$ $\cos \theta_{213}$.

Definition 5. Let $F_{1}=\frac{W_{24}-R_{13} W_{24}}{1+W_{34}-R_{13}-W_{24}}$ and $F_{2}=\frac{W_{24}-R_{23} R_{14}}{1+W_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}}$.
Definition 6. Let $F\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{14}\right)=F_{1}-F_{2}$.
Note that $R_{0}=F_{1}=F_{2}$ is the condition for the consistency equations to be satisfied for the fourth point on the boundary of the exterior triangle.

Definition 7. Let $\Omega$ be the set of $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{14}\right) \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}$ for which $1<r_{23}^{2}<r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$, $r_{13}^{2}<1+r_{23}^{2}$, and $r_{13} / 2<r_{14}<\frac{1}{2 \cos \theta_{213}}$.

More explicitly, the variables in $\Omega$ must satisfy the conditions $\frac{1}{2}<\frac{r_{13}}{2}<r_{14}<\frac{1}{2 \cos \theta_{213}} \leq$ $1<r_{23}<r_{13}<2$ as well as $\left(r_{13}^{2}-1\right)<r_{23}^{2}<r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$. The condition on $r_{23}$ corresponds to the third point being below the diagonal in the region $Q$ (cf. Figure 6.2).

Note that the denominators of both $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ are always positive on the domain $\Omega$.
Definition 8. Configurations in which three points are collinear will be referred to as border configurations.

Definition 9. Let $\Pi(\Omega)$ be the projection of $\Omega$ onto its first two coordinates. I.e. $\Pi(\Omega)$ is the set of $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$ satisfying the inequalities $1<r_{23}<r_{13}<2$ and $\left(r_{13}^{2}-1\right)<r_{23}^{2}<r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$.

The inequalities in the above definitions are somewhat redundant, in order to supply the reader with all the relevant relationships.

Theorem 9. The set $F=0$ in the domain $\Omega$ can be written as the graph of a continuous function $Y_{14}\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$ over $\Pi(\Omega)$.

Proof. First we will show that there is at least one zero of $F$ in $\Omega$ for any fixed $r_{13}$ and $r_{23}$. We simply compute the values at the endpoints, and find that

$$
\begin{gathered}
F\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, \frac{r_{13}}{2}\right)=\frac{8 R_{13}-R_{13} W_{24}}{1+7 R_{13}-W_{24}}-8 R_{13} \\
=\frac{R_{13}\left(8-W_{24}-8\left(1+7 R_{13}-W_{24}\right)\right)}{1+7 R_{13}-W_{24}} \\
=-\frac{7 R_{13}\left(8 R_{13}-W_{24}\right)}{1+7 R_{13}-W_{24}}<0
\end{gathered}
$$

and

$$
\begin{gathered}
F\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, \frac{1}{2 \cos \theta_{213}}\right)=\frac{W_{34}-R_{13} R_{14}}{1+W_{34}-R_{13}-R_{14}}-\frac{W_{34}-R_{23} R_{14}}{1+W_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}} \\
=\frac{\left(R_{23}-R_{13}\right)\left(R_{14}-1\right)\left(W_{34}-R_{14}\right)}{\left(1+W_{34}-R_{13}-R_{14}\right)\left(1+W_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right)}>0
\end{gathered}
$$

on $\Omega$.
Next we compute the derivative of $F$ with respect to $r_{14}$, at $F=0$, in order to use the implicit function theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d F}{d r_{14}} \mid F=0= & 3\left(1+W_{34}-R_{13}-W_{24}\right)^{-1}\left(1+W_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right)^{-1} \\
& {\left[w_{34}^{-4}\left(R_{0}-1\right)\left(R_{23}+R_{14}-R_{13}-W_{24}\right)\right.} \\
& +r_{14}^{-4}\left(R_{0}-R_{23}\right)\left(1+W_{34}-R_{13}-W_{24}\right) \\
& \left.-w_{24}^{-5}\left(r_{14}-\cos \theta_{213}\right)\left(R_{0}-R_{13}\right)\left(1+W_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right)\right] \\
= & 3\left(1+W_{34}-R_{13}-W_{24}\right)^{-1}\left(1+W_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right)^{-1} \\
& {\left[w_{34}^{-4}\left(1+W_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right)^{-1}\left(R_{14}-1\right)\right.} \\
& \left.(1-R_{23})\left(R_{23}+R_{14}-R_{13}-W_{24}\right)\right. \\
& +r_{14}^{-4}\left(R_{14}-1\right)^{-1}\left(W_{34}-R_{23}\right)\left(1-R_{13}\right)\left(W_{24}-1\right) \\
& \left.-w_{24}^{-5}\left(W_{34}-W_{24}\right)^{-1}\left(r_{14}-\cos \theta_{213}\right)\right. \\
& \left.\left(W_{34}-R_{23}\right)\left(1-R_{13}\right)\left(W_{34}-R_{14}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

In order to obtain the last line of (8.1) we have used substitutions derived from the equation $F_{1}=F_{2}$. As noted above, $R_{0}$ is the common value of $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ on the set $F=0$. For the term with the coefficient $r_{14}^{-4}$, the substitution $R_{0}=F_{1}$ is used, and for the term with the coefficient $w_{24}^{-5}$ the substitution $R_{0}=F_{2}$ is used. Then the resulting identity can be verified by expanding and rearranging

$$
\left(W_{34}-R_{13} W_{24}\right)\left(1+W_{34}-R_{23}-R_{14}\right)-\left(W_{34}-R_{23} R_{14}\right)\left(1+W_{34}-R_{13}-W_{24}\right)=0
$$

which is obtained by cross-multiplying the equation $F_{1}=F_{2}$ by its denominators.
We will now show that (8.1) is positive on the domain $\Omega$ we are interested in. Every term in parentheses has been written so that it is positive on this domain, which makes it clear that the first two terms within the brackets are positive and the third is negative. We will see that the sum of the second and third terms is positive. After factoring out the common factor of $-\left(W_{34}-R_{23}\right)\left(1-R_{13}\right)$ we are left with the expression

$$
-\frac{\left(W_{24}-1\right)}{r_{14}^{4}\left(R_{14}-1\right)}+\frac{\left(r_{14}-\cos \theta_{213}\right)\left(W_{34}-R_{14}\right)}{w_{24}^{5}\left(W_{34}-W_{24}\right)}
$$

After factoring out some positive terms and clearing some fractions, the sign of (8.2) is determined by the sign of

$$
-r_{14}^{2}\left(1-w_{24}^{3}\right)\left(w_{24}^{3}-w_{34}^{3}\right)+w_{24}\left(r_{14}-\cos \theta_{213}\right)\left(1-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{14}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)
$$

Now let us make a change of variables from $\left(r_{14}, r_{13}, r_{23}\right)$ to $\left(r_{14}, r_{13}, \alpha\right)$, where $\alpha=$ $\cos \theta_{213}$. Then $w_{24}$ is a function of $r_{14}$ and $\alpha$, whereas $w_{34}$ is function of $r_{14}$ and $r_{13}$. Let us denote the function of these arguments in (8.3) by $G\left(r_{14}, r_{13}, \alpha\right)$.

In our new variables, the inequalities defining $\Omega$ can be written as $\frac{1}{2}<\alpha<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 2 \alpha<$ $r_{13}<\frac{1}{\alpha}$, and $\frac{r_{13}}{2}<r_{14}<\frac{1}{2 \alpha}$.

A simple computation yields that

$$
\frac{\partial G}{\partial r_{13}}=3\left(r_{13}-r_{14}\right)^{2}\left(r_{14}^{2}+w_{24}\left(1+r_{14}\right)\left(\alpha\left(1-r_{14}+r_{14}^{2}\right)-r_{14}\right)\right)
$$

which will always be positive if $G_{1}=r_{14}^{2}+w_{24}\left(1+r_{14}\right)\left(\alpha\left(1-r_{14}+r_{14}^{2}\right)-r_{14}\right)$ is positive on $\Omega$.

Since $\frac{\partial G_{1}}{\partial \alpha}=\left(1+r_{14}^{2}\left(2+2 r_{14}+r_{14}^{3}\right)-3 \alpha\left(r_{14}+r_{14}^{4}\right)\right) / w_{24}$, the sign of $\frac{\partial G_{1}}{\partial \alpha}$ is determined by the sign of

$$
G_{2}\left(r_{14}, \alpha\right)=1+r_{14}^{2}\left(2+2 r_{14}+r_{14}^{3}\right)-3 \alpha\left(r_{14}+r_{14}^{4}\right)
$$

It is easy to see that $\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial \alpha}<0$, so to compute a lower bound for $G_{2}\left(r_{14}, \alpha\right)$ we can examine $G_{2}\left(r_{14}, 1 / \sqrt{2}\right)$.

Now if we look at $\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial r_{14}}\left(r_{14}, 1 / \sqrt{2}\right)$ we get a quartic in $r_{14}$ :

$$
q\left(r_{14}\right)=-\frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}+4 r_{14}+6 r_{14}^{2}-6 \sqrt{2} r_{14}^{3}+5 r_{14}^{4}
$$

and the only real roots of this quartic occur at $r_{14}$ less than $1 / 2$. There are many ways to see this, but one elementary way is to notice that the second derivative of $q$ is $12\left(5 r_{14}^{2}-3 \sqrt{2} r_{14}+\right.$ 1) which is always positive, and since $\left.\frac{d q}{d r_{14}}\right|_{r_{14}=\frac{1}{2}}=(25-9 \sqrt{2}) / 2>0$ and $q\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{61-36 \sqrt{2}}{4}>0$ the polynomial $q$ is positive for all $r_{14}>\frac{1}{2}$.

Thus the sign of $\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial r_{14}}$ is positive on $\Omega$. So the minimum of $G_{2}$ occurs at $r_{14}=r_{13} / 2$ and $\alpha=1 / \sqrt{2}$. This lets us compute $G_{2} \geq G_{2}\left(r_{13} / 2,1 / \sqrt{2}\right)>G_{2}(1 / 2,1 / \sqrt{2})=\frac{57-27 \sqrt{2}}{32}>0$. So $\frac{\partial G_{1}}{\partial \alpha}>0$, which implies that $G_{1}\left(r_{14}, \alpha\right)>G_{1}\left(r_{14}, 1 / 2\right)$.

We now need to show that $G_{1}\left(r_{14}, 1 / 2\right)=r_{14}^{2}+\left(1+r_{14}\right) \sqrt{1-r_{14}+r_{14}^{2}}\left(1-3 r_{14}+r_{14}^{2}\right) / 2$ is always positive on the interval $\left(\frac{1}{2}, 1\right)$. The argument is by contradiction. If $G_{1}\left(r_{14}, 1 / 2\right)=0$ then the following polynomial $p\left(r_{14}\right)$ would also be zero at the same value of $r_{14}$

$$
p_{1}\left(r_{14}\right)=\left(1-r_{14}\right)^{2}\left(1-3 r_{14}-2 r_{14}^{2}+5 r_{14}^{3}-2 r_{14}^{4}-3 r_{14}^{5}+r_{14}^{6}\right)
$$

This is obtained by rearranging, squaring, and simplifying the equation $G_{1}\left(r_{14}, 1 / 2\right)=0$. Let $p\left(r_{14}\right)=1-3 r_{14}-2 r_{14}^{2}+5 r_{14}^{3}-2 r_{14}^{4}-3 r_{14}^{5}+r_{14}^{6}$. Now we compute that $\frac{d^{2} p}{d r_{14}^{2}}=$ $-4+30 r_{14}-24 r_{14}^{2}-60 r_{14}^{3}+30 r_{14}^{4}$. Computing a few values of the quartic $\frac{d^{2} p}{d r_{14}^{2}}$ :

| $r_{14}$ | -1 | 0 | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | 2 | 3 |
| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
| $\left.\frac{d^{2} p}{d r_{14}^{2}}\right|_{r_{14}}$ | 32 | -4 | $\frac{40}{27}$ | $-\frac{5}{8}$ | -40 | 680 |

shows that there are four real roots of the second derivative outside the interval $\left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right]$ so $\frac{d^{2} p}{d r_{14}^{2}}<0$ in that interval. Since $\left.\frac{d p}{d r_{14}}\right|_{r_{14}=\frac{1}{2}}=-3$ we also have that $\frac{d p}{d r_{14}}<0$ on the interval. Finally, since $p\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-37 / 64<0$, we see that $p$ cannot be zero in the interval $\left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right]$. So $p_{1}$ is also never zero in the interval, which is a contradiction.

So $G_{1}$ is positive on $\Omega$, which implies that $\frac{\partial G}{\partial r_{13}}$ is positive on the domain $\Omega$. So $G$ will be less than its values on the boundary of $\Omega$ with largest $r_{13}$, which is when $r_{13}=2 r_{14}$. It is easy to see from (8.3) that $G \leq 0$ at those points since $w_{34}=r_{14}$, so it must be negative on the interior of the domain $\Omega$. This in turn implies that $\left.\frac{d F}{d r_{14}}\right|_{F=0}>0$ so there is exactly one zero of $F$ for each $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right) \in \Pi(\Omega)$. The implicit function theorem then lets us describe the set $F=0$ as the continuous graph of $Y_{14}\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$ over $\Pi(\Omega)$.

Since $R_{0}=F_{1}=F_{2}$ on the set $F=0$, Theorem 9 implies that there is a function $R_{I}\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$ which is continuous in $\Pi(\Omega)$, and such that for $R_{0}=R_{I}\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$ there is a configuration satisfying the consistency equations with the fourth point collinear with first and third points.

We will also need to understand the behavior of the function $R_{I}$ on the boundary of the region $\Pi(\Omega)$.

The easiest case is when $r_{13}^{2}=r_{23}^{2}+1$. Here the required interval for $r_{14}$ shrinks to $r_{13} / 2=r_{C}$, which means

$$
\lim _{r_{13} \rightarrow \sqrt{r_{23}^{2}+1}=\frac{1}{n}} Y_{14}=R_{C}
$$

This in turn means that we can simply extend the value of $R_{I}$ to be $R_{C}$ on these boundary points.

The next type of boundary point we will examine is a point $p_{0}=\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$ such that $r_{23}=1$ and $r_{13} \neq 1$. As one would hope and expect, as these isosceles configurations are approached the limit of $Y_{14}$ equals its value in the isosceles case $\left(\left(r_{13} / 2\right)^{-3}=8 R_{13}\right)$, as the following lemma shows.

Lemma 9. $\lim _{p \rightarrow\left(1, r_{13}\right)} Y_{14}=8 R_{13}$ for $r_{13} \neq 1$ and $p \in \Pi(\Omega)$.
Proof. Let us write the components of $p$ as $\left(\tilde{r}_{23}, \tilde{r}_{13}\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$. It has already been noted that $F\left(\tilde{r}_{23}, \tilde{r}_{13}, \tilde{r}_{13} / 2\right)<0$ (in the beginning of the proof of Theorem 9). Now it will be shown that $F\left(1+\epsilon^{2}, \tilde{r}_{13}, \tilde{r}_{13} / 2+\epsilon+O\left(\epsilon^{2}\right)\right)>0$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon$, which implies the lemma since for each fixed $\tilde{r}_{23}$ and $\tilde{r}_{13}$ there is only one zero of $F$ in the interval $\left(\tilde{r}_{13} / 2, \frac{1}{2 \cos \theta_{213}}\right)$.

Instead of using $\epsilon$, let us work in the capital variables (the inverse cubes) with $\tilde{R}_{23}=$ $1-E_{23}$ and $R_{14}=8 \tilde{R}_{13}-E_{14}$. Then we have $W_{34}=8 \tilde{R}_{13}+E_{14}+O\left(E_{14}^{2}\right)$ and $F_{2}$ becomes

$$
\frac{2 E_{14}+8 \tilde{R}_{13} E_{23}-E_{14} E_{23}+O\left(E_{14}^{2}\right)}{2 E_{14}+E_{23}+O\left(E_{14}^{2}\right)}
$$

If we let $E_{14}=\sqrt{E_{23}}$, then $F_{2}=1+O\left(E_{14}\right)$ and since $F_{1}>1$ (even at $E_{14}=0$ ) we have $F>0$ for sufficiently small $E_{14}$. So for sufficiently small $E_{14}$ there will be a zero of $F$ for $R_{14}$ in the interval $\left(8 \tilde{R}_{13}, 8 \tilde{R}_{13}+E_{14}\right)$. If we choose $\epsilon=\tilde{r}_{13}^{4} E_{14} / 48$ we have $F\left(1+\epsilon^{2}, \tilde{r}_{13}, \tilde{r}_{13} / 2+\epsilon+O\left(\epsilon^{2}\right)\right)>0$ as desired.

The penultimate category of boundary point consists of $p_{0}$ for which $\alpha=1 / 2$, or equivalently when $r_{23}^{2}=r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$. We have already examined this case from a somewhat different perspective, in Lemma 8. The calculations in that lemma suggest that $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} Y_{14}=1$. The following lemma makes that intuition precise.

Lemma 10. For $r_{13} \neq 1, \lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} Y_{14}=1$, where $p_{0}=\left(\sqrt{r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1}, r_{13}\right)$.
Proof. Recall that for each $p=\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$ we define $Y_{14}$ as the unique value of $r_{14} \in$ $\left(r_{13} / 2,1 / 2 \alpha\right)$ for which $F\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{14}\right)=0$.

In order to examine where $F$ changes sign, we expand around the point where $R_{14}=$ $W_{24}=(2 \alpha)^{3}$, writing $R_{14}=(2 \alpha)^{3}+E_{14}=1+E_{\alpha}+E_{14}$ and $W_{24}=(2 \alpha)^{3}+E_{24}=1+E_{\alpha}+E_{24}$. For a border configuration it is easy to show that in fact $1+E_{\alpha}+E_{24}=1+E_{\alpha}+E_{14} / 2+$ $O\left(E_{14}^{2}\right)$.

Now consider the sign of $F\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, 1+E_{\alpha}+E_{14}\right)$. After clearing the positive denominators, the sign of $F$ is determined by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& E_{\alpha}\left(R_{23}-R_{13}\right)\left(W_{34}-1-3 E_{14} / 2-E_{\alpha}\right) \\
& -E_{14}\left(W_{34}\left(R_{13}+1-2 R_{23}\right)+\left(R_{23}+R_{23} R_{13}-2 R_{13}\right)\right) / 2 \\
& +O\left(E_{14}^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

For $p$ sufficiently close to the diagonal (where $\alpha=1 / 2$ ) note that $R_{13}+1-2 R_{23}>0$ by Lemma 7. Since $W_{34} \geq 1$, we have $W_{34}\left(R_{13}+1-2 R_{23}\right)+\left(R_{23}+R_{23} R_{13}-2 R_{13}\right) \geq$ $\left(1-R_{23}\right)\left(1-R_{13}\right)>0$. For sufficiently small $E_{\alpha}$, this means that $F\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, 1+E_{\alpha}+E_{14}\right)$ changes sign at

$$
E_{14}=E_{\alpha} \frac{2\left(R_{23}-R_{13}\right)\left(\left(r_{13}-1\right)^{-3}-1\right)}{\left(\left(r_{13}-1\right)^{-3}\left(R_{13}+1-2 R_{23}\right)+\left(R_{23}+R_{23} R_{13}-2 R_{13}\right)\right)}+O\left(\alpha^{2}\right)
$$

The coefficient of $E_{\alpha}$ in (8.8) is nonzero for $r_{13} \neq 1$, so the zero of $F$ is located at $1+O\left(E_{\alpha}\right)$, which proves the lemma.

Finally, we will examine $R_{I}$ on the blowup of the point where $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)=(1,1)$. For this we introduce $c=\frac{1-R_{23}}{1-R_{13}}$. For admissible outer triangles we have $c \in(0,1 / 2)$, and $\left(c, r_{13}\right)$ may be used as coordinates instead of $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}\right)$.

Theorem 10. For admissible outer triangles there is a continuous function $Y_{14 b}\left(r_{13}, c\right)$ defining the border configurations near the blowup $r_{23}=r_{13}=1$.

Proof. The consistency equations for a border configuration on the blowup can be written, using the variables $c$ and $E_{13}=1-R_{13}$, as

$$
\left(W_{34}-R_{14}\right)\left(W_{24}-1\right)-c\left(W_{34}-W_{24}\right)\left(R_{14}-1\right)+c E_{13}\left(R_{14}-R_{24}\right)=0
$$

Consider instead the above equation with $E_{13}=0$.

$$
\left(W_{34}-R_{14}\right)\left(W_{24}-1\right)-c\left(W_{34}-W_{24}\right)\left(R_{14}-1\right)=0
$$

Let us denote the function in (8.10) as $F_{b}$. We will show that at the relevant zeros of $F_{b}$ its derivative is non-zero. This property is stable under perturbations, and so the function in (8.9) will also have that property for sufficiently small $E_{13}$.

There is at least one zero of $F_{b}$ with $r_{14}$ in the interval $(1 / 2,1)$, for $c \in(0,1 / 2)$. To see this we simply compute values at the endpoints. At $r_{14}=1 / 2$, we have $R_{14}=W_{34}=8$ and $F_{b}=-56 c\left(1-3^{-3}\right)<0$. At the other end, $W_{34}$ becomes infinite and we must take a limit. If $r_{14}=1-\epsilon_{14}$ for $0<\epsilon_{14}<<1$, then $R_{14} \approx 1+3 \epsilon_{14}$ and $W_{24} \approx 1+3 \epsilon_{14} / 2$. The coefficient of $W_{34}$ will determine the sign of $F_{b}$ in the limit as $\epsilon_{14} \rightarrow 0$, and it is $3 \epsilon_{14}(1 / 2-c)>0$ to first order in $\epsilon_{14}$.

Now we turn to the derivative of $F_{b}$. We can solve for $c$ in the equations $F_{b}=0$ and plug it into $\frac{d F_{b}}{d r_{14}}$ to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\frac{d F_{b}}{d r_{14}}\right|_{F_{b}=0, r_{13}=1}=3\left[w_{24}^{3}\left(2-r_{14}\right)\right. & \left.\left(1+r_{14}\right)\left(1-r_{14}\left(1-r_{14}\right)\left(4-7 r_{14}+7 r_{14}^{2}\right)\right)-\right. \\
2\left(1-r_{14}\left(1-r_{14}\right)\left(5+r_{14}\left(1-r_{14}\right)\left(-8+r_{14}^{2}\left(1-r_{14}\right)^{2}\right)\left(3-r_{14}+r_{14}^{2}\right)\right)\right)\right] / & \\
& \left.\left(2\left(\left(1-r_{14}\right)^{4}\left(1+r_{14}+r_{14}^{2}\right)-w_{24}^{3}\left(1-r_{14}^{3}\right)\right)\right) .\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to show that the derivative $\left.\frac{d F_{b}}{d r_{14}}\right|_{F_{b}=0}$ is not zero for $r_{14} \in(1 / 2,1)$. First we show that the denominator in (8.11) is never zero on $(1 / 2,1)$. Any zero of the denominator would also be a zero of the polynomial

$$
r_{14}\left(1+r_{14}+r_{14}^{2}\right)^{2}\left(3-9 r_{14}+13 r_{14}^{2}-9 r_{14}^{3}+3 r_{14}^{4}\right)
$$

which is obtained by setting the denominator to zero, rearranging and squaring to get rid of the square root in $W_{24}$, and factoring. It is easy to see that any zeros in $(1 / 2,1)$ would have to come from the quartic factor $p_{d}$ in (8.12). But the symmetry of the coefficients of

$p_{d}$ implies that if there were a zero in $(1 / 2,1)$, there would also be a zero in $(1,2)$. This is impossible since $p_{d}(1)=1, \frac{d p_{d}}{d r_{14}}(1)=2$, and $\frac{d^{2} p_{d}}{d r_{14}^{2}}>0$ on $(1 / 2,1)$.

Now it must be shown that the numerator of (8.11) has no zeros in the interval. We use the same technique of setting the numerator to zero, and rearranging and squaring to eliminate the square roots to obtain a polynomial in $r_{14}$ which has all the zeros of the numerator. If we ignore factors which do not have zeros in the interval in question, and we make the change of variables $z=\left(r_{14}-1 / 2\right)^{2}$, we are left with the polynomial

$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{n}(z)=32768 z^{8}-270336 z^{7}+653312 z^{6}+1041920 z^{5}-1603968 z^{4} \\
-2648672 z^{3}-892760 z^{2}-184702 z-23569
\end{gathered}
$$

On $(0,1 / 4), p_{n}(z)$ is less than the value obtained by evaluating all the positive terms in $p_{n}(z)$ at zero and all the negative terms at $z=1 / 4$. Since this value is $-22391.5, p_{n}(z)$ has no zeros on $(0,1 / 4)$. This is equivalent to the numerator of (8.11) having no zeros in $(1 / 2,1)$.

The implicit function theorem then guarantees the continuity of the resulting function $Y_{14 b}\left(c, r_{13}\right)$.

We will need Theorem 10 in Chapter 10, where its relevance will be explained.

# Chapter 9 

## TOPOLOGICAL LEMMA

In many of the arguments in the following chapters, and indeed for the main result of this paper, a topological lemma will be used. This can be thought of as one possible extension of the intermediate value theorem to higher dimensions. Note that here, and throughout this paper, $D^{n}$ is the closed unit disk in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

Lemma 11. A continuous map $f: D^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n}$, that restricts to a degree one map $\left.f\right|_{S^{n-1}}$ : $S^{n-1} \rightarrow S^{n-1}$, is surjective onto $D^{n}$.

Proof. The proof is by contradiction. Assume that the map is not surjective onto $D^{n}$. Then at least one point, $p$, is not in the image. However, the induced map on the homology groups is the identity on $H_{n-1}\left(S^{n-1}\right)=\mathbb{Z}$. As seen in the commutative diagram below, this is impossible since the map factors through 0 .
![img-5.jpeg](img-5.jpeg)

For more information on differential topology and the degree of a map see the excellent introduction by Hirsch $[\mathrm{Hr}]$.

# Chapter 10 

## EXTENSION OF THE MASS MAP

The goal of this chapter is to apply Lemma 11 to the map from the set of configurations which are canonical concave central configurations to the space of masses.

Definition 10. Let the set $T$ be defined as the $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right) \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}$ for which $r_{23}$ and $r_{13}$ are determined by a point in $Q$ (see (7.1)), $r_{0} \in\left(r_{C}, r_{I}\right)$ for $r_{23}^{2} \leq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$, and $r_{0} \in\left(r_{C}, 1\right)$ for $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$.

Recall that $\mathcal{M}=\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right) \mid \sum m_{i}=1, m_{i} \geq 0\right\}$.
Definition 11. Let $\mathcal{M}_{c}=\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right) \mid \sum m_{i}=1, m_{i} \geq 0, m_{1} \geq m_{2}, m_{1} \geq m_{3}\right\}$.

Definition 12. Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{c}$ be the union of $\mathcal{M}_{c}$ and the five subsets of $\mathcal{M}$ given by $m_{4}=0$, $m_{2}=0, m_{3}=0, m_{1}=m_{2}$, and $m_{1}=m_{3}$.

Definition 13. Let $\sigma_{j i}=\frac{\Delta_{j} S_{i k}}{\Delta_{i} S_{j k}}$, for $1 \leq k \leq 4, k \neq i$, and $k \neq j$. The $Z_{i 4}$ variables are to be substituted for the $R_{i 4}$ variables in these expressions.

Note that the $\sigma_{j i}$ are simply the mass ratios as given in (4.3).
Recall that $Z_{i 4}=z_{i 4}^{-3}$ are the smooth functions of $r_{0}, r_{23}$, and $r_{13}$ constructed in Chapter 7 which give the distances from the points of the outer triangle to the (interior) fourth point. By construction configurations with these distances are concave central configurations.

Definition 14. The mass map $\mathcal{F}: T \rightarrow \mathcal{M}$ is defined by $m_{i}=1 /\left(1+\sum_{j \neq i} \sigma_{j i}\right)$.
The set $T$ parameterizes the set of concave central configurations. We would like to extend the mass map to the boundary of this set, but this is not possible on the natural closure of $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. We must at least blow up $\bar{T}$ at the point $(1,1,1)$.

Definition 15. In coordinates $(r, \theta, \phi)$, define $U=[0, \infty) \times[0, \pi / 2] \times[0, \pi / 4]$.

Definition 16. Let $\beta: U \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{3}$ be the blow-down map given by $\beta(r, \theta, \phi) \mapsto(1+$ $r \tan (\phi) \cos (\theta), 1+r \cos (\theta), 1-r \sin (\theta))$.

Definition 17. Let $T_{b}=\overline{\beta^{-1}(T)}$.
In order to apply Lemma 11 we must first prove the following theorem:
Theorem 11. The map $\mathcal{F}$ extends continuously to the boundary of $T_{b}$.
Since the proof of Theorem 11 is rather long, it will be broken up into sections 10.1 10.9. The remainder of this section will lay the groundwork for these arguments.

Instead of $(r, \theta, \phi)$, we will use local coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right),\left(r_{0}, a, c\right),\left(r_{13}, d, c\right)$, or $\left(r_{0}, a, b\right)$, where $a=\left(1-R_{13}\right) /\left(R_{0}-1\right), b=\left(1-R_{23}\right) /\left(R_{0}-1\right), c=\left(1-R_{23}\right) /\left(1-R_{13}\right)$, and $d=a^{-1}=\left(R_{0}-1\right) /\left(1-R_{13}\right)$. Although $a, b, c$, and $d$ are defined in terms of $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$ they extend smoothly to most of $T_{b}$. In particular, $a$ and $b$ are smooth everywhere on $T_{b}$ except where $\theta=0$ (face 7), $d$ smoothly extends everywhere but $\theta=\pi / 2$, and $c$ extends smoothly to all of $T_{b}$. Note that $a=\cot (\theta)+O(r), b=\tan (\phi) \cot (\theta)+O(r), c=\tan (\phi)+O(r)$, and $d=\tan (\theta)+O(r)$.

Definition 18. For $(r \cos (\theta) \cos (2 \phi)) \geq \cos ^{2}(\phi)(2 \tan (\phi)-1)$ let $d_{i}\left(r_{13}, c\right)=\left(W_{24}-\right.$ $\left.R_{I}\right) /\left(W_{34}-W_{24}\right)$.

Note that the condition $(r \cos (\theta) \cos (2 \phi)) \geq \cos ^{2}(\phi)(2 \tan (\phi)-1)$ is simply the inequality $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$ extended to the blowup. Outer triangles satisfying the inequality have their third point above the diagonal in $Q$ (cf. Figure 6.2). The arguments in Chapter 8 insure that $Y_{14}$ is a continuous function of $r_{13}$ and $c$. Note also that some functional dependence was suppressed in Definition 18; $R_{I}$ and $Y_{14}$ are functions of $r_{13}$ and $c$, and $W_{24}$ and $W_{34}$ are functions of $Y_{14}$ and $r_{13}$.

Lemma 12. The set $T_{b}$ is homeomorphic to $D^{3}$, and its boundary consists of the following seven two-dimensional pieces:

1. A face $T_{1}$ contained in the plane $\phi=\pi / 4$ whose image points under $\beta$ have $r_{23}=r_{13}$.
2. A face $T_{2}$ contained in the plane $\phi=0$ whose image points under $\beta$ have $r_{23}=1$.

3. A face $T_{3}$ contained in the plane $\theta=\pi / 2$ whose image points under $\beta$ have $r_{23}=$ $r_{13}=1$.
4. A surface $T_{4}$ whose image points under $\beta$ have $r_{0}=r_{I}$ and $r_{23}^{2}<r_{13}^{2}=r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$.
5. A face $T_{5}$ contained in the plane $r=0$.
6. A surface $T_{6}$ whose image points under $\beta$ have $r_{0}=r_{C}$.
7. A face $T_{7}$ contained in the plane $\theta=0$ whose image points under $\beta$ have $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}=$ $r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$ and $r_{0}=1$.

Proof. The fact that $T_{b}$ is homeomorphic to a closed ball follows immediately from the fact that $\beta^{-1}$ is a diffeomorphism on the interior and $T^{\text {circ }}$ is homeomorphic to a ball. Likewise, the pre-images of boundary faces $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{4}, T_{6}$, and $T_{7}$ are all mapped diffeomorphically to the boundary of $T_{b}$ except for their boundary components which have $r_{23}=r_{13}=1$. We will use the word face for all the boundary components $T_{i}$ even they are not all polygons.

It is not hard to compute the properties of the remaining faces, $T_{3}$ and $T_{5}$. For later use we will explicitly describe the all the edges $T_{i j}$ and vertices $T_{i j k}$ where two or three of the faces intersect.

There are ten vertices where three of the faces meet. The following list names the vertices by which faces they are boundaries of, and then gives their coordinates $(r, \theta, \phi)$.

- Faces $T_{1}, T_{6}, T_{7}$ meet at $T_{167}=(\sqrt{2+\sqrt{3}}-1,0, \pi / 4)$.
- Faces $T_{1}, T_{3}, T_{6}$ meet at $T_{136}=\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \pi / 2, \pi / 4\right)$.
- Faces $T_{2}, T_{3}, T_{6}$ meet at $T_{236}=\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \pi / 2,0\right)$.
- Faces $T_{2}, T_{4}, T_{6}$ meet at $T_{246}=\left(\sqrt{3}\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right), \arccos \left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right), 0\right)$.
- Faces $T_{4}, T_{6}, T_{7}$ meet at $T_{467}=(1,0, \arctan (\sqrt{3}-1))$.
- Faces $T_{1}, T_{5}, T_{7}$ meet at $T_{157}=(0,0, \pi / 4)$.

- Faces $T_{1}, T_{3}, T_{5}$ meet at $T_{135}=(0, \pi / 2, \pi / 4)$.
- Faces $T_{2}, T_{3}, T_{5}$ meet at $T_{235}=(0, \pi / 2,0)$.
- Faces $T_{2}, T_{4}, T_{5}$ meet at $T_{245}=\left(0, \arctan \left(\frac{21 \sqrt{3}-19)}{208}, 0\right)\right.$.
- Faces $T_{4}, T_{5}, T_{7}$ meet at $T_{457}=\left(0,0, \arctan \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)$.

There are fifteen edges $T_{i j}$. Eight of these are simply line segments between their vertices, namely $T_{23}, T_{13}, T_{36}, T_{35}, T_{25}, T_{57}, T_{15}$, and $T_{17}$.

The edge $T_{24}$ is given by $r_{23}=1$ and $r_{0}=r_{I}\left(1, r_{13}\right)$, where

$$
r_{I}\left(1, r_{13}\right)=\frac{8\left(r_{13}^{6}-12 r_{13}^{4}+48 r_{13}^{2}-56\right)}{r_{13}^{9}-12 r_{13}^{7}+7 r_{13}^{6}+48 r_{13}^{5}-84 r_{13}^{4}+336 r_{13}^{2}-448}
$$

The edge $T_{47}$ consists of points $\left(\sqrt{r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1}, r_{13}, 1\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$.
The edge $T_{16}$ is given by $r_{23}=r_{13}$ and $r_{0}=r_{C}$. For these configurations $r_{C}=$ $r_{13}^{2} / \sqrt{4 r_{13}^{2}-1}$.

Similarly $T_{26}$ consists of points $\left(1, r_{13}, r_{C}\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$. In this case $r_{C}=$ $1 / \sqrt{4-r_{13}^{2}}$.

For the edge $T_{46}$ we can also use $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$ coordinates, with points $\left(\sqrt{r_{13}^{2}-1}, r_{13}\right.$, $\left.r_{13} / 2\right)$. These configurations have right-angled outer triangles with $r_{0}=r_{I}=r_{C}$.

The edge $T_{67}$ consists of points $\left(\sqrt{3} r_{13} / 2+\sqrt{4-r_{13}^{2}} / 2\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$.
The only edge for which we lack an explicit description is $T_{45}$. In coordinates $\left(r_{13}, d, c\right)$, points on this edge have the form $\left(1, d_{i}(c), c\right)$.

Our goal is to extend the mass map $\mathcal{F}$ to $T_{b}$. We will take this one face of the boundary of $T_{b}$ at a time, starting with the isosceles boundaries. After examining the interior of each face we will consider each edge and then each vertex. Each face of the boundary is mapped by the extension to a point, a line, or a face of the boundary of $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{c} \subset \mathcal{M}$. Note that for some convenience of exposition, $T$ has been blown up more than is strictly necessary for the purpose of extending $\mathcal{F}$; i.e. $T_{b}$ is slightly larger than necessary.

In most cases the first step will be to extend the functions $z_{i 4}\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$, the interior interparticle distances, to the boundary points in question. Then the extension of $\mathcal{F}$ will be examined.

We will commit a mild abuse of notation by denoting the extension of $\mathcal{F}$ by $\mathcal{F}$ as well.
A schematic diagram of $T_{b}$ is shown in Figure 10.1. The vertices are accurate; two of the faces are depicted as flat although they are curved surfaces. These will be discussed in more detail below. Figure 10.2 is an accurate depiction of some of the curved boundary lines, and includes the image of the diagonal in $Q$ where $r_{23}^{2}=r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$.

For reference we list here the most frequently used expressions for the components of $\mathcal{F}$.

Figure 10.1: Schematic of $T_{b}$ structure
![img-7.jpeg](img-7.jpeg)

Figure 10.2: $T_{b}$ structure showing diagonal

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m_{1}=\left(1+\frac{\Delta_{2} S_{13}}{\Delta_{1} S_{23}}+\frac{\Delta_{3} S_{12}}{\Delta_{1} S_{23}}+\frac{\Delta_{4} S_{13}}{\Delta_{1} S_{34}}\right)^{-1} \\
& m_{2}=\left(1+\frac{\Delta_{1} S_{23}}{\Delta_{2} S_{13}}+\frac{\Delta_{3} S_{12}}{\Delta_{2} S_{13}}+\frac{\Delta_{4} S_{23}}{\Delta_{2} S_{34}}\right)^{-1} \\
& m_{3}=\left(1+\frac{\Delta_{1} S_{23}}{\Delta_{3} S_{12}}+\frac{\Delta_{2} S_{13}}{\Delta_{3} S_{12}}+\frac{\Delta_{4} S_{13}}{\Delta_{3} S_{14}}\right)^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
m_{4}=\left(1+\frac{\Delta_{1} S_{34}}{\Delta_{4} S_{13}}+\frac{\Delta_{2} S_{34}}{\Delta_{4} S_{23}}+\frac{\Delta_{3} S_{14}}{\Delta_{4} S_{13}}\right)^{-1}
$$

Note that we are free to substitute a different $S_{i j} / S_{i k}$ in each term from the consistency equations.

# 10.1 Face 1: First isosceles case 

Definition 19. Type-1 isosceles configurations have $r_{12}=1,1 \leq r_{13}=r_{23} \leq \sqrt{2+\sqrt{3}}$, and $1 / \sqrt{3} \leq r_{14}=r_{24} \leq 1$.

The first face of $T_{b}$, where $\phi=\pi / 4$, parameterizes the type-1 configurations. On the interior of this face $\mathcal{F}$ is already defined so no extension is necessary. The symmetry of these configurations implies that $\mathcal{F}_{1}=\mathcal{F}_{2}$.
![img-8.jpeg](img-8.jpeg)

Figure 10.3: Isosceles type-1 face and part of its image in $\mathcal{M}$ (schematic)

# 10.2 Face 2: Second isosceles case 

Definition 20. Type-2 isosceles configurations are configurations with $r_{12}=r_{23}=1<$ $r_{13}<\sqrt{2}$ and $\frac{r_{13}}{2}<r_{14}=r_{34}<r_{C}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-r_{13}^{2}}}$.

Just as for the type-1 configurations, we already have the $z_{i 4}$ defined on the interior of the second face, where $\phi=0$, which corresponds to type- 2 configurations. All of the components of $\mathcal{F}$ are continuous and well-defined on interior points of $T_{2}$.
![img-9.jpeg](img-9.jpeg)

Figure 10.4: Type-2 isosceles face $T_{2 b}$ and part of its image (schematic)

### 10.3 Face 3: Outer equilateral triangle

The third face of the boundary of $T_{b}$ consists of points with $\theta=\pi / 2$, that is points $p_{0}=$ $\left(r_{0}, 0, c\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{0}, a, c\right)$. These configurations have an equilateral outer triangle $\left(r_{23}=r_{13}=1\right)$. As the following lemma shows, we can smoothly extend the $z_{i 4}$ functions so that the fourth point is at the circumcenter of the outer triangle.

Lemma 13. For $p \in T_{b}, \lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{i 4}=1 / \sqrt{3}$.

Proof. We simply examine the consistency equations (4.2) and note that at $p_{0}$ we have $S_{12}=S_{13}=S_{23} \neq 0$, which implies that $S_{14}=S_{24}=S_{34}$. That, in turn, implies that the inner distances $z_{i 4}$ must become equal as $p \rightarrow p_{0}$, which means they will be equal to the circumradius $1 / \sqrt{3}$.

It follows that the outer masses must be equal $\left(\mathcal{F}_{1}=\mathcal{F}_{2}=\mathcal{F}_{3}\right)$, and $m_{4} / m_{1}$ is determined by the value of $r_{0}$. Since the limit is independent of $c$ the blowup is somewhat redundant, but this does not cause any problems.
![img-10.jpeg](img-10.jpeg)

Figure 10.5: Outer equilateral face of $T_{b}$ and its image in $\mathcal{M}$ (schematic)

Figure 10.5 shows the third face in our schematic of $T_{b}$, and part of its image under the extended mass map $\mathcal{F}$. The redundancy of the blowup is seen by the one-dimensionality of the image.

# 10.4 Face 4: Border configuration boundary 

For points in the interior of the fourth face, where $r_{0}=r_{I}$, we have $D_{2}=0$ and $z_{34}+z_{14}=r_{13}$ by definition. For all these points we can extend $m_{2}$ to be zero. The other components of $\mathcal{F}$ extend continuously as well, with the simplification that $\sigma_{2 i}=0$ for $i \in\{1,3,4\}$, since the strict inequalities $z_{34}<z_{14}<z_{24}<r_{0}<1<r_{23}<r_{13}, D_{1}>0, D_{3}>0$, and $D_{4}>0$ prevent any terms of $\mathcal{F}$ from becoming singular.

Figure 10.6 schematically depicts the points of the fourth face along with the part of their image in $\mathcal{M}_{c}$. It should be pointed out that this face of $T_{b}$ is not actually flat in the $(r, \theta, \phi)$ coordinates. It is a smooth surface $\theta_{i}(r, \phi)$, and from numerical studies it appears to be fairly close to a flat face (cf. Figure 10.2). Its size has also been somewhat exaggerated for clarity.

![img-11.jpeg](img-11.jpeg)

Figure 10.6: Border configuration face of $T_{b}$ and part of its image in $\mathcal{M}$ (schematic)

# 10.5 Face 5: $r=0$ boundary 

For the interior of the fifth face, where $r=0$, let $p_{0}=(0, a, b)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{0}, a, b\right)$. This is part of the blowup of the point $(1,1,1)$ in the original coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$. These points are shown in Figure 10.7 along with the part of their image under $\mathcal{F}$ which is in $\mathcal{M}_{c}$.

Lemma 14. The functions $z_{14}, z_{24}$, and $z_{34}$ extend continuously to the interior of the fifth face of $T_{b}$.

Proof. The proof of Theorem 7 is sufficient for this lemma once we change into the $\left(r_{0}, a, b\right)$ coordinates. Then $F_{14}=R_{0}+(1+a)\left(R_{24}-R_{0}\right) /(1+b)$ and $F_{34}=R_{0}+(1+a)\left(R_{24}-R_{0}\right)$. These functions are well behaved on the interior of the fifth face, and the proof of Theorem 7 goes through, mutatis mutandis. In fact the construction also goes through for the interior of edges $T_{15}, T_{25}$, and $T_{35}$, where $b=0, b=a$, and $a=b=0$ respectively.

### 10.6 Face 6: $R_{0}=R_{C}$ boundary

The case of the interior of the sixth face, where $R_{0}=R_{C}$, is particularly simple. Lemma 4 implies that the $z_{i 4}$ all continuously extend to be equal to $R_{C}$. This in turn implies that

Lemma 15. For $p_{0}=\left(r_{C}, r_{13}, r_{23}\right) \in T_{b}$ and a point $p \in T_{b}$,

$$
\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} m_{4}=1
$$

![img-12.jpeg](img-12.jpeg)

Figure 10.7: $r=0$ face of $T_{b}$ and part of its image in $\mathcal{M}$ (schematic)

Proof. Since $S_{14}=S_{24}=S_{34}=0$, the result follows immediately from (10.4) since the other quantities are non-zero.

Of course, Lemma 15 implies that the other masses must be zero, i.e. $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} m_{i}=0$ for $i=1,2,3$.
![img-13.jpeg](img-13.jpeg)

Figure 10.8: $R_{0}=R_{C}$ face of $T_{b}$ and its image in $\mathcal{M}$

Figure 10.8 shows the sixth face shaded in our schematic of $T_{b}$, along with part of its image (the point $m_{4}=1$ in $\mathcal{M}$ ).

# 10.7 Face 7: $R_{0}=1$ boundary 

For the interior of the seventh face, we examine points $p_{0}=\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, 1\right)$ in our original coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$, where $r_{23}^{2} \geq r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1$. Lemma 3 implies that the $z_{i 4}$ extend

smoothly to this part of $T_{b}$, with $z_{14}=z_{24}=1$ and

$$
z_{34}=1+r_{23}^{2}+r_{13}^{2}-\sqrt{3\left[2\left(r_{13}^{2}+r_{23}^{2}\right)-1-\left(r_{13}^{2}-r_{23}^{2}\right)^{2}\right]}
$$

We can compute that $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} m_{3}=0$ from (10.3) and by noting that $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} S_{14}=$ $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} S_{24}=\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} S_{12}=0$ while the other $S_{i j}$ and the $\Delta_{i}$ stay non-zero.

The other masses have well-defined limits as $p \rightarrow p_{0}$ that do not simplify much except for the disappearance of the $m_{3} / m_{i}$ term.

In Figure 10.9 this face is depicted along with part of its image in $\mathcal{M}$.
![img-14.jpeg](img-14.jpeg)

Figure 10.9: $R_{0}=1$ face of $T_{b}$ and part of its image in $\mathcal{M}$

# 10.8 Edges 

In this section we see what the previous extensions of $\mathcal{F}$ to the faces imply for the extension to the edges.

As with the interior of the sixth face, we can extend $\mathcal{F}$ to all the edges $T_{i 6}$ with the constant value of $(0,0,0,1)$. The continuity of this extension is easy to check, since $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{i 4}=r_{C}$ for any $p \in T_{b}$ and $p_{0} \in T_{i 6}$.

The extension of $\mathcal{F}$ to edges $T_{13}$ and $T_{23}$ is also relatively simple. To preserve continuity with our extension to $T_{3}$ we must let $\mathcal{F}\left(p_{0}\right)=\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, m_{1}, 1-3 m_{1}\right)$, where $p_{0} \in T_{23}$ or $p_{13}$ and $m_{1}=\left(3+\frac{3\left(R_{0}-1\right)}{R_{C}-R_{0}}\right)^{-1}$.

As noted in the proof of Lemma 14, we can extend the functions $z_{i 4}$ continuously to the edges $T_{15}, T_{25}$, and $T_{35}$. We can then extend $\mathcal{F}$ to these edges without difficulty, as any

singular expressions can be avoided by an appropriate choice of the $\sigma_{i j}$. On $T_{15}$ we then have

$$
\mathcal{F}_{1}=\mathcal{F}_{2}=\frac{z_{34}^{-2}-z_{34}}{2\left(z_{34}^{-2}-z_{34}\right)+\sqrt{4 z_{14}^{2}-1}\left(z_{14}^{-3}-1\right)}
$$

where $z_{34}=\sqrt{1 / 2+z_{14}^{2}-\sqrt{3\left(4 z_{14}^{2}-1\right)}}$. Since $\mathcal{F}_{4}=0$ on this edge, $\mathcal{F}_{3}=1-2 \mathcal{F}_{1}$. The formulae for $T_{25}$ are identical up to the substitution of $z_{24}$ for $z_{34}$. On the edge $T_{35}, \mathcal{F}$ extends continuously to the value $(1 / 3,1 / 3,1 / 3,0)$.

For points on $T_{17}$, we can apply Lemma 3 to see that we can continuously extend the $z_{i 4}$ by letting $z_{14}=z_{24}=1$ and $z_{34}=\sqrt{1 / 2+r_{13}^{2}-\sqrt{3\left(4 r_{13}^{2}-1\right)}}$. $\mathcal{F}$ continuously extends to be $\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, 0,1-2 m_{1}\right)$, in which the expression $m_{1}=\left(2+\frac{D_{4}\left(1-R_{13}\right)}{D_{1}\left(Z_{34}-1\right)}\right)^{-1}$ does not appreciably simplify further.

By the definition of $r_{I}$ we know that the $z_{i 4}$ extend continuously to a point $p_{0}=T_{24}$ with $z_{34}=z_{14}=r_{13} / 2$ and $z_{24}=\sqrt{1-r_{13}^{2} / 4}$. Recall that $p_{0}=\left(r_{13}, r_{13}, r_{I}\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$. As on the rest of the face $T_{4}$, since $\Delta_{2}=0$ we extend by setting $\mathcal{F}_{2}\left(p_{0}\right)=0$. There are no other singular terms in the $\mathcal{F}_{i}$, and we find that $\mathcal{F}_{1}\left(p_{0}\right)=\mathcal{F}_{3}\left(p_{0}\right)=(2+$ $\left.2 \frac{R_{I}-R_{13}}{8 R_{13}-R_{I}}\right)^{-1}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{4}\left(p_{0}\right)=1-2 \mathcal{F}_{1}\left(p_{0}\right)$.

The points $p_{0} \in T_{47}$ consist of points $\left(\left(r_{13}^{2}-r_{13}+1\right), r_{13}, 1\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{23}, r_{13}, r_{0}\right)$. By considering the behavior of the $z_{i 4}$ on the faces $T_{4}$ and $T_{7}$ it is clear that we can extend $z_{14}\left(p_{0}\right)=z_{24}\left(p_{0}\right)=1$ and $z_{34}\left(p_{0}\right)=r_{13}-1$. So just as for the interior of $T_{7}$ at $p_{0}$ we have $S_{14}=S_{24}=S_{12}=0$.

For points on the edge $T_{45}$ we know that the $z_{i j}$ extend continuously by the arguments in Chapter 8. These points have the form $\left(1, d_{i}(c), c\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{13}, d, c\right)$. Recall that for these points $D_{2}=0 . F$ extends continuously to these points with $\mathcal{F}_{2}=\mathcal{F}_{4}=0, \mathcal{F}_{4}=1-\mathcal{F}_{1}$, and $\mathcal{F}_{1}=\left(1+\frac{\left(\sqrt{3} / 4-D_{1}\right)\left(Y_{14}-1\right)}{\left(D_{1}\right)\left(W_{34}-1\right)}\right)^{-1}$. In the expression for $\mathcal{F}_{1}$ note that $Y_{14}$ is a function of $c$ and $W_{34}=\left(1-Y_{14}^{-1 / 3}\right)^{-3}$.

The edge $T_{57}$ consists of points $p_{0}=(1,0, c)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{13}, d, c\right)$. Note that for this edge the coordinate $c$ is in the interval $(1 / 2,1)$. Here the extension is a bit trickier. We begin with the following lemma.

Lemma 16. For $p \in T_{b}$ and $p_{0} \in T_{57}, \lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{14}=\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{24}=1$ and $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{34}=0$.

Proof. If we let $1+\epsilon_{13}=r_{13}$ then we have $r_{23}=1+c \epsilon_{13}+O\left(\epsilon_{13}^{2}\right)$. In terms of our coordinates $\left(r_{13}, d, c\right)$ we have $r_{0}=1-d \epsilon_{13}+O\left(\epsilon_{13}^{2}\right), F_{14}=1+(1+d)\left(R_{24}-1\right) /(d+c)+O\left(\epsilon_{13}\right)$ and $F_{34}=1+(1+d)\left(R_{24}-1\right) / d+O\left(\epsilon_{13}\right)$. Recall that $F_{14}$ and $F_{34}$ are used to define the $z_{i 4}$ in Theorem 7 .

Using these expansions we compute that for $r_{24}=(1-5 d)$ we have

$$
P\left(1, r_{23}, F_{34}^{-1 / 3}, F_{14}^{-1 / 3}, r_{13}, 1-5 d\right)=-6 d+O(d) O\left(\epsilon_{13}\right)+O\left(d^{2}\right)
$$

which is negative for sufficiently small $d$ and $\epsilon_{13}$. Recall from the proof of Theorem 7 that at the endpoint where $r_{24}=r_{0}$ that $P>0$. Thus we know that for sufficiently small $d$ and $\epsilon_{13}, z_{24}$ is between $\left(1-d \epsilon_{13}\right)$ and $(1-5 d)$, which means that $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{24}=1$. From the expression for $F_{14}$ we can see that this implies that $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{14}=1$. Finally, the fact that $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{34}=0$ follows from planarity.

With Lemma 16 in hand, we now examine the behavior of $z_{i 4}$ near $p_{0}$ in more detail. We will use the same expansions for $r_{13}$ and $r_{23}$ as in Lemma 16. From the relation $S_{13} / S_{23}=S_{14} / S_{24}$ we find that if $z_{14}=1+\epsilon_{14}$ then $z_{24}=1+c \epsilon_{14}+O(d)$. Using these expansions we find that

$$
\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} \sigma_{21}=\frac{(2 c-1)}{c(2-c)}
$$

after which it is easy to compute that $\mathcal{F}$ extends continuously to $T_{57}$ with values

$$
\begin{gathered}
\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} m_{1}=c(2-c) /\left(4 c-c^{2}-1\right) \\
\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} m_{2}=(2 c-1) /\left(4 c-c^{2}-1\right) \\
\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} m_{3}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

and

$$
\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} m_{4}=0
$$

# 10.9 Vertices 

We can complete our continuous extension of $\mathcal{F}$ by studying its behavior near the vertices.
It is easy to see from previous sections that we can let $\mathcal{F}\left(T_{i j 6}\right)=(0,0,0,1)$. It is also trivial to determine that we can let $\mathcal{F}\left(T_{235}\right)=\mathcal{F}\left(T_{135}\right)=(1 / 3,1 / 3,1 / 3,0)$.

The vertex $T_{245}$ can be described as $\left(1, \frac{21 \sqrt{3}-19}{208}, 0\right)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{13}, d, c\right)$. To see that the $z_{14}$ have a continuous extension to this point we must again revisit the functions $F_{14}$ and $F_{34}$ from the proof of Theorem 7 .

Lemma 17. For $p \in T_{b}$ and $p_{0}=T_{245}$, $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{14}=\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{34}=1 / 2$ and $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{24}=$ $\sqrt{3} / 2$.

Proof. Let $p=\left(r_{13}, d, c\right)$, with $r_{13}=1+\epsilon_{13}$ and $d=\frac{21 \sqrt{3}-19}{208}+\epsilon_{d}=d_{0}+\epsilon_{d}$. Then both $F_{14}$ and $F_{34}$ are of the form $1+\left(1+1 / d_{0}\right)\left(R_{24}-1\right)+O\left(\epsilon_{13}\right)+O\left(\epsilon_{d}\right)+O(c)$. We can compute that

$$
P\left(1,1+O\left(\epsilon_{13}\right), F_{34}^{-1 / 3}, F_{14}^{-1 / 3}, 1+\left.\epsilon_{13}, r_{24}\right)\right|_{r_{24}=\sqrt{3} / 2}=O\left(\epsilon_{13}\right)+O\left(\epsilon_{d}\right)+O(c)
$$

By Lemma 5 this means that $\lim _{p \rightarrow p_{0}} z_{24}=\sqrt{3} / 2$. It is then easy to compute from the expressions for $F_{14}$ and $F_{34}$ the rest of the lemma.

With Lemma 17 in hand, we can continuously extend $\mathcal{F}$ to this vertex by $\mathcal{F}\left(T_{245}\right)=$ $(1 / 2,0,1 / 2,0)$.

The extension of $\mathcal{F}$ to the vertices $T_{157}$ and $T_{457}$ is covered by the arguments for the edge $T_{57}$. The point $T_{157}$ is $(1,0,1)$ in coordinates $\left(r_{13}, d, c\right)$, and the formulae for $\mathcal{F}\left(T_{57}\right)$ specialize to $\mathcal{F}\left(T_{157}\right)=(1 / 2,1 / 2,0,0)$. Likewise we can let $\mathcal{F}\left(T_{457}\right)=(1,0,0,0)$.

Proof of Theorem 11. The preceding sections (10.1 - 10.9) have shown that $\mathcal{F}$ extends continuously to the boundary of $T_{b}$ by examining its behavior on every boundary piece.

In this chapter we examine the degree of the extended map $\mathcal{F}$ on the boundary of its domain, in order to prove the following theorem.

Theorem 12. Every point in $\mathcal{M}_{c}$ has a preimage of $\mathcal{F}$ in $T_{b}$.

Definition 21. Let $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ denote the set $\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right) \mid \sum m_{i}=1, m_{i} \geq 0, m_{1}=\right.$ $\left.m_{2}, m_{1} \geq m_{3}\right\}$. Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1}$ denote the set $\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right) \mid \sum m_{i}=1, m_{i} \geq 0, m_{1}=m_{2}\right\}$.

Note that $\partial \mathcal{M}_{1}$ is the union of the segments $\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, 1-2 m_{1}, 0\right) \mid \frac{1}{3} \leq m_{1} \leq \frac{1}{2}\right\}$, $\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, 0,1-2 m_{1}\right) \mid 0 \leq m_{1} \leq \frac{1}{2}\right\}$, and $\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, m_{1}, 1-3 m_{1}\right) \mid 0 \leq m_{1} \leq \frac{1}{3}\right\}$.

From section 10.8 we know that the image of $T_{13}$ under $\mathcal{F}$ is contained in the segment $\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, m_{1}, 1-3 m_{1}\right) \mid 0 \leq m_{1} \leq \frac{1}{3}\right\}$.
