obtained by rotating each of the $q_{i}$. Consequently the solutions of (2) are always degenerate in the sense that the derivative matrix

$$
A=M^{-1} D \nabla U(q)+I
$$

is singular (here $I$ denotes the $2 n \times 2 n$ identity matrix). A relative equilibrium will be called nondegenerate if $A$ has a one-dimensional kernel, that is, all of the degeneracy is due to the symmetry. By using the implicit function theorem in a quotient space under the symmetry group, a nondegenerate relative equilibrium can be continued smoothly as the masses are varied.
![img-0.jpeg](img-0.jpeg)

Fig. 1. Relative equilibria with clusters of small masses.

The study of relative equilibria goes back to Euler and Lagrange [3,5]. Each relative equilibrium gives rise to a simple periodic orbit of the $n$-body problem in the original nonrotating coordinates. The configuration simply rotates rigidly returning to the initial state after time $2 \pi$. By scaling one can construct relative equilibria with any period.

Equations (2) are so complicated that complete solutions are known only for $n=1,2,3$. For $n \geqslant 4$ there are many examples but no systematic classification. This paper is concerned with the limiting case when most of the masses $m_{i}$ are small. Previous studies of this case were done by Hall [4] and the author [7] in the case of one large mass and $n-1$ small ones and by Xia [10] in the case of 2 or 3 large masses followed by a sequence of small masses, each taken small relative to the previous one. This paper is mainly concerned with the case of 2 or more large masses together with small masses of similar size. Some examples are shown in Fig. 1.

# 2. RELATIVE EQUILIBRIA WITH SMALL MASSES 

Assume that the masses of the $n$ bodies depend on a small parameter $\varepsilon$. For technical reasons, it will be assumed that $m_{i}^{\varepsilon}$ is a smooth function of $\varepsilon^{3}$. The limiting masses $m_{i}^{0}$ will be denoted $\bar{m}_{i}$. It will be assumed that $m_{i}^{\varepsilon}>0$ for $\varepsilon>0$ but some of the limiting masses, $\bar{m}_{i}$, may vanish. Let $v=\left\{i: \bar{m}_{i} \neq 0\right\}$ and $\tau=\left\{i: \bar{m}_{i}=0\right\}$, be the indices of the asymptotically nontrivial and trivial masses respectively. Then for $i \in v, m_{i}^{\varepsilon}=\bar{m}_{i}+O\left(\varepsilon^{3}\right)$, whereas for $i \in \tau, m_{i}^{\varepsilon}=\mu_{i} \varepsilon^{3}+O\left(\varepsilon^{6}\right)$ for some constants $\mu_{i}$. It will be assumed that the $\mu_{i} \neq 0$.

Suppose that $q^{\varepsilon}$ is a family of relative equilibria for the masses $m^{\varepsilon}$ for $\varepsilon>0$. If $q^{\varepsilon}$ converges as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$, the limiting configuration will be denoted $\bar{q}$. It is possible that in the limiting configuration some of the masses have coalesced. Some notation will be introduced to describe this. A cluster will be a subset $\gamma \subset\{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that $\bar{q}_{i}=\bar{q}_{j}$ if $i, j \in \gamma$ and $\bar{q}_{i} \neq \bar{q}_{j}$ if $i \in \gamma$ but $j \notin \gamma$. Clearly the clusters form a partition of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$. The number of masses in the cluster will be denoted by $|\gamma|$. The total mass of the cluster will be called $m_{\gamma}^{\varepsilon}$ and the center of mass $c_{\gamma}^{\varepsilon}$. Their limiting values are $\bar{m}_{\gamma}$, and $\bar{c}_{\gamma}$, respectively. Then $q_{i}^{\varepsilon} \rightarrow \bar{c}_{\gamma}$ for $i \in \gamma$. Using this terminology, a mass $q_{i}^{\varepsilon}$ which does not coalesce in the limit forms its own cluster, that is, $\gamma=\{i\}$ is a cluster with $|\gamma|=1$.

Proposition 1. If $q^{\varepsilon}$ is a family of relative equilibria as above, then $\left|q^{\varepsilon}\right|$ remains bounded as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ and so there is a convergent subsequence.

Proof. The superscript $\varepsilon$ will be suppressed to simplify the notation. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there is a subsequence with $|q| \rightarrow \infty$. Define $u=q /|q|$. Then $u$ satisfies

$$
|q| u_{i}+\frac{1}{|q|^{2}} \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{m_{j}\left(u_{j}-u_{i}\right)}{\left|u_{i}-u_{j}\right|^{3}}=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

Since $|u|=1$ one can choose a convergent subsequence: $u \rightarrow \bar{u}$. Since $|\bar{u}|=1, \bar{u} \neq 0$, and so there is some cluster $\gamma$ with $c_{\gamma} \neq 0$. Summing over $i \in \gamma$ with weights $m_{i} / m_{\gamma}$ leads to

$$
|q| c_{\gamma}+\frac{1}{m_{\gamma}|q|^{2}} \sum_{i \in \gamma} \sum_{j \notin \gamma} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}\left(u_{j}-u_{i}\right)}{\left|u_{i}-u_{j}\right|^{3}}=0
$$

because the terms involving $i, j \in \gamma$ cancel in pairs. It follows from the definition of a cluster that the sum is bounded and hence $|q|$ is bounded, a contradiction.

From now on it will be assumed that $q^{\varepsilon}$ converges. The next proposition shows that in the limit, only the asymptotically trivial masses can form clusters.

Proposition 2. If $\gamma$ is a cluster of two or more masses, then $\gamma \subset \tau$.

Proof. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $|\gamma| \geqslant 2$ and that $\gamma$ contains a nontrivial mass: $\bar{m}_{k} \neq 0, k \in \gamma$. Choose $i \in \gamma$ with $\left|q_{i}-q_{k}\right|$ maximal ( $i$ may depend on $\varepsilon$ ) and consider the dot product of (3) with $q_{i}-q_{k}$ :

$$
q_{i} \cdot\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)-\frac{m_{k}}{r_{i k}}+\sum_{\substack{j \in \gamma \\ j \neq i, k}} \frac{m_{j}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right) \cdot\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}+\sum_{j \notin \gamma} \frac{m_{j}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right) \cdot\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}=0
$$

All $q_{j}$ in the first sum are in the ball of radius $\left|q_{i}-q_{k}\right|$ around $q_{k}$ and it follows that all of the dot products in this sum are negative. Hence

$$
\frac{m_{k}}{r_{i k}} \leqslant q_{i} \cdot\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)+\sum_{j \notin \gamma} \frac{m_{j}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right) \cdot\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}
$$

Now by the definition of clusters, the right side of this inequality remains bounded as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$. But $r_{i k} \rightarrow 0$, and since we are assuming $\bar{m}_{k} \neq 0$, the left side tends to infinity. This is a contradiction.

The following proposition gives the limiting behavior of the nontrivial masses. Let $q_{v}^{\varepsilon} \in \mathbf{R}^{2|v|}$ denote the vector formed from the $q_{i}^{\varepsilon}, i \in v$, and let $\bar{q}_{v}$ be its limit as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$.

Proposition 3. $\bar{q}_{v}$ is a relative equilibrium of the $|v|$-body problem for masses $\bar{m}_{i}, i \in \gamma$.

Proof. It follows from Proposition 2 that for $i \in v$, all of the denominators in (3) are bounded away from zero for $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small. Hence taking the limit eliminates the asymptotically trivial masses from the sum and gives

$$
\bar{q}_{i}+\sum_{\substack{j \in v \\ j \neq i}} \frac{\bar{m}_{j}\left(\bar{q}_{j}-\bar{q}_{i}\right)}{\bar{r}_{i j}^{3}}=0, \quad i \in v
$$

where $\bar{r}_{i j}=\left|\bar{q}_{i}-\bar{q}_{j}\right|$. These are the equations for a $|v|$-body relative equilibrium.

Let $U_{v}\left(q_{v}, \varepsilon\right)$ denote the $|v|$-body Newtonian potential. Let $M_{v}$ be the $2|v| \times 2|v|$ mass matrix formed from the $m_{i}^{\varepsilon}, i \in v$, and $\bar{M}_{v}$ its limit as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$. Then Eqs. (4) can be written:

$$
\bar{M}_{v}^{-1} \nabla U_{v}\left(\bar{q}_{v}, 0\right)+\bar{q}_{v}=0
$$

As above, $\bar{q}_{v}$ is nondegenerate provided

$$
A=\bar{M}^{-1} v D \nabla U_{v}\left(\bar{q}_{v}, 0\right)+I
$$

has a one-dimensional kernel.
Next consider a cluster $\gamma \subset \tau$ of asymptotically trivial masses. As in the proof of Proposition 1, summing (3) for $i \in \gamma$ with weights $m_{i} / m_{\gamma}$ causes the terms with $i, j \in \gamma$ to drop out. Since the denominators of the other terms are bounded away from 0 , one can take the limit as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ to get

$$
\bar{c}_{\gamma}+\sum_{j \in v} \frac{\bar{m}_{j}\left(\bar{q}_{j}-\bar{c}_{\gamma}\right)}{\bar{r}_{j y}^{3}}=0
$$

where $\bar{c}_{\gamma}$ is the limiting position of the cluster and $\bar{r}_{j y}=\left|\bar{q}_{j}-\bar{c}_{\gamma}\right|$. This can be written

$$
\nabla V\left(\bar{c}_{\gamma}\right)=0
$$

where $V(\xi)$ is the function on $\mathbf{R}^{2}$ :

$$
V(\xi)=\frac{1}{2}|\xi|^{2}+\sum_{j \in v} \frac{\bar{m}_{j}}{\left|\xi-\bar{q}_{j}\right|}
$$

$V(\xi)$ is called the effective potential of the relative equilibrium $\bar{q}_{v}$. Thus:

Proposition 4. Let $\gamma \subset \tau$ be a cluster of trivial masses. Then the limiting position of the cluster, $\bar{c}_{\gamma}$, is a critical point of effective potential of the relative equilibrium formed by the nontrivial masses.

Note that the sum in (7) would give a harmonic function if $\xi$ were taken to lie in $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ instead of $\mathbf{R}^{2}$. It is not difficult to see that if $\xi \in \mathbf{R}^{2}$, then moving $\xi$ vertically out of the plane in $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ decreases the effective potential. It follows that the second partial derivative of $V$ with respect to the third coordinate is nonpositive and hence the sum of the other two second partials is nonnegative. In other words, $V(\xi)$ is a superharmonic function in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$. In particular, it has no local maxima.

It remains to study the limiting shape of a cluster of trivial masses. For this it is necessary to rescale. For later use, the equations of motion will be rescaled, not just the relative equilibrium equations. A clustering scheme will be a data structure containing

- a relative equilibrium, $\bar{q}_{v}$, of the $|v|$-body problem,
- a partition $\Gamma=\left\{\gamma_{1}, \ldots, \gamma_{k}\right\}$ of $\tau$, and
- a set of distinct critical points, $\left\{\xi_{\gamma}: \gamma \in \Gamma\right\}$, of the effective potential of $\bar{q}_{v}$
(later an additional item will be added to the structure). Given a clustering scheme, define a vector $q_{v} \in \mathbf{R}^{2|v|}$ by collecting the $q_{i}, i \in v$ and, for each cluster $\gamma \in \Gamma$, a vector $q_{\gamma} \in \mathbf{R}^{2|v|}$ consisting of the $q_{i}, i \in \gamma$. The velocity vectors can be collected in a similar way to form vectors $w_{v}$ and $w_{\gamma}$. The notation $q_{v i}, w_{v i}, q_{\gamma i}, w_{v i}$ will be used to refer to the individual position and velocity vectors of the bodies.

Introduce rescaled coordinates as follows. For the nontrivial masses define $x_{v}, y_{v} \in \mathbf{R}^{2|v|}$ by

$$
q_{v}=\bar{q}_{v}+\varepsilon^{2} x_{v}, \quad w_{v}=-K \bar{q}_{v}+\varepsilon^{2} y_{v}
$$

For each cluster $\gamma$ of trivial masses define $x_{\gamma}, y_{\gamma} \in \mathbf{R}^{2|v|}$ by

$$
q_{\gamma i}=\xi_{\gamma}+\varepsilon x_{\gamma i}, \quad w_{\gamma i}=-K \xi_{\gamma}+\varepsilon y_{\gamma i}, \quad i=1, \ldots,|\gamma|
$$

Note that if the $x_{v i}$ and $x_{y i}$ are restricted to some finite ball, $B \subset \mathbf{R}^{2}$, then for $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, masses from distinct clusters will be bounded away from one another.

Let $U(q, \varepsilon)$ denote the Newtonian potential with masses $m^{\varepsilon}$ and, as above, let $U_{\nu}\left(q_{v}, \varepsilon\right)$ be the Newtonian potential of the asymptotically nontrivial masses. The equations of motion for the nontrivial masses are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x}_{v}=y_{v}+K x_{v} \\
& \dot{y}_{v}=\varepsilon^{-2}\left[\ddot{q}_{v}+M_{v}^{-1} \nabla U_{v}\left(q_{v}, \varepsilon\right)+O\left(\varepsilon^{3}\right)\right]+K y_{v}
\end{aligned}
$$

where the $O\left(\varepsilon^{3}\right)$ represents the contributions of the trivial masses. Using (5), the rest of the quantity in brackets can be written

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_{v}^{-1} & \nabla U_{v}\left(q_{v}, \varepsilon\right)-\bar{M}_{v}^{-1} \nabla U_{v}\left(\ddot{q}_{v}, 0\right) \\
& =\bar{M}_{v}^{-1} \nabla U_{v}\left(q_{v}, 0\right)-\bar{M}_{v}^{-1} \nabla U_{v}\left(\ddot{q}_{v}, 0\right)+O\left(\varepsilon^{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding $\bar{M}_{v}^{-1} \nabla U_{v}\left(q_{v}, 0\right)$ in a Taylor series aroung $\ddot{q}_{v}$ and using $q_{v}=$ $\ddot{q}_{v}+\varepsilon^{2} x_{v}$, the equations of motion become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x}_{v}=y_{v}+K x_{v} \\
& \dot{y}_{v}=(A-I) x_{v}+K y_{v}+O(\varepsilon)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is a $2|v| \times 2|v|$ block diagonal matrix with blocks $\kappa$ and, as above,

$$
A=M_{v}^{-1} D \nabla U_{v}\left(\ddot{q}_{v}, 0\right)+i
$$

Thus in the limit as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ the deviation of the nontrivial masses from the relative equilibrium $\bar{q}_{v}$ is governed by linear differential equations which are independent of the trivial masses.

The equations of motion for the trivial masses in a cluster $\gamma$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x}_{y i}=\gamma_{y i}+\kappa x_{y i} \\
& \dot{y}_{y i}=\varepsilon^{-1}\left[\xi_{\gamma}+m_{i}^{-1} U_{i}(q, \varepsilon)\right]+\kappa y_{y i}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{i}^{-1} U_{i}(q, \varepsilon) & =\sum_{j \neq i} \frac{m_{j}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}} \\
& =\sum_{j \in v} \frac{\tilde{m}_{j}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}+\varepsilon \sum_{\substack{j \in v \\
j \neq i}} \frac{\mu_{j}\left(x_{v j}+x_{v i}\right)}{\left|x_{v i}-x_{v j}\right|^{3}}+O\left(\varepsilon^{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

In the first sum, replacing $q_{j}$ by $\bar{q}_{j}$ gives an error $O\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right)$ and the sum becomes

$$
\nabla V\left(q_{i}\right)-q_{i}
$$

where $V(\xi)$ is the effective potential of $\bar{q}_{e}$. Since $\xi_{y}$ is a critical point of $V$ and $q_{i}=\xi_{y}+\varepsilon x_{y i}$, the quantity in brackets becomes

$$
\xi_{y}+\nabla V\left(q_{i}\right)-q_{i}=\varepsilon\left(D V\left(\xi_{y}\right)-I\right) x_{y i}+O\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right)
$$

Thus the equations of motion become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x}_{y i}=y_{y i}+\kappa x_{y i} \\
& \dot{y}_{y i}=\left(\beta_{y}-I\right) x_{y i}+\sum_{\substack{j \in y \\
j \neq i}} \frac{\mu_{j}\left(x_{y j}-x_{y i}\right)}{\left|x_{y i}-x_{y j}\right|^{3}}+\kappa y_{y i}+O(\varepsilon)
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\beta_{y}=D \nabla V\left(\xi_{y}\right)
$$

Defining a potential

$$
U_{y}\left(x_{y}\right)=\sum_{\substack{i, j \in y \\ i<j}} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\left|x_{y i}-x_{y j}\right|}
$$

and $2|\gamma| \times 2|\gamma|$ matrices $B_{y}$ with blocks $\beta_{y}$ and $\bar{M}_{y}=\operatorname{diag}\left(\mu_{1}, \mu_{1}, \ldots\right.$, $\left.\mu_{|y|}, \mu_{|y|}\right)$, these equations can be written

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x}_{y}=y_{y}+K x_{y} \\
& \dot{y}_{y}=\left(B_{y}-I\right) x_{y}+\bar{M}_{y}^{-1} \nabla U_{y}\left(x_{y}\right)+K y_{y}+O(\varepsilon)
\end{aligned}
$$

In the limit $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ these equations are very similar to the equations of the $|\gamma|$-body problem with masses $\mu_{i}$, differing from them only by the term $\left(B_{y}-I\right) x_{y}$.

Thus the (rescaled) deviations of the masses in a trivial cluster $\gamma$ from the critical point $\xi_{\gamma}$ are governed by the equations of the $|\gamma|$-body problem with an extra linear term representing the influence of the nontrivial masses. These equations will be studied in more detail in the next section. Now they will be applied to find the asymptotic shape of a cluster in the family $q^{e}$ of relative equilibria.

If $\gamma$ is a cluster of the family of relative equilibria $q^{\varepsilon}$, then the rescaled vector $x_{\gamma}^{\varepsilon}$ satifies

$$
\bar{M}_{\gamma}^{-1} \nabla U_{\gamma}\left(\bar{x}_{\gamma}\right)+B_{\gamma} \bar{x}_{\gamma}=0
$$

A solution of (11) will be called a generalized relative equilbrium of the $|\gamma|$-body problem with matrix $\beta_{\gamma}$. Thus:

Proposition 5. Let $\gamma \subset \tau$ be a cluster converging to a critical point $\xi_{\gamma}$ of the effective potential $V(\xi)$. Then the resealed positions $x_{\gamma}^{\varepsilon}$, converge to a generalized relative equilibrium of the $|\gamma|$-body problem with masses $\mu_{j}$ and matrix $\beta_{\gamma}=D \nabla V\left(\xi_{\gamma}\right)$.

A generalized relative equilibrium will be called nondegenerate if

$$
C_{\gamma}=\bar{M}_{\gamma}^{-1} D \nabla U_{\gamma}\left(\bar{x}_{\gamma}\right)+B_{\gamma}
$$

is nonsingular.
Having determined the limiting behavior of an arbitrary convergent sequence of relative equilibria, consider the converse problem: Given a clustering scheme, under what conditions is it the limit of a family $q^{\varepsilon}$ of relative equilibria? First an additional item should be added to the clustering scheme data structure:
for each $\gamma \in \Gamma$ a generalized relative equilibrium $\bar{x}_{\gamma}$ of the $|\gamma|$-body problem with masses $\mu_{i}, i \in \gamma$, and matrix $\beta_{\gamma}=D \nabla V\left(\xi_{\gamma}\right)$.

A clustering scheme will be called nondegenerate if the relative equilibrium $\bar{q}_{\nu}$ and each of the generalized relative equilibria $\bar{x}_{\gamma}, \gamma \in \Gamma$, is nondegenerate. Then

Proposition 6. If $C$ is a nondegenerate clustering scheme, then there is exists a smooth one-parameter family of relative equilibria, $q^{\varepsilon}$, for masses $m^{\varepsilon}$ such that as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0 q_{\gamma}^{\varepsilon} \rightarrow \bar{q}_{\gamma}$ and for each cluster $\gamma \in \Gamma$ and each $i \in \gamma, q_{i}^{\varepsilon} \rightarrow \xi_{\gamma}$ and $x_{\gamma}^{\varepsilon} \rightarrow \bar{x}_{\gamma}$.

Proof. In rescaled coordinates the equations for relative equilibria take the form

$$
A x_{\nu}+O(\varepsilon)=0
$$

for the asymptotically nontrivial masses and

$$
M_{\gamma}^{-1} \nabla U_{\gamma}\left(x_{\gamma}, \varepsilon\right)+B_{\gamma} x_{\gamma}+O(\varepsilon)=0
$$

for each cluster of asymptotically trivial masses. To eliminate the rotational symmetry, restrict $x_{v}$ to a subspace complementary to the one-dimensional kernel of $A$. Then the hypothesis that $C$ is nondegenerate is just what is needed to apply the implicit function theorem to solve for $x_{v}$ and the $x_{\gamma}$ as smooth functions of $\varepsilon$.

Note that the nondegeneracy condition for generalized relative equilibria does not allow for a symmetry. This leads to two simple necessary conditions on the symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrix $\beta_{\gamma}$. First note that the $|\gamma|$-body potential, $U_{\gamma}$, is invariant under translations and rotations of all $|\gamma|$ masses in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$. In fact under translations even $\nabla U_{\gamma}$ is invariant. It follows that if $\beta_{\gamma}$ were singular, translation in the direction of its kernel would leave (11) invariant. Hence $C_{\gamma}$ would also be singular. Thus nonsingularity of $\beta_{\gamma}$ is a necessary condition for nondegeneracy of a generalized relative equilibrium. Similarly, if $\beta_{\gamma}$ were a multiple of the identity, (11) would be invariant under rotation and this would mean that $C_{\gamma}$ would be singular. Thus another necessary condition for the nondegeneracy of a generalized relative equilibrium is that the eigenvalues of $\beta_{\gamma}$ be distinct. In particular, if a relative equilibrium is viewed as a special case of a generalized relative equilibrium, it is degenerate.

# 3. LINEAR STABILITY 

As mentioned in Section 1, each relative equilibrium determines a simple periodic solution of the $n$-body problem for which the mass configuration simply rotates rigidly around the center of mass. The gravitational attraction is exactly balanced by the centrifugal force of the rotation. The last section was devoted to constructing relative equilibria with clusters of small masses. Now the linear stability of the resulting periodic orbits will be investigated.

The rescaled equations of motion (8) and (10) will be used. Let $C$ be a nondegenerate clustering scheme with $|v|$-body relative equilbrium $\bar{q}_{v}$ and resealed generalized relative equilibria $\bar{x}_{\gamma}, \gamma \in \Gamma$. Note that $q_{v}=\bar{q}_{v}$ corresponds to $x_{v}=0$. Let $x_{v}^{\varepsilon}$ and $x_{\gamma}^{\varepsilon}$ denote the smooth family of relative equilibria guaranteed by Proposition 6. Then

$$
x_{v}^{\varepsilon}=\bar{x}_{v}+O(\varepsilon), \quad x_{\gamma}^{\varepsilon}=\bar{x}_{\gamma}+O(\varepsilon)
$$

The velocity variables of the equilibrium are given by

$$
y_{v}=-K x_{v}, \quad y_{\gamma}=-K x_{\gamma}
$$

To study linear stablity it is necessary to linearize Eqs. (8) and (10) near this equilibrium. The linearized equations will be represented by a $4 n \times 4 n$ matrix, $L^{n}$.

In the limit $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$, (8) and (10) decouple. Hence $L^{n} \rightarrow \bar{L}$ where $\bar{L}$ is block-diagonal with blocks of size $4|v|$ and $4|\gamma|, \gamma \in \Gamma$. The $4|v| \times 4|v|$ block corresponding to Eqs. (8) can be written in block form as

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc}
K & I \\
A-I & K
\end{array}\right]
$$

where the blocks are all $2|v| \times 2|v|$. The $4|\gamma| \times 4|\gamma|$ block corresponding to Eqs. (10) can be written

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc}
K & I \\
C_{\gamma}-I & K
\end{array}\right]
$$

where the blocks are all $2|\gamma| \times 2|\gamma|$ and $C_{\gamma}$ is given by (12).
To facilitate the study of the linear stability it is important to use the Hamiltonian structure of the system. In the Hamiltonian approach to mechanics one replaces the velocity vector, $v$, by the momentum vector $M v$. This has been avoided until now because the asymptotically trivial masses make $M$ noninvertible in the limit $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$. This can be fixed by using the matrices $\bar{M}_{v}$ and $\bar{M}_{\gamma}$ instead of $M$. Changing to momentum variables amounts to conjugating the matrices (13) and (14) by block diagonal matrices of the form $\operatorname{diag}\left(I, \bar{M}_{v}\right)$ and $\operatorname{diag}\left(I, \bar{M}_{\gamma}\right)$ respectively, to obtain matrices of the form

$$
L=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
K & M_{*}^{-1} \\
D & K
\end{array}\right]
$$

where $M_{*}=\bar{M}_{v}$ or $\bar{M}_{\gamma}$ and $D=D \nabla U_{v}\left(\bar{q}_{v}\right)$ or $D \nabla U_{\gamma}\left(\bar{x}_{v}\right)+\bar{M}_{\gamma}\left(B_{\gamma}-I\right)$. In both cases, $D$ is a symmetric matrix. Matrix (15) can be written as $-J S$, where (using $K^{T}=-K$ )

$$
J=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
0 & -I \\
I & 0
\end{array}\right], \quad S=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
-D & K^{T} \\
K & M_{*}^{-1}
\end{array}\right]
$$

Note that $S^{T}=S . J$ is the matrix of the symplectic form (skew inner product)

$$
\Omega(v, w)=v^{T} J w
$$

used in Hamiltonian mechanics. A matrix of the form $L=-J S$ with $S^{T}=S$ is called Hamiltonian. In this case the linear differential equation with matrix $L$ is a Hamiltonian system with quadratic Hamiltonian function

$$
H(v)=\frac{1}{2} v^{T} S v
$$

It is well-known that $H$, which represents the total energy of the system, is constant along solutions. This fact facilitates the study of linear stability.

A Hamiltonian matrix is called strongly stable of parametrically stable if all of its eigenvalues are imaginary and if the Hamiltonian function is either positive or negative definite on every eigenspace. The algebraic sign of $H(v)$ on a certain eigenspace will be called the Hamiltonian sign of the corresponding eigenvalue. In this case, conservation of energy can be used to show that there cannot be a nontrivial Jordan block [6]. Moreover, strong stability persists under perturbations. Thus if $L^{e} \rightarrow \bar{L}$ and $\bar{L}$ is strongly stable, then $L^{e}$ is strongly stable for all $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small.

Because of the symmetries of the $n$-body problem, some modification of the concept of linear stability is appropriate. The translation symmetry of the problem implies the conservation of the two-dimensional total momentum vector. Also, the center of mass moves uniformly with velocity given by the total momentum over the total mass. This implies that every restpoint is unstable since, by changing the total momentum, one obtains a system which gradually drifts away from the original one. one can eliminate this drift by restricting attention to the set of configurations with center of mass at the origin and with zero total momentum. Similarly, the rotational symmetry of the problem implies that the angular momentum is constant and orbits with different angular momenta drift away from one another. This could be eliminated by restricting to a manifold of constant angular momentum and passing to a quotient space under the action of the rotation group.

Instead of carrying out these reductions of the full nonlinear equations and then linearizing, one can restrict the linearized equations to an appropriate subspace of $\mathbf{R}^{4 n}$. Consider the four-dimensional subspace $W_{1}$ spanned by the vectors

$$
(\xi, 0), \quad(0, M \xi), \quad(\eta, 0), \quad(0, M \eta)
$$

where $\xi=(1,0,1,0, \ldots) \in \mathbf{R}^{2 n+2}$ and $\eta=(0,1,0,1, \ldots) \in \mathbf{R}^{2 n+2}$. This subspace is invariant under $L$ and the eigenvalues of $\left.L\right|_{W_{1}}$ are $\pm i, \pm i$ with a nontrivial Jordan block. Clearly this is associated to a drift in the center of mass.

Similarly, the four-dimensional subspace $W_{2}$ spanned by the vectors

$$
(q, 0), \quad(0, M q), \quad(K q, 0), \quad(0, K M q)
$$

is invariant (this uses the homogeneity of the Newtonian potential). The eigenvalues of $\left.L\right|_{W_{2}}$ are $0,0, \pm i$ and there is a nontrivial Jordan block associated to the repeated 0 . In the quotient space, the repeated zero disappears and the $\pm i$ remains. The Hamiltonian sign of this imaginary pair is positive.

Let $W$ be the skew orthogonal complement of the eight-dimensional subspace $W_{1} \oplus W_{2}$. A relative equilibrium of the $|v|$-body problem will be called strongly stable if the restriction of its linearization to $W$ is strongly stable and if the Hamiltonian sign of the eigenvalue $\pm i$ (if it occurs) is positive. No such modification of the definition of linear stability is necessary for generalized relative equilibria since they are always taken relative to some relative equilibrium whose symmetries will already have been eliminiated. Thus a generalized relative equilibrium of the $|\gamma|$-body problem will be called strongly stable if its linearization is strongly stable on all of $\mathbf{R}^{4|v|}$. Then the following proposition reduces the strong linear stability of the relative equilibria $q^{e}$ to that of its nontrivial masses and its clusters plus a consistency check of the Hamiltonian sign.

Proposition 7. Suppose $\bar{q}_{v}$ is a strongly linearly stable relative equilibrium of the $v$-body problem and, for each $\gamma \in \Gamma, \bar{x}_{v}$ is a strongly linearly stable generalized relative equilibrium of the $|\gamma|$-body problem. Moreover, suppose that any repeated eigenvalues are always occur with the same Hamiltonian sign. Then for a sufficiently small, $q^{e}$ is a strongly linearly stable relative equilibrium of the $N$-body problem.

# 4. EXAMPLES 

In this section, the results above will be applied to some simple examples. These results show how a relative equilibrium with clusters of small masses can be constructed from a nondegenerate clustering scheme $C$. To find such a clustering scheme one must find a relative equilibrium of the $|v|$-body problem and generalized relative equilibria of the $|\gamma|$-body problem, $\gamma \in \Gamma$. As mentioned in Section 1, the equations for relative equilibria are difficult to solve when there are more that three bodies. The equations for generalized relative equilibria are even more complicated. Consequently the examples deal with small values of $|v|$ and $|\gamma|$.

First some well-known facts about relative equilibria and their effective potentials will be reviewed. When $|v|=1$, then only relative equilibrium is $\bar{q}_{v}=0$. The associated effective potential is

$$
V(\xi)=\frac{1}{2}|\xi|^{2}-\frac{\bar{m}}{|\xi|}
$$

which has a circle of degenerate critical points of radius $1 / \bar{m}$. The asymptotically trivial masses must all converge to this circle possibly forming clusters. This is the $(1+n)$-body problem studied by Hall [4]. It turns out that there are restrictions on the possible limiting positions of the trivial cluster within the circle, but these do not follow from the methods of this paper. In case the asymptotically trivial masses do not form clusters, the linear stability of the resulting periodic solutions was determined in Ref. 7. If they form clusters, the problem is still open. It will not be discussed further here.

Next consider $|v|=2$. If $u=q_{v 2}-q_{v 1}$, then (5) gives

$$
\left(1-\frac{\bar{m}_{v}}{|u|^{3}}\right) u=0
$$

where $\bar{m}_{v}=\bar{m}_{v 1}+\bar{m}_{v 2}$. This determines $|u|$ and this, together with the fact that the center of mass is at the origin, determines $q_{v 1}$ and $q_{v 2}$ up to a rotation. Without loss of generality, one can assume that $\bar{m}_{v}=1$ and that the masses lie on the first coordinate axis in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$. Define a parameter $\alpha$ by

$$
\bar{m}_{v 1}=1-\alpha, \quad \bar{m}_{v 2}=\alpha
$$

Then

$$
\bar{q}_{v 1}=(-\alpha, 0), \quad \bar{q}_{v 2}=(1-\alpha, 0)
$$

The effective potential is

$$
V(\xi)=\frac{1}{2}|\xi|^{2}+\frac{1-\alpha}{r_{1}^{3}}+\frac{\alpha}{r_{2}^{3}}
$$

where

$$
r_{1}^{2}=\left(\xi_{1}+\alpha\right)^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2}, \quad r_{2}^{2}=\left(\xi_{1}+\alpha-1\right)^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2}
$$

This is just the effective potential of the restricted three-body problem. A plot of the level curves of $V(\xi)$ for $\alpha=0.25$ is in Fig. 4, upper left (it is

qualitatively the same for all or; figures were produced with the help of Mathematica).

It is well-known that there are five critical points, three along the $\xi_{1}$-axis and two forming equilateral triangles with the nontrivial masses. All five are nondegenerate critical points. The three collinear critical points are saddle points of the effective potential. Hence the matrix $\beta$ has eigenvalues $\beta_{1}>0$ and $\beta_{2}<0$. The equilateral critical points are minima. Some computation shows that the eigenvalues there are

$$
\beta_{1,2}=\frac{3}{2}(1+ \pm \sqrt{1-3 \alpha(1-\alpha)})
$$

Note that $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}=3$. The two-body relative equilibrium is strongly stable because the subspace $W$ to which one is supposed to restrict the matrix (13) is trivial.

Up to rotation, there are five relative equilibria of the 3-body problem. There is a unique collinear relative equilbrium for each of the three rotationally distince orderings of the masses along a line. These are not linearly stable. In fact the restriction of $\bar{L}$ to the four-dimensional subspace, $W$, has two imaginary eigenvalues and two real eigenvalues of opposite sign. The only noncollinear relative equilibria are the two rotationally distinct equilateral triangles. The eigenvalues of $\left.L\right|_{W}$ are either all imaginary or all complex hyperbolic depending on the masses. Assuming $\bar{m}_{1}+\bar{m}_{2}+\bar{m}_{3}=1$, the purely imaginary case occurs for

$$
\bar{m}_{1} \bar{m}_{2}+\bar{m}_{1} \bar{m}_{3}+\bar{m}_{2} \bar{m}_{3}<\frac{1}{27}
$$

This condition is satisfied only when two of the three masses are small. The effective potential of the three-body problem was studied by Arenstorff [2]. The number of critical points depends on the masses. The eigenvalues $\beta_{i}$ have not been studied.

Next consider generalized relative equilibria with matrix $\beta$. As noted in Section 2, the nondegeneracy of a generalized relative equilibrium implies that $\beta$ is nonsingular and not a multiple of the identity. Since $\beta$ is symmetric, it can be diagonalized by an appropriate choice of axes in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$. Thus it can be assumed without loss of generality that $\beta=\operatorname{diag}\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right), \beta_{1} \neq \beta_{2}$.

For $|\gamma|=1$ Eq. (11) becomes (dropping the subscript for simplicity) $\beta \bar{x}=0$. Since $\beta$ is nonsingular there is only one generalized relative equilibrium, $\bar{x}=0$, and it is nondegenerate. To analyze linear stability, consider the $4 \times 4$ matrix:

$$
C=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\kappa & I \\
\beta-I & \kappa
\end{array}\right]
$$

![img-1.jpeg](img-1.jpeg)

Fig. 2. Stability diagram for a cluster of one mass.

The eigenvalues satisfy

$$
\lambda^{4}-\left(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}-4\right) \lambda^{2}+\beta_{1} \beta_{2}=0
$$

They are imaginary provided

$$
\beta_{1}>0, \quad \beta_{2}>0, \quad \beta_{1}+\beta_{2}<4, \quad\left(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}-4\right)^{2} \geqslant 4 \beta_{1} \beta_{2}
$$

In particular, it is necessary for linear stability that $\beta$ be positive definite, that is, that the asymptotically trivial mass converges to a local minimum of the effective potential. If $\beta_{1}>0$ and $\beta_{2}<0$ or vice versa, there are two imaginary eigenvalues and two real eigenvalues of opposite sign. The case $\beta_{1}<0$ and $\beta_{2}<0$ never occurs since, as noted above, the effective potential has no local maxima. Assuming $\beta_{1}>0$ and $\beta_{2}>0$, the other conditions in (18) determine a region in the ( $\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}$ )-plane shown in Fig. 2. Also shown in the figure is the line $\beta_{1}+\beta+2=3$, which contains the eigenvalues of the equilateral critical points of the effective potential of the two-body problem.

Clusters of $|\gamma|=2$ masses are determined by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \beta x_{1}+\frac{\mu_{2}\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)}{\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|}=0 \\
& \beta x_{2}+\frac{\mu_{1}\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)}{\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming that $\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}=1$ and introducing the center of mass $c=$ $\mu_{1} x_{1}+\mu_{2} x_{2}$ and the relative position $u=x_{2}-x_{1}$, these equations become

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta c & =0 \\
\left(\beta-|u|^{-3} I\right) u & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\beta$ is nonsingular, the first equation implies $c=0$. Assuming that $\beta=\operatorname{diag}\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right)$, the second equation gives

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
u=\left( \pm \beta_{1}^{-1 / 3}, 0\right) & \text { if } \quad \beta_{1}>0 \\
u=\left(0, \pm \beta_{2}^{-1 / 3}\right) & \text { if } \quad \beta_{2}>0
\end{array}
$$

These generalized relative equilibria are shown in Fig. 3. If the $\beta_{i}$ are of opposite sign, there is only one solution. To analyze the linear stability, introduce the total momentum $d=\mu_{1} w_{1}+\mu_{2} w_{2}$ and the relative velocity $v=w_{2}-w_{1}$. Then (10) decouple into

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{c}=d+\kappa c \\
& \dot{k}=(\beta-I) c+\kappa d
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{u}=v+\kappa u \\
& \dot{v}=(\beta-I) u-\frac{u}{|u|^{3}}+\kappa v
\end{aligned}
$$

The first set of equations has the same matrix (17) analyzed above. The same stability analysis applies. Assume that $\beta$ is diagonal and that $\beta_{1}>0$. Then the linearization of (20) at the equilibria $u=\left( \pm \beta_{1}^{-1 / 3}, 0\right)$ has matrix

$$
C=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\kappa & I \\
D & \kappa
\end{array}\right]
$$

where

$$
D=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
3 \beta_{1}-1 & 0 \\
0 & \beta_{2}-\beta_{1}-1
\end{array}\right]
$$

The characteristic polynomial of $C$ is

$$
\lambda^{4}-\left(2 \beta_{1}+\beta_{2}-4\right) \lambda^{2}+3 \beta_{1}\left(\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}\right)=0
$$

![img-2.jpeg](img-2.jpeg)

Fig. 3. Clusters of two masses.

If $\beta_{2}<\beta_{1}$, then there are two imaginary eigenvalues and two real eigenvalues of opposite sign. Thus $\beta_{1}<\beta_{2}$ is necessary for linear stability. In particular, $\beta_{2}$ is also positive. The conditions for all eigenvalues to be imaginary are

$$
0<\beta_{1}<\beta_{2}, \quad 2 \beta_{1}+\beta_{2}<4, \quad\left(2 \beta_{1}+\beta_{2}-4\right)^{2} \geqslant 12 \beta_{1}\left(\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}\right)
$$

Figure 4 shows the region of the $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right)$-plane where both (18) and (21) hold. The curve connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ shows the parameter values where some of the eigenvalues are equal. It turns out, however, that the equal eigenvalues have the same Hamiltonian sign except along the small section of the curve near $(1,1)$ between its tangencies with the parabolas forming the boundaries of the shaded region. For $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right)$ on this section, linear stability may not persist for $\varepsilon>0$.
![img-3.jpeg](img-3.jpeg)

Fig. 4. Stability diagram for a cluster of two masses.

The idea of introducing the center of mass can be applied for any $|\gamma|$ and one obtains equations (19). The argument used above for $|\gamma|=2$ applies to show that the center of mass of any nondegenerate generalized relative equilibrium is at the origin and that the conditions (18) (illustrated in Fig. 4) are necessary for linear stability. In particular, the observation that the cluster must be located at a local minimum of the effective potential holds for all $|\gamma|$.

Next consider collinear generalized relative equilibria with any number of masses. Since the center of mass is at the origin, each of the resealed position vectors and each of their difference vectors is a multiple of some fixed vector $u \in \mathbf{R}^{2}$ which determines the line. It follows easily from (11) that $u$ must be an eigenvector of $\beta_{\gamma}$. Since $\beta_{\gamma}$ has distinct eigenvalues (by the nondegeneracy hypothesis), the masses must be located on one of the two principal axes. Note that on the principal axes, the matrix $B_{\gamma}$ in eqs. (11) acts like $\beta_{i} I$.

A collinear generalized relative equilibrium is possible on the principal axis of $\beta_{i}$ only if $\beta_{i}>0$. To see this, consider the body, $x_{j}$, farthest from the origin. The forces due to the other bodies clearly point toward the origin and these must be balanced by the term $\beta_{i} x_{j}$. But if $\beta_{i}<0$, this term also points toward the origin. Next suppose $\beta_{i}>0$. As noted above, one may replace $B_{\gamma}$ by $\beta_{i} I$ in Eqs. (10). Then a simple resealing reduces $\beta_{i} I$ to $I$. Thus the equations for generalized relative equilibria reduce to to the usual equations for relative equilibria. According to the results of Moulton, there is unique collinear relative equilibrium for each of the $|\gamma|$ ! orderings of the masses along the line [8]. The spacing of the bodies along the line is difficult to compute explicitly. One simple case is the three-body problem with equal masses where the three bodies are equally spaced. In case both $\beta_{1}>0$ and $\beta_{2}>0$, there will be $2|\gamma|$ ! collinear generalized relative equilibria (see Fig. 5).

An argument similar to the one in the last paragraph shows that in case $\beta_{1}>0$ and $\beta_{2}<0$ or vice versa, the only generalized relative equilibrium is the collinear one. Let $\beta_{1}$ be the positive eigenvalue and suppose for the sake of contradiction that there is a noncollinear generalized relative equilibrium. Consider the body, $x_{j}$, which has the largest second coordinate. Then the forces on $x_{j}$ have a second component whose sign is
![img-4.jpeg](img-4.jpeg)

Fig. 5. Clusters of three equal masses.

opposite to that of $x_{j}$. These must be balanced by the second coordinate of $\beta_{2} x_{j}$, but this has the same sign, giving the contradiction.

Because the collinear configurations cannot be found explicitly, it is difficult to be precise about their linear stability. However, some general results can be proved. Early work showed that the collinear relative equilibria with $|\gamma| \geqslant 3$ are not linearly stable [1]. As will be shown below, this is no longer the case for generalized relative equilibria: the stability depends on the values of $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$. The key to the analysis is the decomposition of the matrix $\bar{M}_{y}^{-1} D \nabla U_{y}\left(x_{y}\right)$ into block diagonal form. Assume that the bodies are located on the first coordinate axis and rearrange the coordinates of $x_{y}$ so that the first coordinates of the $x_{y i}$ come first followed by their second coordinates. Then it can be shown [9] that

$$
\bar{M}_{y}^{-1} D \nabla U_{y}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
2 C & 0 \\
0 & -C
\end{array}\right]
$$

where $C$ is a $|\gamma| \times|\gamma|$ symmetric matrix with eigenvalues $0, \beta_{1}, \alpha_{2} \beta_{1}, \ldots$, $\alpha_{|y|} \beta_{1}$ where the $\alpha_{i}>1$. If $\alpha \beta_{1}$ denotes one of these eigenvalues and $u \in \mathbf{R}^{|y|}$ is an eigenvector for $\alpha \beta_{1}$, then the vectors $(u, 0,0,0),(0, u, 0,0)$, $\left(0,0, \bar{M}_{y} u, 0\right)$, and $\left(0,0,0, \bar{M}_{y} u\right)$ span a four-dimensional invariant subspace for the matrix $L$ in (15). The eigenvalues of the restriction of $L$ to this subspace satisfy

$$
\lambda^{4}-\left(\beta_{1}(1+\alpha)+\beta_{2}-4\right) \lambda^{2}+\beta_{1}(1+2 \alpha)\left(\beta_{2}-\alpha \beta_{1}\right)=0
$$

The eigenvalue $\alpha=0$ leads to conditions (18) associated to the center of mass. Likewise, $\alpha=1$ leads to (21). The other $\alpha_{i}$ lead to further conditions necessary for linear stability:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\alpha \beta_{1}<\beta_{2}, \quad \beta_{1}(1+\alpha)+\beta_{2}<4 \\
\left(\beta_{1}(1+\alpha)+\beta_{2}-4\right)^{2} \geqslant 4 \beta_{1}(1+2 \alpha)\left(\beta_{2}-\alpha \beta_{1}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

The details of these conditions will depend upon the exact values of the $\alpha_{i}$, which depend in turn on the spacing of the masses in the relative equilibrium. However, it is easy to see that these conditions are satisfied if $0<\beta_{2}<4$ and $\beta_{1}$ is sufficiently small. Thus there is an open set in the $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right)$-plane for which any given collinear generalized relative equilibrium is linearly stable.

The equations for noncollinear generalized relative equilibria of $|\gamma| \geqslant 3$ bodies are at least as hard to solve as those for relative equilibria. For $|\gamma| \geqslant 3$ there are exactly five relative equilibria which have been known since the time of Lagrange. It will now be shown that the situation for

generalized relative equilibria is more complicated. In particular, the number of relative equilibria depends on $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right)$.

Assume that $\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}+\mu_{3}=1$ and introduce Jacobi coordinates: $c$, the center of mass, $u=x_{2}-x_{1}$, and $v=x_{3}-\alpha_{1} x_{1}-\alpha_{2} x_{2}$, where $\alpha_{i}=$ $\mu_{i} /\left(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right), i=1,2$. The center of mass is governed by Eqs. (19), and at a generalized relative equilibrium, $c=0$. The other two Jacobi coordinates at a generalized relative equilibrium satisfy

$$
\begin{gathered}
\beta u-\frac{\left(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right) u}{|u|^{3}}+\frac{\mu_{3}\left(v-\alpha_{1} u\right)}{\left|v-\alpha_{1} u\right|^{3}}-\frac{\mu_{3}\left(v+\alpha_{2} u\right)}{\left|v+\alpha_{2} u\right|^{3}}=0 \\
\beta v-\frac{\alpha_{1}\left(v+\alpha_{2} u\right)}{\left|v+\alpha_{2} u\right|^{3}}-\frac{\alpha_{2}\left(v-\alpha_{1} u\right)}{\left|v-\alpha_{1} u\right|^{3}}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Because of the difficulty of solving these equations, the discussion below will be confined to the limiting case $\mu_{3} \rightarrow 0$ (the generalized $2+1$-body problem). In the limit, $\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}=1$ and the first equation becomes the equation for generalized relative equilibria of the 2 -body problem. Recall that this equation has two solutions if the $\beta_{i}$ are of opposite sign and four if both are positive. Assume that $\beta_{1}>0$ and that $u=\left(\beta_{1}^{-1 / 3}, 0\right)$. Introduce a parameter $\alpha$ with $\alpha_{1}=1-\alpha$ and $\alpha_{2}=\alpha$. Then $x_{1}=\beta_{1}^{-1 / 3}(-\alpha, 0)$ and $x_{2}=\beta_{1}^{-1 / 3}(1-\alpha, 0)$. Writing $v=\beta_{1}^{-1 / 3}\left(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}\right)$, the second equation in (23) becomes

$$
\begin{gathered}
\xi_{1}-\frac{(1-\alpha)\left(\xi_{1}+\alpha\right)}{r_{1}^{3}}-\frac{\alpha\left(\xi_{1}+\alpha-1\right)}{r_{2}^{3}}=0 \\
\rho \xi_{2}-\frac{(1-\alpha) \xi_{2}}{r_{1}^{3}}-\frac{\alpha \xi_{2}}{r_{2}^{3}}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

where $\rho=\beta_{2} / \beta_{1}$ and

$$
r_{1}^{2}=\left(\xi_{1}+\alpha\right)^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2}, \quad r_{2}^{2}=\left(\xi_{1}+\alpha-1\right)^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2}
$$

These are the equations for the critical point of the function

$$
W(\xi)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\xi_{1}^{2}+\rho \xi_{2}^{2}\right)+\frac{1-\alpha}{r_{1}}+\frac{\alpha}{r_{2}}
$$

which will be called the effective potential of the generalized $2+1$-body problem. When $\rho=1$ it is identical to the effective potential of the restricted three-body problem discussed above. In that case it had five critical points. As shown below, the general case is more complicated. In

particular, the number of critical points and their classification depend on the values of $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$.

In the noncollinear case, Eqs. (24) become

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\right) \xi_{1}+\alpha(1-\alpha) {\left[\frac{1}{r_{2}^{3}}-\frac{1}{r_{1}^{3}}\right] } & =0 \\
\frac{(1-\alpha)}{r_{1}^{3}}+\frac{\alpha}{r_{2}^{3}} & =\beta_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\xi_{1}$ can be expressed in terms of the distances using

$$
2 \xi_{1}=r_{1}^{2}-r_{2}^{2}+1-2 \alpha
$$

Eqs. (25) are equivalent to polynomial equations in $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$. These distances can be used as coordinates for the noncollinear configurations subject to the triangle inequalities:

$$
r_{1}+r_{2} \geqslant 1, \quad\left|r_{1}-r_{2}\right| \leqslant 1
$$

The equalities are satisfied when the configurations are collinear. In addition, the distances determine the configuration only up to reflection in the $\xi_{1}$-axis.

A further change of coordinates decouples the equations. Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& s=\frac{(1-\alpha)}{r_{1}^{3}}+\frac{\alpha}{r_{2}^{3}} \\
& t=\frac{1}{r_{2}^{3}}-\frac{1}{r_{1}^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then (25) can be written

$$
\begin{aligned}
s & =\beta_{2} \\
f(t) & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
f(t)=(1-\rho)\left[(1-\alpha t)^{-2 / 3}-(1+(1-\alpha) t)^{-2 / 3}+1-2 \alpha\right]+2 \alpha(1-\alpha) t
$$

Note that $s$ and $t$ uniquely determine $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$. Finding noncollinear generalized relative equilibria of the $(2+1)$-body problem amounts to finding roots of $f(t)$ in the interval $J=[1 /(\alpha-1), 1 / \alpha]$.

When $\rho<1, f^{\prime}(t)>0$ and $f(t)$ has exactly one root in $J$. In this case there are just two noncollinear generalized relative equilibria as is the case for the ordinary ( $2+1$ )-body problem. However, the triangle formed by the masses is not equilateral in general. When $\rho>1, f^{\prime \prime \prime}(t)>0$, so $f(t)$ has at most three roots in $J$. It is not difficult to see that for various choices of the parameters $(\alpha, \rho)$, there can be either 1,2 , or 3 roots of $f(t)$ in $J$ leading to distances $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ satisfying the triangle inequalities. Thus there can be 2,4 , or 6 noncollinear generalized relative equilibria. With the 3 collinear generalized relative equilibria, there are either 5,7 , or 9 generalized relative equilibria in all.

Further insight into the bifurcations of these generalized relative equilibria can be obtained by plotting the level curves of the effective potential for various choices of the parameters. The sequence of computer-generated pictures in Fig. 6 shows the level curves and critical points of $W(\xi)$ for
![img-5.jpeg](img-5.jpeg)

Fig. 6. Effective potentials of the generalized ( $2+1$ )-body problem for parameters $\alpha=0.25$ and $\rho=1,2,3,8$.

$\alpha=0.25$ and various values of $\rho$. For $\rho \geqslant 1$ there are five critical points as in the usual $2+1$-body problem ( $\rho=1$ is the usual problem). This persists until one of the collinear critical points bifurcates, producing 2 new noncollinear critical points. Another bifurcation produces 2 more, for a total of 9 . Finally, the 2 original noncollinear critical points merge with the middle collinear critical point, leaving 7 critical points for $\rho$ large. Note, however, that the collinear points are now minima and the noncollinear points saddles. Figure 6 shows the regions of the $(\alpha, \rho)$-plane where various numbers of generalized relative equilibria exist.

These facts about simple relative equilibria and generalized relative equilibria will be combined using the results of the earlier sections of this paper to construct new families $q^{e}$ of relative equilibria and to analyze their linear stability. For simplicity, only the case of two nontrivial masses will be considered with emphasis on linearly stable examples.

To apply the theory, a nondegenerate clustering scheme should be specified. As noted above, there is only one choice for the relative equilibrium $\bar{q}_{n}$ of the $v=2$-body problem. Then there are five critical points, $\xi$, of the associated effective potential, three collinear saddle points, and two local minima at the equilateral points. At the saddle points one can specify any collinear generalized relative equilibrium of the $|\gamma|$-body problem. Since the principal axis associated to the positive eigenvalue is the axis containing the nontrivial masses, the resulting configuration is still collinear. At the equilateral points one could put a collinear generalized relative equilibrium aligned with either of the two principal axes of the Hessian. Or one could put one of the as yet undiscovered noncollinear generalized relative equilibria, provided it is nondegenerate. According to Proposition 6 any such scheme will be realized by a family of relative equilibria $q^{e}$. Some computergenerated examples of relative equilibria of this type are shown in Fig. 7.

If one wants to produce a linearly stable relative equilibrium, then according to the results described above, one cannot put any clusters at the saddle points. Furthermore, one must put linearly stable generalized relative equilibria at the equilateral points. A cluster of $|\gamma|=1$ mass at the equilateral point will be linearly stable provided the eigenvalues $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right)$ lie in the shaded region in Fig. 4. Now as mentioned above, these eigenvalues lie on the line $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}=3$ which is indicated in the figure. If $\beta_{1}$ is the smaller of the two eigenvalues, then $\beta_{1}$ ranges over the interval $\left[0, \frac{3}{4}\right]$ as $\alpha$ ranges over $\left[0, \frac{1}{2}\right]$ then traces the same interval backward as $\alpha$ ranges over $\left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right]$. Thus for $\alpha$ sufficiently small (or sufficiently close to 1 ), ( $\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}$ ) does indeed lie in the shaded region. In fact, assuming $\alpha<\frac{1}{2}$, the cluster is stable provided

$$
\alpha<\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\sqrt{69}}{9}\right) \approx 0.038521
$$

![img-6.jpeg](img-6.jpeg)

Fig. 7. Bifurcation diagram for generalized relative equilibria of the $2+1$-body problem.
which is, the classical stability criterion of Routh for the restricted threebody problem. By putting one mass at each of the equilateral points one can find a linearly stable periodic orbit of the four-body problem, as well (the Hamiltonian signs of the equal eigenvalues agree).

If one chooses a cluster $|\gamma|=2$ masses, then for linear stability, $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right)$ must lie in the shaded region in Fig. 4. A similar argument shows that this is so provided

$$
\alpha<\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\sqrt{15681+7104 \sqrt{21}}}{225}\right) \approx 0.011942
$$

A single cluster of this kind produces a linearly stable periodic orbit of the four-body problem. Two such clusters produces a linearly stable orbit of the six-body problem. Combining a cluster of two masses at one equilateral point with a single mass at the other gives a five-body orbit.

The discussion of collinear generalized relative equilibria showed that such a configuration along the first principal axis would be linearly stable provided $0<\beta_{2}<4$ and $\beta_{1}$ is sufficiently small. This can be achieved by making the mass parameter sufficiently small. Exactly how small depends

on the details of the collinear cluster. For a cluster of three equal masses the condition is

$$
\alpha<\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\sqrt{3328967+89760 \sqrt{2030}}}{1587 \sqrt{3}}\right) \approx 0.006077
$$

It is interesting to note that when $\alpha$ is small, one of the principal axes at the equilateral critical points toward the $1-\alpha$ mass and the other is perpendicular. The linearly stable collinear clusters are aligned with the latter axis and the resulting relative equilibria give the impression of a lumpy ring of masses clustered near the equilateral points (see Fig. 1).

To lend some astronomical perspective to these results, note that if the two nontrivial masses are the Sun and Jupiter, then $\alpha \approx 0.001$, whereas for the Earth and the Moon $\alpha \approx 0.01215$.


RICHARD MOECKEL

## 1. The Newtonian $n$-body Problem

Celestial mechanics can be defined as the study of the solution of Newton's differential equations formulated by Isaac Newton in 1686 in his Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica.

The setting for celestial mechanics is three-dimensional space:

$$
\mathbb{R}^{3}=\{q=(x, y, z): x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}\}
$$

with the Euclidean norm:

$$
|q|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}
$$

A point particle is characterized by a position $q \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ and a mass $m \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$. A motion of such a particle is described by a curve $q(t)$ where $t$ runs over some interval in $\mathbb{R}$; the mass is assumed to be constant. Some remarks will be made below about why it is reasonable to model a celestial body by a point particle. For every motion of a point particle one can define:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { velocity: } v(t) & =\dot{q}(t) \\
\text { momentum: } p(t) & =m v(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

Newton formulated the following laws of motion:
Lex.I. Corpus omne perservare in statu suo quiescendi vel movendi uniformiter in directum, nisi quatenus a viribus impressis cogitur statum illum mutare ${ }^{1}$
Lex.II. Mutationem motus proportionem esse vi motrici impressae et fieri secundem lineam qua vis illa imprimitur. ${ }^{2}$
Lex.III Actioni contrarium semper et aequalem esse reactionem: sive corporum duorum actiones in se mutuo semper esse aequales et in partes contrarias dirigi. ${ }^{3}$
The first law is statement of the principle of inertia. The second law asserts the existence of a force function $F: \mathbb{R}^{4} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{3}$ such that:

$$
\dot{p}=F(q, t) \quad \text { or } \quad m \ddot{q}=F(q, t)
$$

In celestial mechanics, the dependence of $F(q, t)$ on $t$ is usually indirect; the force on one body depends on the positions of the other massive bodies which in turn depend on $t$. The third law postulates the symmetry of the mutual interaction of two bodies which will apply, in particular, to the gravitational interaction.

${ }^{1}$ Every body continues in its quiescent state or moves uniformly in direction, unless it is compelled by impressed forces to change its state.
${ }^{2}$ The change of momentum is proportional to the motive force impressed and takes place along the line where this force is impressed.
${ }^{3}$ To every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction: the actions of two bodies on one another are always equal and aimed in opposite directions.

The $n$-body problem is about the motion of $n$ point particles under the influence of their mutual gravitational attraction. Each particle has a mass $m_{i}>0$ and position, velocity and momentum vectors $q_{i}, v_{i}, p_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$. The whole system can be described using the vectors $q, v, p \in \mathbb{R}^{3 n}$ where

$$
q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \quad v=\left(v_{1}, v_{2}, \ldots, v_{n}\right) \quad p=\left(m_{1} v_{1}, m_{2} v_{2}, \ldots, m_{n} v_{n}\right)
$$

According to Newton, the gravitational force acting on particle $i$ due to the presence of particle $j$ is

$$
F_{i j}=\frac{G m_{i} m_{j}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right)}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|^{3}}
$$

where $G$ is a constant. Note that $F_{i j}$ acts along the line containing the masses. It's proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the distance between them (see Figure 1). The force produced on $m_{j}$ by $m_{i}$ is $F_{j i}=-F_{i j}$ by Newton's third law. By choosing the units of mass, one can arrange that $G=1$ and this will be assumed from now on (see Exercise 1.1).
![img-0.jpeg](img-0.jpeg)

Figure 1. Newtonian gravitational forces.
The force on the $i$-th mass due to the other $n-1$ masses is:

$$
F_{i}=\sum_{j \neq i} F_{i j}=\sum_{j \neq i} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right)}{\left|q_{j}-q_{i}\right|^{3}}
$$

This can be written:

$$
F_{i}(q)=\nabla_{i} U(q)
$$

where

$$
U(q)=\sum_{\substack{i, j \\ i<j}} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|}
$$

and $\nabla_{i}$ is the partial gradient operator:

$$
\nabla_{i} U=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x_{i}}, \frac{\partial U}{\partial y_{i}}, \frac{\partial U}{\partial z_{i}}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}
$$

The function $U(q)$ will be called the Newtonian gravitational potential function. $V(q)=-U(q)$ is the gravitational potential energy. Newton's second law becomes

$$
\dot{p}_{i}=m_{i} \tilde{q}_{i}=\nabla_{i} U(q) \quad \mathrm{i}=1, \ldots, \mathrm{n}
$$

or, more concisely

$$
\dot{p}=\nabla U(q) \quad \text { or } \quad M \ddot{q}=\nabla U(q)
$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient operator in $\mathbb{R}^{3 n}$ and $M$ is the $3 n \times 3 n$ mass matrix

$$
M=\operatorname{diag}\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}, m_{n}, m_{n}\right)
$$

It is worth digressing at this point to note two important, special features of the Newtonian interparticle potential:

$$
\frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|}
$$

First of all, the presence of the factor $m_{i} m_{j}$ has the effect that the equation for the acceleration of the $i$-th mass,

$$
\ddot{q}_{i}=\frac{1}{m_{i}} F_{i}
$$

is independent of $m_{i}$. This corresponds to the observation, notably by Galileo, that the trajectory of a falling body is independent of its mass.
![img-1.jpeg](img-1.jpeg)

Figure 2. Masses falling from a tower.

Second, the fact that the potential is inversely proportional to the distance between the particles provides some justification for the modeling of celestial bodies by point particles. While such bodies are not even approximately pointlike, they are approximately spherically symmetric. It turns out that with the Newtonian potential, spherically symmetric bodies behave as if their total mass were concentrated at their centers.

To see this, consider a more general massive body, specified by giving a bounded subset $\mathcal{B} \subset \mathbb{R}^{3}$ together with a continuous mass density functions $\rho$. The gravitational force exerted by such a mass distribution on a point mass $m$ at position $q$ is $F=\nabla U(q)$ where

$$
U(q)=\int_{\mathcal{B}} \frac{m}{|q-p|} d m
$$

where the triple integral is over $p=(x, y, z) \in \mathcal{B}$ and $d m=\rho(x, y, z) d x d y d z$.

Proposition 1.1. Suppose $\mathcal{B}$ is a ball of radius $R$ centered at $q_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ and $\rho$ is a spherically symmetric density function. Then the mutual Newtonian potential of the ball and a mass $m$ at any point $q$ with $|q|>R$ is

$$
U(q)=\frac{m_{0} m}{\left|q_{0}-q\right|}
$$

where $m_{0}$ is the total mass in the ball.
Proof. Using the symmetry of the Euclidean distance under rotations and translations, it is no loss of generality to assume $q_{0}=(0,0,0)$ and $q=(0,0, z), z>R$. Using spherical coordinates $(x, y, z)=r(\cos \theta \sin \phi, \sin \theta \sin \phi, \cos \phi)$, the spherical symmetry means that the density function depends only on $r$ and then

$$
U(q)=\int_{0}^{R} \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} \frac{m_{i} \rho(r) r^{2} \sin \phi d \theta d \phi d r}{\sqrt{r^{2}+z^{2}-2 r z \cos \phi}}
$$

It is an exercise to carry out the first two integrals to show

$$
U(q)=\frac{m_{0} m}{z} \quad m_{0}=\int_{0}^{R} 4 \pi r^{2} \rho(r) d r
$$

There is an alternative proof of this result, based on the fact that $f(x, y, z)=$ $1 /|q-p|$ is a harmonic function of $p=(x, y, z)$, that is, $f_{x x}+f_{y y}+f_{z z}=0$. The well-known mean value theorem for harmonic functions states that the average value of a harmonic function over a sphere is equal to the value at the center of the sphere, which can be proved using the divergence theorem (see exercise 1.3). Fixing a value of $r$ and applying this to the function $f(x, y, z)=m \rho(r) /|q-p|$ and the sphere $S_{r}=\left\{\left|q-q_{0}\right|=r\right\}$ gives

$$
\int_{S_{r}} f=\frac{4 \pi r^{2} \rho(r) m}{\left|q_{0}-q\right|}
$$

Then integration over $0 \leq r \leq R$ completes the proof.
Although $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the natural home of celestial mechanics, it is useful and interesting to consider the point-mass $n$-body problem in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for any positive integer $d$. In this case the position vectors are $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ and the vectors $q, v, p$ are elements of $\mathbb{R}^{d n}$. Newton's equations (2) form a system of real-analytic, second order differential equations on the configuration space, $X=\mathbb{R}^{d n} \backslash \Delta$, where

$$
\Delta=\left\{q: q_{i}=q_{j} \text { for some } i \neq j\right\}
$$

is the collision set. It can be transformed in the usual way into a first-order system in the phase space:

$$
T X=X \times \mathbb{R}^{d n}=\left\{(q, v): q \in X \text { and } v \in \mathbb{R}^{d n}\right\}
$$

namely:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{q}=v \\
& \dot{v}=M^{-1} \nabla U(q)
\end{aligned}
$$

The notation $T X$ takes note of the fact that the phase space is the tangent bundle of $X$. The Newtonian $n$-body problem is to study the solutions of equations (3).

A solution to (3) is a differentiable curve $(q(t), v(t))$ where the time $t$ lies in some interval $I$. Since the differential equation is given by real-analytic functions on phase space, the solutions will be real-analytic functions of time and of their

initial conditions, that is, they are given locally by convergent power series. Since the phase space is not compact, it may not be possible to extend solutions for all time $t \in \mathbb{R}$. In general the maximal interval of existence will be of the form $I=(a, b)$ with $-\infty \leq a<b \leq \infty$. By the general theory of ordinary differential equations, if $b<\infty$ then as $t \rightarrow b_{-},(q(t), v(t))$ must leave every compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d n} \backslash \Delta \times \mathbb{R}^{d n}$ and similarly for $a>-\infty$. For example, this can happen if $q(t)$ converges to a collision configuration $\bar{q} \in \Delta$ (see exercise 1.5).

# 2. Variational Formulations 

Newton's laws of motion can be derived from the variational principles of Lagrange or Hamilton. This is of some philosophical interest, but also has the practical effect of simplifying the computation of the equations of motion in non-Cartesian coordinate systems
2.1. Lagrangian Formulation. Lagrangian mechanics is based on the principle of "least" action. The this section contains some of the general theory of Lagrangian Mechanics. Let $X$ be an open subset of a Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ (such as the configuration space of the $n$-body problem where $m=3 n$ ) and let $T X=X \times \mathbb{R}^{m}$ denote the tangent bundle. A Lagrangian is a smooth function $L: T X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, that is, a smooth real-valued function $L(q, v)$. More generally, one can also allow Lagrangians $L(q, v, t)$ which depend explicitly on time. The dimension of the configuration space, $m$, is called the number of degrees of freedom.

For the $n$-body problem the Lagrangian will be

$$
L(q, v)=\frac{1}{2} v \cdot M v+U(q)=\frac{1}{2} v^{T} M v+U(q)
$$

where, in the second formula, $v$ is viewed as a column vector and its transpose $v^{T}$ is the corresponding row vector. The first term $K=\frac{1}{2} \sum m_{i}\left|v_{i}\right|^{2}$ is the kinetic energy and the second $U(q)=-V(q)$ where $V(q)$ is the gravitational potential energy. The recipe

$$
\text { Lagrangian }=\text { Kinetic Energy }- \text { Potential Energy }
$$

holds for many other physical systems as well.
Given a Lagrangian and a curve $q(t) \in X$, the action of the curve on the interval $[a, b]$ is:

$$
A(q)=\int_{a}^{b} L(q(t), \dot{q}(t), t) d t
$$

Thus the action is a function on the space of curves in $X$. For now, it is sufficient to work with $C^{2}$ curves. A variation of a curve $q(t)$ on $[a, b]$ is a $C^{2}$ family of curves $q_{s}(t)$ in $X$, where $t \in[a, b]$ and $s \in(\delta, \delta)$ for some $\delta>0$. The variation has fixed endpoints if $q_{s}(a)=q(a)$ and $q_{s}(b)=q(b)$. If $q_{s}(t)$ is a variation of $q$ then to first order in $s$

$$
q_{s}(t)=q(t)+s \alpha(t)+\ldots \quad \alpha(t)=\left.\frac{\partial q_{s}(t)}{\partial s}\right|_{s=0}
$$

$\alpha(t)$ can be viewed a vectorfield along the curve $q(t)$ (see Figure 3). It will be called the variation vectorfield corresponding to the variation $q_{s}(t)$. Note every vectorfield $\alpha(t)$ along $q$ is the variation vectorfield of some variation, for example $q_{s}(t)=q(t)+s \alpha(t)$.

The principle of least action states that if $q(t)$ is a possible motion of Lagrangian system then the first variation of the action should be zero, for every fixed endpoint variation. That is, for every fixed endpoint variation $q_{s}(t)$ satisfies

$$
\delta A=\left.\frac{d}{d s} A(q_{s})\right|_{s=0}=0
$$

This is a necessary but not sufficient condition for $q$ to have the least action among all nearby curves with the same endpoints. In any case, $q(t)$ can be called a stationary curve or critical curve of $A$ on $[a, b]$.

![img-2.jpeg](img-2.jpeg)

Figure 3. Variation of a curve and the variation vectorfield.

The following proposition is a standard result in the calculus of variations:
Proposition 2.1. A curve, $q(t)$, is a stationary curve of $A$ on $[a, b]$ if and only if the conjugate momentum

$$
p(t)=L_{v}(q(t), v(t), t)
$$

satisfies the Euler-Lagrange (EL) equation on $[a, b]$ :

$$
\dot{p}(t)=L_{q}(q(t), v(t), t)
$$

Before giving a proof, a digression on covectors is in order. The subscripts in this proposition denote partial derivatives with respect to the vectors $q, v \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. The derivative of the real-valued function $L(q, v)$ is a linear function $D L(q, v): \mathbb{R}^{2 m} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and the partial derivatives $L_{q}, L_{v}$ are linear functions from $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Using other terminologies, they are linear forms, one forms, dual vectors or covectors rather than vectors. Thus the Euler-Lagrange equation is fundamentally an equation between two covectors. The space of all covectors on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the also called the dual space and is denoted $\mathbb{R}^{m *}$.

A partial derivative covector like $p=L_{v}$ can be represented in coordinates as a vector of partial derivatives

$$
p=\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m}\right)=\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\partial L}{\partial v_{m}}\right)
$$

Alternatively, it can be represented as the $1 \times m$ Jacobian matrix

$$
p=\left[\begin{array}{lll}
p_{1} & \ldots & p_{m}
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_{1}} & \ldots & \frac{\partial L}{\partial v_{m}}
\end{array}\right]
$$

Ordinary vectors $w \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ can also be represented in two ways, as coordinate vectors or $m \times 1$ matrices

$$
w=\left(w_{1}, \ldots, w_{n}\right)=\left[\begin{array}{c}
w_{1} \\
\vdots \\
w_{m}
\end{array}\right]
$$

Then the value of the linear function $p$ on the vector $w$ is

$$
p(w)=p_{1} w_{1}+\ldots+p_{m} w_{m}=\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m}\right) \cdot\left(w_{1}, \ldots, w_{m}\right)=\left[\begin{array}{lll}
p_{1} & \ldots & p_{m}
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}
w_{1} \\
\vdots \\
w_{m}
\end{array}\right]
$$

Thus, evaluating a covector on a vector amounts to taking the dot product of their coordinate vectors or multiplying their matrices.

Proof of Proposition 2.1. The action of $q_{s}$ is

$$
A\left(q_{s}\right)=\int_{a}^{b} L\left(q_{s}(t), \dot{q}_{s}(t), t\right) d t
$$

Differentiating with respect to $s$ under the integral sign and using the chain rule gives

$$
\delta A=\int_{a}^{b} L_{q}(q(t), v(t), t) \cdot \alpha(t)+p(t) \cdot \dot{\alpha}(t) d t
$$

where $v(t)=\dot{q}(t), \alpha(t)$ is the variation vectorfield and $p(t)=L_{v}(q(t), v(t), t)$. Since $q(t)$ is $C^{2}, p(t)$ is $C^{1}$, and the second term can be integrated by parts. Using the fact that $\alpha(a)=\alpha(b)=0$ this gives

$$
\delta A=\int_{a}^{b}\left[L_{q}(q(t), v(t), t)-\dot{p}(t)\right] \cdot \alpha(t) d t
$$

Since $\alpha(t)$ is an arbitrary $C^{2}$ fixed endpoint vectorfield along $q(t)$, the following lemma shows that the function in square brackets must vanish, which is equivalent to the Euler-Lagrange equation (7).

Lemma 2.1. Suppose $f:[a, b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is a continuous function such that

$$
\int_{a}^{b} f(t) \cdot \alpha(t) d t=0
$$

for all $C^{\infty}$ functions $\alpha:[a, b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{m}$ with $\alpha(a)=\alpha(b)=0$. Then $f(t)=0$ for all $t \in[a, b]$.

Proof. Exercise 2.1.
QED
Newton's equation (2) are the Euler-Lagrange equations for the Lagrangian (4). In fact, let $U(q)$ be any smooth function on an open set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and $M$ any invertible, symmetric $m \times m$ matrix. The $1 \times m$ partial derivative matrices of the Lagrangian (4) are

$$
L_{v}=v^{T} M \quad L_{q}=D U(q)
$$

and the Euler-Lagrange equation is $\dot{v}^{T} M=D U(q)$. Taking transposes gives Newton's equation $M \dot{v}=\nabla U(q)$.

In this case, the Euler-Lagrange equations amount to a second order differential equation for $q$ on $X$ or, equivalently, a first-order differential equation for $(q, v)$ on $T X$. More generally, this will be true whenever it is possible to invert the equation $p=L_{v}(q, v)$ defining the conjugate momentum.

Definition 2.1. A Lagrangian $L(q, v)$ is nondegenerate if the equation $p=L_{v}(q, v)$ can be solved for $v$ as a smooth function $v(q, p)$.

The utility of the Lagrangian point of view lies in the fact that the EulerLagrange equations are invariant under changes of coordinates. Consider a timeindependent Lagrangian $L(q, v)$ and a smooth coordinate change given by a diffeomorphism $Q=\phi(q), \phi: X \rightarrow Y$ where $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is another open set. The inverse map will be written $q=\psi(Q)$. The velocity variables are related by $v=D \psi(Q) V$ and the Lagrangian becomes

$$
\tilde{L}(Q, V)=L(\psi(Q), D \psi(Q) V)
$$

Writing things like this in terms of the "backward" coordinate change map $\psi$ instead of $\phi$, it actually suffices to assume that $\psi$ is a local diffeomophism.

Proposition 2.2. Let $\psi: Y \rightarrow X$ be a local diffeomorphism. $A C^{2}$ curve $Q(t)$ solves the Euler-Lagrange equations for $\tilde{L}$ if and only if the corresponding curve $q(t)=\psi(Q(t))$ solves the Euler-Lagrange equations for $L$.

Proof. First suppose $\psi$ is really a diffeomorphism with inverse $\phi$. It suffices to show that $q$ is a stationary curve for the action $A$ if and only if $Q$ is a stationary curve for the action $\tilde{A}$ of $\tilde{L}$. Suppose $q$ is stationary for $L$ and let $Q_{s}(t)$ be any fixed endpoint variation of $Q$. Then $q_{s}(t)=\psi\left(Q_{s}(t)\right)$ is a fixed endpoint variation of $q$ with $\dot{q}_{s}(t)=D \psi\left(Q_{s}(t)\right) \tilde{Q}_{s}(t)$. The actions satisfy
$A\left(q_{s}\right)=\int_{a}^{b} L\left(q_{s}, \dot{q}_{s}\right) d t=\int_{a}^{b} L\left(\psi\left(Q_{s}\right), D \psi\left(Q_{s}\right) \tilde{Q}_{s}\right) d t=\int_{a}^{b} \tilde{L}\left(Q_{s}, \dot{Q}_{s}\right) d t=\tilde{A}\left(Q_{s}\right)$
It follows that $\delta \tilde{A}(Q)=\delta A(q)=0$, so $Q$ is stationary for $\tilde{A}$. Reversing the roles of $q, Q$ completes the proof when $\psi$ is a diffeomorphism.

To handle the case of a local diffeomorphism, let $t_{0} \in[a, b]$ and let $U, V$ be neighborhoods of $q\left(t_{0}\right), Q\left(t_{0}\right)$ such that $\psi: V \rightarrow U$ is a diffeomorphism. There is some interval $I=[c, d]$ with $t_{0} \in I \subset[a, b]$ such that $q(t) \in U, Q(t) \in V$ for all $t \in I$. The previous proof applies to fixed endpoint variations on the interval $I$, so at time $t_{0}, q$ solve the EL equations for $L$ if and only if $Q$ solves the EL equations for $\tilde{L}$. Since $t_{0}$ is arbitrary, the proof is complete.

Actually, this result is still true for time-dependent Lagrangians and time-dependent coordinate changes (see exercise 2.5). Its main practical consequence is that to find the transformed differential equations, it suffices to transform the Lagrangian and then compute the Euler-Lagrange equation in the new variables. Here is a simple example - the central force problem in the plane.

Example 2.1. Consider a point particle with mass $m$ and position vector $q \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ subjected to a force $F(q)=f(|q|) q$ where $f$ is a real-valued function. Thus the force vector is always pointing toward or away from the "center", $q=0$. Suppose further that $F(q)=\nabla U(|q|)$ for some potential function depending only on $|q|$. Newton's equations are the Euler-Lagrange equations for the Lagrangian

$$
L(q, v)=\frac{m}{2}|v|^{2}+U(|q|)
$$

Let $r, \theta$ be the usual polar coordinates in the plane. Then the backward coordinate change is a local diffeomorphism away from the origin:

$$
q=r(\cos \theta, \sin \theta) \quad v=\dot{r}(\cos \theta, \sin \theta)+r \dot{\theta}(-\sin \theta, \cos \theta)
$$

and the transformed Lagrangian is

$$
\tilde{L}(r, \theta, \dot{r}, \dot{\theta})=\frac{m}{2}\left(\dot{r}^{2}+r^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2}\right)+U(r)
$$

The conjugate momentum vector is

$$
p=\left(p_{r}, p_{\theta}\right)=\left(L_{\dot{r}}, L_{\dot{\theta}}\right)=\left(m \dot{r}, m r^{2} \dot{\theta}\right)
$$

and the Euler-Lagrange equations are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{p}_{r}=m \ddot{r}=L_{r}=U^{\prime}(r)+2 r \dot{\theta}^{2} \\
& \dot{p}_{\theta}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

The zero in the second equation comes from the fact that the $\hat{L}$ is independent of the position variable $\theta$. It follows that

$$
p_{\theta}=r^{2} \dot{\theta}=C
$$

for some constant, $C$ and the equations become

$$
m \ddot{r}=U^{\prime}(r)+\frac{2 C^{2}}{r^{3}} \quad \dot{\theta}=\frac{C}{r^{2}}
$$

Using the coordinate invariance property of the Euler-Lagrange equations, it is also possible to generalize to Lagrangian systems on manifolds. If $X$ is an $m$ dimensional manifold then it is covered by a system of local coordinate patches diffeomorphic to open subsets in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$. Using local coordinate, the tangent bundle $T X$ is parametrized by variables $(q, v)$ as above and a Lagrangian $L: T X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ takes the form $L(q, v)$ as above. Assuming the Lagrangian is nondegenerate, the Euler-Lagrange equations define a first order system of differential equations in each coordinate patch. Proposition 2.2 shows that these locally defined differential equations fit together consistently to give a differential equation on $T X$. In practice, it is better to use some tricks to avoid local coordinates.

Example 2.2. Consider a pendulum consisting of a mass $m$ attached to a rigid rod of length $l$ swinging in a vertical plane, say the $(x, z)$ plane. The configuration manifold is the circle $X=\left\{(x, z): x^{2}+z^{2}=l^{2}\right\}$. Instead of using local coordinates, $X$ can be parametrized by an angle $\theta$ using $(x, z)=l(\sin \theta,-\cos \theta)$ and then the velocity is $(\dot{x}, \dot{z})=l(\cos \theta, \sin \theta) \dot{\theta}$ (the parametrization is such that $\theta=0$ represents the bottom of the circle). Assume that the gravitational force is given by $F=(0,-m g)$ where $g$ is constant. This is the gradient of $U(z)=-m g z$. The Lagrangian is of the standard form (5)

$$
L=\frac{1}{2} m\left(\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{z}^{2}\right)-m g z=\frac{1}{2} m l^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2}+m g l \cos \theta
$$

and the EL equation is

$$
\ddot{\theta}+\frac{g}{l} \sin \theta=0
$$

For a spherical pendulum, that is, not confined to the plane, the configuration manifold is $X=\left\{(x, y, z): x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=l^{2}\right\}$. This time there is no global parametrization. Spherical coordinates

$$
(x, y, z)=l(\sin \theta \cos \phi, \sin \theta \sin \phi,-\cos \theta)
$$

cover the sphere but have singularities at $\{\theta=0\}$. Stereographic projections $(x, y, z)=l\left(2 u, 2 v, \pm\left(1-u^{2}-v^{2}\right) /\left(1+u^{2}+v^{2}\right)\right.$ could be used to give nonsingular local coordinates omitting only $(0,0, \pm l)$. An alternative is to find a Lagrangian system on $T \mathbb{R}^{3}$ for which $T X$ is invariant and whose Lagrangian has the right values on $T X$.

Let $q=(x, y, z)$ and $v=\dot{q}$ and consider the "homogenized" Lagrangian

$$
L(q, v)=\frac{1}{2} \frac{m l^{2}|v|^{2}}{|q|^{2}}-\frac{m g l z}{|q|}
$$

If $(q, v) \in T X=\{|q|=l, q \cdot v=0\}$ then the homogenizing factors cancel out and $L(q, v)$ give the correct standard Lagrangian (5). Moreover, $T X$ is an invariant set for the EL equations of $L$. It follows that restricting $L$ to $T X$ gives the correct solutions for the spherical pendulum (see exercise 2.2).

The method used in this example is justified by the following proposition, whose proof is exercise 2.3

Proposition 2.3. Let $L: T \mathbb{R}^{m} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a nondegenerate Lagrangian and let $X \subset$ $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ be submanifold such that $T X$ is invariant under the EL equations of L. Let $\hat{L}: T X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be the restriction of $L$ to $T X$. Suppose a curve $(q(t), v(t)) \in T X$ solves the EL equations for L. Then it solves the EL equations for $\hat{L}$ (in every local coordinate system).

Let $X$ be an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ and consider a Lagrangian $L: T X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ of the form

$$
L(q, v)=\frac{1}{2} v^{T} M v+U(q)
$$

where $M$ is an invertible $m \times m$ matrix. The tangent bundle of $X$ is just the product space

$$
T X=X \times \mathbb{R}^{m}=\left\{(q, v): q \in X, v \in \mathbb{R}^{m}\right\}
$$

Using matrix representations, the conjugate momentum covector $p=L_{v}(q, v) \in$ $\mathbb{R}^{m *}$ and the velocity $v \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are related by

$$
p=v^{T} M \quad v=M^{-1} p^{T}
$$

The transformation $(x, v) \mapsto(x, p)$ can be viewed as a diffeomorphism $T X \simeq T^{*} X$ where

$$
T^{*} X=X \times \mathbb{R}^{m *}=\left\{(q, p): q \in X, p \in \mathbb{R}^{m *}\right\}
$$

is the cotangent bundle of $X$.
More generally, for any nondegenerate Lagrangian, one can solve the equation $p=L_{v}(q, v)$ for $v=v(q, p)$. Then define the Hamiltonian function $H: T^{*} X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by

$$
H(x, p)=\left.p \cdot v-L(q, v)\right|_{v=v(q, p)}
$$

where the $\cdot$ denotes multiplication of $1 \times m$ and $m \times 1$ matrices or, equivalently, the result of evaluating the covector $p$ on the vector $v$. If $L(q, v)=\frac{1}{2} v^{T} M v+U(q)$, as in the $n$-body problem, then

$$
H(q, p)=\frac{1}{2} p M^{-1} p^{T}-U(q)
$$

Hamiltonian $=$ Kinetic Energy + Potential Energy $=$ Total Energy.
The process of going from $L(q, v)$ to $H(q, p)$ is sometimes called the Legendre transform. One can recover the Lagrangian from the Hamiltonian by

$$
