\left(r_{k l}^{-1}\right)^{\prime}=r_{k l}^{-3}\left\{\left(x_{k}-x_{l}\right)\left(\dot{x}_{l}-\dot{x}_{k}\right)+\left(y_{k}-y_{l}\right)\left(\dot{y}_{l}-\dot{y}_{k}\right)+\left(z_{k}-z_{l}\right)\left(\dot{z}_{l}-\dot{z}_{k}\right)\right\} \\
=O\left(t^{-\frac{4}{2}} \cdot t^{-\frac{4}{2}}\right)=O\left(t^{-\frac{4}{2}}\right) \\
\dot{T}=\dot{U}=O\left(t^{-\frac{4}{3}}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

and

$$
\bar{I}=2 T+2 h=O\left(t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)
$$

all this being true for $\tau_{2 j} \leqq t \leqq \tau_{2 j-1}, j \rightarrow \infty$. These estimates together with (10) and (11) show that

$$
\dot{g}<b t^{-1} \quad\left(\tau_{2 j} \leqq t \leqq \tau_{2 j-1} ; j=1,2, \ldots\right)
$$

for some positive constant $b$.
From (10) and (12) we now have

$$
\begin{gathered}
\varepsilon=g\left(\tau_{2 j-1}\right)-g\left(\tau_{2 j}\right)=\int_{\tau_{2 j}}^{\tau_{2 j-1}} \dot{g}(t) d t<b \int_{\tau_{2 j}}^{\tau_{2 j-1}} \frac{d t}{t} \\
\int_{\tau_{2 j}}^{\tau_{2 j-1}} g(t) \frac{d t}{t}>\varepsilon \int_{\tau_{2 j}}^{\tau_{2 j-1}} \frac{d t}{t}>\varepsilon^{2} b^{-1}
\end{gathered}
$$

which upon summation over $j$ contradicts convergence of the integral $G$. This proves statements (9) and (7) and in turn leads to the estimates

$$
r_{k l}^{-1}=O\left(t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right), \quad \dot{q}=O\left(t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

which up to now were known only in the intervals $\tau_{2 j} \leqq t \leqq \tau_{2 j-1}$ for $j \rightarrow \infty$.

An important consequence of (8), (9) and $(6 ; 3)$ is the asymptotic formula

$$
p \dot{q}-q \dot{p}=o\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

valid for any two coordinates $p$ and $q$. This, in particular, shows once more that in the case of triple collision all 3 angular momentum constants are 0 .

Since according to (1) and (4) we have

$$
q=O\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)
$$

it is convenient to introduce

$$
\bar{q}=q t^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \quad \bar{p}=p t^{-\frac{1}{2}} \quad(t>0)
$$

Then

$$
\bar{q}=O(1), \quad \bar{p}=O(1) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

and (14) becomes

$$
\bar{p} \dot{\bar{q}}-\bar{q} \bar{p}=(p \dot{q}-q \dot{p}) t^{-\frac{1}{2}}=o\left(t^{-1}\right) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

In general, for $f$ a homogeneous function of degree $v$ in the coordinates $q$, let $\bar{f}$ denote the corresponding function in the variables $\bar{q}$,

so that

$$
\bar{f}=f t^{\frac{-2 v}{3}}
$$

By (4) and (6) then

$$
\bar{I}=I t^{-\frac{1}{2}} \rightarrow \varkappa, \quad \bar{I}=\dot{I} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{4}{3} I t^{-\frac{1}{2}}=o\left(t^{-1}\right) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

while on the other hand

$$
\bar{I}=\sum_{\vec{q}} m \bar{q}^{2}, \quad \frac{1}{2} \dot{\bar{I}}=\sum_{\vec{q}} m \bar{q} \dot{\bar{q}}
$$

so that (15), (16), and (17) give

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{1}{2} \bar{p} \dot{\bar{I}}-\bar{I} \dot{\bar{p}}=\sum_{\vec{q}} m \bar{q}(\bar{p} \dot{\bar{q}}-\bar{q} \dot{\bar{p}})=o\left(t^{-1}\right) \\
\bar{I} \dot{\bar{p}}=o\left(t^{-1}\right), \quad \bar{p}=o\left(t^{-1}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus for each coordinate $q$ we have

$$
\dot{\bar{q}}=o\left(t^{-1}\right) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

In addition to the triangle $\Delta$ formed by the three particles $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}$, we consider the triangle $\bar{\Delta}$ whose vertices $\bar{P}_{1}, \bar{P}_{2}, \bar{P}_{3}$ have the corresponding coordinates $\bar{q}$. Thus, the new triangle is obtained from the original one by a dilatation in the ratio of 1 to $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$. At triple collision $\Delta$ collapses to the origin of the coordinate system, while in the end it will be shown that also the large triangle $\bar{\Delta}$ has a definite limiting position as $t \rightarrow 0$. First we will show that the lengths of the three sides of $\bar{\Delta}$ have positive limits, which we will also determine. For this we consider the equations of motion

$$
m \ddot{q}=U_{q}
$$

and express these in terms of $\bar{q}$ in place of $q$.
The relations

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{U}=U t^{\frac{1}{2}}, \quad \bar{U}_{\bar{q}}=U_{q} t^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
\bar{q}=\left(\bar{q} t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{\prime \prime}=\ddot{\bar{q}} t^{\frac{1}{2}}+\frac{4}{3} \dot{\bar{q}} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{2}{9} \bar{q} t^{-\frac{3}{2}}=\left(\ddot{\bar{q}} t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{\prime} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{2}{9} \bar{q} t^{-\frac{3}{2}}
\end{gathered}
$$

combine to give

$$
\left(\ddot{\bar{q}} t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{\prime} t^{\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{2}{9} \bar{q}=m^{-1} \bar{U}_{\bar{q}}
$$

We now take the mean value of both sides of this differential equation over the interval from $t$ to $2 t$, where $0<2 t \leqq \tau$. In view of (18), integration

by parts leads to the estimate

$$
\int_{t}^{2 t}\left(\dot{\bar{q}} t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{\prime} t^{\frac{1}{2}} d t=\left[\dot{\bar{q}} t^{\frac{1}{2}} t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]_{t}^{2 t}-\frac{2}{3} \int_{t}^{2 t} \dot{\bar{q}} t^{\frac{1}{2}} t^{-\frac{1}{2}} d t=o(t) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

while for $t \leqq t^{*} \leqq 2 t$ also

$$
\bar{q}\left(t^{*}\right)-\bar{q}(t)=\int_{t} \dot{\bar{q}} d t=o(1)
$$

To estimate the mean value of the function $\bar{U}_{\bar{q}}$ we use the relations

$$
\bar{U}_{\bar{q}}\left(t^{*}\right)-\bar{U}_{\bar{q}}(t)=\int_{t} \dot{\bar{U}}_{\bar{q}} d t, \quad \dot{\bar{U}}_{\bar{q}}=\sum_{\bar{p}} \bar{U}_{\bar{q} \bar{p}} \dot{\bar{p}}
$$

and note that according to (13) and (18) we then have

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{r}_{k l}^{-1}=O(1) \\
\bar{U}_{\bar{q} \bar{p}}=O(1), \quad \dot{\bar{U}}_{\bar{q}}=o\left(t^{-1}\right), \quad \bar{U}_{\bar{q}}\left(t^{*}\right)-\bar{U}_{\bar{q}}(t)=o(1) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus (19) in conjunction with (20) and (21) leads to the formula

$$
-\frac{2}{9} \bar{q}=m^{-1} \bar{U}_{\bar{q}}+o(1) \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

This, of course, is no longer a differential equation but rather an algebraic relation asymptotically satisfied by the coordinates $\bar{q}$.

It was shown already in $\S 6$ that in case of a triple collision the three particles move in a fixed plane, and this may be taken as the $z=0$ plane, so that $z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}$ are identically 0 and only the 6 coordinates $x_{k}, y_{k}$ $(k=1,2,3)$ have to be considered. From their derivation, or from a direct calculation, the corresponding 6 equations (23) are seen to be invariant under arbitrary rotations of the coordinate axes in the $(x, y)$-plane. Let us introduce new coordinates $X_{k}, Y_{k}$ in place of $\bar{x}_{k}, \bar{y}_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ with the same origin as before, but with the new abscissa axis always parallel to the direction of the vector $P_{3} P_{1}$. In this new moving coordinate system $Y_{1}=Y_{3}$, while (23) leads to the 3 equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{2}{9} Y_{1}=m_{2}\left(Y_{1}-Y_{2}\right) \bar{r}_{12}^{-3}+m_{3}\left(Y_{1}-Y_{3}\right) \bar{r}_{13}^{-3}+o(1) \\
\frac{2}{9} Y_{2}=m_{1}\left(Y_{2}-Y_{1}\right) \bar{r}_{12}^{-3}+m_{3}\left(Y_{2}-Y_{3}\right) \bar{r}_{23}^{-3}+o(1) \\
\frac{2}{9} Y_{3}=m_{1}\left(Y_{3}-Y_{1}\right) \bar{r}_{13}^{-3}+m_{2}\left(Y_{3}-Y_{2}\right) \bar{r}_{23}^{-3}+o(1)
\end{array}\right.
$$

and 3 analogous equations for $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}$. According to (15) all 6 coordinates $X_{k}(t), Y_{k}(t)(k=1,2,3)$ remain bounded as $t \rightarrow 0$. Consider an arbitrary sequence of values for $t \rightarrow 0$ along which these coordinates tend to definite limits $\hat{X}_{k}, \hat{Y}_{k}$. The distances $\bar{r}_{k l}=r_{k l} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ then also have limits $\bar{r}_{k l}$ which in view of (22) are all positive. Because $Y_{1}=Y_{3}$, subtrac-

tion of the third equation in (24) from the first leads to the relation

$$
m_{2}\left(\hat{Y}_{1}-\hat{Y}_{2}\right)\left(\hat{r}_{12}^{-3}-\hat{r}_{23}^{-3}\right)=0
$$

Consequently either $\hat{r}_{12}=\hat{r}_{23}$ or $\hat{Y}_{1}=\hat{Y}_{2}$.
If $\hat{r}_{12} \neq \hat{r}_{23}$, then $\hat{Y}_{1}=\hat{Y}_{2}$ and, since also $\hat{Y}_{1}=\hat{Y}_{3}$ and $m_{1} \hat{Y}_{1}+m_{2} \hat{Y}_{2}$ $+m_{3} \hat{Y}_{3}=0$, it follows that $\hat{Y}_{k}=0$ for all three ordinates. Thus in this case, as $t \rightarrow 0$ along the sequence considered, the 3 points $\bar{P}_{1}, \bar{P}_{2}, \bar{P}_{3}$ tend to limiting positions on the abscissa axis of the new coordinate system. In the other case $\hat{r}_{12}=\hat{r}_{13}$, while the previous analysis repeated relative to a coordinate system with abscissa axis parallel to $P_{1} P_{2}$ then shows that also $\hat{r}_{13}=\hat{r}_{23}$. The limiting configuration in the second case is therefore an equilateral triangle. Thus we see that as $t \rightarrow 0$ along the chosen sequence, either all three angles of the triangle $\bar{A}$ go to $\frac{\pi}{3}$; or one angle goes to $\pi$ and the other two to 0 . Moreover, because for $t>0$ the angles are continuous functions of $t$, their limit values do not depend on the choice of the sequence $t \rightarrow 0$. The two possible configurations will in the future be referred to as the equilateral case and the collinear case. In addition, set

$$
m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}=M
$$

For the equilateral case, let $\hat{r}_{12}=\hat{r}_{13}=\hat{r}_{23}=r$. From (24) we then have

$$
\frac{2}{9} \hat{Y}_{k} r^{3}=M \hat{Y}_{k} \quad(k=1,2,3)
$$

and since not all the $\hat{Y}_{k}$ are 0 it follows that

$$
r^{3}=\frac{9}{2} M
$$

Thus $r$ has a well determined value, while from (7) we also have

$$
\varkappa=\frac{9}{2}\left(m_{1} m_{2}+m_{1} m_{3}+m_{2} m_{3}\right) r^{-1}
$$

If, in addition, the orientation of the coordinate system is so chosen that upon traversal of the triangle $\bar{A}$ in the positive direction the vertices $\bar{P}_{1}, \bar{P}_{2}, \bar{P}_{3}$ follow in that order, then

$$
\begin{gathered}
\hat{X}_{1}-\hat{X}_{3}=r, \quad \hat{X}_{2}-\hat{X}_{3}=\frac{1}{2} r, \quad \hat{Y}_{1}-\hat{Y}_{3}=0, \quad \hat{Y}_{2}-\hat{Y}_{3}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} r \\
0=\sum_{k=1}^{3} m_{k} \hat{X}_{k}=M \hat{X}_{1}-\frac{1}{2} m_{2} r-m_{3} r, 0=\sum_{k=1}^{3} m_{k} \hat{Y}_{k}=M \hat{Y}_{1}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} m_{2} r \\
\hat{X}_{1}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} m_{2}+m_{3}}{M} r, \quad \hat{X}_{2}=\frac{m_{3}-m_{1}}{2 M} r, \quad \hat{X}_{3}=-\frac{m_{1}+\frac{1}{2} m_{2}}{M} r \\
\hat{Y}_{1}=\hat{Y}_{3}=-\frac{\sqrt{3} m_{2}}{2 M} r, \quad \hat{Y}_{2}=\sqrt{3} \frac{m_{1}+m_{3}}{2 M} r
\end{gathered}
$$

For the collinear case let $\hat{r}_{12}=\hat{X}_{1}-\hat{X}_{3}=a$ be the longest side, so that $\hat{r}_{12}=\hat{X}_{1}-\hat{X}_{2}=\varrho a, \hat{r}_{23}=\hat{X}_{2}-\hat{X}_{3}=\sigma a$ with $\varrho+\sigma=1,0<\varrho<1$. The corresponding equations (24) for the abscissas then become
$\frac{3}{9} \hat{X}_{1} a^{2}=m_{2} \varrho^{-2}+m_{3}, \frac{3}{9} \hat{X}_{2} a^{2}=-m_{1} \varrho^{-2}+m_{3} \sigma^{-2}, \frac{3}{9} \hat{X}_{3} a^{2}=-m_{1}-m_{2} \sigma^{-2}$,
and upon subtraction these give
(27) $\frac{3}{9} a^{3}=m_{1}+m_{2}\left(\varrho^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}\right)+m_{3}, \frac{3}{9} \sigma a^{3}=m_{1}\left(1-\varrho^{-2}\right)+m_{2} \sigma^{-2}+m_{3} \sigma^{-2}$.

Elimination of $a$ now leads to the fifth degree equation

$$
m_{1} \sigma^{2}\left(\varrho^{3}-1\right)+m_{2}\left(\varrho^{3}-\sigma^{3}\right)+m_{3} \varrho^{2}\left(1-\sigma^{3}\right)=0 \quad(\sigma=1-\varrho)
$$

for $\varrho$. If this equation is written as

$$
\frac{m_{1}+m_{2} \sigma}{m_{1}+m_{2} \sigma^{-2}}=\frac{m_{3}+m_{2} \varrho}{m_{3}+m_{2} \varrho^{-2}}
$$

it can be seen that in the interval $0 \leqq \varrho \leqq 1$ the left side, as a function of $\varrho$, decreases monotonically from 1 to 0 , while the right side monotonically increases from 0 to 1 . Hence (28) has exactly one positive solution $\varrho<1$, and (27) then also uniquely determines the length $a$. Equation (7) now implies that

$$
x=\frac{9}{2}\left(m_{1} m_{2} \varrho^{-1}+m_{1} m_{3}+m_{2} m_{3} \sigma^{-1}\right) a^{-1}
$$

while the coordinates are given by

$$
\begin{gathered}
0=\sum_{k=1}^{3} m_{k} \hat{X}_{k}=M \hat{X}_{1}-m_{2} \varrho a-m_{3} a, \quad \hat{X}_{1}=\frac{m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}}{M} a \\
\hat{X}_{2}=\frac{m_{3} \sigma-m_{1} \varrho}{M} a, \quad \hat{X}_{3}=-\frac{m_{1}+m_{2} \sigma}{M} a, \quad \hat{Y}_{1}=\hat{Y}_{2}=\hat{Y}_{3}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

These values correspond to the assumption that at $t=0$ the point $\bar{P}_{2}$ lies between $\bar{P}_{1}$ and $\bar{P}_{3}$. The two other possibilities in the collinear case are obtained from this by cyclic permutation of $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$.

Thus we have proved that in both the equilateral and the collinear cases the coordinates $X_{k}, Y_{k}$ of $\bar{P}_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ have well determined limit values that do not depend on the initially considered sequence $t \rightarrow 0$. Consequently in reference to the moving coordinate system the triangle $\bar{A}$ tends to a limiting position that in both cases depends only on the values $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$.

In this section we have derived the results of Sundman [1] insofar as they relate to triple collisions; in particular, the theorem that the sides of the triangle, when expanded in the ratio of 1 to $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, have definite limits that correspond to either the equilateral or the collinear case. It does

not follow, however, that the old coordinates $\bar{x}_{k}, \bar{y}_{k}$ of the points $\bar{P}_{k}$ $(k=1,2,3)$ themselves have limit values. For this it remains to show that as $t \rightarrow 0$ the angle between the old and the new coordinate systems also tends to a limit. Moreover, in complete analogy to the case of a simple collision, it will be possible also in this case to obtain suitable series expansions for the coordinates $x_{k}, y_{k}$, and thereby collectively determine the possible triple-collision orbits. This will be carried out in the next section.

# § 13. Triple-Collision Orbits 

First we will construct a special solution to the planar three-body problem which will show that both the equilateral case of a triple collision as well as the collinear case with its 3 possible permutations actually do occur. For this, let the 6 coordinates $q=x_{k}, y_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ have the form

$$
q=q(t)=\hat{q} w, \quad w=w(t)
$$

where $w$ is a twice differentiable positive function in the interval $0<t \leqq \tau$ and the 6 constants $\hat{q}$ are such that for $t>0$ the 3 points are distinct. Also, to have triple collision at $t=0$, assume that $w(t) \rightarrow 0$ as $t \rightarrow 0$. In view of (1), the function

$$
\hat{U}=U w
$$

depends only on the parameters $\hat{q}$ and is a homogeneous function of degree -1 in these values. Consequently

$$
\sum_{\hat{q}} \hat{q} \hat{U}_{\hat{q}}=-\hat{U}<0
$$

and therefore $\hat{q} \hat{U}_{\hat{q}}<0$ for at least one coordinate. With assumption (1) the equations of motion $(5 ; 3)$ become

$$
m \hat{q} \ddot{w}=\hat{U}_{\hat{q}} w^{-2}
$$

implying that the expression $\ddot{w} w^{2}$ must be a negative constant $b_{1}$. If $w$ is multiplied by a positive factor to achieve the normalization $b_{1}=-\frac{2}{9}$, we are left with the equations

$$
\ddot{w}=-\frac{2}{9} w^{-2}, \quad-\frac{2}{9} \hat{q}=m^{-1} \hat{U}_{\hat{q}}
$$

Integration of the differential equation in (2) gives

$$
\dot{w}^{2}=\frac{4}{9}\left(w^{-1}+b_{2}\right)
$$

where $b_{2}$ is an arbitrary constant. If the constant is taken to be 0 , it follows that

$$
\frac{3}{2} w^{\frac{1}{2}} \dot{w}=1, \quad w^{\frac{1}{2}}=t, \quad w=t^{\frac{1}{2}}
$$

The second equation in (2), on the other hand, coincides with (12;23) if the functions $\bar{q}=\bar{q}(t)$ are replaced by the constants $\dot{q}$. From our earlier result the solutions are given by three fixed points $\hat{P}_{1}, \hat{P}_{2}, \hat{P}_{3}$ with coordinates $\hat{q}$, corresponding either to the equilateral or the collinear case. If the abscissa axis is chosen in the direction of the vector $\hat{P}_{3} \hat{P}_{1}$, the values of the $\hat{q}$ are precisely those found for $\hat{X}_{k}, \hat{Y}_{k}(k=1,2,3)$. This shows that each of the individual cases for a triple collision does indeed appear as a special solution to the three-body problem.

One can still introduce an arbitrary real parameter into the above solutions by not assuming that $b_{2}=0$ in (3) and using the series expansion

$$
\left(1+b_{2} w\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}=1-\frac{1}{2} b_{2} w+\cdots \quad\left(\left|b_{2} w\right|<1\right)
$$

Then

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{3}{2}\left(w^{\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{1}{2} b_{2} w^{\frac{3}{2}}+\cdots\right) \dot{w}=1, w^{\frac{3}{2}}-\frac{3}{10} b_{2} w^{\frac{1}{2}}+\cdots=t, w-\frac{1}{2} b_{2} w^{2}+\cdots=t^{\frac{3}{2}} \\
w=t^{\frac{3}{2}} \bar{w}, \quad \bar{w}=1+\frac{1}{2} b_{2} t^{\frac{3}{2}}+\cdots, \quad q=\bar{q} t^{\frac{3}{2}}, \quad \bar{q}=\hat{q} \bar{w}
\end{gathered}
$$

with $\bar{w}$ a power series in $b_{2} t^{\frac{3}{2}}$ that converges for sufficiently small positive values of $t$. Moreover, the quantity $b_{2}$ can readily be expressed in terms of the energy constant $h$.

The following investigation will show that the particular solutions to the three-body problem appearing in (4) are still not the most general triple-collision orbits $[1,2,3]$. In determining all of them one may assume that for the collinear case, with the notation of the previous section, the point $\bar{P}_{2}$ at $t=0$ lies between $\bar{P}_{3}$ and $\bar{P}_{1}$, since the other two possibilities can be reduced to this by a cyclic permutation of the indices.

In accordance with $\S 7$ we introduce the relative coordinates

$$
\xi_{1}=x_{1}-x_{3}, \quad \xi_{2}=x_{2}-x_{3}, \quad \xi_{3}=y_{1}-y_{3}, \quad \xi_{4}=y_{2}-y_{3}
$$

of $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ with respect to $P_{3}$, whereupon

$$
r_{13}^{2}=\xi_{1}^{2}+\xi_{3}^{2}, \quad r_{23}^{2}=\xi_{2}^{2}+\xi_{4}^{2}, \quad r_{12}^{2}=\left(\xi_{1}-\xi_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\xi_{3}-\xi_{4}\right)^{2}
$$

and because the center of mass was taken to rest at the origin, we also have

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{c}
M x_{1}=\left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right) \xi_{1}-m_{2} \xi_{2}, \quad M x_{2}=-m_{1} \xi_{1}+\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right) \xi_{2} \\
M x_{3}=-m_{1} \xi_{1}-m_{2} \xi_{2} \\
M y_{1}=\left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right) \xi_{3}-m_{2} \xi_{4}, \quad M y_{2}=-m_{1} \xi_{3}+\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right) \xi_{4} \\
M y_{3}=-m_{1} \xi_{3}-m_{4} \xi_{4}
\end{array}\right.
$$

where again $M=m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}$. If in addition

$$
\eta_{1}=m_{1} \dot{x}_{1}, \quad \eta_{2}=m_{2} \dot{x}_{2}, \quad \eta_{3}=m_{1} \dot{y}_{1}, \quad \eta_{4}=m_{2} \dot{y}_{2}
$$

then

$$
\begin{gathered}
m_{3} \dot{x}_{3}=-\eta_{1}-\eta_{2}, \quad m_{3} \dot{y}_{3}=-\eta_{3}-\eta_{4} \\
T=\frac{1}{2 m_{1}}\left(\eta_{1}^{2}+\eta_{3}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2 m_{2}}\left(\eta_{2}^{2}+\eta_{4}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2 m_{3}}\left\{\left(\eta_{1}+\eta_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\eta_{3}+\eta_{4}\right)^{2}\right\}
\end{gathered}
$$

As was already established in $\S 7$, this leads for the variables $\xi_{k}, \eta_{k}$ to the Hamiltonian system

$$
\dot{\xi}_{k}=E_{\eta_{k}}, \quad \dot{\eta}_{k}=-E_{\xi_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 4)
$$

with $E=T-U$, or more explicitly

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\dot{\xi}_{k}=\left(\frac{1}{m_{1}}+\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right) \eta_{k}+\frac{1}{m_{3}} \eta_{k+1}, \quad \dot{\xi}_{k+1}=\left(\frac{1}{m_{2}}+\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right) \eta_{k+1}+\frac{1}{m_{3}} \eta_{k} \\
\dot{\eta}_{k}=U_{\xi_{k}} \quad(k=1,2,3,4)
\end{array}\right.
$$

For a further discussion of triple collision it is necessary to introduce a new rectangular coordinate system whose origin coincides with $P_{3}$ and whose abscissa axis always passes through $P_{1}$. Let the new abscissa axis form an angle $p_{4}$ relative to the old one, with $p_{1}, 0$ and $p_{2}, p_{3}$ the new coordinates of $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$. Abbreviating

$$
\cos p_{4}=c, \quad \sin p_{4}=s
$$

we then have

$$
\begin{gathered}
\xi_{1}=p_{1} c, \quad \xi_{2}=p_{2} c-p_{3} s, \quad \xi_{3}=p_{1} s, \quad \xi_{4}=p_{2} s+p_{3} c \\
r_{13}=p_{1}, \quad r_{23}^{2}=p_{2}^{2}+p_{3}^{2}, \quad r_{12}^{2}=\left(p_{1}-p_{2}\right)^{2}+p_{3}^{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

To extend the transformation (9) of the variables $\xi_{1}, \ldots, \xi_{4}$ into $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{4}$ to a canonical transformation of the 8 independent variables $\xi_{k}, \eta_{k}$ $(k=1, \ldots, 4)$, one considers the generating function

$$
W=W(p, \eta)=\eta_{1} p_{1} c+\eta_{2}\left(p_{2} c-p_{3} s\right)+\eta_{3} p_{1} s+\eta_{4}\left(p_{2} s+p_{3} c\right)
$$

Then the four-by-four determinant

$$
\left|W_{\eta_{k} p_{1}}\right|=-p_{1} \neq 0
$$

In accordance with $\S 3$, the expression

$$
W_{p_{k}}=q_{k}, \quad W_{\eta_{k}}=\xi_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 4)
$$

then gives a canonical transformation that clearly satisfies (9) and contributes the 4 additional equations

$$
\begin{cases}q_{1}=\eta_{1} c+\eta_{3} s, \quad q_{2}=\eta_{2} c+\eta_{4} s, \quad q_{3}=-\eta_{2} s+\eta_{4} c \\
q_{4}=p_{1}\left(-\eta_{1} s+\eta_{3} c\right)+p_{2}\left(-\eta_{2} s+\eta_{4} c\right)-p_{3}\left(\eta_{2} c+\eta_{4} s\right)
\end{cases}
$$

With the aid of the auxiliary variable

$$
q_{0}=-\eta_{1} s+\eta_{3} c
$$

these lead to

$$
\begin{gathered}
q_{4}=p_{1} q_{0}+p_{2} q_{3}-p_{3} q_{2}, \quad q_{0}=\left(q_{4}-p_{2} q_{3}+p_{3} q_{2}\right) p_{1}^{-1} \\
\eta_{1}=q_{1} c-q_{0} s, \quad \eta_{2}=q_{2} c-q_{3} s, \quad \eta_{3}=q_{1} s+q_{0} c, \quad \eta_{4}=q_{2} s+q_{3} c
\end{gathered}
$$

and
(14) $T=\frac{1}{2 m_{1}}\left(q_{1}^{2}+q_{0}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2 m_{2}}\left(q_{2}^{2}+q_{3}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2 m_{3}}\left\{\left(q_{1}+q_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(q_{0}+q_{3}\right)^{2}\right\}$.

It should be observed that here and henceforth the $q_{k}$ have a different meaning than the symbol $q$ used earlier.

The real advantage in the canonical transformation defined by (9) and (11) is that as a consequence of (10), (13), and (14) the function $E$ in its dependence on the 8 new variables $p_{k}, q_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 4)$ no longer contains the angle $p_{4}$. As seen from $\S 2$, the new Hamiltonian system becomes

$$
\dot{p}_{k}=E_{q_{k}}, \quad \dot{q}_{k}=-E_{p_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 4)
$$

and, because $E_{p_{4}}=0$, it follows that $q_{4}$ is constant. On the other hand, $(5 ; 8)$ in conjunction with (5), (7), (9), and (11) says that

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{4}= & \xi_{1} \eta_{3}+\xi_{2} \eta_{4}-\xi_{3} \eta_{1}-\xi_{4} \eta_{2}=m_{1}\left(x_{1}-x_{3}\right) \dot{y}_{1}+m_{2}\left(x_{2}-x_{3}\right) \dot{y}_{2} \\
& -m_{1}\left(y_{1}-y_{3}\right) \dot{x}_{1}-m_{2}\left(y_{2}-y_{3}\right) \dot{x}_{2} \\
= & m_{1}\left(x_{1} \dot{y}_{1}-y_{1} \dot{x}_{1}\right)+m_{2}\left(x_{2} \dot{y}_{2}-y_{2} \dot{x}_{2}\right)+m_{3}\left(x_{3} \dot{y}_{3}-y_{3} \dot{x}_{3}\right)=\gamma=0
\end{aligned}
$$

since for a triple collision the angular momentum constants are 0 . Thus (15) reduces to the system

$$
\dot{p}_{k}=\left(E_{q_{k}}\right)_{q_{4}=0}, \quad \dot{q}_{k}=-\left(E_{p_{k}}\right)_{q_{4}=0} \quad(k=1,2,3)
$$

of only 6 equations, free from $p_{4}$ and $q_{4}$, plus the supplementary equation

$$
\dot{p}_{4}=\left(E_{q_{4}}\right)_{q_{4}=0}
$$

to be solved by quadrature. For the purpose of investigating these differential equations we now determine the asymptotic behavior of $p_{k}$ and $q_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ as $t \rightarrow 0$.

The quantities

$$
p_{k} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}=\bar{p}_{k} \quad(k=1,2,3)
$$

correspond in the notation of the previous section to

$$
\bar{p}_{1}=X_{1}-X_{3}, \quad \bar{p}_{2}=X_{2}-X_{3}, \quad \bar{p}_{3}=Y_{2}-Y_{3}
$$

and therefore have at $t=0$ the limit values

$$
\dot{p}_{1}=r, \quad \dot{p}_{2}=\frac{1}{2} r, \quad \dot{p}_{3}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} r
$$

in the equilateral case, and

$$
\dot{p}_{1}=a, \quad \dot{p}_{2}=\sigma a, \quad \dot{p}_{3}=0
$$

in the collinear case, where $r, a, \sigma$ have the old connotation. Next, let

$$
q_{k} t^{\dagger}=\bar{q}_{k} \quad(k=0,1,2,3)
$$

It is very significant that also the $\bar{q}_{k}$ have limits at $t=0$, and these will now be determined.

First, from $(12 ; 1)$ and $(5),(7),(9),(11)$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2} \dot{I} & =\sum_{k=1}^{3} m_{k}\left(x_{k} \dot{x}_{k}+y_{k} \dot{y}_{k}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{2} m_{k}\left(\left(x_{k}-x_{3}\right) \dot{x}_{k}+\left(y_{k}-y_{3}\right) \dot{y}_{k}\right) \\
& =\sum_{k=1}^{4} \xi_{k} \eta_{k}=\sum_{k=1}^{3} p_{k} q_{k}=t^{\dagger} \sum_{k=1}^{3} \bar{p}_{k} \bar{q}_{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

which in view of $(12 ; 6)$ shows that

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{3} \bar{p}_{k} \bar{q}_{k} \rightarrow \frac{2}{3} \varkappa \quad(t \rightarrow 0)
$$

Here the positive constant $\varkappa$ is given by $(12 ; 26)$ in the equilateral case, and $(12 ; 29)$ in the collinear case. Because $q_{4}=0$, it follows from (13) that also

$$
\bar{p}_{1} \bar{q}_{0}+\bar{p}_{2} \bar{q}_{3}-\bar{p}_{3} \bar{q}_{2}=0
$$

Additional asymptotic relations can be obtained from $(12 ; 14)$, which in particular says that

$$
\begin{gathered}
x_{1} \dot{y}_{1}-y_{1} \dot{x}_{1}=o\left(t^{\dagger}\right), \quad x_{2} \dot{y}_{2}-y_{2} \dot{x}_{2}=o\left(t^{\dagger}\right) \\
x_{1} \dot{x}_{2}-x_{2} \dot{x}_{1}+y_{1} \dot{y}_{2}-y_{2} \dot{y}_{1}=o\left(t^{\dagger}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

With the aid of (6), (9), (11), (12), (16) and (17) this leads to

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right)\left(\xi_{1} \eta_{3}-\xi_{3} \eta_{1}\right)-m_{2}\left(\xi_{2} \eta_{3}-\xi_{4} \eta_{1}\right)=o\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) \\
& \left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right)\left(\xi_{2} \eta_{4}-\xi_{4} \eta_{2}\right)-m_{1}\left(\xi_{1} \eta_{4}-\xi_{3} \eta_{2}\right)=o\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) \\
& m_{1}\left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right)\left(\xi_{1} \eta_{2}+\xi_{3} \eta_{4}\right)-m_{2}\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right)\left(\xi_{2} \eta_{1}+\xi_{4} \eta_{3}\right) \\
& +m_{1} m_{2}\left(\xi_{1} \eta_{1}+\xi_{3} \eta_{3}-\xi_{2} \eta_{2}-\xi_{4} \eta_{4}\right)=o\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right) \bar{p}_{1} \bar{q}_{0}-m_{2}\left(\bar{p}_{2} \bar{q}_{0}-\bar{p}_{3} \bar{q}_{1}\right) \rightarrow 0 \\
& \left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right)\left(\bar{p}_{2} \bar{q}_{3}-\bar{p}_{3} \bar{q}_{2}\right)-m_{1} \bar{p}_{1} \bar{q}_{3} \rightarrow 0 \\
& m_{1}\left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right) \bar{p}_{1} \bar{q}_{2}-m_{2}\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right)\left(\bar{p}_{2} \bar{q}_{1}+\bar{p}_{3} \bar{q}_{0}\right) \\
& +m_{1} m_{2}\left(\bar{p}_{1} \bar{q}_{1}-\bar{p}_{2} \bar{q}_{2}-\bar{p}_{3} \bar{q}_{3}\right) \rightarrow 0
\end{aligned}
$$

all for $t \rightarrow 0$. On the basis of $(12 ; 13)$ and $(7),(11),(12),(17)$ we also have

$$
\bar{q}_{k}=O(1) \quad(k=0,1,2,3)
$$

In the equilateral case (18), (19), (20), (21) and (23) combine to give the relations

$$
\begin{gathered}
2 \bar{q}_{1}+\bar{q}_{2}+\sqrt{3} \bar{q}_{3} \rightarrow \frac{4}{3} \times r^{-1}, \quad 2 \bar{q}_{0}-\sqrt{3} \bar{q}_{2}+\bar{q}_{3} \rightarrow 0 \\
2 \sqrt{3} m_{2} \bar{q}_{1}+\left(m_{2}+2 m_{3}\right)\left(\sqrt{3} \bar{q}_{2}-\bar{q}_{3}\right) \rightarrow 0, \sqrt{3}\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right) \bar{q}_{2}+\left(m_{1}-m_{3}\right) \bar{q}_{3} \rightarrow 0
\end{gathered}
$$

If we then set

$$
\bar{q}_{3}=\frac{m_{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right) \bar{q}
$$

it follows that

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{q}_{2}=\frac{m_{2}}{3}\left(m_{3}-m_{1}\right) \bar{q}+o(1), \quad \bar{q}_{1}=\frac{m_{1}}{3}\left(m_{2}+2 m_{3}\right) \bar{q}+o(1) \\
\frac{4}{3}\left(m_{1} m_{2}+m_{1} m_{3}+m_{2} m_{3}\right) \bar{q} \rightarrow \frac{4}{3} \times r^{-1}
\end{gathered}
$$

so that by $(12 ; 25)$ and $(12 ; 26)$ we have

$$
\bar{q} \rightarrow \frac{r}{M}
$$

Consequently in the equilateral case $\bar{q}_{1}, \bar{q}_{2}, \bar{q}_{3}$ have the limit values

$$
\hat{q}_{1}=\frac{m_{1}}{3 M}\left(m_{2}+2 m_{3}\right) r, \quad \hat{q}_{2}=\frac{m_{2}}{3 M}\left(m_{3}-m_{1}\right) r, \quad \hat{q}_{3}=\frac{m_{2}}{\sqrt{3} M}\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right) r
$$

while

$$
\bar{q}_{0} \rightarrow \hat{q}_{0}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \hat{q}_{2}-\frac{1}{2} \hat{q}_{3}=-\frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{\sqrt{3} M} r
$$

Just like $\hat{p}_{1}, \hat{p}_{2}, \hat{p}_{3}$, these values depend only on the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$.

In the collinear case one obtains from (19), (20), (22), and (23) the relations

$$
\bar{q}_{0}+\sigma \bar{q}_{3} \rightarrow 0,\left(m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}\right) \bar{q}_{0} \rightarrow 0, m_{2}\left(m_{1} \varrho-m_{3} \sigma\right) \bar{q}_{1}+m_{1}\left(m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}\right) \bar{q}_{2} \rightarrow 0
$$

and therefore

$$
\bar{q}_{0} \rightarrow 0, \quad \bar{q}_{3} \rightarrow 0
$$

If this time we set

$$
\bar{q}_{1}=m_{1}\left(m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}\right) \bar{q}
$$

then

$$
\bar{q}_{2}=m_{2}\left(m_{3} \sigma-m_{1} \varrho\right) \bar{q}+o(1)
$$

and it follows from (18) that

$$
\left\{m_{1}\left(m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}\right)+m_{2} \sigma\left(m_{3} \sigma-m_{1} \varrho\right)\right\} \bar{q} \rightarrow \frac{2}{3} \times a^{-1}
$$

On the other hand, in view of $(12 ; 27)$ and $(12 ; 29)$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{2}{9} a^{3} m_{1}\left(m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}\right)+\frac{2}{9} \sigma a^{3} m_{2}\left(m_{3} \sigma-m_{1} \varrho\right) \\
& =M\left(m_{1} m_{2} \varrho^{-1}+m_{1} m_{3}+m_{2} m_{3} \sigma^{-1}\right)=\frac{2}{9} M \times a
\end{aligned}
$$

so that finally

$$
\bar{q} \rightarrow \frac{2 a}{3 M}
$$

Thus in the collinear case $\bar{q}_{0}, \bar{q}_{1}, \bar{q}_{2}, \bar{q}_{3}$ have the limits

$$
\hat{q}_{0}=0, \quad \hat{q}_{1}=\frac{2 m_{1}}{3 M}\left(m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}\right) a, \quad \hat{q}_{2}=\frac{2 m_{2}}{3 M}\left(m_{3} \sigma-m_{1} \varrho\right) a, \quad \hat{q}_{3}=0
$$

which likewise depend only on the three masses.
Next, with $q_{4}$ again arbitrary, we introduce into the differential equations (15) the substitutions

$$
p_{k}=\bar{p}_{k} t^{\frac{1}{2}}(k=1,2,3), \quad q_{k}=\bar{q}_{k} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}(k=0,1,2,3), \quad q_{4}=\bar{q}_{4} t^{\frac{1}{2}}, \quad p_{4}=\bar{p}_{4}
$$

as well as

$$
t=e^{-u}, \quad d t=-t d u
$$

The function $\bar{E}$, obtained from $E$ through direct replacement of the 7 variables $p_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ and $q_{k}(k=1,2,3,4)$ by $\bar{p}_{k}$ and $\bar{q}_{k}$, then satisfies

$$
E=\bar{E} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

and the differential equations transform into the system

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{d \bar{p}_{k}}{d u}=\frac{2}{3} \bar{p}_{k}-\bar{E}_{\bar{q}_{k}}, \quad \frac{d \bar{q}_{k}}{d u}=-\frac{1}{3} \bar{q}_{k}+\bar{E}_{\bar{p}_{k}} \quad(k=1,2,3) \\
\frac{d \bar{p}_{4}}{d u}=-\bar{E}_{\bar{q}_{4}}, \quad \frac{d \bar{q}_{4}}{d u}=\frac{1}{3} \bar{q}_{4}
\end{array}\right.
$$

Now let

$$
\begin{cases}\bar{p}_{k}=\hat{p}_{k}+\delta_{k}, & \bar{q}_{k}=\hat{q}_{k}+\delta_{k+2} \quad(k=1,2) \\ \bar{p}_{3}=\hat{p}_{3}+\delta_{5}, & \bar{q}_{3}=\hat{q}_{3}+\delta_{6}, \quad \bar{q}_{4}=\delta_{7}, \quad \bar{p}_{4}=\delta_{8}\end{cases}
$$

where $\hat{p}_{k}, \hat{q}_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ are the previously derived limits for either the equilateral or the collinear case. The values $\delta_{k}=0(k=1, \ldots, 8)$ correspond precisely to the coordinates of the special triple-collision orbits found in the beginning of this section, and because these too lead to solutions of (24), it follows that the right sides of the 8 differential equations, as functions of the $\delta_{k}$, all vanish at the point $\delta_{k}=0(k=1, \ldots, 8)$. On the other hand, in a sufficiently small complex neighborhood of this point the right sides are regular and therefore have convergent series expansions in powers of the $\delta_{k}$. The system (24) thus takes on the form

$$
\frac{d \delta_{k}}{d u}=\sum_{l=1}^{8} a_{k l} \delta_{l}+\phi_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 8)
$$

where the $\phi_{k}$ are power series in $\delta_{1}, \ldots, \delta_{7}$ beginning with quadratic terms, and the $a_{k l}$ are real constants. Here

$$
a_{k 8}=0(k=1, \ldots, 8), \quad a_{77}=\frac{1}{3}, \quad a_{7 l}=0(l \neq 7)
$$

giving the eight-by-eight matrix $\left(a_{k l}\right)$ the structure

$$
\mathfrak{A}=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathfrak{B} & * & 0 \\
0 & \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\
* & * & 0
\end{array}\right)
$$

with $\mathfrak{B}$ a six-by-six matrix. Moreover, $\phi_{7}=0$.
Since $u=\log t^{-1}$, as $t$ decreases to 0 the variable $u$ increases to $\infty$. Moreover, $\delta_{7}=q_{4} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}=0$ for every triple-collision orbit. Thus, to obtain all triple-collision orbits, one solves the 6 differential equations

$$
\frac{d \delta_{k}}{d u}=\sum_{l=1}^{6} a_{k l} \delta_{l}+\phi_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 6)
$$

with $\delta_{7}=0$, to find all solutions $\delta_{k}=\delta_{k}(u)(k=1, \ldots, 6)$ that are defined for $u$ sufficiently large and asymptotically approach the solution $\delta_{k}=0$ as $u \rightarrow \infty$.

To solve this problem we appeal to a result that will first be derived in $\S 28$ independently of the present considerations. According to (27), the linear part of the right side in (28) has the coefficient matrix $\mathfrak{B}$. Let $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{6}$ be the eigenvalues of $\mathfrak{B}$, that is, the roots of the polynomial $|\lambda \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{B}|$, with $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{f}$ the ones having a negative real part. In view of the restrictions imposed in $\S 28$, it is further assumed that the eigenvalues

$\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{6}$ are all simple, none is purely imaginary or 0 , and for all systems of nonnegative integers $n_{1}, \ldots, n_{f}$ with $n_{1}+\cdots+n_{f}>1$ we have

$$
\sum_{l=1}^{f} n_{l} \lambda_{l} \neq \lambda_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, f)
$$

In accordance with $\S 28$, the desired solutions of (28) are then given by

$$
\delta_{k}=\psi_{k}\left(v_{1}, \ldots, v_{f}\right)(k=1, \ldots, 6), \quad v_{l}=c_{l} e^{\lambda_{l} u}(l=1, \ldots, f)
$$

where the $\psi_{k}$ are convergent power series in the variables $v_{1}, \ldots, v_{f}$ without a constant term, and the $c_{l}$ are arbitrary constants sufficiently small in absolute value. The coefficients in the series $\psi_{k}$ are uniquely determined by a recursive process. Once the desired solutions $\delta_{1}, \ldots, \delta_{6}$ of (28) have been found from (30), the angle $p_{4}=\bar{p}_{4}=\delta_{6}$ is obtained by quadrature from the last equation in (26), which with $\delta_{7}=0$ reads
(31) $\frac{d p_{4}}{d u}=-\left(\frac{1}{m_{1}}+\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right) \frac{\bar{q}_{0}}{\bar{p}_{1}}-\frac{1}{m_{3}} \frac{\bar{q}_{3}}{\bar{p}_{1}}, \quad \bar{q}_{0}=\frac{\bar{q}_{2} \bar{p}_{3}-\bar{p}_{2} \bar{q}_{3}}{\bar{p}_{1}}$.

In light of (30) the right side of this differential equation is again a power series in $v_{1}, \ldots, v_{f}$ without a constant term, and because $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{f}$ have negative real parts, the integral converges up to $u=\infty$. Consequently for each solution resulting in a triple collision also $p_{4}$ has a finite limit $\hat{p}_{4}$ as $t \rightarrow 0$. This finally proves that collision of the three particles takes place in definite directions.

The calculation of the 6 eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{6}$ is facilitated by a return to the earlier variables. From (27) we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
\lambda \mathfrak{E}_{6}-\mathfrak{A}=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\lambda \mathfrak{E}_{6}-\mathfrak{B} & * & 0 \\
0 & \lambda-\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\
* & * & \lambda
\end{array}\right) \\
\left|\lambda \mathfrak{E}_{6}-\mathfrak{U}\right|=\lambda\left(\lambda-\frac{1}{3}\right)\left|\lambda \mathfrak{E}_{6}-\mathfrak{B}\right|
\end{gathered}
$$

We will transform the 8 variables $\delta_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 8)$ via a substitution

$$
\omega_{k}=\sum_{l=1}^{8} c_{k l} \delta_{l}+\chi_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 8)
$$

where the coefficients $c_{k l}$ form an invertible constant matrix $\mathfrak{C}$ and the $\chi_{k}$ are convergent power series in the $\delta_{l}(l=1, \ldots, 8)$ beginning with quadratic terms. This results in (26) being replaced by the new differential equations

$$
\frac{d \omega_{k}}{d u}=\sum_{l=1}^{8} g_{k l} \omega_{l}+\cdots \quad(k=1, \ldots, 8)
$$

whose coefficient matrix $\mathfrak{G}=\left(g_{k l}\right)$ is determined from the relation

$$
\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{C}^{-1} \mathfrak{G} \mathfrak{C}
$$

This assertion is purely algebraic in nature, and has nothing to do with properties of solutions to the differential equations. In defining $\omega_{k}$ we refer back to the previously used canonical transformation

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\xi_{1}=p_{1} c, \quad \xi_{2}=p_{2} c-p_{3} s, \quad \xi_{3}=p_{1} s, \quad \xi_{4}=p_{2} s+p_{3} c \\
\eta_{1}=q_{1} c-q_{0} s, \quad \eta_{2}=q_{2} c-q_{3} s, \quad \eta_{3}=q_{1} s+q_{0} c, \quad \eta_{4}=q_{2} s+q_{3} c \\
q_{0}=\left(q_{4}-p_{2} q_{3}+p_{3} q_{2}\right) p_{1}^{-1}, \quad c=\cos p_{4}, \quad s=\sin p_{4}
\end{array}\right.
$$

and carry out the additional invertible homogeneous linear substitution

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{c}
-\left(\frac{1}{m_{1}}+\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right) \eta_{k}-\frac{1}{m_{3}} \eta_{k+1}=\xi_{k+4} \\
-\frac{1}{m_{3}} \eta_{k}-\left(\frac{1}{m_{2}}+\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right) \eta_{k+1}=\xi_{k+5} \quad(k=1,3)
\end{array}\right.
$$

In terms of

$$
\bar{\xi}_{k}=\xi_{k} t^{-\frac{s}{2}}, \quad \bar{\xi}_{k+4}=\xi_{k+4} t^{\frac{s}{2}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 4)
$$

with $t=e^{-u}$, the system (8) then becomes

$$
\frac{d \bar{\xi}_{k}}{d u}=\frac{2}{3} \bar{\xi}_{k}+\bar{\xi}_{k+4}, \quad \frac{d \bar{\xi}_{k+4}}{d u}=-\frac{1}{3} \bar{\xi}_{k+4}-F_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 4)
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
F_{k}= \begin{cases}\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right) R_{2} \bar{\xi}_{k}+m_{2} R_{1} \bar{\xi}_{k+1}+m_{2} R_{3}\left(\bar{\xi}_{k}-\bar{\xi}_{k+1}\right) & (k=1,3) \\
m_{1} R_{2} \bar{\xi}_{k-1}+\left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right) R_{1} \bar{\xi}_{k}+m_{1} R_{3}\left(\bar{\xi}_{k}-\bar{\xi}_{k-1}\right) & (k=2,4) \\
R_{1}=\left(\bar{\xi}_{2}^{2}+\bar{\xi}_{4}^{2}\right)^{-\frac{s}{2}}, \quad R_{2}=\left(\bar{\xi}_{1}^{2}+\bar{\xi}_{3}^{2}\right)^{-\frac{s}{2}}, \quad R_{3}=\left\{\left(\bar{\xi}_{1}-\bar{\xi}_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\bar{\xi}_{3}-\bar{\xi}_{4}\right)^{2}\right\}^{-\frac{s}{2}} .
\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, let $\bar{\xi}_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 8)$ be the value at $\delta_{l}=0$ of $\bar{\xi}_{k}$ as a function of the eight variables $\delta_{l}(l=1, \ldots, 8)$, and define

$$
\omega_{k}=\bar{\xi}_{k}-\bar{\xi}_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 8)
$$

The right sides of (36) then lead to convergent power series in the $\omega_{k}$ without a constant term, with the corresponding coefficient matrix

$$
\mathfrak{G}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{2}{3} \mathfrak{E}_{4} & \mathfrak{E}_{4} \\
-\mathfrak{S} & -\frac{1}{3} \mathfrak{E}_{4}
\end{array}\right)
$$

where the elements $s_{k l}(k, l=1, \ldots, 4)$ in the four-by-four matrix $\mathfrak{S}$ are the partial derivatives $\frac{\partial F_{k}}{\partial \bar{\xi}_{l}}$ evaluated at $\bar{\xi}_{r}=\bar{\xi}_{r}(r=1, \ldots, 4)$.

From (34) we have $\hat{\zeta}_{1}=\hat{p}_{1}, \hat{\zeta}_{2}=\hat{p}_{2}, \hat{\zeta}_{3}=0, \hat{\zeta}_{4}=\hat{p}_{3}$, and therefore in the equilateral case

$$
r^{3} \cong=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\frac{1}{4} m_{2}-2\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right) & 0 & \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4} m_{2} & -\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2} m_{2} \\
-\frac{9}{4} m_{1} & \frac{1}{4}\left(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}\right) & -\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4} m_{1} & \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4}\left(m_{1}-m_{2}-m_{3}\right) \\
\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4} m_{2} & -\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2} m_{2} & m_{1}+m_{3}-\frac{5}{4} m_{2} & 0 \\
-\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4} m_{1} & \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4}\left(m_{1}-m_{2}-m_{3}\right) & \frac{9}{4} m_{1} & -\frac{5}{4}\left(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}\right)
\end{array}\right)
$$

while in the collinear case

$$
a^{3} \mathfrak{S}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
-2 \mathfrak{Q} & 0 \\
0 & \mathfrak{Q}
\end{array}\right), \quad \mathfrak{Q}=\left(\begin{array}{ll}
m_{1}+m_{3}+m_{2} \varrho^{-3} & m_{2}\left(\sigma^{-3}-\varrho^{-3}\right) \\
m_{1}\left(1-\varrho^{-3}\right) & m_{1} \varrho^{-3}+\left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right) \sigma^{-3}
\end{array}\right)
$$

With the abbreviation

$$
\left(\lambda+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(\lambda-\frac{2}{3}\right)=\zeta
$$

one sees from (32), (33), (38) that

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left|\lambda \mathfrak{E}_{8}-\mathfrak{B}\right|=\left|\lambda \mathfrak{E}_{8}-\mathfrak{B}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{cc}
\left(\lambda-\frac{2}{3}\right) \mathfrak{E}_{4} & -\mathfrak{E}_{4} \\
\mathfrak{S} & \left(\lambda+\frac{1}{3}\right) \mathfrak{E}_{4}
\end{array}\right| \\
\left(\zeta+\frac{2}{9}\right)\left|\lambda \mathfrak{E}_{6}-\mathfrak{B}\right|=\left|\zeta \mathfrak{E}_{4}+\mathfrak{S}\right|
\end{gathered}
$$

whereupon a direct calculation of the four-by-four determinant gives

$$
\left|\zeta \mathfrak{E}_{4}+\mathfrak{S}\right|=\left(\zeta+\frac{2}{9}\right)\left(\zeta-\frac{4}{9}\right)\left(\zeta^{2}-\frac{2}{9} \zeta-\frac{8}{81}+\frac{1}{3} \mu\right)
$$

with

$$
\mu=\frac{m_{1} m_{2}+m_{1} m_{3}+m_{2} m_{3}}{\left(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}\right)^{2}}
$$

in the equilateral case, and

$$
\left|\zeta \mathfrak{E}_{4}+\mathfrak{S}\right|=\left(\zeta+\frac{2}{9}\right)\left(\zeta-\frac{4}{9}\right)\left(\zeta+\frac{2}{9}+\frac{2}{9} v\right)\left(\zeta-\frac{4}{9}-\frac{4}{9} v\right)
$$

with

$$
v=\frac{m_{1}\left(1+\varrho^{-1}+\varrho^{-2}\right)+m_{3}\left(1+\sigma^{-1}+\sigma^{-2}\right)}{m_{1}+m_{2}\left(\varrho^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}\right)+m_{3}}
$$

in the collinear case. The determinant $\left|\lambda \mathfrak{E}_{6}-\mathfrak{B}\right|$ is then obtained from these two polynomials by discarding the factor $\left(\zeta+\frac{2}{9}\right)$. Thus in the

equilateral case the 6 eigenvalues of $\mathfrak{B}$ are
$\lambda_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}, \lambda_{2}=\frac{1}{6}(1-\sqrt{13+12 \sqrt{1-3 \mu}}), \lambda_{3}=\frac{1}{6}(1-\sqrt{13-12 \sqrt{1-3 \mu}})$,
$\lambda_{4}=\frac{1}{6}(1+\sqrt{13-12 \sqrt{1-3 \mu}}), \lambda_{5}=\frac{1}{6}(1+\sqrt{13+12 \sqrt{1-3 \mu}}), \lambda_{6}=1$,
while in the collinear case they are

$$
\begin{gathered}
\lambda_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}, \quad \lambda_{2}=\frac{1}{6}(1-\sqrt{25+16 v}), \quad \lambda_{3}=\frac{1}{6}(1-\sqrt{1-8 v}) \\
\lambda_{4}=\frac{1}{6}(1+\sqrt{1-8 v}), \quad \lambda_{5}=\frac{1}{6}(1+\sqrt{25+16 v}), \quad \lambda_{6}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The identity

$$
2 M^{2}(1-3 \mu)=\left(m_{1}-m_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(m_{1}-m_{3}\right)^{2}+\left(m_{2}-m_{3}\right)^{2}
$$

shows that in the equilateral case the 6 eigenvalues are all real, with $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \lambda_{3}$ negative and $\lambda_{4}, \lambda_{5}, \lambda_{6}$ positive. Moreover, unless $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}$, the eigenvalues are all distinct, while condition (29) is easily seen to coincide here with the stipulation that neither $\lambda_{1} / \lambda_{3}$ nor $\lambda_{2} / \lambda_{3}$ be an integer. With these exceptions excluded, the previously named result from $\S 28$ then gives the coordinates in the equilateral case of a triple collision as power series in the three variables

$$
v_{1}=c_{1} t^{\frac{2}{3}}, \quad v_{2}=c_{2} t^{-\lambda_{2}}, \quad v_{3}=c_{3} t^{-\lambda_{3}}
$$

containing three arbitrary real constants $c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}$. Another constant, which fixes the direction of collision for the 3 points in the orbital plane, comes from determining $p_{4}$ by quadrature. Furthermore, one can undertake an arbitrary orientation of the $(x, y)$-plane in space and impart to it a translation with constant velocity, obtaining in this way 8 additional constants. The equilateral case of a triple collision thus contains altogether 12 independent real parameters. Finally, observe that for an arbitrary constant $c_{0}>0$ the transformation $t \rightarrow c_{0} t, c_{k} \rightarrow c_{k} c_{0}^{\lambda_{k}}$ leaves the variables $v_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ in (39) unchanged, so that also the functions $\bar{p}_{k}, \bar{q}_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ constructed from these through (25) and (30) remain unaltered, whereas the $p_{k}=\bar{p}_{k} t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ themselves do not. On account of the independent variable $t$, the triple-collision orbits in the equilateral case then form a 13-dimensional manifold in an 18-dimensional space.

In the collinear case the two eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}$ are real and negative, $\lambda_{5}, \lambda_{6}$ real and positive, while $\lambda_{3}, \lambda_{4}$ are either real and positive or complex conjugate with the positive real part $\frac{1}{6}$. To have the eigenvalues all distinct, it is necessary to stipulate that $v \neq \frac{1}{6}$, whereas (29) means here that $\lambda_{2} / \lambda_{1}$ must not be an integer. The coordinates are then given as power series in the two variables

$$
v_{1}=c_{1} t^{\frac{2}{3}}, \quad v_{2}=c_{2} t^{-\lambda_{2}}
$$

with two arbitrary real constants $c_{1}, c_{2}$.

In conclusion we show that in the collinear case of a triple collision the angle $p_{4}$ is constant, so that the 3 particles move along a fixed line. For this, in addition to equation (31) for $p_{4}$, we isolate the two differential equations for $\bar{p}_{3}$ and $\bar{q}_{3}$, which in view of (10), (13), (14) and (24) are explicitly given by

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\frac{d \bar{p}_{3}}{d u}= & \frac{2}{3} \bar{p}_{3}+\left\{\left(\frac{1}{m_{1}}+\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right) \frac{\bar{p}_{2}}{\bar{p}_{1}}-\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right\} \bar{q}_{0}+\left(\frac{1}{m_{3}} \frac{\bar{p}_{2}}{\bar{p}_{1}}-\frac{1}{m_{2}}-\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right) \bar{q}_{3} \\
\frac{d \bar{q}_{3}}{d u}= & -\frac{1}{3} \bar{q}_{3}+m_{2} m_{3}\left(\bar{p}_{2}^{2}+\bar{p}_{3}^{2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \bar{p}_{3}+m_{1} m_{2}\left\{\left(\bar{p}_{1}-\bar{p}_{2}\right)^{2}+\bar{p}_{3}^{2}\right\}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \bar{p}_{3} \\
& +\left(\frac{1}{m_{1}}+\frac{1}{m_{3}}\right) \frac{\bar{q}_{2}}{\bar{p}_{1}} \bar{q}_{0}+\frac{1}{m_{3}} \frac{\bar{q}_{2}}{\bar{p}_{1}} \bar{q}_{3}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with

$$
\bar{q}_{0}=\left(\bar{q}_{4}-\bar{p}_{2} \bar{q}_{3}+\bar{q}_{2} \bar{p}_{3}\right) \bar{p}_{1}^{-1}
$$

Because in the collinear case $\hat{p}_{3}=0, \hat{q}_{3}=0$, and by (25) therefore $\bar{p}_{3}=\delta_{5}$, $\bar{q}_{3}=\delta_{6}$, the right sides of both equations in (41) for $\delta_{7}=0$ are of the form $\Phi \delta_{5}+\Psi \delta_{6}$, with $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ convergent power series in $\delta_{1}, \ldots, \delta_{6}$. If now the two eigenvalues corresponding to the linear part in the right side of (41) both have a positive real part, the considerations in $\S 28$ imply that the solutions $\delta_{5}=\delta_{5}(u)$ and $\delta_{6}=\delta_{6}(u)$, subject to the conditions $\delta_{k} \rightarrow 0(k=1, \ldots, 6)$ as $u \rightarrow \infty$, must vanish identically in $u$. The condition on the two eigenvalues, on the other hand, will follow from the contention that these are just $\lambda_{3}$ and $\lambda_{4}$. Since a direct calculation of the eigenvalues using (41) appears too laborious, it is better to proceed as we did in determining the 6 eigenvalues of $\mathfrak{B}$. One verifies from (24) and (25) that in the collinear case the coefficients $a_{k l}$ in (26) are 0 if $k=1, \ldots, 4$ and $l=5, \ldots, 8$. Now if in the definition of the $\omega_{k}$ in (37) one interchanges the indices 3 and 5 as well as 4 and 6 on the left side, then according to (34) and (35) the correspondingly constructed new matrix $\mathfrak{E}$ decomposes like $\mathfrak{A}$, while in place of (38) one now has

$$
\mathfrak{G}=\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
\frac{2}{3} \mathfrak{E}_{2} & \mathfrak{E}_{2} & 0 & 0 \\
2 a^{-3} \mathfrak{Q} & -\frac{1}{3} \mathfrak{E}_{2} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \frac{2}{3} \mathfrak{E}_{2} & \mathfrak{E}_{2} \\
0 & 0 & -a^{-3} \mathfrak{Q} & -\frac{1}{3} \mathfrak{E}_{2}
\end{array}\right)
$$

From this one verifies the contention about the two eigenvalues in question, whereupon it follows that in the collinear case $\bar{p}_{3}=0, \bar{q}_{3}=0$. Since then also $\bar{q}_{0}=0$, equation (31) now does indeed imply that $p_{4}=\hat{p}_{4}$ is constant.

To obtain the general solution in the collinear case one has to replace the orbital line by any straight line in the old coordinate system moving parallel to itself with constant velocity. This gives 7 new constants, in addition to $c_{1}, c_{2}, p_{4}$, altogether 10 independent real parameters, whereas there are 12 parameters in the equilateral case.

The exponents $-\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{3}$ in (39) for the equilateral case, and also the exponent $-\lambda_{2}$ in (40) for the collinear case, are in general irrational, namely, whenever the quantities $\mu, v$, which depend on the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$, avoid a certain countable set of exceptional values. Thus, generally, a triple collision gives rise to an essential singularity in the coordinates $x_{k}, y_{k}(k=1,2,3)$. On the other hand, by setting $c_{2}=0$, $c_{3}=0$ in (39) and $c_{2}=0$ in (40) one obtains special triple-collision solutions with the same type of singularity as in simple collisions, for the coordinates are then power series in the variable $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$. A closer inspection shows these special solutions to be the same as those given in (4), with the constant $b_{2}$ there bearing a simple relation to $c_{1}$.

The considerations in $\S 28$ can be extended to give analogous results for the case when the 6 eigenvalues are not all distinct or do not satisfy condition (29), a case that up to now has been excluded. This, however, will not be pursued here any further.

A final point to be discussed is the possibility of a singularity in the three-body problem due to simple collisions at a sequence of times $t=t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots$ decreasing to 0 . It follows from the reasoning in $\S 8$ that a triple collision would then have to occur at $t=0$. But the reasoning of $\S 12$, appropriately translated to this case, would now show $(12 ; 7)$ again to be true, contradicting that $U=U(t)$, on the other hand, would have to become infinite at all $t_{k}(k=1,2, \ldots)$. Thus, extending the result obtained in $\S 8$, we have proved that simple collisions in the three-body problem do not accumulate at a finite time, even if the angular momentum constants with respect to the fixed center of mass are all 0 .

This concludes our investigation into the singularities of the threebody problem. The restriction of $t$ to real values was essential here, and a satisfactory extension of this analysis to the complex case appears hopeless.

# Chapter Two 

## Periodic Solutions

## § 14. The Solutions of Lagrange

The theorem of Sundman discussed in chapter one represents the most far reaching result yet known about general solutions to the threebody problem. Unfortunately his ingenious method cannot be extended to the case $n>3$. Although the results in $\S 6$ can be used to exclude at the outset the simultaneous collision of all $n$ bodies, the investigations of $\S 12, \S 13$ show that already a triple collision may give rise to essential singularities.

In this chapter we will develop methods that go beyond the $n$-body problem and apply to many general questions in mechanics as well. The methods deal with finding periodic solutions for a given problem. A solution of period $\tau$ has the special property that it is completely determined by knowledge over a finite time interval of length $\tau$, and therefore difficulties arising from the unboundedness of time, as for example in Sundman's first lemma, are no longer present. Because planetary motion is approximately periodic, periodic solutions to the $n$-body problem are important also in astronomy.

The simplest periodic solutions are ones whose coordinates do not depend on time. These are known as equilibrium solutions. We observe first that there are no such solutions to the $n$-body problem ( $n>1$ ), for if each coordinate $q$ were constant in time, then from $\bar{q}=0$ the equations of motion $(5 ; 3)$ would imply that $U_{q}=0$, and it would follow from Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions that

$$
\sum_{q} q U_{q}=-U=0
$$

whereas from its definition $U$ must certainly be positive. Since there are no equilibrium solutions to the $n$-body problem, we look for the next simplest periodic solutions. Restricting ourselves again to three particles $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}$, we ask: Does the three-body problem have solutions for which the particles move uniformly along circular orbits in a fixed plane? In answering this question affirmatively, we will obtain a special class of

solutions to the three-body problem that were given already by Lagrange [1] in the year 1772.

In the plane in question we introduce a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system and denote the coordinates of $P_{k}$ by $q_{2 k-1}, q_{2 k}(k=1,2,3)$. Again let
(1) $T=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{3} m_{k}^{-1}\left(p_{2 k-1}^{2}+p_{2 k}^{2}\right), \quad U=\sum_{k<l} m_{k} m_{l} r_{k l}^{-1}, \quad E=T-U$,
with $r_{k l}$ the distance between $P_{k}$ and $P_{l}$, so that the equations of motion take the Hamiltonian form

$$
\dot{q}_{k}=E_{p_{k}}, \quad \dot{p}_{k}=-E_{q_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 6)
$$

Retaining the same origin, we introduce a new rectangular Cartesian coordinate system that rotates uniformly about the origin in the given plane. The rotational velocity is to be determined so that in the new coordinate system the particles are at rest. The new coordinates $x_{2 k-1}, x_{2 k}$ of $P_{k}$ are given by

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left\{\begin{array}{c}
x_{2 k-1}=q_{2 k-1} c+q_{2 k} s, \quad x_{2 k}=-q_{2 k-1} s+q_{2 k} c \quad(k=1,2,3) \\
c=\cos \lambda, \quad s=\sin \lambda
\end{array}\right.
\end{gathered}
$$

where the angle of rotation $\lambda$ takes the form $\lambda=\omega t$, with $\omega \neq 0$ a real constant still to be determined. To introduce these coordinates into the equations of motion (2), we complete (3) to a canonical transformation by choosing suitable additional variables $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{6}$. For this purpose we base a canonical transformation on the representation given by $(3 ; 4)$, and readily obtain

$$
w=w(q, y)=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\left\{\left(q_{2 k-1} c+q_{2 k} s\right) y_{2 k-1}+\left(-q_{2 k-1} s+q_{2 k} c\right) y_{2 k}\right\}
$$

as an appropriate generating function. The matrix of the binary bilinear form in the curved bracket being orthogonal, the 6 -by-6 determinant $\left|w_{q_{k} y_{l}}\right|$ has the value $1 \neq 0$. In accordance with $(3 ; 4)$, the corresponding canonical transformation then reads

$$
p_{k}=w_{q_{k}}, \quad x_{k}=w_{y_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 6)
$$

so that (3) is augmented by

$$
p_{2 k-1}=y_{2 k-1} c-y_{2 k} s, \quad p_{2 k}=y_{2 k-1} s+y_{2 k} c \quad(k=1,2,3)
$$

It follows that

$$
p_{2 k-1}^{2}+p_{2 k}^{2}=y_{2 k-1}^{2}+y_{2 k}^{2}
$$

and to introduce the new coordinates into $T$ one has merely to replace $p_{k}$ by $y_{k}$ in expression (1). Similarly, since $U$ depends only on the distances

between the particles, $q_{k}$ has merely to be replaced by $x_{k}$ in the corresponding expression for $U$. Moreover, the derivatives of $c, s$ are $c_{t}=-\omega s, s_{t}=\omega c$, so that by $(3 ; 4)$ the new Hamiltonian function is

$$
F=E+w_{t}=E+\omega \sum_{k=1}^{3}\left(x_{2 k} y_{2 k-1}-x_{2 k-1} y_{2 k}\right)
$$

and the equations of motion become

$$
\dot{x}_{k}=F_{y_{k}}, \quad \dot{y}_{k}=-F_{x_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 6)
$$

or

$$
\begin{cases}\dot{x}_{2 k-1}=E_{y_{2 k-1}}+\omega x_{2 k}, & \dot{y}_{2 k-1}=-E_{x_{2 k-1}}+\omega y_{2 k} \\ \dot{x}_{2 k}=E_{y_{2 k}}-\omega x_{2 k-1}, & \dot{y}_{2 k}=-E_{x_{2 k}}-\omega y_{2 k-1} \quad(k=1,2,3)\end{cases}
$$

Here

$$
E_{x_{k}}=-U_{x_{k}}(k=1, \ldots, 6), E_{y_{2 k-1}}=m_{k}^{-1} y_{2 k-1}, E_{y_{2 k}}=m_{k}^{-1} y_{2 k}(k=1,2,3)
$$

Note that the expression

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{3}\left(x_{2 k} y_{2 k-1}-x_{2 k-1} y_{2 k}\right)=Q
$$

appearing in the definition of $F$ is just the angular momentum integral, for in accordance with (3), (4), this expression is unaltered if $x$ and $y$ are replaced by $q$ and $p=m \dot{q}$. That $\dot{Q}=0$ can of course also be verified directly from (5).

The equilibrium solutions to (5) arise from the twelve conditions

$$
\begin{gathered}
m_{k}^{-1} y_{2 k-1}+\omega x_{2 k}=0, \quad U_{x_{2 k-1}}+\omega y_{2 k}=0, \quad m_{k}^{-1} y_{2 k}-\omega x_{2 k-1}=0 \\
U_{x_{2 k}}-\omega y_{2 k-1}=0 \quad(k=1,2,3)
\end{gathered}
$$

which upon elimination of $y_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 6)$ become

$$
m_{k} \omega^{2} x_{2 k-1}=-U_{x_{2 k-1}}, \quad m_{k} \omega^{2} x_{2 k}=-U_{x_{2 k}} \quad(k=1,2,3)
$$

Conversely, each solution $x_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 6)$ of the above system of equations leads to an equilibrium solution, while addition over $k$ in (6) in conjunction with $(5 ; 6)$ shows that the center of mass of the three bodies lies at the origin. The solving of equations (6), which we now undertake, was carried out in a different setting already in $\S 12$.

Let us first assume that the triangle $P_{1} P_{2} P_{3}$ is not equilateral, and select the indices so that $r_{13} \neq r_{23}$. If in addition the abscissa axis is taken to pass through $P_{3}$, then $x_{6}=0$ and the second equation of (6) for $k=3$ gives rise to the condition

$$
m_{1} x_{2} r_{13}^{-3}+m_{2} x_{4} r_{23}^{-3}=0
$$

Since

$$
m_{1} x_{2}+m_{2} x_{4}+m_{3} x_{6}=0, \quad x_{6}=0
$$

it follows that

$$
m_{1} x_{2}\left(r_{13}^{-3}-r_{23}^{-3}\right)=0
$$

hence $x_{2}=0$ and also $x_{4}=0$. Therefore, if the three particles do not form an equilateral triangle they are collinear.

For the case of an equilateral triangle, let $r_{12}=r_{23}=r_{31}=r$, so that from (6) and the condition on the center of mass we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
\omega^{2} x_{2 k-1}=r^{-3} \sum_{l=1}^{3} m_{l}\left(x_{2 k-1}-x_{2 l-1}\right)=M r^{-3} x_{2 k-1} \\
\omega^{2} x_{2 k}=M r^{-3} x_{2 k} \quad(k=1,2,3)
\end{gathered}
$$

where $M=m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}$. Because the $x_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 6)$ are not all 0 , it follows that

$$
M=\omega^{2} r^{3}, \quad \omega= \pm \sqrt{M r^{-3}}
$$

Conversely, (7) leads back to (6), so that we have indeed found a solution to the three-body problem for which $P_{1} P_{2} P_{3}$ is an equilateral triangle with side $r$, while $\omega$ is determined from (7). This is known as the equilateral solution.

It remains to investigate the case when the three particles lie on a straight line. Selecting this line as the abscissa axis, we have $x_{2 k}=0$ $(k=1,2,3)$, whereby the second equation of (6) is automatically satisfied. Assume now that $P_{2}$ lies between $P_{1}$ and $P_{3}$, while the positive direction along the abscissa axis is from $P_{1}$ to $P_{3}$. If $r_{13}=a, r_{12}=\varrho a, r_{23}=\sigma a$, then $\varrho+\sigma=1,0<\varrho<1$, and the first equation in (6) for $k=1,2,3$ gives rise to the formulas

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
-m_{2}(\varrho a)^{-2}-m_{3} a^{-2} & =\omega^{2} x_{1}, \quad m_{1}(\varrho a)^{-2}-m_{3}(\sigma a)^{-2}=\omega^{2} x_{3} \\
m_{1} a^{-2}+m_{2}(\sigma a)^{-2} & =\omega^{2} x_{5}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

One of these, say the middle one, can be replaced by the condition $m_{1} x_{1}+m_{2} x_{3}+m_{3} x_{5}=0$ on the center of mass, which also says that

$$
M x_{1}+m_{2} \varrho a+m_{3} a=0, \quad M x_{5}-m_{2} \sigma a-m_{1} a=0
$$

where again $M=m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}$. Using this to eliminate $x_{1}$ and $x_{5}$ in the first and third equation of (8), we obtain

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
m_{2} \varrho^{-2}+m_{3}=M^{-1} \omega^{2} a^{3}\left(m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}\right) \\
m_{2} \sigma^{-2}+m_{1}=M^{-1} \omega^{2} a^{3}\left(m_{2} \sigma+m_{1}\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$

and because $\sigma=1-\varrho$, finally

$$
M^{-1} \omega^{2} a^{3}=\frac{m_{2} \varrho^{-2}+m_{3}}{m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}}=\frac{m_{2}(1-\varrho)^{-2}+m_{1}}{m_{2}(1-\varrho)+m_{1}}, \quad 0<\varrho<1
$$

Since in the interval $0<\varrho<1$ the difference

$$
\frac{m_{2} \varrho^{-2}+m_{3}}{m_{2} \varrho+m_{3}}-\frac{m_{2}(1-\varrho)^{-2}+m_{1}}{m_{2}(1-\varrho)+m_{1}}=f(\varrho)
$$

is a monotonically decreasing function of $\varrho$ which tends to $+\infty$ as $\varrho \rightarrow 0$ and to $-\infty$ as $\varrho \rightarrow 1$, the equation $f(\varrho)=0$ has exactly one root $\varrho$ in this interval. Setting $M^{-1} \omega^{2} a^{3}$ equal to the value given by (10) and determining $x_{1}, x_{3}, x_{5}$ from (8), we obtain a solution to (6). Thus again this leads to an actual solution of the three-body problem, with $\omega$ determined up to sign by the value of $a$. This is known as the collinear solution. To determine $\varrho$ one has to solve a fifth degree equation with coefficients depending on the masses. We saw that there is only one solution in the interval $0<\varrho<1$. It was assumed here that $P_{2}$ lies between $P_{1}$ and $P_{3}$, and two additional solutions can be obtained by a cyclic permutation of the indices.

In the opinion of Lagrange the solutions he found had no significance in astronomy. However, more recently it was discovered that the sun, Jupiter, and the small planets of the Trojan group form an approximately equilateral triangle, and it is therefore of interest to study solutions of the three-body problem near the Lagrange solutions. This will be done in $\S 18$.

Lagrange generalized the above solutions further by asking for, and constructing, all additional solutions for which the triangles formed by the particles remain similar throughout the motion. We will consider the analogous question for the planar $n$-body problem, assuming, in view of the center of mass integral, that the center of mass is at rest. The rectangular Cartesian coordinates $x_{k}, y_{k}$ of $P_{k}$ then take the form

$$
x_{k}+i y_{k}=z_{k}=\zeta_{k} q \quad(k=1, \ldots, n)
$$

where $\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}$ are distinct complex constants and $q$ is an unknown complex function of the real variable $t$. The distances are then given by

$$
r_{k l}=\left|z_{k}-z_{l}\right|=\left|\zeta_{k}-\zeta_{l}\right||q|
$$

and the complex form of the equations of motion

$$
\ddot{z}_{k}=\sum_{l \neq k} m_{l} \frac{z_{l}-z_{k}}{r_{k l}^{3}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, n)
$$

leads for $q \neq 0$ to the equations

$$
\zeta_{k} \ddot{q}=q|q|^{-3} \sum_{l \neq k} m_{l} \frac{\zeta_{l}-\zeta_{k}}{\left|\zeta_{l}-\zeta_{k}\right|^{3}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, n)
$$

Because the $\zeta_{k}$ are not all 0 , the expression

$$
\ddot{q} q^{\frac{1}{2}} \bar{q}^{\frac{1}{2}}=c
$$

is independent of $t$, while

$$
\zeta_{k} c=\sum_{l \neq k} m_{l} \frac{\zeta_{l}-\zeta_{k}}{\left|\zeta_{l}-\zeta_{k}\right|^{3}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, n)
$$

The problem is thereby reduced to solving the differential equation (12), which is independent of $n$, together with the system of algebraic equations (13). For the case $n=2$ this leads to the general solution of the twobody problem, since the segments $P_{1} P_{2}$ trivially remain similar throughout. In addition, we have $m_{1} \zeta_{1}+m_{2} \zeta_{2}=0$, hence $\zeta_{1}=m_{2} \zeta, \zeta_{2}=-m_{1} \zeta$ with a complex $\zeta \neq 0$, and it follows from (13) that in this case the quantity $c=-\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right)^{-2}|\zeta|^{-3}$ is real and negative.

The solution of the two-body problem is now assumed as known. If $q=q(t)$ is any solution of the differential equation (12) with $c$ a negative constant, and if $\zeta \neq 0$ is a complex constant, then

$$
x+i y=z=\zeta q
$$

is a parametric representation of a conic section in the $(x, y)$-plane, and, indeed, of one for which the origin is a focus. Let $n$ again be arbitrary and suppose that $\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}$ are $n$ distinct complex numbers satisfying the system of equations (13) with $c<0$. Each solution of (12) then gives, by means of (11), a solution to the $n$-body problem, whereby each particle describes a conic section and the polygons formed by the $n$ points remain similar throughout. In particular, if the conic section is taken to be an ellipse, $q(t)$ is periodic, and one obtains in this way a periodic solution.

For the case $n=3$ all solutions of (13) with a negative constant $c$ are already known to us, for this system of equations corresponds to (6) with $\omega^{2}=-c$ and $x_{2 k-1}+i x_{2 k}=\zeta_{k}$, and therefore leads to solutions of the three-body problem in which $\zeta_{1}, \zeta_{2}, \zeta_{3}$ are either vertices of an equilateral triangle or three collinear points with the ratio $\varrho$ of their distances determined by (10). These are then the generalized solutions of Lagrange, with the special case of circular orbits obtained by setting $q=e^{i \omega t}$. Another special case arises from taking the solution $q(t)$ of (12) to be real, and this was already considered in $\S 13$. The collinear case of the latter was treated already by Euler [2], who thus became the first to find a particular solution to the three-body problem. In this connection the fifth degree equation $f(\varrho)=0$ also appears in his work.

# § 15. Eigenvalues 

We consider a system of $m$ first order differential equations expressed in vector form as

$$
\dot{x}=f(x)
$$

where $x$ and $f(x)$ are columns with entries $x_{k}$ and $f_{k}(x)(k=1, \ldots, m)$ respectively. Let $x=x^{(0)}$ be an equilibrium solution to (1), and assume that the $f_{k}$ are regular functions of $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{m}$ in a neighborhood of $x^{(0)}$ which do not depend explicitly on $t$. It may be assumed without loss of generality that $x^{(0)}=0$, so that the Taylor series of $f_{k}(x)$ at $x=0$ takes the form

$$
f_{k}(x)=\sum_{l=1}^{m} a_{k l} x_{l}+\cdots
$$

or in vector notation

$$
f(x)=\mathfrak{A} x+\cdots, \quad \mathfrak{A}=\left(a_{k l}\right)
$$

At first we shall neglect the higher order terms and, instead of (1), solve the linear system

$$
\dot{x}=\mathfrak{A} x
$$

From these solutions we will try to arrive at solutions to the nonlinear system (1), although this will not always be possible. It will be shown, however, that if (1) is a Hamiltonian system, then one can, in general, construct a periodic solution of (1) from a periodic solution of (2).

To solve (2), we use a known algebraic result about the normal form of a square matrix. The eigenvalues of $\mathfrak{A}$ are the $m$ solutions $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{m}$ of the $m$-th degree characteristic equation

$$
|\lambda \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{U}|=0
$$

with $\mathfrak{E}$ the identity matrix of $m$ rows, and henceforth it will be assumed that these $m$ roots are distinct from one another. According to the result mentioned, there exists an invertible complex matrix $\mathfrak{C}$ of $m$ rows such that

$$
\mathfrak{C}^{-1} \mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{R}=\left[\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{m}\right]
$$

is the diagonal matrix with the entries $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{m}$. We still want to investigate the extent to which $\mathfrak{C}$ is determined by $\mathfrak{A}$. If $c^{(1)}, \ldots, c^{(m)}$ are the individual columns of $\mathfrak{C}$, the matrix equation $\mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{C} \mathfrak{R}$ is equivalent to the $m$ vector equations

$$
\mathfrak{A} c^{(k)}=c^{(k)} \lambda_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, m)
$$

hence also to

$$
\left(\lambda_{k} \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{A}\right) c^{(k)}=0
$$

Because the $\lambda_{k}$ are distinct, the matrix

$$
\lambda_{k} \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{C}\left(\lambda_{k} \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{R}\right) \mathfrak{C}^{-1}
$$

has rank $m-1$, and consequently (5) determines $c^{(k)}$ up to an arbitrary scalar factor $p_{k}$. If, on the other hand,

$$
\mathfrak{P}=\left[p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m}\right], \quad \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{C} \mathfrak{B}
$$

with the $p_{k} \neq 0$ arbitrary, then also $|\mathfrak{B}| \neq 0$ and $\mathfrak{B}^{-1} \mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{R}$. Thus the $c^{(k)}$ are determined precisely up to nonzero scalar factors. This algebraic reasoning applies to any complex $\mathfrak{A}$.

If $\mathfrak{A}$ is real, the characteristic equation (3) has real coefficients and hence for each root $\lambda_{k}$ also the complex conjugate $\bar{\lambda}_{k}$ appears as one of the roots $\lambda_{l}$. In this way, to each $k=1, \ldots, m$ there corresponds a unique $l=l_{k}$ in the range $1, \ldots, m$ such that $\bar{\lambda}_{k}=\lambda_{l}$; in particular, $k=l$ if $\lambda_{k}$ is real. The $\lambda_{k}$ being distinct, this correspondence between $k$ and $l_{k}$ is one-to-one. Now, according to (5), we have

$$
\left(\lambda_{l} \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{A}\right) \overline{c^{(k)}}=0 \quad\left(l=l_{k}\right)
$$

and consequently

$$
c^{(l)}=\overline{c^{(k)}} \varrho_{k} \quad\left(l=l_{k}\right)
$$

with $\varrho_{k}$ a scalar. Similarly $c^{(k)}=\overline{c^{(l)}} \varrho_{l}$, and since $|\mathfrak{C}| \neq 0$ implies that $c^{(k)} \neq 0$, it follows that

$$
\bar{\varrho}_{k} \varrho_{l}=1
$$

By replacing $c^{(k)}$ with $c^{(k)} \varrho_{l}^{k}$ one may achieve the normalization $\varrho_{k}=1$ and therefore have $c^{(l)}=\overline{c^{(k)}}$, a possibility that can also be inferred directly from (5). For subsequent application to Hamiltonian systems, however, it is more convenient not to assume as yet that $\varrho_{k}=1$.

The linear substitution

$$
x=\mathfrak{C} y, \quad y=\mathfrak{C}^{-1} x
$$

transforms (2) into the system

$$
\dot{y}=\mathfrak{R} y
$$

whose complete solution is given by

$$
y_{k}=\alpha_{k} e^{\lambda_{k} t} \quad(k=1, \ldots, m)
$$

where $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{m}$ are elements of the column $y$, and $\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{m}$ are $m$ integration constants. In particular, if $\lambda_{k}$ is purely imaginary, then $y_{k}$ is a periodic function of the real variable $t$. To discuss reality conditions, i.e. conditions under which the solutions are real, one has to consider the relation (6). For

$$
x=\sum_{k=1}^{m} c^{(k)} y_{k}
$$

to be real, it must be true that

$$
x=\sum_{k=1}^{m} \overline{c^{(k)}} \overline{y_{k}}
$$

and because $|\mathfrak{C}| \neq 0$, if $\mathfrak{A}$ is real we need $\bar{y}_{k}=\varrho_{k} y_{l_{k}}$. The integration constants must therefore be chosen so that $\bar{\alpha}_{k}=\varrho_{k} \alpha_{l_{k}}$.

Let us again consider the general nonlinear system

$$
\dot{x}=\mathfrak{A} x+\cdots
$$

and introduce new variables $y$ by a transformation

$$
x_{k}=\phi_{k}(y) \quad(k=1, \ldots, m)
$$

analytic in a neighborhood of $y_{1}=0, \ldots, y_{m}=0$ and taking $y=0$ into $x=0$. If the corresponding Taylor series is

$$
x=\mathfrak{B} y+\cdots
$$

with $|\mathfrak{B}| \neq 0$, then in a neighborhood of $x=0$ there is an inverse transformation $y=\mathfrak{B}^{-1} x+\cdots$, also analytic, and the system (9) becomes

$$
\dot{y}=\mathfrak{B}^{-1} \mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{B} y+\cdots
$$

This shows that under analytic transformation of the differential equation (1) the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{m}$ remain invariant.

We now specialize (1) to a Hamiltonian system

$$
\dot{u}_{k}=H_{v_{n}}, \quad \dot{v}_{k}=-H_{u_{n}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, n)
$$

To express this in vector form, let $w$ be the column with the $2 n$ entries $u_{1}, \ldots, u_{n}, v_{1}, \ldots, v_{n}$ and $H_{w}$ the column having the corresponding derivatives of $H$ as entries. If $\mathfrak{E}$ is again the $n \times n$ identity matrix and

$$
\mathfrak{J}=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & \mathfrak{E} \\
-\mathfrak{E} & 0
\end{array}\right)
$$

then (11) can be written in the abbreviated form

$$
\dot{w}=\mathfrak{J} H_{w}
$$

The Hamiltonian function $H=H(w)$ is assumed to be regular in a neighborhood of $w=0$. Because the constant term of the Taylor expansion of $H$ at $w=0$ plays no role in the differential equation (11), it may as well be set equal to 0 . Moreover, if $w=0$ is to be an equilibrium solution of (11), then all the first derivatives of $H$ must vanish there. The power series of $H$ therefore begins with quadratic terms and can be expressed in the form

$$
H=\frac{1}{2} w^{\prime} \mathfrak{S} w+\cdots
$$

where $\mathfrak{S}$ is a symmetric matrix of $2 n$ rows and $w^{\prime}$ is the transpose of $w$. Consequently

$$
H_{w}=\mathfrak{S} w+\cdots
$$

so that (12) becomes

$$
\dot{w}=\mathfrak{A} w+\cdots, \quad \mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}
$$

and the characteristic polynomial to be considered is $p(\lambda)=|\lambda| \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}|$.
Since $\mathfrak{J}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J}^{-1}=-\mathfrak{J},|\mathfrak{J}|=1, \mathfrak{S}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{S}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\lambda \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S})^{\prime} & =\lambda \mathfrak{E}+\mathfrak{S} \mathfrak{J}=\mathfrak{J}(-\lambda \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}) \mathfrak{J} \\
p(\lambda) & =|\lambda \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}|=|-\lambda \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}|=p(-\lambda)
\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $p(\lambda)$ is an even function. Thus if $\lambda$ is a root of $p(\lambda)$, so also is $-\lambda$, with both having the same multiplicity, while if 0 is a root its multiplicity must be even. If all the eigenvalues are again assumed to be simple, and therefore $\neq 0$, after a suitable reordering they can be denoted by $\lambda_{k}, \lambda_{k+n}=-\lambda_{k}(k=1, \ldots, n)$. Setting $\mathfrak{R}_{0}=\left[\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}\right]$, we can then find an invertible complex matrix $\mathfrak{C}$, of $2 n$ rows, such that the normal form of $\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}$ becomes

$$
\mathfrak{C}^{-1} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S} \mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{R}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathfrak{R}_{0} & 0 \\
0 & -\mathfrak{R}_{0}
\end{array}\right)
$$

whereby upon transposition we have

$$
\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{S} \mathfrak{J}=-\mathfrak{R}^{\prime}
$$

On the other hand, since the matrix

$$
-\mathfrak{R} \mathfrak{J}^{-1}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
0 & \mathfrak{R}_{0} \\
\mathfrak{R}_{0} & 0
\end{array}\right)
$$

is symmetric, it follows that

$$
\mathfrak{R} \mathfrak{J}^{-1}=\left(\mathfrak{R} \mathfrak{J}^{-1}\right)^{\prime}=\left(\mathfrak{J}^{-1}\right)^{\prime} \mathfrak{R}=\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{R}
$$

and together with (15) this gives

$$
\left(\mathfrak{J}^{-1} \mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}\right) \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}=\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{S}=-\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{R}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}^{-1}=\mathfrak{R}\left(\mathfrak{J}^{-1} \mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}\right)
$$

Thus, setting $\mathfrak{B}=\left(\mathfrak{J}^{-1} \mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J}\right)^{-1}$, we have $|\mathfrak{B}| \neq 0$ and

$$
\mathfrak{B}^{-1} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S} \mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{R}
$$

Our earlier result about the extent to which $\mathfrak{C}$ is determined implies that $\mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{B}$, where $\mathfrak{B}$ is an invertible diagonal matrix which we will express in the form

$$
\mathfrak{P}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathfrak{P}_{1} & 0 \\
0 & \mathfrak{P}_{2}
\end{array}\right)
$$

with $\mathfrak{P}_{1}, \mathfrak{P}_{2}$ two $n \times n$ diagonal matrices. It follows that

$$
\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{B}^{-1} \mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{P}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
0 & \mathfrak{P}_{2} \\
-\mathfrak{P}_{1} & 0
\end{array}\right)
$$

and since $\mathfrak{J}$, and therefore also $\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{C}$, is alternating, we have $\mathfrak{P}_{1}=\mathfrak{P}_{2}$. Consequently, if

$$
\mathfrak{Q}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathfrak{P}_{1} & 0 \\
0 & \mathfrak{C}
\end{array}\right)
$$

then $\mathfrak{Q}^{\prime} \mathfrak{I} \mathfrak{Q}=\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{P}$. Finally, with $\mathfrak{C} \mathfrak{Q}^{-1}$ again denoted by $\mathfrak{C}$, equation (14) remains as is, while now

$$
\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{J}
$$

and therefore $\mathfrak{C}$ is symplectic. Furthermore,

$$
\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{S} \mathfrak{C}=-\left(\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{C}\right) \mathfrak{C}^{-1} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S} \mathfrak{C}=-\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{R}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
0 & \mathfrak{R}_{0} \\
\mathfrak{R}_{0} & 0
\end{array}\right)
$$

so that $\mathfrak{S}$ is brought into the above normal form, and indeed through a symplectic transformation.

Let $z$ now be a column with the $2 n$ entries $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}, y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n}$, and consider the linear substitution

$$
w=\mathfrak{C} z
$$

Because the Jacobian matrix $\mathfrak{C}$ is symplectic, $(2 ; 20)$ implies that the transformation (19) is canonical. The Hamiltonian system (12) then becomes

$$
\dot{z}=\mathfrak{J} H_{z}
$$

with (13), (18) combining to give

$$
H=\frac{1}{2} z^{\prime} \mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{S} \mathfrak{C} z+\cdots=\sum_{k=1}^{n} \lambda_{k} x_{k} y_{k}+\cdots
$$

Thus the quadratic terms of $H$ take the above normal form.

If the power series $H(w)$ has only real coefficients, the matrices $\mathfrak{S}$ and $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}$ are real, whereas to have also $w$ real, $z$ must satisfy the condition $\mathfrak{C} z=\overline{\mathfrak{C}} \bar{z}$. Now $\mathfrak{C}$ is not yet uniquely determined by equations (14), (15), for it may still be multiplied on the right by an arbitrary symplectic diagonal matrix

$$
\mathfrak{R}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathfrak{R}_{0} & 0 \\
0 & \mathfrak{R}_{0}^{-1}
\end{array}\right), \quad \mathfrak{R}_{0}=\left[r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n}\right]
$$

of $2 n$ rows. By a suitable choice of $\mathfrak{R}$ the reality condition on $z$ can be simplified as follows. First, suppose that an eigenvalue $\lambda_{k}(k \leqq n)$ is not purely imaginary and that $\lambda_{i}=\bar{\lambda}_{k}\left(l=l_{k}\right)$. If $l>n$, it follows that $\lambda_{k} \neq-\lambda_{i}$ $=\lambda_{l-n}$ and $\lambda_{k} \neq \lambda_{i}$, so that an interchange of $\lambda_{l-n}, \lambda_{i}$ leads to the case $l \leqq n$. It may therefore be assumed at the outset that $l \leqq n$, and thus also that $\lambda_{i+n}=\bar{\lambda}_{k+n}$. On the other hand, for $\lambda_{k}$ purely imaginary we have $\bar{\lambda}_{k}=-\lambda_{k}=\lambda_{k+n}$. With the columns of $\mathfrak{C}$ again denoted by $c^{(1)}, \ldots, c^{(2 n)}$, the identity $\mathfrak{C}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{J}$ gives

$$
c^{(k) \prime} \mathfrak{J} c^{(k+n)}=1 \quad(k=1, \ldots, n)
$$

If $\lambda_{k}$ is not purely imaginary, (6) now implies that

$$
1=c^{(l) \prime} \mathfrak{J} c^{(l+n)}=\varrho_{k} \overline{c^{(k) \prime}} \mathfrak{J} \overline{c^{(k+n)}} \varrho_{k+n}=\varrho_{k} \varrho_{k+n}
$$

while if $\lambda_{k}$ is purely imaginary, then $l_{k}=k+n$ and

$$
-1=-\left(c^{(k) \prime} \mathfrak{J} c^{(k+n)}\right)^{\prime}=c^{(k+n) \prime} \mathfrak{J} c^{(k)}=\varrho_{k} \overline{c^{(k) \prime}} \mathfrak{J} \overline{c^{(k+n)}} \varrho_{k+n}=\varrho_{k} \varrho_{k+n}
$$

Let $\mathfrak{C} \mathfrak{R}$ again be replaced by $\mathfrak{C}$, so that the original columns $c^{(k)}, c^{(k+n)}$ are now multiplied by the scalar factors $r_{k}, r_{k}^{-1}$. For $\lambda_{k}$ not purely imaginary, (6) shows that $\varrho_{k}$ then gets multiplied by the factor $r_{l} \bar{r}_{k}^{-1}$. If in addition $\lambda_{k}$ is not real and $k<l_{k}$, the choice $r_{k}=\bar{\varrho}_{k}, r_{l}=1$ leads to the normalization $\varrho_{k}=1$, and by (7), (22) then also $\varrho_{k+n}=1, \varrho_{l}=1, \varrho_{l+n}=1$; whereas if $\lambda_{k}$ is real, then $k=l_{k}$ and by (7) the absolute value of $\varrho_{k}$ is 1 , so that the same normalization is achieved by taking $r_{k}=\varrho_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Finally, for $\lambda_{k}$ purely imaginary, $\varrho_{k}$ takes on the positive factor $\left(r_{k} \bar{r}_{k}\right)^{-1}$, and the identity $\bar{\varrho}_{k}=-\varrho_{k}$ coming from (7),(23) remains valid, showing that $\varrho_{k}$ is purely imaginary. Consequently, in this case one can normalize $\varrho_{k}=\varrho_{k+n}= \pm i$, and since an interchange of $\lambda_{k}$ and $\lambda_{k+n}$ replaces $c^{(k)}, c^{(k+n)}$ by $c^{(k+n)},-c^{(k)}$ with $\mathfrak{C}$ remaining symplectic and $-\varrho_{k+n}$ replacing $\varrho_{k}$, it is possible to have $\varrho_{k}=-i$. The above process thus leads to the factor $\varrho_{k}=-i$ for each purely imaginary eigenvalue $\lambda_{k}$, and $\varrho_{k}=1$ otherwise.
