The reality condition $\mathfrak{C} z=\overline{\mathfrak{C}} \bar{z}$, which is equivalent to $\bar{z}_{k}=\varrho_{k} z_{l_{k}}$, then becomes $x_{l}=\bar{x}_{k}, y_{l}=\bar{y}_{k}$ if $\lambda_{l}=\bar{\lambda}_{k} \neq-\lambda_{k}\left(l=l_{k} ; k=1, \ldots, n\right)$ and $y_{k}=i \bar{x}_{k}$ if $\bar{\lambda}_{k}=-\lambda_{k}$.

If on the right side of (20) only the linear term is retained, one has the linear system $\dot{z}=\mathfrak{L} z$, or, more exactly, the system

$$
\dot{x}_{k}=\lambda_{k} x_{k}, \quad \dot{y}_{k}=-\lambda_{k} y_{k} \quad(k=1, \ldots, n)
$$

whose complete solution is given by

$$
x_{k}=\xi_{k} e^{\lambda_{k} t}, \quad y_{k}=\eta_{k} e^{-\lambda_{k} t}
$$

with $\xi_{k}, \eta_{k}$ constants of integration. Should one of the eigenvalues, say $\lambda_{1}$, be purely imaginary, then

$$
x_{k}=y_{k}=0(k=2, \ldots, n), \quad x_{1}=\xi_{1} e^{\lambda_{1} t}, \quad y_{1}=\eta_{1} e^{-\lambda_{1} t}
$$

gives a periodic solution to the linear system, with the condition $\eta_{1}=i \bar{\zeta}_{1}$ making $w$ real. Our aim in the next two sections will be to find near this solution a periodic solution to the general nonlinear Hamiltonian system (11).

Incidentally, if the system of differential equations (1) is not Hamiltonian, it may well happen that apart from the equilibrium solution there are no periodic solutions, even if the corresponding linear system does have nonconstant periodic solutions. This, for example, can be seen from the system

$$
\dot{x}=-y+x\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{g}, \quad \dot{y}=x+y\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{g}
$$

for two unknown functions $x$ and $y$, wherein $g$ is a fixed natural number. The corresponding linear system $\dot{x}=-y, \dot{y}=x$ has only periodic solutions, namely, $x=\alpha \cos t+\beta \sin t, y=\alpha \sin t-\beta \cos t$ with $\alpha, \beta$ constants of integration. The corresponding orbits in the $(x, y)$-plane are concentric circles centered at the origin and traversed with constant angular velocity 1 . On the other hand, in polar coordinates $r, \phi$ with $x=r \cos \phi$, $y=r \sin \phi$ the nonlinear system (24) becomes

$$
r \dot{r}=x \dot{x}+y \dot{y}=\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{g+1}=r^{2 g+2}, \quad r^{2} \dot{\phi}=x \dot{y}-y \dot{x}=x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}
$$

and apart from the trivial solution $r=0$, its solutions are given by

$$
\dot{r}=r^{2 g+1}, \quad r=(a-2 g t)^{-\frac{1}{2 g}}, \quad \dot{\phi}=1, \quad \phi=b+t
$$

with two integration constants $a, b$. These solutions are spirals, and therefore certainly not periodic. Since the parameter $g=1,2, \ldots$ is still free, this example shows also that the property of the system $\dot{x}=-y$, $\dot{y}=x$ having periodic solutions can be destroyed by adding suitable terms of arbitrarily high order to the right sides. The system in this example, however, is not canonical. In what follows we will investigate how to obtain a periodic solution to a Hamiltonian system, under the assumption that the corresponding linear system has such a solution and satisfies a certain additional condition.

# § 16. An Existence Theorem 

Consider a Hamiltonian system $\dot{w}=\mathfrak{J} H_{w}$ satisfying the same conditions as in the previous section. Thus, $H=\frac{1}{2} w^{\prime} \mathfrak{S} w+\cdots$ is a real power series that begins with quadratic terms and converges in some neighborhood of $w=0$, while the $2 n$ eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n},-\lambda_{1}, \ldots,-\lambda_{n}$ of $\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}$ are distinct. Our aim is to prove the following existence theorem:

Let $\lambda_{1}$ be purely imaginary, and assume that none of the $n-1$ quotients $\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\lambda_{n}}{\lambda_{1}}$ is an integer. Then there exists a family of real periodic solutions to the Hamiltonian system which depend analytically on one real parameter $\varrho$, with $\varrho=0$ corresponding to the equilibrium solution. The period $\tau(\varrho)$, likewise, is analytic in $\varrho$ and, moreover, $\tau(0)=\frac{2 \pi}{\left|\lambda_{1}\right|}$.

To prove this theorem we will assume the desired solutions in the form of power series with undetermined coefficients and work as in $\S 4$ with formal power series, proving their convergence only in the next section. For now the variables are to be viewed as finitely many indeterminates $z_{1}, \ldots, z_{m}$ having no definite numerical values, and the coefficients as certain complex numbers. With equality, sum, and product defined as between convergent series, the formal power series form a ring $R(z)$ without zero divisors. If new variables $\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{q}$ are introduced as power series in $z_{1}, \ldots, z_{m}$ without constant terms, each series in the new variables $\zeta$ can be rearranged to become a series in the old variables $z$, the process thus giving rise to an isomorphism between $R(\zeta)$ and a subring of $R(z)$. In addition, we define partial differentiation with respect to $z_{1}, \ldots, z_{m}$ in $R(z)$ by applying this operation termwise to each series, observing that for polynomials differentiation can be defined purely algebraically. The usual rules for differentiating sums and products then remain valid, as does the chain rule.

First, instead of a Hamiltonian system, let us consider again the general nonlinear system $(15 ; 1)$, this time under the assumption that the matrix $\mathfrak{A}$ has two eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}=-\lambda_{1}$ differing in sign only. We look for a particular solution where $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{m}$ are power series in two unknown functions $\xi=\xi(t), \eta=\eta(t)$, whereby $(15 ; 1)$ takes the form

$$
x_{\xi} \dot{\xi}+x_{\eta} \dot{\eta}=f(x)
$$

Under the additional assumption that the functions $\xi, \eta$ satisfy the two differential equations

$$
\dot{\xi}=\alpha \xi, \quad \dot{\eta}=\beta \eta
$$

with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ power series in $\xi, \eta$, our search for the particular solution is divided into two steps. Namely, suitably adjusting $\alpha(\xi, \eta), \beta(\xi, \eta)$, we

first consider the linear partial differential equation

$$
x_{\xi} \xi \alpha+x_{\eta} \eta \beta=f(x)
$$

for $x(\xi, \eta)$, and after that integrate the system (1). One advantage to this approach is that (2) can be treated within the ring of formal power series, without initial concern about convergence. The linear substitution $x=\mathbb{C} y$ transforms (2) into

$$
y_{\xi} \xi \alpha+y_{\eta} \eta \beta-\mathfrak{R} y=g(y)
$$

where the power series

$$
g(y)=\mathbb{C}^{-1} f(\mathbb{C} y)-\mathfrak{R} y
$$

begins with quadratic terms and, as before, $\mathfrak{R}=\left[\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{m}\right]$. In order that the $m+2$ power series $y_{k}(\xi, \eta)(k=1, \ldots, m), \alpha(\xi, \eta), \beta(\xi, \eta)$ be uniquely determined by comparison of coefficients in (3), we impose the following three conditions: The series $y_{1}-\xi, y_{2}-\eta$, and $y_{k}(k=3, \ldots, m)$ shall all begin with quadratic terms; there shall be no term of the form $\xi(\xi \eta)^{i}$ in $y_{1}-\xi$, and no term of the form $\eta(\xi \eta)^{i}$ in $y_{2}-\eta$; the series for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ shall be in powers of the product $\xi \eta=\omega$ only. The $m$ eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}=-\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{3}, \ldots, \lambda_{m}$ have already been assumed to be distinct, and in addition we stipulate that none of the $m-2$ ratios $\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\lambda_{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\lambda_{m}}{\lambda_{1}}$ be an integer.

Inserting the $m+2$ power series $y_{k}, \alpha, \beta$ with undetermined coefficients into equation (3) and comparing the linear parts, we see that the constant terms in $\alpha, \beta$ must be $\lambda_{1},-\lambda_{1}$. For $s$ a natural number, suppose that by comparing the coefficients of order $\leqq s$ in (3) we have already uniquely determined the terms up to order $s$ in $y$ and order $s-1$ in $\alpha, \beta$. Comparing the coefficients in terms of the form $\xi^{p} \eta^{q}(p+q=s+1)$ in (3), we observe that, since $g(y)$ begins with quadratic terms, for $g(y)$ the coefficient in question is a polynomial in the already known coefficients of $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{m}$. Let $\gamma$ be the desired coefficient of $\xi^{p} \eta^{q}$ in $y_{k}$. This term contributes $\left\{\lambda_{1}(p-q)-\lambda_{k}\right\} \gamma$ to the corresponding coefficient on the left side of (3). If it is not the case that both $k=1$ and $p=q+1$, nor that both $k=2$ and $q=p+1$, then only a polynomial in the already known coefficients of $y, \alpha, \beta$ must still be added to the left side, and because the factor in front of $\gamma$ is different from 0 , the coefficient $\gamma$ is uniquely determined. On the other hand, if either $k=1, p=q+1$ or $k=2, q=p+1$, then the second of our three conditions says that $\gamma=0$. Now, however, one must still add to the left side the unknown coefficient of $\omega^{q}$ in $\alpha$ if $k=1$, or the coefficient of $\omega^{p}$ in $\beta$ if $k=2$, while the other terms there are already known. Thus the inductive assumption holds also for $s+1$ in place of $s$,

and because the assumption is valid for $s=1$, equation (3) can be uniquely solved under the above conditions.

Let us now assume that the series $f(x)$ has only real coefficients and, furthermore, let $\lambda_{1}$ be purely imaginary, so that $\lambda_{2}=\bar{\lambda}_{1}$. We wish to investigate the effect of this on the series $y(\xi, \eta), \alpha(\xi, \eta), \beta(\xi, \eta)$. Setting $\mathfrak{C}^{-1} \overline{\mathfrak{C}}=\mathfrak{I}$ and $\mathfrak{I}^{-1} y=y^{*}$, we observe that by $(15 ; 6),(15 ; 7)$ the latter substitution has the simple form

$$
y_{l}=\bar{\varrho}_{l} y_{k}^{*} \quad\left(l=l_{k} ; k=1, \ldots, m\right)
$$

so that, in particular, $y_{1}=\bar{\varrho}_{1} y_{2}^{*}, y_{2}=\bar{\varrho}_{2} y_{1}^{*}, \bar{\varrho}_{1} \varrho_{2}=1$. Let us consider identity (3) transformed by complex conjugation of the coefficients, with the indeterminates $\xi, \eta$ remaining fixed. Since

$$
\overline{\mathfrak{C}}^{-1} \bar{f}(\overline{\mathfrak{C}} \bar{y})=\mathfrak{I}^{-1} \mathfrak{C}^{-1} f(\mathfrak{C} \mathfrak{I} \bar{y})
$$

where $\bar{y}=\bar{y}(\xi, \eta)$, equation (3) in context with (4) remains valid if $y, \alpha, \beta$ are replaced by $\mathfrak{I} \bar{y}, \bar{\alpha}, \bar{\beta}$. The first two components of the vector $\mathfrak{I} \bar{y}$ are $\bar{\varrho}_{1} \bar{y}_{2}=\bar{\varrho}_{1} \eta+\cdots, \bar{\varrho}_{2} \bar{y}_{1}=\bar{\varrho}_{2} \xi+\cdots$, while the other components again begin with quadratic terms. If $\xi, \eta$ are now replaced by $\varrho_{1} \eta, \varrho_{2} \xi$, it is apparent that also $\mathfrak{I} \bar{y}\left(\varrho_{1} \eta, \varrho_{2} \xi\right), \bar{\beta}\left(\varrho_{1} \eta, \varrho_{2} \xi\right), \bar{\alpha}\left(\varrho_{1} \eta, \varrho_{2} \xi\right)$ represent a solution of (3) fulfilling our three conditions, and it follows from the established uniqueness that

$$
\mathfrak{C} y(\xi, \eta)=\overline{\mathfrak{C}} \bar{y}\left(\varrho_{1} \eta, \varrho_{2} \xi\right), \quad \alpha(\xi, \eta)=\bar{\beta}\left(\varrho_{1} \eta, \varrho_{2} \xi\right)
$$

Therefore, if $\bar{\xi}=\varrho_{1} \eta$, then in case of convergence the values $\alpha(\xi, \eta), \beta(\xi, \eta)$ are complex conjugates and $\mathfrak{C} y(\xi, \eta)=x(\xi, \eta)$ is real.

The case where the series $f(x)$ has only real coefficients and $\lambda_{1}$ is real, whereby $\bar{\lambda}_{1}=\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}=-\lambda_{1}=\bar{\lambda}_{2}$, can be treated analogously. In that case $l_{1}=1, l_{2}=2$ and normalization achieves that $\varrho_{1}=\varrho_{2}=1$, whereupon $y_{1}=y_{1}^{*}, y_{2}=y_{2}^{*}$. The first two components of $\mathfrak{I} \bar{y}$ then already have the form $\bar{y}_{1}=\xi+\cdots, \bar{y}_{2}=\eta+\cdots$, so that this time

$$
\mathfrak{C} y(\xi, \eta)=\overline{\mathfrak{C}} \bar{y}(\xi, \eta), \quad \alpha(\xi, \eta)=\bar{\alpha}(\xi, \eta), \quad \beta(\xi, \eta)=\bar{\beta}(\xi, \eta)
$$

and, in case of convergence, for $\xi, \eta$ real also the values $x(\xi, \eta), \alpha(\xi, \eta)$, $\beta(\xi, \eta)$ are real.

Next we again neglect the reality requirement on $f(x)$, and consider the special case of a Hamiltonian system. It will be shown that then $\alpha(\xi, \eta)=-\beta(\xi, \eta)$. Accordingly, we alter the above notation to have the $2 n$ variables $z_{k}=x_{k}, z_{k+n}=y_{k}(k=1, \ldots, n)$ enter in place of the $m$ variables $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{m}$, with $x_{1}, y_{1}$ appearing in place of $y_{1}, y_{2}$ and correspondingly $\lambda_{n+1}=-\lambda_{1}$ replacing $\lambda_{2}=-\lambda_{1}$. The Hamiltonian function $H$ is considered with the linear canonical transformation already carried out, so that the quadratic terms have the normal form given in $(15 ; 21)$. Equa-

tions (3), (4) are now replaced by

$$
z_{\xi} \xi \alpha+z_{\eta} \eta \beta=\mathfrak{J} H_{z}
$$

and from this the formally constructed differential $d H=H_{\xi} d \xi+H_{\eta} d \eta$ becomes

$$
d H=H_{z}^{\prime} d z=\left(\alpha \xi z_{\xi}^{\prime}+\beta \eta z_{\eta}^{\prime}\right) \mathfrak{J}\left(z_{\xi} d \xi+z_{\eta} d \eta\right)=(\alpha \xi d \eta-\beta \eta d \xi) z_{\xi}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J} z_{\eta}
$$

Abbreviating $z_{\xi}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J} z_{\eta}=\Delta$, we then have

$$
\begin{gathered}
H_{\xi}=-\beta \eta \Delta, \quad H_{\eta}=\alpha \xi \Delta \\
\alpha \xi H_{\xi}+\beta \eta H_{\eta}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

whereby $H$ is now viewed as a power series in $\xi, \eta$.
With the aid of (6) we will show that $H$ is a series in $\omega=\xi \eta$ alone. Assume that it has already been shown that the terms of order $\leqq s$ in $H$ form a polynomial in $\omega$. Since

$$
H=\sum_{k=1}^{n} \lambda_{k} x_{k} y_{k}+\cdots=\lambda_{1} \omega+\cdots
$$

this is true for $s=2$. Let $\gamma \xi^{p} \eta^{q}(p+q=s+1)$ be a term of order $s+1$. Because $\alpha=\lambda_{1}+\cdots, \beta=-\lambda_{1}+\cdots$, in the identity

$$
\lambda_{1}\left(\eta H_{\eta}-\xi H_{\xi}\right)=\left(\alpha-\lambda_{1}\right) \xi H_{\xi}+\left(\beta+\lambda_{1}\right) \eta H_{\eta}
$$

the factors $\alpha-\lambda_{1}, \beta+\lambda_{1}$ are power series in $\omega$ with no constant term, and therefore, under the induction hypothesis, the terms of order $\leqq s+2$ on the right form a polynomial in $\omega$ alone, while on the left the coefficient of $\xi^{p} \eta^{q}$ is $\lambda_{1}(q-p) \gamma$. Therefore $\gamma=0$ when $p \neq q$, and the assertion is valid for $s+1$ in place of $s$.

Now that $H$ depends on $\omega$ only, we have

$$
H_{\xi}=\eta H_{\omega}, \quad H_{\eta}=\xi H_{\omega}
$$

and (6) becomes

$$
(\alpha+\beta) \omega H_{\omega}=0
$$

Since the series $\omega H_{\omega}=\lambda_{1} \omega+\cdots$ is not identically 0 , if follows that

$$
\alpha+\beta=0
$$

We return once more to the general case (2) and this time assume that our solution also fulfills (7). It will be shown in the next section that in that case, if $f(x)$ is convergent, also the series $y(\xi, \eta), \alpha, \beta$ converge for complex $\xi, \eta$ sufficiently small in absolute value. The differential

equations (1) thereby acquire meaning, while (7) now says that

$$
\dot{\omega}=\dot{\xi} \eta+\xi \dot{\eta}=(\alpha+\beta) \xi \eta=0
$$

so that $\omega, \alpha, \beta$ are independent of $t$. Consequently

$$
\xi=\xi_{0} e^{\alpha t}, \quad \eta=\eta_{0} e^{\beta t}
$$

If again the series $f(x)$ has only real coefficients and $\lambda_{1}$ is purely imaginary, the initial values $\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}$ of $\xi, \eta$ at $t=0$ are chosen so that $\bar{\xi}_{0}=\varrho_{1} \eta_{0}$ and $\left|\xi_{0}\right|$ is sufficiently small. By our earlier result the numbers $\alpha=\alpha(\xi, \eta)$ $=\alpha\left(\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}\right)$ and $\beta=\beta(\xi, \eta)=\beta\left(\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}\right)$ are then complex conjugates, and therefore, by (7), purely imaginary. Consequently, in view of (8), we have $\bar{\xi}=\varrho_{1} \eta$ for all real $t$, while $|\xi|=\left|\xi_{0}\right|$, so that, by the result mentioned, $x(\xi, \eta)$ is real. Thus (8) gives a family of real periodic solutions of the system $(15 ; 1)$ that depend on the complex parameter $\xi_{0}$. Since the right sides of this system of differential equations are independent of $t$, each solution curve is transformed into itself if $t$ is replaced by $t+c$ for an arbitrary real $c$, and therefore it is sufficient to choose $\xi_{0}=\varrho \geqq 0$. The value of the period is $\tau(\varrho)=\frac{2 \pi}{|\alpha|}$, with $\alpha=\lambda_{1}+\cdots$, so that $\tau(0)=\frac{2 \pi}{\left|\lambda_{1}\right|}$.
In the initial formulation we had $y_{1}=\xi+\cdots, y_{2}=\eta+\cdots$, which shows that, for $\varrho>0$ sufficiently small, $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$ do in fact depend on $t$, with $\tau(\varrho)$ being the primitive period. In view of (8), the power series obtained can be written as Fourier series in multiples of the angle $|\alpha| t$. Once we carry out the still missing convergence proof in the next section, we will, in particular, have the assertions of the existence theorem.

On the other hand, should $f(x)$ have real coefficients and $\lambda_{1}$ be real, so that also $\lambda_{2}=-\lambda_{1}$ is real, we choose the initial values $\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}$ real with $\left|\xi_{0}\right|,\left|\eta_{0}\right|$ sufficiently small. In that case the numbers $\alpha=\alpha(\xi, \eta)$ $=\alpha\left(\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}\right)$ and $\beta=-\alpha$ are real, and by (8) we have $\xi, \eta$ real for all real $t$. Thus, for $|t|$ sufficiently small, the series $x(\xi, \eta)$ converges and is real. In the $(\xi, \eta)$-plane (8) then defines a family of equilateral hyperbolas that depend on the real parameter $\xi_{0} \eta_{0}$, or, to be more exact, if the signs of $\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}$ are taken into account, four families of hyperbola branches. This gives four one-parameter families of real solution curves for the system $(15 ; 1)$. If, say, $\alpha>0$ and $\beta=-\alpha<0$, then $e^{\alpha t}$ or $e^{\beta t}$ goes to $\infty$ as $t \rightarrow \infty$ or $t \rightarrow-\infty$ respectively. Thus, according to (8), for $\xi_{0} \eta_{0} \neq 0$ the point $\xi, \eta$ remains in a given bounded neighborhood of the origin for a finite time interval only, while it moves into the origin along the $\eta$-axis if $\xi_{0}=0$, $\eta_{0} \neq 0, t \rightarrow \infty$, or along the $\xi$-axis if $\xi_{0} \neq 0, \eta_{0}=0, t \rightarrow-\infty$. The two possible signs for $\eta_{0}$ or $\xi_{0}$ in the latter case then give four solutions $x(t)$ that asymptotically approach the equilibrium solution as $t \rightarrow \infty$ or $t \rightarrow-\infty$ respectively. In contrast, for $\xi_{0} \eta_{0} \neq 0$ our solutions $x(t)$ have

the property that they remain in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $x=0$ only for a bounded time interval, being, so to speak, first captured and then cast out. This, however, does not mean that there are no periodic solutions among these, but only that their periodicity can no longer be determined by local analysis. With $e^{\alpha t}=q$, the $x_{k}(t)(k=1, \ldots, m)$ are Laurent series in the variable $q$ and have the purely imaginary period $\frac{2 \pi i}{\alpha}$ in $t$. To examine this result more closely, we introduce for comparison a system constructed analogously to $(15 ; 24)$; namely,

$$
\dot{x}=x+x(x y)^{g}, \quad \dot{y}=-y+y(x y)^{g}
$$

with $g$ again a given natural number. Then

$$
(x y)^{\prime}=2(x y)^{g+1}, \quad y \dot{x}-x \dot{y}=2 x y
$$

For $x y \neq 0$, it follows that

$$
x y=(a-2 g t)^{-\frac{1}{g}}, \quad x=b y e^{2 t}
$$

with $a, b \neq 0$ two integration constants, and therefore

$$
x=b^{\frac{1}{2}} e^{t}(a-2 g t)^{-\frac{1}{2 g}}, \quad y=b^{-\frac{1}{2}} e^{-t}(a-2 g t)^{-\frac{1}{2 g}}
$$

while for $x y=0$, there are the special solutions $x=0, y=c e^{-t}$ and $x=c e^{t}, y=0$ with $c$ a constant. Here $\lambda_{1}=1, \lambda_{2}=-1$, yet no solution of the two-parameter family (9) has a complex period. Thus, also for $\lambda_{1}$ real we have exhibited an analytic property of solutions to a Hamiltonian system that need not appear for $(15 ; 1)$ in general.

For a recursive determination of the coefficients of $y, \alpha, \beta$ by comparison of coefficients, it was essential that none of the $m-2$ quotients $\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\lambda_{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\lambda_{m}}{\lambda_{1}}$ be an integer, which in the Hamiltonian case is equivalent to none of the $n-1$ quotients $\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\lambda_{n}}{\lambda_{1}}$ being an integer. We wish to show by an example that in general this assumption is necessary for the validity of the existence theorem. With the cubic polynomial

$$
H=\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}\right)-x_{2}^{2}-y_{2}^{2}+x_{1} y_{1} x_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{1}^{2}-y_{1}^{2}\right) y_{2}
$$

as our Hamiltonian function, the corresponding system becomes

$$
\begin{cases}\dot{x}_{1}=y_{1}+x_{1} x_{2}-y_{1} y_{2}, & \dot{y}_{1}=-x_{1}-y_{1} x_{2}-x_{1} y_{2} \\ \dot{x}_{2}=-2 y_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{1}^{2}-y_{1}^{2}\right), & \dot{y}_{2}=2 x_{2}-x_{1} y_{1}\end{cases}
$$

with the obvious equilibrium solution $x_{1}=x_{2}=y_{1}=y_{2}=0$ and corresponding eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}=-\lambda_{3}=i, \lambda_{2}=-\lambda_{4}=2 i$. If $\lambda_{2}$ is taken as the

purely imaginary eigenvalue used in the existence theorem, then the assumption that $\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$ not be an integer is valid, implying the existence of a one-parameter family of periodic solutions with approximate period $\frac{2 \pi i}{\lambda_{2}}=\pi$. These solutions can be readily exhibited. Indeed, the uniqueness theorem for differential equations implies that for initial values $x_{1}=y_{1}=0$ the general solution is

$$
x_{1}=0, \quad y_{1}=0, \quad x_{2}=\alpha \cos 2 t-\beta \sin 2 t, \quad y_{2}=\alpha \sin 2 t+\beta \cos 2 t
$$

with $\alpha, \beta$ constant, i.e. a circle in the $\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$-plane traversed in time $\pi$, with no restriction on the radius. These are precisely the solutions given by the existence theorem, and here the period is equal to $\pi$ exactly, rather than only in the first approximation. On the other hand, if $\lambda_{1}$ is taken as the eigenvalue in the existence theorem, then, as we will show, there is no periodic solution with approximate period $\frac{2 \pi i}{\lambda_{1}}=2 \pi$, apart from the trivial equilibrium solution. Because in this case only one condition from the hypothesis of the existence theorem is violated, namely, that $\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}$ not be an integer, whereas here we have $\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}=2$, we see that the condition is essential. As we have just seen, all solutions with initial values $x_{1}=y_{1}=0$ have period $\pi$, and we now show that there are no other periodic solutions. By the uniqueness theorem for differential equations, the quantity $p=x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}$ remains positive throughout for the other solutions. With $q=x_{2}^{2}+y_{2}^{2}$, a simple calculation, aided by a suitable combination of the terms in complex form, leads from (10) to the differential equation

$$
\ddot{p}=4 p q+p^{2}
$$

Because $p^{2}>0,4 p q \gtrsim 0$, it follows that $p$ is a strictly convex function of $t$ and therefore certainly not periodic. Thus, in fact, apart from the given circular orbits, there are no additional periodic solutions to this system.

# § 17. The Convergence Proof 

Using the method of majorants already employed in $\S 4$, we now prove convergence of the formal power series constructed in the previous section. For this it will be assumed that the solution to $(16 ; 3)$ satisfies also the relation $\alpha+\beta=0$, which according to $(16 ; 7)$ is always the case for a Hamiltonian system.

For $h=h(\xi, \eta)$ a power series in $\xi, \eta$, the coefficient of $\xi^{p} \eta^{q}$ in $h(\xi, \eta)$ will be denoted by $\{h\}_{p q}$. According to $(16 ; 3)$, with the constructed power series inserted for $y$ and $\alpha$, we have

$$
\left\{\left(y_{\xi} \xi-y_{\eta} \eta\right) \alpha-\mathfrak{R} y\right\}_{p q}=\{g(y)\}_{p q}
$$

or more exactly, because

$$
\alpha=\lambda_{1}+\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\{\alpha\}_{r r}(\xi \eta)^{r}
$$

is a power series in $\xi \eta$ alone,

$$
\left((p-q) \lambda_{1}-\lambda_{k}\right)\left\{y_{k}\right\}_{p q}+\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(p-q)\{\alpha\}_{r r}\left\{y_{k}\right\}_{p-r, q-r}=\left\{g_{k}(y)\right\}_{p q}
$$

for $k=1, \ldots, m$, the sum here really breaking off with the term $r=\min (p, q)$. First, suppose that not simultaneously $k=1, p=q+1$ nor $k=2, q=p+1$. Then $(p-q) \lambda_{1}-\lambda_{k} \neq 0$, and there is a number $c_{1}>0$ independent of $k, p, q$ such that

$$
\left|\frac{1}{(p-q) \lambda_{1}-\lambda_{k}}\right|<c_{1}, \quad\left|\frac{p-q}{(p-q) \lambda_{1}-\lambda_{k}}\right|<c_{1}
$$

whereupon (1) implies that

$$
\left|\left\{y_{k}\right\}_{p q}\right| \leqq c_{1}\left|\left\{g_{k}(y)\right\}_{p q}\right|+c_{1} \sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left|\{\alpha\}_{r r}\left\{y_{k}\right\}_{p-r, q-r}\right|
$$

In the remaining cases, when $k=1, p=q+1$ or $k=2, q=p+1$, we always have $\left\{y_{k}\right\}_{p q}=0$ if $p+q>1$, while $\left\{y_{1}\right\}_{10}=\left\{y_{2}\right\}_{01}=1$, so that (1) gives

$$
\begin{cases}\left|\{\alpha\}_{q q}\right|=\left|\left\{g_{1}(y)\right\}_{p q}\right| & (p=q+1>1) \\ \left|\{\alpha\}_{p p}\right|=\left|\left\{g_{2}(y)\right\}_{p q}\right| & (q=p+1>1)\end{cases}
$$

For $h$ again a power series in $\xi, \eta$, let

$$
|\bar{h}|=\sum_{p, q}\left|\{h\}_{p q}\right| \xi^{p} \eta^{q}
$$

Thus $|\bar{h}|$ is obtained from $h$ by replacing all coefficients by their absolute values. Moreover, let $y_{1}^{*}=y_{1}-\xi, y_{2}^{*}=y_{2}-\eta, y_{k}^{*}=y_{k}(k=3, \ldots, m)$, and $\alpha^{*}=\alpha-\lambda_{1}$. Multiplication of (2), (3) by $\xi^{p} \eta^{q}$ and summation over $k, p, q$ then leads to the majorant relation

$$
(\xi+\eta)\left|\overline{\alpha^{*}}\right|+\sum_{k=1}^{m}\left|\overline{y_{k}^{*}}\right|<c_{1}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{m} \overline{\left|g_{k}(y)\right|}+\left|\overline{\alpha^{*}}\right| \sum_{k=1}^{m}\left|\overline{y_{k}^{*}}\right|\right)
$$

which no longer contains any derivatives.

We require an estimate for $\left[\overline{g_{k}(y)}\right]$, and will denote by $c_{2}, \ldots, c_{8}$ suitable positive constants. The $m$ functions $f_{k}(x)(k=1, \ldots, m)$ are by assumption regular in a neighborhood of $x=0$, and therefore the functions $g_{k}(y)$ defined by $(16 ; 4)$ are regular at $y=0$. If $g_{k}(y)$ is regular for $\left|y_{l}\right| \leqq c_{2}(l=1, \ldots, m)$ and in absolute value $\leqq c_{3}$, then Cauchy's estimate gives the relation

$$
g_{k}(y)<c_{3} \prod_{l=1}^{m}\left(1-\frac{y_{l}}{c_{2}}\right)^{-1}
$$

with $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{m}$ treated here as independent variables. Moreover, abbreviating $s=y_{1}+\cdots+y_{m}$, we have

$$
\prod_{l=1}^{m}\left(1-\frac{y_{l}}{c_{2}}\right)^{-1}<\left(1-\frac{s}{c_{2}}\right)^{-m}<\frac{c_{4}}{1-c_{5} s}
$$

and because $g_{k}(y)$ begins with quadratic terms, it follows that

$$
g_{k}(y)<\frac{c_{6} s^{2}}{1-c_{5} s} \quad(k=1, \ldots, m)
$$

On the other hand, with

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{m}\left[\overline{y_{k}^{*}}\right]=S
$$

certainly

$$
|\bar{s}|<\xi+\eta+S
$$

and hence (4), (5), (6) imply that

$$
(\xi+\eta)\left[\overline{\alpha^{*}}\right]+S<c_{1}\left(\frac{c_{6}(\xi+\eta+S)^{2}}{1-c_{5}(\xi+\eta+S)}+\left|\overline{\alpha^{*}}\right| S\right)
$$

In view of (6) it is sufficient to prove convergence of $S$ and $\left[\overline{\alpha^{*}}\right]$ in a neighborhood of $\xi=0, \eta=0$, and since here all the coefficients are $\geqq 0$, it is enough to consider the case $\xi=\eta$. Because $S$ also begins with quadratic terms in $\xi, \eta$, the expression

$$
2\left|\overline{\alpha^{*}}\right|+\xi^{-1} S=U
$$

is now a power series in $\xi$ with nonnegative coefficients and having no constant term, while (7) implies that

$$
U<c_{7}\left(\frac{\xi(1+U)^{2}}{1-2 c_{5} \xi(1+U)}+U^{2}\right)
$$

For

$$
\xi+U+\xi U=V
$$

so that

$$
2 \xi U+2 \xi U^{2}+U^{2}<V^{2}
$$

this gives

$$
\begin{gathered}
V<\xi+U+V^{2}<\xi+V^{2}+c_{7}\left(\frac{\xi+V^{2}}{1-2 c_{5} V}+V^{2}\right) \\
V<c \frac{2 \xi+V^{2}}{4-c V}, \quad c=c_{8}
\end{gathered}
$$

and it is enough to prove that $V$ converges for sufficiently small positive $\xi$. Instead of (8), let us consider the equation

$$
W=c \frac{2 \xi+W^{2}}{4-c W}
$$

for an unknown power series

$$
W=W(\xi)=\sum_{l=1}^{\infty} \gamma_{l} \xi^{l}
$$

If the right side of (9) is expanded in powers of $W$ and the series $W(\xi)$ then inserted, comparison of coefficients leads uniquely to a recursive determination of the coefficients $\gamma_{l}$, with the recursion formulas showing that, in view of (8), the series $W$ majorizes $V$. On the other hand, by (9) we have

$$
c W^{2}-2 W+c \xi=0, \quad(1-c W)^{2}=1-c^{2} \xi
$$

so that

$$
2 c W<(1-c W)^{-2}-1=\frac{c^{2} \xi}{1-c^{2} \xi}
$$

which proves convergence of $W(\xi)$ for $|\xi|<c^{-2}$. To make the computations as short as possible, we chose to forgo determining $c$ explicitly. However, by making a few of the estimates more precise one can obtain also a practical result by the above method.

# § 18. An Application to the Solutions of Lagrange 

The existence theorem formulated in $\S 16$ will now be applied to the planar three-body problem to prove existence of periodic solutions near the circular orbits of Lagrange. We again use the notation of $\S 14$, whereby the three particles in the given plane have coordinates $q_{2 k-1}$, $q_{2 k}(k=1,2,3)$ and, with $E=T-U$ defined by $(14 ; 1)$, the equations of motion in Hamiltonian form read

$$
\dot{q}_{k}=E_{p_{k}}, \quad \dot{p}_{k}=-E_{q_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 6)
$$

The canonical transformation $(14 ; 3),(14 ; 4)$ corresponded to a rotation of the coordinate system with constant angular velocity $\omega$ in the plane, and the transformed differential equations were

$$
\dot{x}_{k}=F_{y_{k}}, \quad \dot{y}_{k}=-F_{x_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 6)
$$

with
(2) $F=E+\omega Q=T-U+\omega Q, \quad Q=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\left(x_{2 k} y_{2 k-1}-x_{2 k-1} y_{2 k}\right)$,

$$
T=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{3} m_{k}^{-1}\left(y_{2 k-1}^{2}+y_{2 k}^{2}\right)
$$

Correspondingly, for the equilibrium solutions we had the equilateral and collinear solutions of Lagrange, with $\omega$ chosen in accordance with the respective conditions $(14 ; 7)$ and $(14 ; 10)$. There is clearly no loss of generality in assuming from now on that $\omega=1$.

For the application of the existence theorem in $\S 16$ to the system (1), we must expand the function $F=F(x, y)$ into a power series in a neighborhood of the corresponding equilibrium solution $x_{k}=x_{k 0}, y_{k}=y_{k 0}$ $(k=1, \ldots, 6)$ and compute the quadratic terms. With $z_{k}=x_{k}-x_{k 0}$, $z_{k+6}=y_{k}-y_{k 0}$, the Taylor expansion has the form

$$
F(x, y)=F\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k, l=1}^{12} s_{k l} z_{k} z_{l}+\cdots
$$

wherein the matrix $\mathfrak{S}=\left(s_{k l}\right)$ is chosen symmetric. According to $\S 15$ the corresponding eigenvalues $\lambda_{k}$ are determined by the twelfth degree equation $|\lambda \mathfrak{S}-\mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{S}|=0$, which can also be expressed as $|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|=0$. Subsequently we will actually carry out the computation of this determinant, but for the moment let us anticipate the result. In the equilateral case

$$
|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|=\lambda^{2}\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)^{3}\left(\lambda^{4}+\lambda^{2}+\gamma\right)
$$

where

$$
\gamma=\frac{27}{4} \frac{m_{1} m_{2}+m_{2} m_{3}+m_{1} m_{3}}{\left(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}\right)^{2}}
$$

while in the collinear case, with $P_{2}$ between $P_{1}$ and $P_{3}$, we have

$$
|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|=\lambda^{2}\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)^{3}\left(\lambda^{4}+(1-\alpha) \lambda^{2}-\alpha(2 \alpha+3)\right)
$$

where

$$
\alpha=\frac{m_{1}\left(1+\varrho^{-1}+\varrho^{-2}\right)+m_{3}\left(1+\sigma^{-1}+\sigma^{-2}\right)}{m_{1}+m_{2}\left(\varrho^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}\right)+m_{3}}
$$

with $\sigma=1-\varrho$, and $\varrho$ again the solution to $(14 ; 10)$. Hence in both cases $\lambda=0$ enters as a double eigenvalue and $\lambda= \pm i$ as a triple eigenvalue, whereas in the existence theorem the $\lambda_{k}$ were all assumed to be simple.

The root $\pm i$ could have been expected at the outset without any calculation. Namely, the original coordinates $q$ in the stationary coordinate system for the related equilibrium solution obviously have period $2 \pi$ with respect to time. Moreover, if the coordinates $q_{2 k-1}, q_{2 k}$ are replaced by $q_{2 k-1}+a, q_{2 k}+b(k=1,2,3)$ with $a$ and $b$ arbitrary linear functions of $t$, the equations of motion remain satisfied, so that by virtue of $(14 ; 3)$, $(14 ; 4)$ in this way each equilibrium solution $x_{k 0}, y_{k 0}$ gives rise to the solution

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
x_{2 k-1}=x_{2 k-1,0}+a c+b s, & y_{2 k-1}=y_{2 k-1,0}+\dot{a} c+\dot{b} s \\
x_{2 k}=x_{2 k, 0}-a s+b c, & y_{2 k}=y_{2 k, 0}-\dot{a} s+\dot{b} c \\
(k=1,2,3) & \text {. }
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

If $a$ and $b$ are chosen constant, this solution has period $2 \pi$ and is trivially seen from (8) to have a power series expansion in $e^{\lambda t}$ and $e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda=i$. On the other hand, the existence theorem in $\S 16$ leads directly to a series expansion of the solutions in powers of $e^{\alpha t}$ and $e^{-\alpha t}$, with $\alpha=\lambda+\cdots$ and $\lambda$ a purely imaginary eigenvalue. Thus the solution (8) makes the appearance of the eigenvalue $\pm i$ at least plausible. Furthermore, the fact that $\pm i$ is a multiple eigenvalue can be correlated to our being able to take any linear function of $t$ for $a$ and $b$ in (8). This observation, however, cannot be further motivated here, since the theory in $\S 16$ was carried out for simple eigenvalues only. There is an intrinsic reason also for the appearance of the eigenvalue $\lambda=0$, and we will later show that the angular momentum integral is responsible for this.

To be able to apply the existence theorem from $\S 16$, we must try to get rid of the multiple eigenvalues, and this can be achieved by reducing the Hamiltonian system (1) with the aid of the center of mass integrals and the angular momentum integral. First, in analogy to $(7 ; 4),(7 ; 5)$, we introduce relative coordinates of $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ with respect to $P_{3}$ by means of the linear substitution

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\xi_{2 k-1} & =x_{2 k-1}-x_{5}, & \xi_{2 k} & =x_{2 k}-x_{6} & & (k=1,2) \\
\xi_{5} & =x_{5}, \quad \xi_{6}=x_{6}, & \eta_{k} & =y_{k} & & (k=1, \ldots, 4) \\
\eta_{5} & =y_{1}+y_{3}+y_{5}, & \eta_{6} & =y_{2}+y_{4}+y_{6}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

whereupon the new equations of motion become

$$
\dot{\xi}_{k}=F_{\eta_{k}}, \quad \dot{\eta}_{k}=-F_{\xi_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 6)
$$

Because $U$ depends only on the differences between the original coordinates, the new variables $\xi_{5}, \xi_{6}$ do not appear in $U$, while from (2), (3) one finds that $F=T-U+Q$ with

$$
Q=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\left(\xi_{2 k} \eta_{2 k-1}-\xi_{2 k-1} \eta_{2 k}\right)
$$

(12) $T=\frac{1}{2} m_{3}^{-1}\left\{\left(\eta_{5}-\eta_{3}-\eta_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(\eta_{6}-\eta_{4}-\eta_{2}\right)^{2}\right\}+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{2} m_{k}^{-1}\left(\eta_{2 k-1}^{2}+\eta_{2 k}^{2}\right)$.

In particular, since $Q_{\xi_{k}}=\eta_{5}, Q_{\xi_{5}}=-\eta_{6}$, it follows from (10) that

$$
\dot{\eta}_{5}=\eta_{6}, \quad \dot{\eta}_{6}=-\eta_{5}
$$

which governs the motion of the center of mass in the rotating coordinate system. If in the original coordinate system the center of mass is now assumed to be at rest, and this is indeed the case for Lagrange's solution, then $\eta_{5}=0, \eta_{6}=0$ and solving (10) simplifies to integrating the reduced Hamiltonian system

$$
\dot{\xi}_{k}=F_{\eta_{k}}, \quad \dot{\eta}_{k}=-F_{\xi_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, 4)
$$

with $\xi_{5}, \xi_{6}$ subsequently determined from

$$
\dot{\xi}_{5}=F_{\eta_{5}}=\xi_{6}-m_{3}^{-1}\left(\eta_{3}+\eta_{1}\right), \dot{\xi}_{6}=F_{\eta_{6}}=-\xi_{5}-m_{3}^{-1}\left(\eta_{4}+\eta_{2}\right)
$$

by quadrature. It now follows from (13), (15) without further calculation that the numbers $i,-i$ appear as simple eigenvalues for the equilibrium solution of the reduced system (14), and therefore after this reduction the factor $\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)^{3}$ in the characteristic polynomials (4) and (6) is replaced by the first power of $\lambda^{2}+1$. The troublesome factor $\lambda^{2}$, however, still remains, but it will be removed next with the aid of the angular momentum integral, which now, because $\eta_{5}=\eta_{6}=0$, reduces to

$$
Q=\sum_{k=1}^{2}\left(\xi_{2 k} \eta_{2 k-1}-\xi_{2 k-1} \eta_{2 k}\right)
$$

First we wish to show that the double root $\lambda=0$ has its origin in the existence of the time-independent integral $Q$. Consider again the general system

$$
\dot{x}_{k}=f_{k}(x) \quad(k=1, \ldots, m)
$$

with $x=0$ an equilibrium solution and the $f_{k}(x)$ regular at $x=0$, so that we have a series expansion $f(x)=\mathfrak{A} x+\cdots$. Furthermore, assume that there exists an integral $\psi(x)$ for (17) that is analytic at $x=0$ and does not depend explicitly on $t$. If $\psi(x)=\psi(0)+c x+\cdots$ is the series for $\psi(x)$, wherein $c$ denotes a row vector, comparison of coefficients in the

linear terms of the partial differential equation

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{m} \psi_{x_{k}} f_{k}(x)=0
$$

shows that $c \mathfrak{A}=0$. If $c \neq 0$, it follows that $|\mathfrak{M}|=0$ and the characteristic equation $|\lambda \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{M}|=0$ has $\lambda=0$ as a root. Now from the expressions (2), (11), (16) for $Q$ it is easily seen that the first order partial derivatives do not all vanish at the equilibrium solution, so that the condition $c \neq 0$ is fulfilled. This explains the appearance of the factor $\lambda$ in (4) and (6), and because $|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|$ is an even function of $\lambda$, actually the factor $\lambda^{2}$ must appear. It should be added that in the rotating coordinate system the center of mass integrals are no longer independent of $t$, and therefore cannot take the place of $Q$ in this reasoning.

To remove the factor $\lambda^{2}$ we will attempt a further reduction of the Hamiltonian system of equations of motion with the aid of the angular momentum integral. For this we will find a canonical transformation that introduces $Q$ as a new variable - an idea carried out already by Jacobi even for the three-body problem in space, where the process is known as elimination of the node. The substitution to be used played an important role already in $\S 13$. To explain the idea, we consider an arbitrary Hamiltonian system $\dot{x}_{k}=H_{y_{k}}, \dot{y}_{k}=-H_{x_{k}}$ with unknown functions $x_{k}, y_{k}(k=1, \ldots, n)$, and assume that it possesses an integral $\psi(x, y)$ independent of $t$. We now pass from $x, y$ to new variables $\xi, \eta$ using a canonical transformation generated, as in $(3 ; 4)$, by $w=w(\xi, y)$ via

$$
\eta_{k}=w_{\xi_{k}}, \quad x_{k}=w_{y_{k}}(k=1, \ldots, n), \quad\left|w_{\xi_{k} y_{1}}\right| \neq 0
$$

In the process we wish to have $\eta_{n}=\psi(x, y)$. This leads to the partial differential equation

$$
w_{\xi_{n}}=\psi\left(w_{y}, y\right)
$$

for the generating function $w$. Suppose now that we have a solution to (19) which satisfies the condition $\left|w_{\xi_{k} y_{1}}\right| \neq 0$. If the columns with the respective variables $x, y$ and $\xi, \eta$ are denoted by $z$ and $\zeta$, and the Jacobian matrix $\zeta_{z}$ by $\mathfrak{M}$, then $\mathfrak{M}$ is symplectic, so that $\mathfrak{M} \mathfrak{J} \mathfrak{M}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{J}$, while $H_{z}=\mathfrak{M}^{\prime} H_{\zeta}$, $\psi_{z}=\mathfrak{M}^{\prime} \psi_{\zeta}$. Hence the expression

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\psi_{x_{k}} H_{y_{k}}-\psi_{y_{k}} H_{x_{k}}\right)=\psi_{z}^{\prime} \mathfrak{J} H_{z}
$$

remains invariant under the transformation from $z$ to $\zeta$; on the other hand, $\psi(x, y)$ being an integral, this expression is identically 0 . By (18), (19), however, $\psi=\eta_{n}$ and therefore $\psi_{\eta_{n}}=1$, while the other partial derivatives of $\psi$ as a function of $\zeta$ are all 0 . It thus follows from (20) that $H_{\xi_{n}}=0$

and consequently $H$ as a function of $\xi, \eta$ is independent of $\xi_{n}$. If in addition the given system has an equilibrium solution in whose neighborhood the Hamiltonian function and the canonical transformation (18) are analytic, the new differential equations

$$
\dot{\xi}_{k}=H_{\eta_{k}}, \quad \dot{\eta}_{k}=-H_{\xi_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, n)
$$

show that in the related matrix $\mathfrak{A}$ the row corresponding to the variable $\eta_{n}$ and the column corresponding to the variable $\xi_{n}$ are both 0 . This again exhibits a factor $\lambda^{2}$ in $|\lambda \mathfrak{E}-\mathfrak{A}|$, which then disappears upon passage to the reduced system

$$
\dot{\xi}_{k}=H_{\eta_{k}}, \quad \dot{\eta}_{k}=-H_{\xi_{k}} \quad(k=1, \ldots, n-1)
$$

Finally, with (22) integrated, the missing function $\xi_{n}$ is obtained from the differential equation $\dot{\xi}_{n}=H_{\eta_{n}}$ by quadrature.

We apply this to the Hamiltonian system (14), whereby $\xi, \eta, u, v, Q, 4$ will appear in place of $x, y, \xi, \eta, \psi, n$. Since by (11) the function $Q$ is bilinear in $\xi, \eta$, we seek $w(u, \eta)$ in the linear form

$$
w=\sum_{k=1}^{4} g_{k} \eta_{k}, \quad g_{k}=g_{k}(u)
$$

with the partial differential equation (19) then becoming

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{4} g_{k u_{4}} \eta_{k}=\sum_{k=1}^{2}\left(g_{2 k} \eta_{2 k-1}-g_{2 k-1} \eta_{2 k}\right)
$$

or

$$
g_{2 k-1, u_{4}}=g_{2 k}, \quad g_{2 k, u_{4}}=-g_{2 k-1} \quad(k=1,2)
$$

This has the particular solution

$$
\begin{gathered}
g_{1}=u_{1} c, \quad g_{2}=-u_{1} s, \quad g_{3}=u_{2} c+u_{3} s, \quad g_{4}=-u_{2} s+u_{3} c \\
c=\cos u_{4}, \quad s=\sin u_{4}
\end{gathered}
$$

with $\left|w_{u_{k} \eta_{1}}\right|=\left|g_{l u_{k}}\right|=-u_{1}$, so that the condition $\left|w_{u_{k} \eta_{1}}\right| \neq 0$ is satisfied if $u_{1} \neq 0$. Under this assumption the desired canonical transformation becomes

$$
\begin{gathered}
\xi_{1}=u_{1} c, \quad \xi_{2}=-u_{1} s, \quad \xi_{3}=u_{2} c+u_{3} s, \quad \xi_{4}=-u_{2} s+u_{3} c \\
\left\{\begin{array}{c}
v_{1}=\eta_{1} c-\eta_{2} s, \quad v_{2}=\eta_{3} c-\eta_{4} s, \quad v_{3}=\eta_{3} s+\eta_{4} c \\
v_{4}=\sum_{k=1}^{2}\left(\xi_{2 k} \eta_{2 k-1}-\xi_{2 k-1} \eta_{2 k}\right)=Q
\end{array}\right.
\end{gathered}
$$

by (18). The last equation transforms to

$$
v_{4}=u_{3} v_{2}-u_{2} v_{3}-u_{1}\left(\eta_{1} s+\eta_{2} c\right)
$$

and defining

$$
\eta_{1} s+\eta_{2} c=v_{0}
$$

we have

$$
v_{0}=u_{1}^{-1}\left(u_{3} v_{2}-u_{2} v_{3}-v_{4}\right)
$$

The fact that in the new coordinates $u, v$ the Hamiltonian function $F$ no longer depends on $u_{4}$ can be easily shown also by direct calculation. Namely, (25), (26) show that

$$
\begin{gathered}
v_{2}^{2}+v_{3}^{2}=\eta_{3}^{2}+\eta_{4}^{2}, \quad v_{1}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}=\eta_{1}^{2}+\eta_{2}^{2} \\
\left(v_{1}+v_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(v_{3}+v_{0}\right)^{2}=\left(\eta_{1}+\eta_{3}\right)^{2}+\left(\eta_{2}+\eta_{4}\right)^{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

and because $\eta_{5}=\eta_{6}=0$, formula (12) becomes

$$
T=\frac{1}{2}\left\{m_{1}^{-1}\left(v_{1}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}\right)+m_{2}^{-1}\left(v_{2}^{2}+v_{3}^{2}\right)+m_{3}^{-1}\left(\left(v_{1}+v_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(v_{3}+v_{0}\right)^{2}\right)\right\}
$$

Hence $T$ and $Q=v_{4}$ are free of $u_{4}$. To show the same for $U$, note that according to (24) the transformation from the $\xi_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 4)$ to the $u_{k}$ corresponds to a rotation through an angle $-u_{4}$ with the particle $P_{3}$ as pivot, whereby the points $\left(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}\right),\left(\xi_{3}, \xi_{4}\right)$ go over to $\left(u_{1}, 0\right),\left(u_{2}, u_{3}\right)$. Thus $\left(u_{1}, 0\right),\left(u_{2}, u_{3}\right)$ are the coordinates of $P_{1}, P_{2}$ in the rectangular Cartesian system with origin at $P_{3}$ and abscissa axis passing through $P_{1}$; in particular, $u_{1} \neq 0$. Because it depends only on the distances between the three particles, $U$ must be a function of $u_{1}, u_{2}, u_{3}$ alone. Upon introduction of these new coordinates the Hamiltonian system (14) now decomposes into the further reduced system

$$
\dot{u}_{k}=F_{v_{k}}, \quad \dot{v}_{k}=-F_{u_{k}} \quad(k=1,2,3)
$$

and the trivial residue

$$
\dot{u}_{4}=F_{v_{4}}, \quad \dot{v}_{4}=0
$$

The constant for $v_{4}$ is chosen in accordance with the original equilibrium solution, whereupon, after (27) is integrated, $u_{4}$ is obtained from (28) by quadrature. For the Hamiltonian system (27) the characteristic polynomials corresponding to the equilateral and collinear equilibrium solutions evidently are

$$
\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)\left(\lambda^{4}+\lambda^{2}+\gamma\right) \quad \text { and } \quad\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)\left(\lambda^{4}+(1-\alpha) \lambda^{2}-\alpha(2 \alpha+3)\right)
$$

where the values of $\gamma$ and $\alpha$ are given by (5) and (7).
First we discuss the equilateral case. Setting

$$
\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}-\gamma}=\varrho, \quad a_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+\varrho, \quad a_{2}=\frac{1}{2}-\varrho
$$

we have

$$
\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)\left(\lambda^{4}+\lambda^{2}+\gamma\right)=\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)\left(\lambda^{2}+a_{1}\right)\left(\lambda^{2}+a_{2}\right)
$$

Because $\gamma>0$, a multiple eigenvalue appears only when $\gamma=\frac{1}{4}$, and this case will be excluded. For $\gamma>\frac{1}{4}$ the numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}$ are distinct complex conjugates, while for $\gamma<\frac{1}{4}$ they satisfy $0<a_{2}<a_{1}<1$. By the existence theorem in $\S 16$, to the eigenvalues $\lambda_{3}=i, \lambda_{6}=-i$ there corresponds a one parameter family of periodic solutions to (27) that lie near the equilibrium solution and have the approximate period $2 \pi$. These solutions, however, are already known to us from the generalized solutions of Lagrange at the end of $\S 14$, emanating there from elliptic orbits in the vicinity of Lagrange's circular solutions. Namely, from the known formulas for the solution to the two-body problem it is easily seen that corresponding to the prescribed fixed value of the angular momentum integral $v_{4}$ there is still a family of elliptic solutions that can be parametrized by, say, the time of traversal $\tau$. With $c=\cos \left(t-u_{4}\right), s=\sin \left(t-u_{4}\right)$, a simple computation leads from $(14 ; 3),(14 ; 4),(9),(24)$ to the formulas

$$
\begin{gathered}
q_{1}-q_{5}=u_{1} c, \quad q_{2}-q_{6}=u_{1} s, \quad q_{3}-q_{5}=u_{2} c-u_{3} s, \quad q_{4}-q_{6}=u_{2} s+u_{3} c \\
p_{1}=v_{1} c-v_{0} s, \quad p_{2}=v_{1} s+v_{0} c, \quad p_{3}=v_{2} c-v_{3} s, \quad p_{4}=v_{2} s+v_{3} c
\end{gathered}
$$

so that $u_{1}, c, s, u_{2}, u_{3}, v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}$ do indeed have period $\tau$. From now on we may therefore restrict ourselves to the two other purely imaginary eigenvalue pairs $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{4}=-\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}, \lambda_{5}=-\lambda_{2}$ present when $\gamma<\frac{1}{4}$; that is, when

$$
27\left(m_{1} m_{2}+m_{2} m_{3}+m_{3} m_{1}\right)<\left(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}\right)^{2}
$$

This inequality is manifestly a definite restriction on $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$, being violated, for example, when $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}$. Even then, however, it does not follow that there are no additional periodic solutions, only that they cannot be obtained from the formulation in $\S 14$ and $\S 16$.

With $\lambda_{1}^{2}=-a_{1}, \lambda_{2}^{2}=-a_{2}$, we now wish to check whether one can satisfy the additional condition that $\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{1}}$ not be an integer for $k=2,3$. It follows from $-\lambda_{3}^{2}=1>-\lambda_{1}^{2}=a_{1}>\frac{1}{2}>a_{2}=-\lambda_{2}^{2}>0$ that $0<\left(\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}\right)^{2}<1$ and $1<\left(\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\lambda_{1}}\right)^{2}<2$, so that the condition is indeed met, and the existence theorem then gives a family of periodic solutions with the approximate period $\frac{2 \pi i}{\lambda_{1}}$. Along the same lines, to examine the ratio $\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{2}}$ for $k=1,3$, let $\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\lambda_{2}}=\varkappa_{2}$, whereupon $\lambda_{2}^{2}=-\varkappa_{2}^{-2}$ and $\varkappa_{2}^{-4}-\varkappa_{2}^{-2}+\gamma=0$. Consequently the inequality

$$
\gamma \neq g^{-2}-g^{-4}
$$

is required to hold for all integers $g>1$. Analogously, if $\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}}=\varkappa$ then $\lambda_{1}^{2}=\varkappa^{2} \lambda_{2}^{2}$, hence $\varkappa^{2}>1$ and $\left(\varkappa \lambda_{2}\right)^{4}+\left(\varkappa \lambda_{2}\right)^{2}+\gamma=0$, which in conjunction with $\lambda_{2}^{4}+\lambda_{2}^{2}+\gamma=0$ gives $\left(\varkappa^{4}-1\right) \lambda_{2}^{4}+\left(\varkappa^{2}-1\right) \lambda_{2}^{2}=0,\left(\varkappa^{2}+1\right) \lambda_{2}^{2}+1=0$, $\left(\varkappa^{2}+1\right)^{-2}-\left(\varkappa^{2}+1\right)^{-1}+\gamma=0$. This leads to the added requirement that

$$
\gamma \neq\left(g+g^{-1}\right)^{-2}
$$

again for all integers $g>1$. Thus, if $\gamma$ satisfies the countably many conditions (29), (30), the existence theorem yields a second family of periodic solutions with the approximate period $\frac{2 \pi i}{\lambda_{2}}$.

A similar analysis leads to periodic solutions in the vicinity of a collinear equilibrium solution. First of all, we have, as before, the family of Lagrange's elliptic solutions near a circular one, these associated with the eigenvalue pair $i,-i$. The other eigenvalues come from the roots $\lambda_{1}^{2}, \lambda_{2}^{2}$ of the quadratic equation

$$
x^{2}+(1-\alpha) x-\alpha(2 \alpha+3)=0
$$

with $\alpha$ defined by (7). Because $\alpha>0$, the roots of this equation are real and of opposite sign, say $\lambda_{1}^{2}<0, \lambda_{2}^{2}>0$. Thus, in addition to $\pm \lambda_{3}=i$, there is one other purely imaginary eigenvalue pair, namely $\pm \lambda_{1}$. Since for $x=-1$ the left side of (31) has the negative value $-2 \alpha(\alpha+1)$, the negative root satisfies $\lambda_{1}^{2}<-1=\lambda_{3}^{2}<0$ and therefore the quotient $\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\lambda_{1}}$ is not an integer. This then leads to a family of periodic solutions in a neighborhood of the collinear solution of Lagrange which have the approximate period $\frac{2 \pi i}{\lambda_{1}}$. Corresponding to the real eigenvalue pair $\pm \lambda_{2}$ there are, according to $\S 16$, four solutions to the three-body problem which asymptotically approach the equilibrium solution as $t \rightarrow \infty$ and $t \rightarrow-\infty$ respectively, as well as a family of solutions that remain in any fixed small neighborhood of the equilibrium solution for a bounded time interval only.

The formulation discussed in $\S 16$ allows these periodic solutions, whose existence we have proved here, to be explicitly expanded into Fourier series.

Finally, it remains to compute the determinant $|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|$. In the equilateral case we use the relative coordinates $\xi_{k}, \eta_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 6)$ and denote their values for Lagrange's solution by $\xi_{k}^{*}, \eta_{k}^{*}$. After a suitable rotation it may be assumed that $\xi_{1}^{*}=-\xi_{3}^{*}=\frac{r}{2}, \xi_{2}^{*}=\xi_{4}^{*}=\frac{r}{2} \sqrt{3}$. Next, replacing $\xi, \eta$ by $\xi+\xi^{*}, \eta+\eta^{*}$, we expand $U$ into powers of the $\xi_{k}$

$(k=1, \ldots, 6)$. For $1 \leqq k<l \leqq 3$, with the abbreviations

$$
\begin{aligned}
& s_{k l}=2 r^{-2}\left\{\left(x_{k}-x_{l}\right)\left(x_{k}^{*}-x_{l}^{*}\right)+\left(x_{k+3}-x_{l+3}\right)\left(x_{k+3}^{*}-x_{l+3}^{*}\right)\right\} \\
& q_{k l}=r^{-2}\left\{\left(x_{k}-x_{l}\right)^{2}+\left(x_{k+3}-x_{l+3}\right)^{2}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
r_{k l}^{-1}=r^{-1}\left(1+s_{k l}+q_{k l}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}=r^{-1}\left(1-\frac{1}{2} s_{k l}-\frac{1}{2} q_{k l}+\frac{3}{8} s_{k l}^{2}+\cdots\right)
$$

so that the terms of $-2 U$ quadratic in the $\xi_{k}$ are given by the expression

$$
\begin{aligned}
V=\frac{m_{1} m_{3}}{4 r^{3}}\left(\xi_{1}^{2}-6 \sqrt{3} \xi_{1} \xi_{2}-5 \xi_{2}^{2}\right) & +\frac{m_{2} m_{3}}{4 r^{3}}\left(\xi_{3}^{2}+6 \sqrt{3} \xi_{3} \xi_{4}-5 \xi_{4}^{2}\right) \\
& +\frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{r^{3}}\left\{\left(\xi_{2}-\xi_{4}\right)^{2}-2\left(\xi_{1}-\xi_{3}\right)^{2}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

By (11), (12) then $\mathfrak{S}$ is the matrix of the quadratic form $V+2 Q+2 T$ in the twelve variables $\xi_{k}, \eta_{k}(k=1, \ldots, 6)$. Setting $m_{k}^{-1}=\mu_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ and introducing the four-by-four matrices

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathfrak{A}=\frac{m_{1} m_{2} m_{3}}{4 r^{3}}\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
\mu_{2}-8 \mu_{3} & -3 \sqrt{3} \mu_{2} & 8 \mu_{3} & 0 \\
-3 \sqrt{3} \mu_{2} & 4 \mu_{3}-5 \mu_{2} & 0 & -4 \mu_{3} \\
8 \mu_{3} & 0 & \mu_{1}-8 \mu_{3} & 3 \sqrt{3} \mu_{1} \\
0 & -4 \mu_{3} & 3 \sqrt{3} \mu_{1} & 4 \mu_{3}-5 \mu_{1}
\end{array}\right), \\
& \mathfrak{B}=\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
\lambda & -1 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & \lambda & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \lambda & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & \lambda
\end{array}\right), \quad \mathfrak{C}=\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
-\lambda & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
-1 & -\lambda & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -\lambda & 1 \\
0 & 0 & -1 & -\lambda
\end{array}\right), \\
& \mathfrak{D}=\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
\mu_{1}+\mu_{3} & 0 & \mu_{3} & 0 \\
0 & \mu_{1}+\mu_{3} & 0 & \mu_{3} \\
\mu_{3} & 0 & \mu_{2}+\mu_{3} & 0 \\
0 & \mu_{3} & 0 & \mu_{2}+\mu_{3}
\end{array}\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

we see that

$$
|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|=\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)^{2}\left|\begin{array}{cc}
\mathfrak{A} & \mathfrak{B} \\
\mathfrak{C} & \mathfrak{D}
\end{array}\right|
$$

and since

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathfrak{E} & -\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{D}^{-1} \\
0 & \mathfrak{E}
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathfrak{A} & \mathfrak{B} \\
\mathfrak{C} & \mathfrak{D}
\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathfrak{A}-\mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{D}^{-1} \mathfrak{C} & 0 \\
\mathfrak{C} & \mathfrak{D}
\end{array}\right)
$$

we have

$$
\left|\begin{array}{ll}
\mathfrak{M} & \mathfrak{B} \\
\mathfrak{C} & \mathfrak{D}
\end{array}\right|=\left|\mathfrak{D} \mathfrak{M}-\mathfrak{D} \mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{D}^{-1} \mathfrak{C}\right|
$$

A direct computation of the last four-by-four determinant now leads to the result given in (4), (5).

In the collinear case one may take the values found in $(14 ; 8)$ for the coordinates $x_{2 k-1}=x_{2 k-1}^{*}(k=1,2,3)$ of the equilibrium solution, while $x_{2 k}^{*}=0$. With

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
u_{k} & =x_{2 k-1}-x_{2 k-1}^{*}, & u_{k+3} & =x_{2 k}-x_{2 k}^{*} \\
u_{k+6} & =y_{2 k-1}-y_{2 k-1}^{*}, & u_{k+9} & =y_{2 k}-y_{2 k}^{*}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

the expansion of $F$ in powers of $u_{1}, \ldots, u_{12}$ takes the form

$$
F(x, y)=F\left(x^{*}, y^{*}\right)+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k, l=1}^{12} r_{k l} u_{k} u_{l}+\cdots
$$

where $\left(r_{k l}\right)=\mathfrak{R}$ is a symmetric matrix of twelve rows. Since the linear substitution (33) is canonical, we have $|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|=|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{R}|$, while on the other hand, using (32), one finds that

$$
\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{R}=\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
-2 \mathfrak{B} & 0 & \lambda \mathfrak{E} & -\mathfrak{E} \\
0 & \mathfrak{B} & \mathfrak{E} & \lambda \mathfrak{E} \\
-\lambda \mathfrak{E} & \mathfrak{E} & \mathfrak{M}^{2} & 0 \\
-\mathfrak{E} & -\lambda \mathfrak{E} & 0 & \mathfrak{M}^{2}
\end{array}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathfrak{B}=m_{1} m_{2} m_{3} a^{-3}\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\mu_{2}+\mu_{3} \varrho^{-3} & -\mu_{3} \varrho^{-3} & -\mu_{2} \\
-\mu_{3} \varrho^{-3} & \mu_{3} \varrho^{-3}+\mu_{1} \sigma^{-3} & -\mu_{1} \sigma^{-3} \\
-\mu_{2} & -\mu_{1} \sigma^{-3} & \mu_{2}+\mu_{1} \sigma^{-3}
\end{array}\right) \\
\mathfrak{E}=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right), \quad \mathfrak{M}=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\mu_{1}^{4} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \mu_{2}^{4} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \mu_{3}^{4}
\end{array}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

and $a, \varrho, \sigma$ have the same meaning as in $\S 14$. The quadratic form in the three real variables $w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}$ constructed from the matrix $\left(m_{1} m_{2} m_{3}\right)^{-1} a^{3} \mathfrak{M}$ is given by

$$
\mu_{1} \sigma^{-3}\left(w_{2}-w_{3}\right)^{2}+\mu_{2}\left(w_{3}-w_{1}\right)^{2}+\mu_{3} \varrho^{-3}\left(w_{1}-w_{2}\right)^{2} \geqq 0
$$

and is therefore nonnegative, albeit degenerate, since it vanishes for $w_{1}=w_{2}=w_{3}$. It follows that $|\mathfrak{B}|=0$. For the twelve-by-twelve diagonal

matrix

$$
\mathfrak{R}=\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
\mathfrak{R} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \mathfrak{R} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \mathfrak{M}^{-1} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \mathfrak{M}^{-1}
\end{array}\right)
$$

we have $|\mathfrak{R}|=1$ and

$$
|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{R}|=|\mathfrak{R}(\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{R}) \mathfrak{R}|=\left|\begin{array}{cccc}
-2 \mathfrak{F} & 0 & \lambda \mathfrak{E} & -\mathfrak{E} \\
0 & \mathfrak{F} & \mathfrak{E} & \lambda \mathfrak{E} \\
-\lambda \mathfrak{E} & \mathfrak{E} & \mathfrak{E} & 0 \\
-\mathfrak{E} & -\lambda \mathfrak{E} & 0 & \mathfrak{E}
\end{array}\right|, \quad \mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{R} \mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{B} \mathfrak{R}
$$

Since the above twelve-by-twelve determinant is made up of three-bythree matrices that mutually commute, it may formally be treated as a four-by-four determinant, whereupon an elementary computation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}| & =\left|\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)^{2} \mathfrak{E}+\left(1-\lambda^{2}\right) \mathfrak{F}-2 \mathfrak{F}^{2}\right| \\
& =\prod_{k=1}^{3}\left(\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)^{2}+\left(1-\lambda^{2}\right) \gamma_{k}-2 \gamma_{k}^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with $\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}, \gamma_{3}$ the eigenvalues of $\mathfrak{F}$. Because $|\mathfrak{B}|=0$, also $|\mathfrak{F}|=0$, so that one of the eigenvalues is 0 , say $\gamma_{3}=0$. To determine $\gamma_{1}$ and $\gamma_{2}$ we recall that from the existence of the angular momentum integral one was able to deduce that $|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|$ vanishes for $\lambda=0$. Hence, after suitable ordering of $\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}$, we have

$$
0=1+\gamma_{2}-2 \gamma_{2}^{2}=\left(1+2 \gamma_{2}\right)\left(1-\gamma_{2}\right)
$$

Now together with $\mathfrak{B B}$ also $\mathfrak{F}$ is nonnegative, so that $\gamma_{2} \geqq 0$, and therefore $\gamma_{2}=1$. On the other hand, the trace of $\mathfrak{F}$ is given by

$$
\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3}=\gamma=a^{-3}\left\{m_{1}\left(1+\varrho^{-3}\right)+m_{2}\left(\varrho^{-3}+\sigma^{-3}\right)+m_{3}\left(1+\sigma^{-3}\right)\right\}
$$

so that $\gamma_{1}=\gamma-1$. Inserting these values of $\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}, \gamma_{3}$ into (34) and setting $\alpha=\gamma-2$, one then obtains the formula

$$
|\lambda \mathfrak{J}+\mathfrak{S}|=\lambda^{2}\left(\lambda^{2}+1\right)^{3}\left\{\lambda^{4}+(1-\alpha) \lambda^{2}-\alpha(2 \alpha+3)\right\}
$$

Since $x_{3}^{*}-x_{1}^{*}=\varrho a, x_{3}^{*}-x_{3}^{*}=\sigma a$, from $(14 ; 8)$ we have

$$
-1=m_{3}(\varrho a)^{-1}(\sigma a)^{-2}-m_{3}(\varrho a)^{-1} a^{-2}-\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right)(\varrho a)^{-3}
$$

$$
-1=m_{1}(\sigma a)^{-1}(\varrho a)^{-2}-m_{1}(\sigma a)^{-1} a^{-2}-\left(m_{2}+m_{3}\right)(\sigma a)^{-3}
$$

and recalling that $\varrho+\sigma=1$, by adding (35), (37), (38) we obtain the

relation

$$
\alpha=m_{1} a^{-3}\left(1+\varrho^{-1}+\varrho^{-2}\right)+m_{3} a^{-3}\left(1+\sigma^{-1}+\sigma^{-2}\right)
$$

Finally, addition of the two equations in $(14 ; 9)$ gives

$$
a^{3}=m_{1}+m_{2}\left(\varrho^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}\right)+m_{3}
$$

and (36), (39), (40) combine to give the result in (6), (7).

# § 19. Hill's Problem 

We seek periodic solutions to the three-body problem other than those found in the previous sections. Restricting ourselves again to planar orbits, we first neglect the particle $P_{2}$ and consider only the motion of two particles $P_{1}, P_{3}$. These travel along conic sections and, in particular, we will assume that they describe circles about their common center of mass $P_{0}$. We now replace the two particles $P_{1}, P_{3}$ by $P_{0}$ and reintroduce the third particle $P_{2}$. Of the possible orbits for $P_{0}$ and $P_{2}$ we again consider the particular case of circles. If $P_{2}$ is far enough from the other two particles, starting with this approximate solution we will arrive at an actual solution to the three-body problem.

A limiting case of the above problem which is easier to handle arises from considering not the general three-body problem, but the so called restricted three-body problem. This is a special case of the planar threebody problem in which the mass of $P_{3}$ is taken to be 0 and $P_{1}, P_{2}$ describe circular orbits. To obtain the differential equations of motion for $P_{3}$, we introduce in the given plane a rotating coordinate system with origin at the center of mass of $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$, so that in the new system $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are at rest. Without loss of generality the rotational velocity may be taken as $\omega=1$, so that by $(14 ; 5)$ the rectangular coordinates $x_{2 k-1}$, $x_{2 k}$ of $P_{k}(k=1,2,3)$ in the rotating coordinate system satisfy the differential equations

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{x}_{2 k-1} & =m_{k}^{-1} y_{2 k-1}+x_{2 k}, & & \dot{y}_{2 k-1}=U_{x_{2 k-1}}+y_{2 k} \\
\dot{x}_{2 k} & =m_{k}^{-1} y_{2 k}-x_{2 k-1}, & & \dot{y}_{2 k}=U_{x_{2 k}}-y_{2 k-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Upon elimination of $y_{2 k-1}, y_{2 k}$ these lead to the second order differential equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\ddot{x}_{2 k-1} & =2 \dot{x}_{2 k}+x_{2 k-1}+m_{k}^{-1} U_{x_{2 k-1}} \\
\ddot{x}_{2 k} & =-2 \dot{x}_{2 k-1}+x_{2 k}+m_{k}^{-1} U_{x_{2 k}}
\end{aligned} \quad(k=1,2,3)\right.
$$

wherein $m_{3}$ is not yet assumed to be 0 nor need $P_{1}, P_{2}$ be at rest. Now

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
m_{k}^{-1} U_{x_{2 k-1}}=\sum_{l \neq k} m_{l}\left(x_{2 l-1}-x_{2 k-1}\right) r_{k l}^{-3} \\
m_{k}^{-1} U_{x_{2 k}}=\sum_{l \neq k} m_{l}\left(x_{2 l}-x_{2 k}\right) r_{k l}^{-3}
\end{array}\right.
$$

and here the right sides make sense also when $m_{3}=0$. In that case formulas (1) with $k=1,2$ reduce to precisely the differential equations of the two-body problem for the particles $P_{1}, P_{2}$. Normalizing $m_{1}+m_{2}=1$, we set $m_{1}=\mu, m_{2}=1-\mu$ with $0<\mu<1$ and obtain $x_{1}=1-\mu, x_{2}=0$, $x_{3}=-\mu, x_{4}=0$ as a particular solution that corresponds to circular orbits for $P_{1}, P_{2}$ in the stationary coordinate system. The equations of motion for the third point $P_{3}$ with coordinates $x_{5}=x, x_{6}=y$ then become

$$
\ddot{x}=2 \dot{y}+x+F_{x}, \quad \ddot{y}=-2 \dot{x}+y+F_{y}
$$

with

$$
F=\frac{1-\mu}{r_{23}}+\frac{\mu}{r_{13}}=(1-\mu)\left\{(x+\mu)^{2}+y^{2}\right\}^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\mu\left\{(x+\mu-1)^{2}+y^{2}\right\}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

These are the differential equations for the restricted three-body problem. Although this is only a fourth order system, we are still far from knowing a complete solution. It is more convenient to express equations (3) in terms of the conjugate complex variables

$$
p=(x+\mu-1)+i y, \quad q=\bar{p}=(x+\mu-1)-i y
$$

where $p$ represents the vector from $P_{1}$ to $P_{3}$ in the complex plane. Then

$$
F=\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{p q}}+\frac{1-\mu}{\sqrt{(1+p)(1+q)}}, \quad F_{x}=F_{p}+F_{q}, \quad F_{y}=i\left(F_{p}-F_{q}\right)
$$

hence

$$
\bar{p}=-2 i \dot{p}+p-\mu+1+2 F_{q}, \quad \bar{q}=2 i \dot{q}+q-\mu+1+2 F_{p}
$$

and with

$$
G=p q+(1-\mu)(p+q)+2 F=p q+(1-\mu)(p+q)+\frac{2 \mu}{\sqrt{p q}}+\frac{2-2 \mu}{\sqrt{(1+p)(1+q)}}
$$

the differential equations assume the abbreviated form

$$
\bar{p}=-2 i \dot{p}+G_{q}, \quad \bar{q}=2 i \dot{q}+G_{p}
$$

To obtain a periodic solution of (5) we introduce yet another simplification which is due to Hill and has its basis in astronomy.

Namely, if $P_{2}$ is taken to be the sun, $P_{1}$ the earth, and $P_{3}$ the moon, then the mass $\mu$ of the earth is small relative to the mass $1-\mu$ of the sun; moreover, the sun and earth move approximately in circles about their common center of mass, while the moon remains nearly in a plane containing these circles. In addition, the mass of the moon is small relative to that of the earth and is taken to be $m_{3}=0$. Thus we seek a periodic solution to (5) for small values of $\mu$. In particular, since $|p|$ corresponds to the distance between the moon and the earth and is therefore small relative to the distance 1 between the sun and the earth, we seek a periodic solution for which $|p|$ is small. If as a first attempt we neglect the terms $-2 i \dot{p}, 2 i \dot{q}$ in (5) and in addition retain only the leading term $2 \mu(p q)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ of $G$, we obtain the system

$$
\ddot{p}=-\mu p(p q)^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \quad \ddot{q}=-\mu q(p q)^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

This is again the complex form of the differential equations of the twobody problem for $P_{1}, P_{3}$, encountered already in $(14 ; 12)$, having the circular orbits $p=\mu^{\frac{1}{2}} e^{i t}, q=\bar{p}=\mu^{\frac{1}{2}} e^{-i t},|p|=|q|=\mu^{\frac{1}{2}}$ as a particular solution. This suggests the transformation of variables

$$
p=\mu^{\frac{1}{2}} u, \quad q=\mu^{\frac{1}{2}} v
$$

whereby (5) becomes

$$
\ddot{u}=-2 i \dot{u}+H_{v}, \quad \ddot{v}=2 i \dot{v}+H_{u}
$$

with

$$
H=\mu^{-\frac{3}{2}} G=u v+\mu^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-\mu)(u+v)+\frac{2}{\sqrt{u v}}+\frac{2 \mu^{-\frac{3}{2}}(1-\mu)}{\sqrt{\left(1+\mu^{\frac{1}{2}} u\right)\left(1+\mu^{\frac{1}{2}} v\right)}}
$$

The expansion of $H$ in ascending powers of $\mu^{\frac{1}{2}}$ takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
H= & u v+\mu^{-\frac{1}{2}}(u+v) \\
& +2 \mu^{-\frac{3}{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{2} \mu^{\frac{1}{2}} u+\frac{3}{8} \mu^{\frac{3}{2}} u^{2}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{2} \mu^{\frac{1}{2}} v+\frac{3}{8} \mu^{\frac{3}{2}} v^{2}\right)+2(u v)^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\cdots \\
= & 2 \mu^{-\frac{3}{2}}+\frac{3}{4}(u+v)^{2}+2(u v)^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\cdots
\end{aligned}
$$

where the remaining terms contain only positive powers of $\mu^{\frac{1}{2}}$. Because $\mu$ is assumed to be small, we neglect these additional terms, and accordingly, instead of (8), consider the system

$$
\ddot{u}=-2 i \dot{u}+\frac{3}{2}(u+v)-u(u v)^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \quad \ddot{v}=2 i \dot{v}+\frac{3}{2}(u+v)-v(u v)^{-\frac{3}{2}}
$$

These are known as Hill's differential equations, and even here the general solution is not known. We will, however, determine periodic solutions to (9) through a power series expansion similar to that in $\S 16$.

To discover a form for this expansion, we consider again the simplified system

$$
\ddot{u}=-u(u v)^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \quad \ddot{v}=-v(u v)^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

which in analogy to (6) is obtained from (9) by neglecting the rest of the terms on the right. We seek periodic solutions for which $\bar{v}=u$, since then by (4), (7) the coordinates $x, y$ are real. One such solution is given by the circular orbits $u=u_{0} e^{\lambda t}, v=v_{0} e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda^{2}=-(u v)^{-\frac{1}{2}}=-\left(u_{0} v_{0}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, $v_{0}=\bar{u}_{0}$. Setting $u=\xi^{4}, v=\eta^{4}$ so as to eliminate roots, we then have $\xi=\xi_{0} e^{\alpha t}, \eta=\eta_{0} e^{-\alpha t}, \dot{\xi}=\alpha \xi, \dot{\eta}=-\alpha \eta$ with $\alpha=\frac{\lambda}{4}= \pm \frac{i}{4}\left(\xi_{0} \eta_{0}\right)^{-3}, \eta_{0}=\bar{\xi}_{0}$.
With this in mind, we now seek an exact solution to (9) in the form of power series

$$
u=\xi^{4}\left(1+\sum_{k, l} a_{k l} \xi^{3 k+4 l} \eta^{3 k-4 l}\right), \quad v=\eta^{4}\left(1+\sum_{k, l} a_{k l} \xi^{3 k-4 l} \eta^{3 k+4 l}\right)
$$

in two new variables $\xi, \eta$, with $k, l$ running over all pairs of integers satisfying $3 k \geqq 4|l|, k>0$, and the coefficients $a_{k l}$ as yet undetermined. The special form of this expression will be justified later. In accordance with the previous heuristic reasoning, the new unknowns $\xi, \eta$ are to satisfy the differential equations

$$
\dot{\xi}=\alpha \xi, \quad \dot{\eta}=-\alpha \eta, \quad \alpha= \pm \frac{i}{4}(\xi \eta)^{-3}
$$

and, since then $(\xi \eta)^{\prime}=\alpha \xi \eta+\xi(-\alpha \eta)=0$, it follows that

$$
\xi=\xi_{0} e^{\alpha t}, \quad \eta=\eta_{0} e^{-\alpha t}, \quad \alpha= \pm \frac{i}{4}\left(\xi_{0} \eta_{0}\right)^{-3}
$$

with $\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}$ nonzero constants.
The derivatives of the series for $u$ and $v$ are obtained by formally differentiating each term with respect to $t$ and then using (12) to express $\dot{\xi}, \dot{\eta}$ again in terms of $\xi, \eta$. With the abbreviation

$$
\zeta_{k l}=\xi^{3 k+4 l} \eta^{3 k-4 l}
$$

this gives

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\dot{u}=4 \alpha \xi^{4}\left\{1+\Sigma(2 l+1) a_{k l} \zeta_{k l}\right\}, & \dot{v}=-4 \alpha \eta^{4}\left\{1+\Sigma(2 l+1) a_{k l} \zeta_{k,-l}\right\} \\
\ddot{u}=(4 \alpha)^{2} \xi^{4}\left\{1+\Sigma(2 l+1)^{2} a_{k l} \zeta_{k l}\right\}, & \ddot{v}=(4 \alpha)^{2} \eta^{4}\left\{1+\Sigma(2 l+1)^{2} a_{k l} \zeta_{k,-l}\right\}
\end{array}
$$

Here, as well as in the rest of this section, the sum is always taken over the previously specified pairs of integers $k, l$, so that the exponents $3 k+4 l, 3 k-4 l$ in (14) are nonnegative and their sum $6 k$ is positive. We will refer to $k$ as the order of $\zeta_{k l}$. In addition, let

$$
A=-\Sigma a_{k l} \zeta_{k l}, \quad B=-\Sigma a_{k l} \zeta_{k,-l}
$$

To get rid of the negative exponents we multiply the first equation in (9) by $\xi^{2} \eta^{6}$ and, observing that $4 \alpha= \pm i(\xi \eta)^{-3}$, obtain for the resulting individual terms the series

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
-\ddot{u} \xi^{2} \eta^{6} & =1+\Sigma(2 l+1)^{2} a_{k l} \zeta_{k l} \\
-2 i \dot{u} \xi^{2} \eta^{6} & = \pm 2\left\{\zeta_{10}+\Sigma(2 l+1) a_{k l} \zeta_{k+1, l}\right\} \\
\frac{3}{2}(u+v) \xi^{2} \eta^{6} & =\frac{3}{2}\left(\zeta_{20}+\Sigma a_{k l} \zeta_{k+2, l}\right)+\frac{3}{2}\left(\zeta_{2,-1}+\Sigma a_{k l} \zeta_{k+2,-l-1}\right) \\
-u^{-\frac{1}{2}} v^{-\frac{3}{2}} \xi^{2} \eta^{6} & =-(1-A)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-B)^{-\frac{3}{2}}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Here the expression

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(1-A)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-B)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
=\left(1+\frac{1}{2} A+\cdots\right)\left(1+\frac{3}{2} B+\cdots\right)=1+\frac{1}{2} A+\frac{3}{2} B+\cdots
\end{array}\right.
$$

is to be expanded in powers of $A, B$ and the latter then replaced by their respective series in the $\zeta_{k l}$. Since $\zeta_{k l} \zeta_{g k}=\zeta_{k+g, 1+k}$, the right side of the last row in (15) also becomes a series of the form $\Sigma c_{k l} \zeta_{k l}$, as is already the case for the other rows. Thus, to satisfy the first equation in (9) formally, we have to determine the constants $a_{k l}$ so that the sum of the expressions in (15) vanish identically in the $\zeta_{k l}$.

Multiplying the second equation in (9) by $\xi^{6} \eta^{2}$, one obtains for the individual terms again series analogous to (15). These, however, can be obtained directly from (15) by interchanging $\xi$ and $\eta$, or equivalently, by writing $\zeta_{k,-l}$ in place of $\zeta_{k l}$. It should be noticed that on the left side of the second row the term $-2 i \dot{u} \xi^{2} \eta^{6}$ is to be replaced by $2 i \dot{v} \xi^{6} \eta^{2}$, so that the sign $\pm$ on the right also remains unchanged. Thus, comparison of coefficients for $\zeta_{k l}$ in the first equation of (9) leads to exactly the same conditions on the $a_{k l}$ as the corresponding comparison for $\zeta_{k,-l}$ in the second equation of (9). It is therefore sufficient to determine the unknown coefficients $a_{k l}$ so that the sum of the four terms on the right side in (15) vanishes identically in the $\zeta_{k l}$. We will show that this can be done in exactly one way, and that the $a_{k l}$ are all rational numbers.

To prove this assertion we proceed by induction on $k$. It is clear from our expression that the coefficients of the constant term do indeed match. Now let $r \geqq 1$, and suppose that it has already been shown that for $0<k \leqq r-1$ the $a_{k l}$ can be uniquely determined so that the coefficients for each of the terms of order $1,2, \ldots, r-1$ match and, furthermore, that these $a_{k l}$ are rational numbers. For $r=1$ the assumption is vacuous. To show that the inductional hypothesis is valid also for the $a_{r l}(4|l| \leqq 3 r)$, we observe that the series expansion of

$$
D=(1-A)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-B)^{-\frac{3}{2}}-1-\frac{1}{2} A-\frac{3}{2} B
$$

in terms of $A, B$ begins with quadratic terms. If $A$ and $B$ in this expression are replaced by their respective series in the $\zeta_{k l}$, the coefficient of $\zeta_{r l}$ in $D$ will then be a polynomial in the $a_{k s}$ with $k<r$, which have already been determined and are rational. Moreover, the coefficients of this polynomial are well defined rational numbers. Consequently the coefficient of $\zeta_{r l}$ on the right side of the last row in (15) is the sum of $\frac{1}{2} a_{r l}+\frac{3}{2} a_{r,-l}$ and an already known rational number. Comparison of coefficients of the corresponding term in the first three rows of (15) now leads to the condition

$$
\left\{(2 l+1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right\} a_{r l}+\frac{3}{2} a_{r,-l}=\varrho_{r l}
$$

where $\varrho_{r l}$ is an already uniquely determined rational number. For $l=0$ this gives

$$
3 a_{r 0}=\varrho_{r 0}
$$

which fixes $a_{r 0}$ as a rational number. On the other hand, for $l \neq 0$ we obtain a second equation

$$
\frac{3}{2} a_{r l}+\left\{(-2 l+1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right\} a_{r,-l}=\varrho_{r,-l}
$$

from (18) by changing the sign of $l$. Since the two linear equations (18), (20) for $a_{r l}, a_{r,-l}$ have the positive determinant

$$
\left\{(2 l+1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right\}\left\{(-2 l+1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right\}-\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{2}=4 l^{2}\left(4 l^{2}-1\right)
$$

and their coefficients are rational, they uniquely determine $a_{r l}, a_{r,-l}$, and indeed as rational numbers. This completes the induction.

We will subsequently prove that these series for $u, v$ converge absolutely if $|\xi|,|\eta|$ are sufficiently small. If in addition $\eta=\bar{\xi}$, then, since the $a_{k l}$ are real, the two quantities $u, v$ are complex conjugates, and therefore the original coordinates $x, y$ are real. This corresponds to choosing $\eta_{0}=\bar{\zeta}_{0}$ in (13).

As in $\S 17$, convergence is proved by using the method of majorants. For

$$
\phi=\Sigma c_{k l} \zeta_{k l}=\Sigma c_{k l} \xi^{3 k+4 l} \eta^{3 k-4 l}
$$

a formal power series with constant coefficients $c_{k l}$, we abbreviate $c_{k l}=[\phi]_{k l}$. Writing down once more the formulas used for comparing coefficients, from (15), (17) we obtain the relation

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\varrho_{k l}= & {\left[D \mp 2\left(\zeta_{10}+\Sigma(2 l+1) a_{k l} \zeta_{k+1, l}\right)+\right.} \\
& \left.-\frac{3}{2} \zeta_{20}(1+A)-\frac{3}{2} \zeta_{2,-1}(1+B)\right]_{k l}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

while, on the other hand,

$$
a_{k 0}=\frac{1}{3} \varrho_{k 0}, \quad a_{k l}=\frac{\left\{(1-2 l)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right\} \varrho_{k l}-\frac{3}{2} \varrho_{k,-l}}{4 l^{2}\left(4 l^{2}-1\right)} \quad(l \neq 0)
$$

To prove absolute convergence of the series for $u$ and $v$ in a complex neighborhood of $\xi=0, \eta=0$, it is enough to consider the particular case of $\xi=\eta$. Then $\zeta_{k l}=\xi^{3 k+4 l} \eta^{3 k-4 l}=\xi^{6 k}=\zeta^{k}$, where $\zeta=\xi^{6}$, and by (11) it is sufficient to prove convergence of

$$
Z=\Sigma\left|a_{k l}\right| \zeta^{k}
$$

for some $\zeta>0$. With this in mind we first majorize $D$. Because $\xi=\eta$, we have $A=B \prec Z$, where $\zeta$ is now treated as an indeterminate. Since, moreover, the expansion of $(1-A)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-B)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ in powers of $A, B$ has only positive coefficients, it follows that

$$
D \prec(1-Z)^{-2}-1-2 Z=\frac{3 Z^{2}}{(1-Z)^{2}}-\frac{2 Z^{3}}{(1-Z)^{2}} \prec \frac{3 Z^{2}}{(1-Z)^{2}} \prec \frac{3 Z^{2}}{1-2 Z}
$$

while in addition

$$
-\frac{3}{2} \zeta_{20}(1+A)-\frac{3}{2} \zeta_{2,-1}(1+B) \prec 3 \zeta^{2}(1+Z)
$$

Noting that $|2 l+1| \geqq 1$, we then obtain from (22), (24), (25) the estimate

$$
\sum_{k, l}\left|\frac{\varrho_{k l}}{2 l+1}\right| \zeta^{k} \prec \frac{3 Z^{2}}{1-2 Z}+3 \zeta^{2}(1+Z)+2 \zeta(1+Z)
$$

One observes next that the two quotients

$$
\frac{(2 l+1)\left\{(1-2 l)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right\}}{4 l^{2}\left(4 l^{2}-1\right)}, \quad \frac{\frac{3}{2}(2 l+1)}{4 l^{2}\left(4 l^{2}-1\right)}
$$

remain bounded over all integers $l \neq 0$, so that (23) and (26) lead to the relation

$$
Z \prec c_{1}\left\{\frac{Z^{2}}{1-2 Z}+\zeta^{2}(1+Z)+\zeta(1+Z)\right\}
$$

Here $c_{1}$, and later also $c_{2}, \ldots, c_{5}$, denotes a positive universal constant. With the aid of $1+Z \prec(1-2 Z)^{-1}$ it follows that

$$
Z \prec c_{1} \frac{Z^{2}+\zeta^{2}+\zeta}{1-2 Z} \prec c_{1} \frac{\zeta+(\zeta+Z)^{2}}{1-2(\zeta+Z)}
$$

and for $V=\zeta+Z$ one obtains

$$
V \prec c_{2} \frac{2 \zeta+V^{2}}{4-c_{2} V}
$$

As we saw in the concluding argument of $\S 17$, this implies convergence of $V$ for $\zeta<c_{3}$. Thus the power series for $u$ and $v$ are absolutely convergent in $|\xi|<c_{4},|\eta|<c_{4}$.

Let us now summarize this result. In the solutions

$$
\xi=\xi_{0} e^{\alpha t}, \quad \eta=\eta_{0} e^{-\alpha t}
$$

of the differential equations (12), choose $\eta_{0}=\bar{\xi}_{0}$ and $0<\left|\xi_{0}\right|=\varrho<c_{4}$. Then the quantity

$$
\alpha= \pm \frac{i}{4}\left(\xi_{0} \eta_{0}\right)^{-3}= \pm \frac{i}{4} \varrho^{-6}
$$

is purely imaginary, and therefore $\eta=\bar{\zeta},|\xi|=\varrho$ remains valid for all real $t$. Consequently the power series for $u$ and $v$ converge, while $v=\bar{u}$, so that in the original coordinates $x, y$ the solution is real. Furthermore $\xi, \eta$ as well as $\xi^{4}=\xi_{0}^{4} e^{4 \alpha t}, \eta^{4}=\eta_{0}^{4} e^{-4 \alpha t}$, and $\zeta_{k l}=\xi_{0}^{3 k+4 l} \eta_{0}^{3 k-4 l} e^{8 l \alpha t}$ are periodic functions of $t$. Inserting these functions into the series (11), one obtains $u, v$ and also $x, y$ as periodic functions of $t$ with period $\left|\frac{2 \pi i}{4 \alpha}\right|=2 \pi \varrho^{6}$. In view of (27), by a suitable translation of the time variable $t$, one evidently can achieve that $\xi_{0}=\eta_{0}=\varrho$. Setting $\varrho^{2}=\sigma$, we can choose this quantity as a free parameter in the interval $0<\sigma<c_{4}^{2}=c_{5}$. The series for $x, y$ are Fourier series in $e^{4 \alpha t}$, with the coefficients being power series in $\sigma$ that likewise converge absolutely for $|\sigma|<c_{5}$. If $t$ is replaced by $-t$, then $\xi$ and $\eta$ are interchanged, as are $u$ and $v$, so that the point $x, y$ goes over to its mirror image $x,-y$ relative to the $x$-axis. In the Fourier series this is expressed by $x$ being a cosine series and $y$ a sine series. In particular, the orbits lie symmetrically about the $x$-axis. One thus has a family of such symmetric solutions, which depend on the real parameter $\sigma$ and have period $2 \pi \sigma^{3}$. Admitting the two possible signs for $\alpha$ in (12), which manifest themselves also in the $\pm$ sign in the second equation (15), we obtain two different families of periodic solutions corresponding to the two directions in the moon's $P_{3}$ motion about the earth $P_{1}$. Namely, for the positive sign the direction is the same as of the earth rotating about the sun, while for the negative sign it is opposite.
