## 2. THE CONSERVATION OF ENERGY: THE LAGRANGE-JACOBI FORMULA

We return to the Eqs. (1.1), assuming, henceforth, that the center of mass is fixed at the origin. Define the function $U$, the negative of the potential energy, by the equation

$$
U=\sum_{1 \leqq j \in \varepsilon \leqq n} \frac{G m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}}
$$

Since $r_{j k}=\left|\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{r}_{k}\right|$, the function $U$ depends only on the positions $\mathbf{r}_{1}, \ldots, \ldots$, $\mathbf{r}_{n}$ of the particles. In any Cartesian coordinate system fixed at $O$, the vector $\mathbf{r}_{k}$ will have components $x_{k}, y_{k}, z_{k}$, so that $U$ can be regarded as a function of $x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1} ; x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2} ; \ldots ; x_{n}, y_{n}, z_{n}$, a total of $3 n$ real variables. By the gradient of $U$ in the direction $\mathbf{r}_{k}$, we shall mean the vector having components

$$
\left[\frac{\partial U}{\partial x_{k}}, \frac{\partial U}{\partial y_{k}}, \frac{\partial U}{\partial z_{k}}\right]
$$

It is convenient to denote this vector by $\partial U / \partial \mathbf{r}_{k}$. In general, if $f\left(\mathbf{a}_{1}, \mathbf{a}_{2}, \ldots\right.$, $\mathbf{a}_{n}$ ) is a function of $n$ vectors, we denote by $\partial f / \partial \mathbf{a}_{k}$ the vector

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{a}_{k}}=\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial \alpha_{k}}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \beta_{k}}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \gamma_{k}}\right]
$$

where $\alpha_{k}, \beta_{k}, \gamma_{k}$ are the components of $\mathbf{a}_{k}$ in a Cartesian coordinate system. This seems more suggestive than the customary symbols $\Delta_{k}{ }^{r j}$ or $\operatorname{grad}_{k} U$.

It is now readily verified that the Eqs. (1.1) become

$$
m_{k} \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_{k}=\frac{\partial U}{\partial \mathbf{r}_{k}}
$$

It follows from this that

$$
\sum_{k} m_{k} \dot{\mathbf{r}}_{k} \cdot \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_{k}=\sum_{k} \frac{\partial U}{\partial \mathbf{r}_{k}} \cdot \frac{d \mathbf{r}_{k}}{d t}
$$

The right-hand side is clearly the total derivative of $U$ with respect to $t$, since it can also be written

$$
\sum_{k}\left[\frac{\partial U}{\partial x_{k}} \frac{d x_{k}}{d t}+\frac{\partial U}{\partial y_{k}} \frac{d y_{k}}{d t}+\frac{\partial U}{\partial z_{k}} \frac{d z_{k}}{d t}\right]
$$

Therefore, because $v_{k}^{2}=\left(\dot{\mathbf{r}}_{k} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{r}}_{k}\right),(2.3)$ can be written

$$
\frac{d}{d t} \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} r_{k} v_{k}^{2}=\dot{U}
$$

Denote by $T$ the kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} m_{k} v_{k}^{2}$, Then $\dot{T}=\dot{U}$ or

$$
T=U+h
$$

when $h$ is a constant, the total energy.
An extremely important form of this law is the Lagrange-Jacobi identity. Define the moment of inertia $2 I$ of the system by the formula

$$
I=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} m_{k} r_{k}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} m_{k}\left(\mathbf{r}_{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}_{k}\right)
$$

Diferentiate the extreme members of this twice with respect to $t$. The result is

$$
\tilde{I}=\sum_{k} m_{k}\left(\mathbf{v}_{k} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{k}\right)+\sum_{k} \mathbf{r}_{k} \cdot m_{k} \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_{k}
$$

or, by the Eqs. (1.1),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{I} & =\sum_{k} m_{k} v_{k}^{2}+\sum_{k} \sum_{j} \frac{G m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}^{2}}\left[\left(\mathbf{r}_{j} \cdot \mathbf{r}_{k}\right)-r_{k}^{2}\right] \\
& =2 T+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} \sum_{j} \frac{G m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}^{2}}\left[r_{j}^{2}-r_{k}^{2}-r_{j k}^{2}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{I}-2 T= & \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} \sum_{j} \frac{G m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}^{2}} r_{j}^{2}-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} \sum_{j} \frac{G m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}^{2}} r_{k}^{2} \\
& -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} \sum_{j} \frac{G m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}}
\end{aligned}
$$

The first two terms on the right cancel one another, since they become identical if in the first one $j$ and $k$ are interchanged. The last term, by (2.1), is simply $-U$. Therefore $\tilde{I}=2 T-U$. By (2.4)

$$
\tilde{I}=T+h=U+2 h
$$

## 3. THE CONSERVATION OF ANGULAR MOMENTUM

The constancy of the energy reduces to the system from order $6 n-6$ to $6 n-7$. We now make a further reduction of three, to order $6 n-10$, by introducing the angular momentum c. Cross multiply each side of (1.1) by $\mathbf{r}_{k}$ and sum on $k$. Since $\mathbf{r}_{k} \times \mathbf{r}_{k}=0$, we conclude that

$$
\sum_{k} m_{k}\left(\mathbf{r}_{k} \times \overline{\mathbf{r}}_{k}\right)=\sum_{j_{u k}} \sum_{j} \frac{G m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}^{2}}\left(\mathbf{r}_{j} \times \mathbf{r}_{k}\right)
$$

The right-hand side vanishes because, with each occurrence of a term $\mathbf{r}_{m} \times \mathbf{r}_{k}$, the term $\mathbf{r}_{k} \times \mathbf{r}_{m}$ also occurs to cancel it. Therefore, the left-hand side is zero. Integration yields

$$
\mathbf{c}=\sum_{k} m_{k}\left(\mathbf{r}_{k} \times \mathbf{v}_{k}\right)
$$

when the constant c is the angular momentum.
Recall that if $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n} ; b_{1}, \ldots, b_{n}$ are $2 n$ real numbers, then the quantities $A, B, C$, defined by

$$
A=\sum_{k} a_{k}^{2}, \quad B=\sum_{k} b_{k}^{2}, \quad C=\sum_{k} a_{k} b_{k}
$$

are related by Cauchy's inequality* $C^{2} \leqq A B$. This has an important consequence, Sundman's inequality:

$$
c^{2} \leqq 4 I(\bar{I}-h)
$$

To prove (3.2) start with (3.1). This tells us that the longth $c$ of c satisfies the inequality

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathbf{c} \leqq \sum_{k} m_{k}\left|\mathbf{r}_{k} \times \mathbf{v}_{k}\right| \\
\leqq \sum_{k} m_{k} r_{k} v_{k}=\sum_{k}\left(\sqrt{m_{k}} r_{k}\right)\left(\sqrt{m_{k}} v_{k}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

*See Ex. 3.1.

Therefore, by Cauchy's inequality,

$$
c^{2} \leqq \sum_{k} m_{k} r_{k}^{2} \sum_{k} m_{k} v_{k}^{2}=(2 I)(2 T)
$$

According to (2.6), an immediate consequence is the inequality (3.2).

$$

## 4. SUNDMAN'S THEOREM OF TOTAL COLLAPSE

In this section we shall study the possibility that the system of particles suffers total collapse. By this we mean that all the particles came together at the same time, finite or infinite. We begin by writing the moment of inertia $2 I$ in a new form. Since

$$
\sum_{j} m_{j}\left(\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{r}_{k}\right)^{2}=\sum_{j} m_{j} r_{j}^{2}-2 \mathbf{r}_{k} \cdot \sum_{j} m_{j} \mathbf{r}_{j}+\sum_{j} m_{j} r_{k}^{2}
$$

we conclude from (1.2) that

$$
\sum_{j} m_{j}\left(\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{r}_{k}\right)^{2}=2 I-0+M r_{k}^{2}
$$

where $M$ is the total mass. Multiply each side by $m_{k}$ and sum. Since $r_{j k}^{2}=$ $\left(\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{r}_{k}\right)^{2}$, the result is

$$
\sum_{k} \sum_{j} m_{j} m_{k} r_{j k}^{2}=2 I M+M(2 I)=4 I M
$$

On the left-hand side we can delete the term for which $j=k$, since then $r_{j k}=0$. Therefore

$$
\sum_{1 \geqq 2 \leq k \leqq n} m_{j} m_{k} r_{j k}^{2}=2 I M
$$

Since total collapse means that all $r_{j k}$ become zero simultaneously, it follows from (4.1) that total collapse means that $I \rightarrow 0$, or that all particles simultaneously meet the origin.

First we show that if total collapse is to occur, it will not take forever to happen. In other words, $I \rightarrow 0$ as $t \rightarrow \infty$ is impossible. To prove this, return to (2.1). If all $r_{j k} \rightarrow 0$ as $t \rightarrow \infty$, then $U \rightarrow \infty$. Therefore, by (2.6), $\bar{I} \rightarrow \infty$ because $h$ is constant. This means that from some time on $\bar{I} \geqq 1$, say for $t \geqq t_{1}$. Integrate both sides and we get $I \geqq \frac{1}{2} t^{2}+A t+B$, where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Therefore, as $t \rightarrow \infty, I \rightarrow \infty$. This contradicts $I \rightarrow 0$.

Now we prove the more profound theorem* of Sundman. Total collapse

- This was known to Weierstrass, who never published a proof.

cannot occur unless the angular momentum is zero. To prove this, suppose that $I \rightarrow 0$ as $t \rightarrow t_{1}$, where $t_{1}$ is finie. Just as before, $U \rightarrow \infty$ and $\bar{I} \rightarrow \infty$ as $t \rightarrow t_{1}$. Therefore (we assume $t_{1}>0$ and let the reader modify the proof if $t_{1}<0$ ), $\bar{I}>0$ for some interval of time $t_{2} \leqq t \leqq t_{1}$. Since $I>0$, it follows from Ex. 3.2 that $-\bar{I} \geqq 0$ for $t_{2} \leqq t \leqq t_{1}$. Now multiply both sides of the inequality (3.2) by the positive number $-\bar{I} I^{-1}$. Therefore,

$$
-\frac{1}{2} c^{2} \bar{I} I^{-1}: \leqq h \bar{I}-\bar{I} \bar{I}
$$

Integrate both sides with respect to $t$, for $t \geqq t_{2}$. Then

$$
\frac{1}{2} c^{2} \log I^{-1} \leqq h I-\frac{1}{2} \bar{I}^{2}+K \leqq h I+K
$$

where $K$ is a constant of integration, so that

$$
\frac{1}{2} c^{2} \leqq \frac{h I+K}{\log I^{-2}}
$$

Now let $t \rightarrow t_{1}$. Since $I \rightarrow 0$, it follows that $c^{2} \rightarrow 0$. But $c$ is a constant. Therefore $c=0$.

## 5. THE VIRAL THEOREM

We now assume (see Ex. 2.6) that the system moves from the instant $t=0$ so that $U$ remains finite. There is a classical result, called the Virial Theorem, which states that if $I$ and $T$ remain bounded for $t>0$, then the two limits

$$
\bar{T}=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{t} T(\tau) d \tau, \quad \bar{U}=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{t} U(\tau) d \tau
$$

exist and $2 \hat{T}=\hat{U}$. Since $T=U+h$, it follows that if one of the limits exists, so does the other and $\hat{T}=\hat{U}+h$. Therefore the conclusion $2 \hat{T}=\hat{U}$ is equivalent to

$$
\hat{T}=-h
$$

In this section we shall prove a sharper form of the theorem which does not require boundedness.*

Theorem: The statement $\hat{T}=-h$ is true if and only if

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} t^{-2} I(t)=0
$$

We start with the Lagrange-Jacobi formula $\bar{I}=T+h$. Integrate once and divide by $t$. Then

$$
t^{-1} \hat{I}=t^{-1} \int_{0}^{t} T(\tau) d \tau+h+t^{-1} k
$$

where $k$ is a constant. Now let $t \rightarrow \infty$. From the definition of $\hat{T}$, the

* H. Pollard, A Sharp Form of the VirialTheorem, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, LXX, (1964), 703-5.
assertion (5.1) means that the right-hand side of (5.3) approaches zero, and hence the left-hand side also. Therefore (5.1) holds if and only if

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} t^{-1} \hat{I}=0
$$

It remains to show that each of (5.2) and (5.4) implies the other.
First suppose that (5.4) is true. Then, for each $\epsilon>0$, it follows that $\bar{I}<\epsilon t$, provided $t$ is large. Integrate both sides of the inequality. Then, $I<\epsilon\left(t^{2} / 2\right)+A t+B$, where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Therefore $t^{-2} I<$ $(\epsilon / 2)+t^{-1} A+t^{-2} B$. The last two terms can be made less than $\epsilon / 2$ by taking $t$ sufficiently large. Hence $t^{-2} I<\epsilon$ for large $t$. This proves (5.2).

Now let (5.2) be true. There is a theorem of Landau* which says that (5.4) is an immediate consequence, provided it is true that $\bar{I} \geqq-M$ for some finite number $M$. But $\bar{I}=T+h$. Since $T \geqq 0, \bar{I} \geqq h$, and the proof is finished.

## 6. GROWTH OF THE SYSTEM

We have seen in the case of the two-body problem that these cases occur: if $h<0$, the system is bounded, that is, the distance $r$ between the masses is bounded; if $h=0$, the distance $r$ grows like $|t|^{2 / 3}$ as $|t| \rightarrow \infty$, and if $h=0$, $r$ grows like $|t|$ as $|t| \rightarrow \infty$. The corresponding problems for three or more bodies is very difficult and we shall only obtain some elementary conclusions. It will be assumed that $U$ remains finite.

First we reconsider the function

$$
U=\Sigma \frac{G m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}}
$$

where the sum is taken over the indices such that $1 \leqq j<k \leqq n$. Since $r \leqq r_{j k}$, it follows that $U \leqq A / r$, where $A$ depends only on the masses.

Here is a simple consequence. Suppose $h<0$. Then $T=U-|h|$. Since $T \geqq 0$, we get $U \geqq|h|$. Therefore $A / r \geqq|h|$, or $r \leqq A|h|^{-1}$. If the energy is negative, the minimum distance is bounded. The converse is false. In general, there is no simple relation between the growth of the system and the sign of the energy.

* For a proof see D. V. Widder, The Laplace Transform, Princeton University Press, 1942, p. 143.

On the other hand, let $m, m^{\prime}$ be the two smallest masses. Then

$$
U \cong \Sigma \frac{G m m^{\prime}}{r_{j k}}=G m m^{\prime} \Sigma \frac{1}{r_{j k}}
$$

Now, at any particular instant, $r$ is one of the $r_{j k}$, so the sum on the right contains the term $1 / r$. Therefore $U \geqq G m m^{\prime} / r$. In summary,

$$
B \leqq r U \leqq A
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are positive constants depending only on the masses. This says, roughly, that $U^{-1}$ is a measure of $r$, the minimum spacing between particles.

We have shown that

$$
I=\frac{1}{2 M} \sum_{1 \leqq j \leqq k \leqq n} m_{j} m_{k} r_{j k}^{2}
$$

Now denote by $R$ the maximum of the $r_{j k}$ at time $t$. Then $I \leqq A_{1} R^{2}$, where $A_{1}$ depends only on the masses. Arguing as in the preceding paragraph, let $m, m^{\prime}$ be the smallest masses. Then

$$
I \geqq \frac{m m^{\prime}}{2 M} \sum r_{j k}^{2}
$$

Since $R$ is one of the $r_{j k}$ at time $t, I \geqq\left(m m^{\prime} / 2 M\right) R^{2}$. Therefore

$$
B_{1} R^{2} \leqq I \leqq A_{1} R^{2}
$$

where $A_{1}$ and $B_{1}$ are positive constants determined by the masses. This means, roughly, that $\sqrt{I}$ is a measure of $R$, the maximum spacing between particles.

The question arises naturally of how rapidly a system can expand. We prove this elementary result: If $r \geqq \delta>0$, then $R \leqq M t$, where $\delta>0$ and $M>0$. This says that if the particles do not get too close together at any time, then the maximum spacing cannot grow faster than the first power of $t$. To prove it, we start once again with the formula $\bar{I}=U+h$. Therefore $\bar{I} \leqq A / r+h$ or $\bar{I} \leqq A / \delta+h$. Integrating twice this says that $I \leqq D t^{2}$, where $D$ is a constant. Therefore, by (16.2), $B_{1} R^{2} \leqq D t^{2}$, or $R \leqq M t$, where $M=\left(D B_{1}^{-1}\right)^{1 / 2}$.

As a final application of these ideas, we repeat an argument used before. Since $\bar{I}=U+2 h, \bar{I} \geqq 2 h$. Suppose $h>0$. Then $I \geqq E t^{2}$, where $E$ is a positive constant. Therefore $A_{1} R^{2} \geqq E t^{2}$. Conclusion: if $h>0$, then $R$ grows at least as fast as the first power of $t$.

$$

## 7. THE THREE-BODY PROBLEM: JACOBI COORDINATES

In the special case $n=3$, the equations of Sec. 1 become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m_{1} \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_{1}=\frac{G m_{1} m_{2}}{r_{12}^{2}}\left(\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1}\right)+\frac{G m_{1} m_{1}}{r_{12}^{2}}\left(\mathbf{r}_{3}-\mathbf{r}_{1}\right) \\
& m_{1} \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_{2}=\frac{G m_{1} m_{2}}{r_{12}^{2}}\left(\mathbf{r}_{1}-\because_{2}\right)+\frac{G m_{2} m_{2}}{r_{22}^{2}}\left(\mathbf{r}_{3}-\mathbf{r}_{2}\right) \\
& m_{1} \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_{1}=\frac{G m_{2} m_{1}}{r_{12}^{2}}\left(\mathbf{r}_{1}-\because_{2}\right)+\frac{G m_{2} m_{2}}{r_{22}^{2}}\left(\mathbf{r}_{3}-\mathbf{r}_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $m_{1} \mathbf{r}_{1}+m_{2} \mathbf{r}_{2}+m_{3} \mathbf{r}_{3}=0$, one oi the $\mathbf{r}_{1}$ can be eliminated. We prefer to proceed in another way. We shall consider the motion of $m_{2}$ relative to $m_{1}$ by use of the vector $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1}$ and of $m_{2}$ relative to the center of mass $O^{\prime}$ of $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$. The location of this center is at $\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right)^{-1}\left(m_{1} \mathbf{r}_{1}+m_{2} \mathbf{r}_{2}\right)$ or $-\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right)^{-1} m_{2} \mathbf{r}_{2}$. The position $\rho$ of $m_{2}$ relative to this center is then $\mathbf{r}_{2}+\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right)^{-1} m_{2} \mathbf{r}_{2}$ or $M \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}_{2}$, where $\mu=m_{1}+m_{2}$. Therefore $\rho=$ $M \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}_{2}$.

It is easily verified, since $m_{1} \mathbf{r}_{1}+m_{2} \mathbf{r}_{2}+m_{3} \mathbf{r}_{3}=0$, that

$$
\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1}=\mathbf{r} ; \quad \mathbf{r}_{3}-\mathbf{r}_{1}=\rho+m_{2} \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r} ; \quad \mathbf{r}_{3}-\mathbf{r}_{2}=\rho-m_{1} \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}
$$

We return to (7.1). Divide the first equation by $m_{1}$, the second by $m_{2}$ and subtract. The result is

$$
\ddot{\mathbf{r}}=-\frac{G \mu}{r^{2}} \cdot \mathbf{r}+G m_{1}\left[\frac{\rho-m_{1} \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}}{r_{22}^{2}}-\frac{\rho+m_{2} \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}}{r_{12}^{2}}\right]
$$

Now multiply the last equation of (7.2) by $M \mu^{-1} m_{2}^{-1}$. This time we get

$$
\ddot{\rho}=-\frac{M G m_{1} \mu^{-1}}{r_{12}^{2}}\left(\rho+m_{2} \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}\right)-\frac{M G m_{2} \mu^{-1}}{r_{22}^{2}}\left(\rho-m_{1} \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}\right)
$$

The vectors $\mathbf{r}$ and $\rho$ are called Jacobi coordinates.
We denote the relative velocity $\dot{\mathbf{r}}$ by $\mathbf{v}$ and $\dot{\rho}$ by $\mathbf{V}$. Let $g_{1}=m_{1} m_{2} \mu^{-1}$, $g_{2}=m_{2} \mu M^{-1}$. It is readily verified that, in terms of the new coordinates $\mathbf{r}$ and $\rho$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbf{c}=g_{1}(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v})+g_{2}(\rho \times \mathbf{V}) \\
& 2 I=g_{1} r^{2}+g_{2} \rho^{2} \\
& 2 T=g_{1} v^{2}+g_{2} v^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

As a simple application, suppose that $c=0$. Then $\mathbf{r} \cdot \rho \times \mathbf{V}=0$ and $\rho \cdot \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}=0$. Therefore $\rho \cdot \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{V}=0$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v} \times \rho=0$. Now let $\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{r} \times$ $\rho$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{u} \times \dot{\mathbf{u}} & =(\mathbf{r} \times \boldsymbol{\rho}) \times(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{V})+(\mathbf{r} \times \boldsymbol{\rho}) \times(\mathbf{v} \times \boldsymbol{\rho}) \\
& =(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{V}) \boldsymbol{\rho}-(\boldsymbol{\rho} \cdot \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{V}) \mathbf{r}+(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v} \times \boldsymbol{\rho}) \boldsymbol{\rho}-(\boldsymbol{\rho} \cdot \mathbf{v} \times \boldsymbol{\rho}) \mathbf{r}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Now according to the formula (2.2) of Chap. 1, it follows that $(d / d t)(\mathbf{u} / u)$ $=0$ when $u \neq 0$. Therefore, as long as $\mathbf{r} \times \boldsymbol{\rho} \neq 0$, the vector perpendicular to $\mathbf{r}$ and $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ is a constant. It follows that all the motion is in one plane. We leave it to the reader to draw the same conclusion if $\mathbf{r} \times \boldsymbol{\rho}=0$ over an interval of time (Ex. 7.1).

## 8. THE LAGRANGE SOLUTIONS

We seek a very special set of solutions of the three-body problem, namely those for which all three purticles are moving uniformly in circles, in the same plane, and with the same angular velocity.

Introduce at $O$ a fixed coordinate system $x, y, z$ such that $z=0$ is the plane of motion. Let $\left(x_{0}, y_{0}, 0\right)$ be the coordinates of the mass $m_{k}$. Then $r_{k}=\left[x_{0}, y_{0}, 0\right]$ and the equations of motion (7.1) become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \ddot{x}_{k}=G \sum_{j \neq k} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{j k}^{2}}\left(x_{j}-x_{k}\right) \\
& \ddot{y}_{k}=G \sum_{j \neq k} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{j k}^{2}}\left(y_{j}-y_{k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $k=1,2,3$, and each sum con ains two terms.

Let the angular velocity of the particles in their plane of motion be $\omega$. Introduce into that plane a coordinate system $(\xi, \eta)$ which is rotating at angular velocity $\omega$. In this coordinate system the particles are at rest. We transfer the Eqs. (8.1) to the new coordinate system, starting with the relations

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{k}=\xi_{k} \cos \omega t-\eta_{k} \sin \omega t \\
& y_{k}=\xi_{k} \sin \omega t+\eta_{k} \cos \omega t
\end{aligned}
$$

We now differentiate each of these twice and substitute into (8.1). The following equations can then be derived for $\xi_{k}, \eta_{k}$. When they have been solved, then (8.2) can be used to find ( $x_{k}, y_{k}$ ).

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \ddot{\xi}_{k}-2 \omega \dot{\eta}_{k}-\omega^{2} \dot{\xi}_{k}=G \sum_{j \neq k} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{j k}^{2}}\left(\dot{\xi}_{j}-\xi_{k}\right) \\
& \ddot{\eta}_{k}+2 \omega \dot{\xi}_{k}-\omega^{2} \eta_{k}=G \sum_{j \neq k} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{j k}^{2}}\left(\eta_{j}-\eta_{k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $k=1,2,3$.
It is convenient to let $z_{k}=\xi_{k}+i \eta_{k}$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Multiply the second of Eqs. (8.3) by $i$ and add it to the first. We obtain

$$
\dot{z}_{k}+2 \omega i z_{k}-\omega^{2} z_{k}=G \sum_{j \neq k} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{j k}^{2}}\left(z_{j}-z_{k}\right)
$$

where, of course, $r_{j k}=\left|z_{j}-z_{k}\right|$.
Since the particles are at rest in the rotating system, each $\dot{z}_{k}$ is identically zero. Therefore the positions $z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}$ we seek satisfy the equations

$$
-z_{k}=\lambda \sum_{j \neq k} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{j k}^{3}}\left(z_{j}-z_{k}\right), \quad k=1,2,3
$$

where $\lambda=G \omega^{-2}$.
Let $\rho_{1}=\lambda r_{22}^{-3}, \rho_{2}=\lambda r_{31}^{-3}, \rho_{3}=\lambda r_{22}^{-3}$. The first and third equations, written out in full, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(1-m_{2} \rho_{2}-m_{1} \rho_{1}\right) z_{1}+m_{2} \rho_{1} z_{2}+m_{3} \rho_{2} z_{3}=0 \\
& m_{1} \rho_{1} z_{1}+m_{2} \rho_{1} z_{2}+\left(1-m_{1} \rho_{2}-m_{2} \rho_{1}\right) z_{3}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the center of mass is fixed at $O$, the missing equation can be replaced by

$$
m_{1} z_{1}+m_{2} z_{2}+m_{3} z_{3}=0
$$

There are two possibilities: (i) the points $z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}$ at some time $t$ are not in a straight line; (ii) they are. In case (i) the coefficients of corresponding $z_{k}$ in the preceding three equations are proportional. It follows immediately that $\rho_{1}=\rho_{2}=\rho_{3}=1 / M$, where $M$ is the total mass $m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}$. In other words, the only possible solution of the form (i) puts the masses at

the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $\left(G M_{10}{ }^{-7}\right)^{1 / 3}$. It is important to observe that this is independent of the size of the masses, so that the center of mass and the center of the triangle need not coincide. This solution is due to Lagrange. Case (ii) will be treated in the next section.
exercise 8.1. Prove in case (i) that the force on each mass passes through the origin.
exercise 8.2. In case (i) compute the quantities $T, U, I, h$. Answer $2 T=U=-2 h=2 \omega^{2} I$, where $U=q\left(m_{1} m_{2}+m_{2} m_{3}+m_{3} m_{1}\right)$ ant $q=(G \omega)^{2 / 3} m^{-1 / 3}$.

## 9. EULER'S SOLUTION

Suppose now that $z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}$ at some instant $t$ lic on a line $L$. Since $L$ must contain the center of mass, it passes through $O$ and we may as well suppose it is the $\xi$-axis so that all $\eta_{k}$ vanish. By retumbering the masses, we can arrange that $\xi_{1}<\xi_{2}<\xi_{3}$ so that $r_{12}=\xi_{2}-\xi_{1}, r_{23}=\xi_{2}-\xi_{3}, r_{13}=\xi_{2}-\xi_{1}$. The Eqs. (8.5) can be written

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\xi_{1} & =\lambda\left[\frac{m_{1}}{\left(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1}\right)^{2}}+\frac{m_{3}}{\left(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1}\right)^{2}}\right] \\
\xi_{2} & =\lambda\left[\frac{m_{1}}{\left(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1}\right)^{2}}+\frac{m_{3}}{\left(\xi_{2}-\xi_{3}\right)^{2}}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
m_{1} \xi_{1}+m_{2} \xi_{2}+m_{3} \xi_{3}=0
$$

Now let $\xi_{2}-\xi_{1}=a, \xi_{2}-\xi_{3}=a \rho, \xi_{3}-\xi_{1}=a(1+\rho)$. Equation (9.2) can be written in either of the forms

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m_{2} a+m_{3} a(1+\rho)=-M \xi_{1} \\
& m_{1} a(1+\rho)+m_{2} a \rho=M \xi_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Obtain $-\xi_{1} / \xi_{2}$ from each pair (9.1) and (9.3) by division. Equate the results to obtain

$$
\frac{m_{2}+m_{3}(1+\rho)}{m_{1}(1+\rho)+m_{2} \rho}=\frac{m_{1}+m_{2}(1+\rho)^{-2}}{m_{1}(1+\rho)^{-2}+m_{2} \rho^{-2}}
$$

The order of events is this. Suppose that $\rho$ can be determined from this equation. Replace $\xi_{1}$ on the left-hand side of (9.1) from its value given by (9.3). We find that

$$
a^{2}\left[m_{2}+m_{3}(1+\rho)\right]=\lambda M\left[m_{2}+m_{3}(1+\rho)^{-2}\right]
$$

This determines $a$. Then (9.1) determines $\xi_{1}$ and $\xi_{2}$. Finally, $\xi_{1}=a+\xi_{1}$.
This reduces the problem to the determination of positive values of $\rho$ which satisfy (9.4). It can be written

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(m_{2}+m_{1}\right)+\left(2 m_{2}+3 m_{1}\right) \rho+\left(3 m_{2}+m_{3}\right) \rho^{2} \\
& \quad-\left(3 m_{1}+m_{2}\right) \rho^{3}-\left(3 m_{1}+2 m_{2}\right) \rho^{4}-\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right) \rho^{5}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

If $\rho=0$, the left-hand side is positive; as $\rho \rightarrow \infty$ it approaches $-\infty$. Therefore it has a positive root. By Descartes' rule of signs it has at most one positive root. Hence there is a unique positive value of $\rho$ which solves the problem. It is clear that, by renumbering the masses, two other solutions to the main problem can be obtained. These collinear solutions are due to Euler.

## 10. THE RESTRICTED THREE-BODY PROBLEM

The three-body problem described by Eqs. (7.2) and (7.3) is a system of order twelve. Its equivalent formulation, given in Ex. 6.3, gives four vector equations (equal to twelve scalar equations), each of the first order. By use of Eq. (7.4) for the conservation of angular momentum and the conservation of energy, the system can be reduced by four, leaving eight. It is possible to eliminate the time from the eight, leaving a system of order seven, and finally, by a device due to Jacobi, it can be cut down to order six. Moreover, if the motion is planar, we use only two of the three dimensions of space and the order is reduced to four. This is the best that is known. After all these reductions, the problem is still extremely complicated and has kept mathematicians busy for over two hundred years.
We shall make an assumption which leads to a more tractable problem. It will be supposed that the mass $m_{2}$ is so small that it does not influence the motion of $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ (known as the primaries), but is affected by them in the usual way. Clearly, this is a sensible approximation to reality only if the path of $m_{2}$ does not come too close to $m_{1}$ or $m_{2}$. Mathematically what we do is to set $m_{2}=0$, or what is equivalent, $M=\mu$. The center of mass of the system is now the center of mass of the primaries. If we let $r_{12}=\rho_{1}$ and $r_{23}=\rho_{2}$, the Eqs. (7.2) and (7.3) become, respectively,

$$
\ddot{\mathbf{r}}=G \mu r^{-2} \mathbf{r}
$$

and

$$
\ddot{\rho}=-G m_{1} \rho_{1}^{-3}\left(\rho+m_{2} \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}\right)-G m_{2} \rho_{2}^{-3}\left(\rho-m_{1} \mu^{-1} \mathbf{r}\right)
$$

The first equation can be solved completely by the methods of Chap. 1 and so $r$ can be taken as a known solution of the two-body problem. Then the motion of $m_{2}$ is completely described by the single Eq. (10.2). This is called the restricted three-body problem. Because of our physical assumption on $m_{2}$, the customary conservation laws do not hold and we cannot use them to reduce the order of (10.2), which is six. We shall make

the further assumption that all the motion occurs in one plane (the planar restricted problem), which makes the order four. Finally, we shall suppose that the primaries rotate uniformly around their center of mass (the circular planar restricted problem).

The mean motion $n$ for the primaties, according to Eq. (10.1), is given by $\sqrt{G \mu} r^{-1 / 2}$, where $r$ is the distalice between the primaries. We may, therefore, use the rotating coordinate system described in Sec. 8 and illustrated in Fig. 11, with $\omega=n$. Th: primaries are at rest in this coordi-

nate system and we shall place them on the $\xi$-axis. Equation (8.4) is applicable with $k=3$. ## 11. THE CIRCULAR RESTRICTED PROBLEM: THE JACOBI CONSTANT

It must not be supposed that the problem described in the last chapter is an artificial one. Two examples will serve to make a rather convincing argument that the problem is worth investigating.

Apart from the sun itself, the heaviest of all the planets is Jupiter, which moves in an ellipse of small eccentricity; call it a circle for a first approximation. There is a group of tiny planets, the Trojan asteroids, whose motion is controlled principally by the sun and Jupiter; a first approximation to their motion is given by a solution of the restricted problem with the sun and Jupiter as primaries.

As another example, consider the motion of the earth around the sun to be circular. Then these two play the role of the primaries and the moon is $m_{2}$, the small mass.

We turn to the main problem of investigating Eqs. (10.5). They are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \ddot{\xi}-2 \dot{\eta}-\xi=\frac{\partial U}{\partial \xi} \\
& \dot{\eta}+2 \dot{\xi}-\eta=\frac{\partial U}{\partial \eta}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $U(\xi, \eta)=\left(1-\mu / \rho_{1}\right)+\left(\mu / \rho_{2}\right)$.
If we define a new "potential" $\Phi$ by

$$
\Phi(\xi, \eta)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\dot{\xi}^{2}+\eta^{2}\right)+U+\frac{1}{2} \mu(1-\mu)
$$

the equations read, more simply,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \ddot{\xi}-2 \dot{\eta}=\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \xi} \\
& \dot{\eta}+2 \dot{\xi}=\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \eta}
\end{aligned}
$$

The constant $\frac{1}{2} \mu(1-\mu)$ appearing in the definition of $\Phi$ is of no importance in these equations, but is convenient later.

We have already explained in Sec. 10 that the usual conservation laws do not hold. But a substitute exists. Define the Jacobi integral as the expression $2 \Phi-\dot{\xi}^{2}-\dot{\eta}^{2}$. Multiply the first of Eqs. (11.2) by $\dot{\xi}$, the second by $\dot{\eta}$ and add. The result is $\dot{\xi} \xi+\dot{\eta} \dot{\eta}=d \Phi / d t$. Therefore

$$
\dot{\xi}^{2}+\dot{\eta}^{2}=2 \Phi-C
$$

where $C$ is a constant, the so-called Jacobi constant. Equation (11.3) says that the Jacobi integral remains equal to $C$ during the motion. It is clearly determined by the initial values $\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}, \dot{\xi}_{0}, \dot{\eta}_{0}$.

The system (11.2) can be written

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{\xi}=\alpha, \quad \dot{\eta}=\beta \\
& \dot{\alpha}=2 \beta+\Phi_{1}, \quad \dot{\beta}=-2 \alpha+\Phi_{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

which is of order four. Now divide the first two by the third to eliminate time. We find that

$$
\frac{d \xi}{d \alpha}=\frac{\alpha}{2 \beta+\Phi_{2}}, \quad \frac{d \eta}{d \alpha}=\frac{\beta}{-2 \alpha+\Phi_{0}}
$$

From (11.3) we know that $\alpha_{2}+\beta^{2}=2 \Phi-C$. This can be solved for $\beta$ and the result substituted into the preceding pair to obtain equations of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{d \xi}{d \alpha}=F(\xi, \eta, \alpha) \\
& \frac{d \eta}{d \alpha}=G(\xi, \eta, \alpha)
\end{aligned}
$$

a second order system. If the solution is given by $\xi=f(\alpha), \eta=g(\alpha)$, then we proceed as follows. Since $\alpha=\dot{\xi}=f^{\prime}(\alpha) \dot{\alpha}$, we can, in theory, determine $\alpha(t)$. Then $\xi=\xi_{0}+\int_{0}^{t} \alpha(\tau) d \tau$, so that $\xi(t)$ is determined. Also $\dot{\eta}=\beta=$
$g^{\prime}(\alpha) \dot{\alpha}=\alpha g^{\prime}(\alpha) / f^{\prime}(\alpha)$. Therefore,

$$
\eta=\eta_{0}+\int_{0}^{t} \frac{\alpha g^{\prime}(\alpha)}{f^{\prime}(\alpha)} d \tau
$$

where $\alpha(\tau)$ must be substituted for $\alpha$ under the integral sign. In practice, this method is of no use since $f(\alpha)$ and $g(\alpha)$ are impossible to determine explicitly. Instead of pursuing this line of thought further, we shall seek some simple explicit solutions, analogous to those found in Secs. 8 and 9 for the unrestricted problem.

$$
\begin{aligned}

& \frac{d \xi}{d t}=p+\eta \\
& \frac{d \eta}{d t}=P-\xi
\end{aligned}
$$

Now define $H(\xi, \eta ; p, P)=\frac{1}{2}(p+\eta)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(P-\xi)^{2}-\Phi(\xi, \eta)$ and verify that the system can be written in the Hamilton-Jacobi form

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\dot{\xi}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, & \dot{p}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial \xi} \\
\dot{\eta}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial P}, & \dot{P}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial \eta}
\end{array}
$$

The initial values are $\xi_{0}, \eta_{0}, p_{0}=\dot{\xi}_{0}-\eta_{0}, \dot{P}_{0}=\dot{\eta}_{0}+\xi_{0}$.

## 12. EQUILIBRIUM SOLUTIONS

We seek solutions of the restricted problem for which the small mass $m_{2}$ remains at rest in the relative coordinate system. These are called equilibrium solutions. Since $\xi$ and $\eta$ are constant, the Eqs. (11.2) become simply

$$
\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \xi}=\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \eta}=0
$$

It is convenient to express $\Phi$ in terms of the so-called bipolar coordinates $\mu$ and $\mu_{1}$ of the point ( $\left.\xi, \eta\right)$ since $0^{\prime}$ ' $\beta$ ' $\beta$ $^{\prime}$ $\eta^{\prime}$, we find that $\xi^{\prime}-\eta^{\prime}=(1-\mu) \cdot-\infty-\infty-\mu$ form $\because \because$ and the definition of $U$, we get

$$
\Phi=(1-\mu)\left(\frac{1}{2} \rho_{1}^{2}+\rho_{1}^{\prime \prime}\right)+\mu\left(\frac{1}{2} \rho_{2}^{2}+\rho_{2}^{\prime \prime}\right)
$$

The relations (12.1) become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (1-\mu)\left[\rho_{1}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{\xi+\mu}{\rho_{1}}+\mu\left[\rho_{2}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{\xi-1+\mu}{\rho_{2}}=0 \\
& (1-\mu)\left[\rho_{1}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{\eta}{\rho_{1}}+\mu\left[\rho_{2}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{\eta}{\rho_{2}}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

First suppose that $\eta \neq 0$. Then

$$
(1-\mu)\left[\rho_{1}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{1}{\rho_{1}}+\mu\left[\rho_{2}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{1}{\rho_{2}}=0
$$

This means that the terms containing $\xi$ in the first of Eqs. (12.3) drop out. In addition, a factor of $\mu(1-\mu)$ cancels and we are left with

$$
\left[\rho_{1}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{1}{\rho_{1}}-\left[\rho_{2}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{1}{\rho_{2}}=0
$$

The only simultaneous solution of this equation and the preceding one is $1=1=1$. Therefore, if $=0$, there are precisely two equilibrium s: in: the ser:ices of :so equilateral triangles based on the line joining $(-\ldots, 0)$ and $(1-\ldots, 0)$. These are the points $L$, and $L$, indicated in lig. 12.

On the other hand, if $\eta=0$ the Eqs. (12.3) reduce to the single one

$$
(1-\mu)\left[\rho_{1}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{\xi+\mu}{\rho_{1}}+\mu\left[\rho_{2}-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}^{\prime}}\right] \frac{\xi-1+\mu}{\rho_{2}}=0
$$

where $\rho_{1}=|\xi+\mu|, \rho_{2}=|\xi-1+\mu|$. There are three cases: $\xi<-\mu$, $-\mu<\xi<1-\mu, \xi>1-\mu$, in which we have, respectively,
(a)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_{1}=-\xi-\mu, \quad \rho_{2}=1-\xi-\mu, \quad \rho_{2}=1+\rho_{1} ; \\
& \rho_{1}=\xi+\mu, \quad \rho_{2}=1-\xi-\mu, \quad \rho_{2}=1-\rho_{1} ; \\
& \rho_{1}=\xi+\mu, \quad \rho_{2}=\xi+\mu-1, \quad \rho_{2}=\rho_{1}-1 .
\end{aligned}
$$

We can rewrite (12.4) in each of the cases as follows.
(a) Let $\rho_{1}=\rho, \rho_{2}=1+\rho$. Then

$$
(1-\mu)\left[\rho-\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\right]+\mu\left[\rho+1-\frac{1}{(\rho+1)^{2}}\right]=0
$$

(b) Let $\rho_{1}=\rho, \rho_{2}=1-\rho$. Then

$$
(1-\mu)\left[\rho^{2}-\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\right]=\mu\left[1-\rho-\frac{1}{(1-\rho)^{2}}\right]
$$

(c) Let $\rho_{2}=\rho, \rho_{1}=1+\rho$. Then

$$
\mu\left[1+\rho-\frac{1}{(1+\rho)^{2}}\right]+(1-\mu)\left[\rho-\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\right]=0
$$

Each of these three equations has a single positive solution for $\rho$. In cases (a) and (c) this can be seen as follows. Each of the equations is of the form

$$
F(\rho)=\frac{\rho-\rho^{-2}}{\rho+1-(\rho+1)^{-2}}=-c
$$

where $c \succ 0$. It is easily verified that $F^{\prime}(\rho)>0$, so that $F$ is strictly increasing. Moreover, $F(0+1 \cdots \cdots, F(1) \cdots 0$. Therefore $F$ assumes the value $-c$ at precisely one value of $\rho$ between 0 and 1 . The solutions are denoted by $L_{1}$ in case (a) and by $L_{2}$ in case (c), as indicated in Fig. 12.

The case (b) is similar. Now the equation is

$$
F_{1}(\rho)=\frac{1-\rho-(1-\rho)^{-2}}{\rho-\rho^{-2}}=\frac{1-\mu}{\mu} \geqq 1
$$

because $\mu \leqq \frac{1}{2}$. The function $F_{1}(\rho)$ is increasing in the interval $\frac{1}{2} \leqq \rho<1$. Moreover, $F_{1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=1, F_{1}(1-)=\infty$, so that $F_{1}$ assumes the value $1-\mu / \mu$ precisely once in the interval $\frac{1}{2} \leqq \rho<1$. This means that the equilibrium point lies closer to the lighter mass than to the other, unless $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$; it is called $L_{2}$ (see Fig. 12).

The five points $L_{1}$ are called libration points. The first three are called he Euler points and the last two the Lagrange points.

## 13. THE CURVES OF ZERO VELOCITY

The equilibrium solutions are the only solutions of (11.2) that are known explicitly. However, by use of the Jacobi integral it is possible to derive some important general properties of all solutions. According to the formula (11.3), it is true that

$$
v^{2}=2 \Phi-C
$$

where $v$ is the relative velocity $\left(\frac{1}{2}^{2}+\dot{\eta}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}, C$ is the Jacobi constant of the motion, and, in bipolar form,

$$
2 \Phi=(1-\mu)\left(\rho_{1}^{2}+2 \rho_{1}^{-1}\right)+\mu\left(\rho_{2}^{2}+2 \rho_{2}^{-1}\right)
$$

We shall consider the level curves $2 \Phi=C$, which, in accordance with (13.1), are called the curves of zero velocity. It will now be proved that the minimum value of $2 \Phi$ is 3 , so that no level curve exists when $C<3$. We start with the assertion that if $0 \leqq \mu \leqq 1, A \geqq 0, B \geqq 0$, then

$$
A \mu+B(1-\mu) \geqq \min (A, B)
$$

For if $A \geqq B$, then $A \mu+B(1-\mu) \geqq B \mu+B(1-\mu)=B=\min (A, B)$, and similarly if $A \leqq B$. Therefore, by (13.2), $2 \Phi \geqq \min \left(\rho_{1}^{2}+2 \rho_{1}^{-1}, \rho_{2}^{2}+\right.$ $\left.2 \rho_{2}^{-1}\right)$. But the minimum of the function $x^{2}+2 x^{-1}$ is 3 , achieved when $x=1$. Hence, $2 \Phi \geqq 3$. Clearly, this minimum is achieved only when $\rho_{1}=$ $\rho_{2}=1$, that is, at the Lagrange libration points. This, incidentally, solves Ex. 12.3.

We shall begin with $C=3$, when the level curve $2 \Phi=C$ consists only of the points $L_{1}, L_{3}$, and describe the shape of the curves as $C$ increased. It will be supposed that $0<\mu<\frac{1}{2}$. It is clear from the definition of $\Phi$ that the curves are symmetric in the axis $\eta=0$, so we have drawn only the upper half of each. In the accompanying Fig. 13, the shaded region corresponds to $2 \Phi<C$. The drawings are schematic and do not pretend to any accuracy.

The importance of the curves is this. Each locus $2 \Phi=C$ divides the plane into the shaded region where $2 \Phi<C$ and the unshaded region, where $2 \Phi>C$. In view of Eq. (13.1), motion is impossible if $2 \Phi<C$, since then $v^{2}<0$. Therefore, the shaded regions indicate for each value of the Jacobian constant $C$ the positions in the $\xi-\eta$ coordinate system where motion cannot take place.

## Chapter Three

## INTRODUCTION TO HAMILTON-JACOBI THEORY

## 1. CANONICAL TRANSFORMATIONS

We begin by recalling some basic facts from advanced calculus. Let the functions

$$
y_{k}=y_{k}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{m}\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, m
$$

denote a transformation of variables in an $m$-dimensional region. It will be supposed that each of the partial derivatives $\partial y_{k} / \partial x_{i}$ exists and is continuous. The matrix $\mathscr{M}$ with entries $\partial y_{k} / \partial x_{i}(k=$ row index, $l=$ column index $)$ is known as the Jacobian matrix of the transformation; in more detail it is

The determinant of $\mathscr{M}$, written $|\mathscr{M}|$, is called the Jacobian of the transformation (1.1). It is known that if the transformation (1.1) carries a particular point $\left(x_{1}^{2}, \ldots, x_{m}^{2}\right)$ into the point $\left(y_{1}^{2}, \ldots, y_{m}^{2}\right)$ and if the Jacobian does not vanish at $\left(x_{1}^{2}, \ldots, x_{m}^{2}\right)$, then the Eqs. (1.1) allow a unique solution for the $x_{k}$ in terms of the $y_{k}$ for all points $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{m}$ sufficiently close to $y_{1}^{2}, \ldots, y_{m}^{2}$. Write it

$$
x_{k}=x_{k}\left(y_{1}, \ldots, y_{m}\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, m
$$

The partial derivatives $\partial x_{k} / \partial y_{i}$ are continuous in a neighborhood of $y_{i}^{\prime \prime}$, $\ldots, y_{i n}^{\prime \prime}$. The matrix of the transformation (1.3) is the inverse* of the matrix $\mathscr{M}$.

If $n$ is an integer, the identity matrix $I_{n}$ is the $n \times n$ matrix consisting of ones along the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. By $J$ or $J_{2 n}$, we shall mean a certain matrix constructed in four blocks from $I_{n}$, namely,

$$
J_{n}=J_{2 n}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
O_{n} & I_{n} \\
-I_{n} & O_{n}
\end{array}\right)
$$

where $O_{n}$ is the $n \times n$ matrix whose entries are all zero. It is easily verified that

$$
J_{2 n}^{\prime \prime}=-J_{2 n}, \quad J_{2 n}=-J_{2 n}^{\prime}
$$

Since $\left|J_{2 n}^{\prime}\right|=\left|J_{2 n}\right|^{2}=\left|I_{2 n}\right|=1$, it follows that $\left|J_{2 n}\right| \neq 0$.
Now let $M_{2 n}$ (we write $M$ for simplicity) denote a $2 n \times 2 n$ matrix. It is called symplectic if

$$
M^{T} J M=J
$$

where $M^{T}$ is the transpose of $M$. Since $\left|M^{T}\right| \cdot|J| \cdot|M|=|J|$ and $\left|M^{T}\right|=|M|$, then the non-vanishing of $|J|$ implies that $|M|^{2}=1,|M|= \pm 1$. Therefore $M$ has an inverse $M^{-1}$, and from (1.5) and (1.6) we obtain

$$
M^{-1}=-J M^{T} J
$$

A transformation (1.1) is called canonical if the corresponding Jacobian matrix $\mathscr{M}$, defined by (1.2), is symplectic. Clearly, for such a transformation $m$ must be even, $m=2 n$. In that case, it is customary to split the variables into $p$ 's and $q$ 's and write (1.1) in the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{k}=p_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{n} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{n}\right) \\
& \text { (1.8) } \\
& \qquad k=1, \ldots, n \\
& q_{k}=q_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{n} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

while the inverse transformation (1.3) takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{k}=P_{k}\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \\
& \text { (1.9) } \\
& \text { (1.9) } \\
& k=1, \ldots, n \\
& Q_{k}=Q_{k}\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{\partial p_{m}}{\partial p_{k}} \frac{\partial q_{m}}{\partial P_{1}}-\frac{\partial p_{m}}{\partial P_{1}} \frac{\partial q_{m}}{\partial P_{k}}\right]=0 \\
& \sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{\partial p_{m}}{\partial Q_{k}} \frac{\partial q_{m}}{\partial Q_{1}}-\frac{\partial p_{m}}{\partial Q_{1}} \frac{\partial q_{m}}{\partial Q_{k}}\right]=0
\end{aligned}
$$

for all $k, l$ and

$$
\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{\partial p_{m}}{\partial P_{k}} \frac{\partial q_{m}}{\partial Q_{1}}-\frac{\partial p_{m}}{\partial Q_{1}} \frac{\partial q_{m}}{\partial P_{k}}\right]=\delta_{k l}
$$

The symbol $\delta_{k l}$ means 1 when $k=l$, and 0 when $k \neq l$.

Then

$$

$$

In the expression

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} p_{k} d q_{k}-P_{k} d Q_{k}
$$

replace $p_{k}$ as given by (1.8) and $d q_{k}$ as just obtained. The result, after rearrangement, is the differential form $K$, defined by

$$
K=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} A_{i} d P_{i}+B_{i} d Q_{i}
$$

where $A_{i}$ and $B_{i}$ are functions only of $P_{k}$ and $Q_{k}$. Prove, by use of Ex. 1.10 that (1.8) defines a canonical transformation if and only if there is a function $w\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{n}\right)$ whose total differential is $K$.

## 2. AN APPLICATION OF CANONICAL TRANSFORMATIONS

We have seen on several occasions that the equations of a system may be put in the form

$$
\dot{q}_{k}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{k}}, \dot{p}_{k}=-\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial_{1} l_{k}}, \quad k=1, \ldots, m
$$

where the function $H$, the Hamilton. $m$ of the system, is a function of

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} . \text { Let } \\
& \begin{aligned}
& p_{k}=p_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right) \\
& q_{k}=q_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right)
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

represent a canonical transformation. With this replacement of the original variables, $H$ becomes a function of $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}$. We shall show tl at the system (2.1) retains its original form under this transformation, that is,

$$
\dot{Q}_{k}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial P_{k}}, \quad \dot{P}_{k}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial Q_{k}}, \quad k=1, \ldots, m
$$

For ease of writing, we adopt the notation $\dot{p}$ for the $n \times 1$ matrix with entries $\dot{p}_{1}, \dot{p}_{2}, \ldots, \dot{p}_{m}$ and similarly for $\dot{q}, \dot{P}, \dot{Q}$. The functions of system (2.2) have the derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{p}_{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[\frac{\partial p_{k}}{\partial P_{1}} \dot{P}_{i}+\frac{\partial p_{k}}{\partial Q_{i}} \dot{Q}_{i}\right] \\
& \dot{q}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[\frac{\partial q_{k}}{\partial P_{1}} \dot{P}_{i}+\frac{\partial q_{k}}{\partial Q_{i}} \dot{Q}_{i}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

If $\mathscr{M}$ is the Jacobian matrix of (2.2), this says that

$$
\binom{\dot{p}}{\dot{q}}=\mathscr{M}\binom{\dot{p}}{\dot{Q}}
$$

Therefore

$$
\binom{\dot{p}}{\dot{Q}}=\mathscr{M}^{-1}\binom{\dot{p}}{\dot{q}}
$$

According to (1.7), this is the same as

$$
\binom{\dot{p}}{\dot{Q}}=-J \mathscr{M}^{T} J\binom{\dot{p}}{\dot{q}}
$$

because $\mathscr{M}$ is symplectic. By Ex. 1.4, this says that

$$
\binom{\dot{p}}{Q}=-J \mathscr{M}^{T}\binom{\dot{q}}{-\dot{p}}
$$

Left-multiply each side by $J$. Since $J^{2}=-I$

$$
\binom{\dot{Q}}{-\dot{P}}=\mathscr{M}^{T}\binom{\dot{q}}{-\dot{p}}
$$

By (2.1), this becomes

$$
\binom{\dot{Q}}{-\dot{P}}=\mathscr{M}^{T}\binom{\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}}{\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}}
$$

Multiplication of the two matrices on the right-hand side shows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{Q}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{i}} \frac{\partial p_{i}}{\partial P_{k}}+\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{i}} \frac{\partial q_{i}}{\partial P_{k}}\right] \\
& \dot{P}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{i}} \frac{\partial p_{i}}{\partial Q_{k}}+\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{i}} \frac{\partial q_{i}}{\partial Q_{k}}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the chain rule for differentiation shows that the right-hand sides of (2.3) and (2.4) are identical. This completes the proof of the assertion that the Hamilton-Jacobi form (2.1) is preserved under a contact transformation, with $H$ undergoing the change of variables (2.2).

As an illustration, we turn to Ex. 11.2 of the preceding chapter, first making a notational change. Write $p_{1}$ for $p, p_{2}$ for $P, q_{1}$ for $\xi, q_{2}$ for $\eta$. The function $H$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}+q_{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{2}-q_{1}\right)^{2}-\Phi\left(q_{1}, q_{2}\right) \\
& =\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2}\right)-\left(q_{1} p_{2}-q_{2} p_{1}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(q_{1}^{2}+q_{2}^{2}\right)-\Phi\left(q, q_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

According to (11.1) of the preceding chapter, this is the same as

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2}\right)-\left(q_{1} p_{2}-q_{2} p_{1}\right)-U\left(q_{1}, q_{2}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \mu(1-\mu)
$$

and the differential equations of the circular restricted problem take the form (2.1) with $m=2$ and $H$ defined by (2.5).

We now apply the canonical transformation of Ex. 1.5, namely

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{1}=P_{1} \cos Q_{2}-P_{2} Q_{1}^{-1} \sin Q_{2} \\
& p_{2}=P_{1} \sin Q_{2}+P_{2} Q_{1}^{-1} \cos Q_{2} \\
& q_{1}=Q_{1} \cos Q_{2} \\
& q_{2}=Q_{1} \sin Q_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Hamiltonian (2.5) becomes

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left(P_{1}^{2}+P_{2}^{2} Q_{1}^{-2}\right)-P_{2}-U\left(Q_{1} \cos Q_{2}, Q_{1} \sin Q_{2}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \mu(1-\mu)
$$

and the equations are (2.3) with $m=2$.
exercise 2.1. By retracing all the variables back to the original (nonrotating) system $x-y$, show that the terms of the Hamiltonian (2.6) of the restricted circular problem have these interpretations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{1}^{2}+P_{2}^{2} Q_{1}^{-2}=v^{2}=\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2} \\
& P_{2}=c=x \dot{y}-y \dot{x}
\end{aligned}
$$

The quantity $v$ is the velocity of the particle in the original coordinate system and $c$ is its angular momentum. Observe also that $Q_{1}, Q_{2}$ represent the polar coordinates of the particle in the (rotating) $\xi-\eta$ system. What do $P_{1}, P_{2}$ mean?

## 3. CANONICAL TRANSFORMATIONS GENERATED BY A FUNCTION

In this section the symbol $\sum$ means $\sum_{k=1}^{n}$;
Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{k}=p_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right) \\
& q_{k}=q_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$k=1, \ldots, m$, denote a transformation. In the preceding section it was shown that the transformation is canonical if and only if the differential form

$$
\sum p_{k} d q_{k}-P_{k} d Q_{k}
$$

after replacement of $p_{k}$ and $d q_{k}$ from (3.1), is exact in the $P_{k}$ and $Q_{k}$. This form is related to three others:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum q_{k} d p_{k}+P_{k} d Q_{k} \\
& \sum p_{k} d q_{k}+Q_{k} d P_{k} \\
& \sum q_{k} d p_{k}-Q_{k} d P_{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote each of the four forms by $F_{i}, i=1,2,3,4$, respectively, it is easy to verify that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& F_{1}=-F_{2}+d \sum p_{k} q_{k} \\
& F_{1}=F_{2}-d \sum P_{k} Q_{k} \\
& F_{1}=-F_{4}+d \sum\left(p_{k} q_{k}-P_{k} Q_{k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

It follows that if any one of the four differential forms after replacement of $p_{k}, q_{k}, d p_{k}, d q_{k}$ from (3.1) is exact, that is, the differential of a function of the $P_{k}$ and $Q_{k}$, so is each of the others. Therefore the transformation (3.1) is canonical if and only if any one of the forms is exact after the replacement.

A subtlety, often overlooked, must be mentioned here. We illustrate with the form (3.3) and $m=2$, although the comments apply in the other cases. To say that (3.3) is exact after replacement of $p_{k}$ and $d q_{k}$ does not mean that there is a function $S\left(p_{1}, p_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)$ whose differential

$$
d S=\frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{1}} d p_{1}+\frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{2}} d p_{2}+\frac{\partial S}{\partial Q_{1}} d Q_{1}+\frac{\partial S}{\partial Q_{2}} d Q_{2}
$$

agrees with (3.3), namely,

$$
q_{1} d p_{1}+q_{2} d p_{2}+P_{1} d Q_{1}+P_{2} d Q_{2}
$$

in the sense that the relations

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{1}}=q_{1}, \quad \frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{2}}=q_{2}, \quad \frac{\partial S}{\partial Q_{1}}=P_{1}, \quad \frac{\partial S}{\partial Q_{2}}=P_{2}
$$

hold identically after the replacement. For example, let $p_{1}=P_{1}, p_{2}=Q_{2}$,

$\sigma_{1}=Q_{1}, q_{2}=-P_{2}$ be a transformation; according to Ex. 1.11, it is canonical. The form (3.3), on replacement of $p_{i}$, and $d q_{i}$, becomes

$$
Q_{1} d P_{1}-P_{2} d Q_{2}+P_{1} d Q_{1}+P_{2} d Q_{2}
$$

which is $d\left(P_{1} Q_{1}\right)$ and exact. But there is no function $S\left(p_{1}, p_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)$ for which (3.6) is satisfied. To show this, lcok at the second equation in $(3,6)$. It says

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{1}}\left(p_{1}, p_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)=q_{2}
$$

or

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{2}}\left(P_{1}, Q_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)=-P_{2}
$$

which is impossible since the left-hand side does not contain $P_{1}$.
On the other hand, it may happen for some canonical transformation that there is a function $S\left(p_{1}, p_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)$ for which (3.6) is satisfied. Consider, for example, the canonical transformation of Ex. 1.5, namely,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{1}=P_{1} \cos Q_{2}-P_{2} Q_{1}^{-1} \sin Q_{2} \\
& p_{2}=P_{1} \sin Q_{2}+P_{2} Q_{1}^{-1} \cos Q_{2} \\
& q_{1}=Q_{1} \cos Q_{2} \\
& q_{2}=Q_{1} \sin Q_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We ask whether there is a function $S\left(p_{1}, p_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)$ satisfying (3.6) identically. The first two equations of (3.6) read

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{1}}=Q_{1} \cos Q_{2} \\
& \frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{2}}=Q_{1} \sin Q_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

It follows that an admissible $S$ must be of the form $p_{1} Q_{1} \cos Q_{2}+p_{2} Q_{1}$ $\sin Q_{2}+T$, where $T$ is a function of $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ only. The last two equations of (3.6) then require that

$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{1} \cos Q_{2}+p_{2} \sin Q_{2}+\frac{\partial T}{\partial Q_{1}}=P_{1} \\
-p_{1} Q_{1} \sin Q_{2}+p_{2} Q_{1} \cos Q_{2}+\frac{\partial T}{\partial Q_{2}}=P_{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

Substituting for $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ from (3.7), we obtain $\partial T / \partial Q_{1}=0, \partial T / \partial Q_{2}=0$, so that $T$ is a constant. Since only the derivatives of $S$ appear in (3.6), we can drop the constant to conclude that $S\left(p_{1}, p_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)$, defined as $Q_{1}\left(p_{1} \cos Q_{2}\right.$ $+p_{2} \sin Q_{2}$ ), accomplishes the desired purpose.

If a function $S$ of the desired form does exist satisfying (3.6), we call it a generating function for the contact transformation. We have concen-
trated on the form (3.3), but analogous results hold for the other forms.

## 4. GENERATING FUNCTIONS

Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{k}=p_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right) \\
& q_{k}=q_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

denote a canonical transformation.
Then
(i) there is a function $S\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right)$ whose differeniial is (3.2), that is, for which

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_{k}}=p_{k}, \quad \frac{\partial S}{\partial Q_{k}}=-P_{k}
$$

or
(ii) there is a function $S\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right)$ whose differential is (3.3), that is, for which

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{k}}=q_{k}, \quad \frac{\partial S}{\partial Q_{k}}=P_{k}
$$

or
(iii) there is a function $S\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} ; P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m}\right)$ whose differential is (3.4), that is, for which

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_{k}}=p_{k}, \quad \frac{\partial S}{\partial P_{k}}=Q_{k}
$$

or
(iv) there is a function $S\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m}\right)$ whose differential is (4.5), that is, for which

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial p_{k}}=q_{k}, \quad \frac{\partial S}{\partial P_{k}}=-Q_{k}
$$

or
(v) none of (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) is true.

We have seen (Ex. 3.2) that case (v) can actually occur.
Now forget the transformation (4.1). Suppose we start with a function $S$ of one of the four forms described in (i)-(iv). For definiteness, let us say $S$ is of the form (iii). Let us define the variables $p_{k}, Q_{k}$ by (4.4). The second of these equations is

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial P_{k}}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} ; P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m}\right)=Q_{k}, \quad k=1, \ldots, m
$$

Suppose, moreover, that the Hessian $\left|\partial^{2} S / \partial P_{k} \partial q_{i}\right|$ does not vanish. Then this system of $m$ equations can be solved for the $q_{k}$ in terms of the $Q_{k}$ and $P_{k}$ yielding functions of the form (4.1). The first of the Eqs. (4.4) can be written

$$
p_{k}=\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_{k}}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} ; P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m}\right)
$$

Replacing the $q_{k}$ by $q_{k}\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right)$ yields for $p_{k}$ of the form (4.1). Clearly, the transformation (4.1) so obtained is generated by the function $S$, and is, therefore, canonical.

The same argument can be applied to the three other forms of $S$. The technique provides a method for obtaining canonical transformations, starting with a function $S$. The implications are very important, as we now show.

Suppose that we are given a system of differential equations

$$
\dot{q}_{k}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{k}}, \quad \dot{p}_{k}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{k}}, \quad k=1, \ldots, m
$$

with Hamiltonian $H\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; q_{1}, q_{1} \ldots, q_{m}\right)$. Then it retains its form under a canonical transformation (4.1); that is, after the change of variables in the Hamiltonian, the system becomes

$$
\dot{Q}_{k}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial P_{k}}, \quad \dot{P}_{k}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial Q_{k}}, \quad k=1, \ldots, m
$$

Now let us try to find a canonical transformation which reduces $H$ to a very simple form so that the system (4.7) is manageable. For example, suppose it is possible to find a substitution (4.1) such that $H$ reduces identically to $Q_{1}$. Then Eqs. (4.7) become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{Q}_{k}=0, \quad k=1, \ldots, m \\
& \dot{P}_{1}=-1, \quad \dot{P}_{k}=0, \quad k=2, \ldots, m
\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{1}=-t+\alpha_{1}, \quad P_{k}=\alpha_{k}, \quad k=2, \ldots, m \\
& Q_{k}=\beta_{k}, \quad k=1, \ldots, m
\end{aligned}
$$

where all the $\alpha_{i}, \beta_{k}$ are constants. Substitution for $P_{k}, Q_{k}$ into (4.1) then gives the solution of (4.6) in terms of $t$ and the "arbitrary" constants $\alpha_{1}$, $\ldots, \alpha_{m} ; \beta_{1}, \ldots, \beta_{m}$

But how can one find a transformation (4.1) which does in fact reduce $H$ to $Q_{1}$ ? A procedure, due to Jacobi, is to search for a generating function $S$ that produces such a transformation. Specifically, let us try for a function $S$ of type (i). If the $p_{k}$ in $H\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}\right)$ are replaced from (4.2), we get

$$
H\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\partial S}{\partial q_{m}} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}\right)
$$

where $S$ is of the form $S\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} ; Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{m}\right)$ and we are asking that

$$
H\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\partial S}{\partial q_{1}} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}\right)=Q_{1}
$$

irrespective of the values of $Q_{2}, \ldots Q_{m}$. This is the Jacobi (partial differential) equation. If we can find such an $S$ and the Hessian $\left|\partial^{2} S / \partial q_{k} \partial Q_{k}\right|$ does not vanish, then $S$ generates a trans ormation (4.1) which has the desired properties.

A fairly simple example may help to make all this clearer. Let $m=1$ (so that we need no subscripts) and let $H=\frac{1}{2}\left(p^{2}+q^{2}\right)$. The differential equations are $\dot{q}=\partial H / \partial p=p, \dot{p}=-\partial H / \partial q=-q$. They are trivial to solve, since $\dot{p}+p=0, p=A \cos (t-B), q=-\dot{p}=A \sin (t-B)$. But we wish to solve them by the method outlined above, because direct integration of a system is seldom possible.

We seek $S(q, Q)$ so that (4.9), in this case

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial q}\right)^{2}+q^{2}\right]=Q
$$

is satisfied. Then $\partial S / \partial q=\left(2 Q-q^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}$ and

$$
S=\frac{1}{2}\left[q\left(2 Q-q^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}+2 Q \operatorname{arc} \sin q(2 Q)^{-1 / 2}\right]
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
-P & =\frac{\partial S}{\partial Q}=\arcsin q(2 Q)^{-1 / 2} \\
p & =\frac{\partial S}{\partial q}=\left(2 Q-q^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

According to (4.8), $P=-t+\alpha, Q=\beta$. Therefore $q=\sqrt{2 \beta} \sin (t-\alpha)$, $p=\sqrt{2 \beta} \cos (t-\alpha)$, which certainly provides a general solution of the equation.

Exercise 4.1. What is the Hessian in the example just worked?
Exercise 4.2. In the general case can the reduction of $H$ to $Q_{1}$ be accomplished by an $S$ of one of the other three types? Suppose we had

tried for a reduction to $P_{1}$. What modifications are needed? Try out your theory on the special example.
*Exercise 4.3. Show that if $S$ satisfies Eq. (4.9), then the solution $p_{k}, q_{k}$ of (4.6) is given "implicitly" by

$$
\begin{aligned}
-t+\alpha_{1} & =-\frac{\partial S}{\partial \beta_{1}}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} ; \beta_{1}, \ldots, \beta_{m}\right) \\
\alpha_{k} & =-\frac{\partial S}{\partial \beta_{k}}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} ; \beta_{1}, \ldots, \beta_{m}\right), \quad k=2, \ldots, m \\
p_{k} & =\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_{k}}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m} ; \beta_{1}, \ldots, \beta_{m}\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, m
\end{aligned}
$$

where the $\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{m} ; \beta_{1}, \ldots, \beta_{m}$ are $2 m$ arbitrary constants.

## 5. APPLICATION TO THE CENTRAL FORCE AND RESTRICTED PROBLEMS

We have seen in Sec. 2 that the restricted three-body problem can be put in the form

$$
\dot{q}_{k}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{k}}, \quad \dot{p}_{k}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{k}}, \quad k=1,2
$$

with

$$
H=\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2} q_{1}^{-2}\right)-p_{2}-U\left(q_{1} \cos q_{2}, q_{2} \sin q_{2}\right)
$$

Observe that we have changed from capital letters to small; this is because another canonical transformation is forthcoming. The constant $\frac{1}{2} \mu(1-\mu)$ has been dropped from the Hamiltonian; no harm is done since it does not appear in the Eqs. (5.1) anyhow.

Recall that, according to Ex. 2.1, the term $\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2} q_{1}^{-2}\right)$ is simply $\frac{1}{2} v^{2}$, where $v$ is the velocity of the particle in the non-rotating system and that $p_{2}=c$, where $c$ is the angular momentum. The variables $q_{1}, q_{2}$ are the polar coordinates of the particle in the rotating coordinate system. In the latter system, $U$ is defined by

$$
U(\xi, \eta)=(1-\mu)\left[(\xi+\mu)^{2}+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1 / 2}+\mu\left[(\xi+\mu-1)^{2}+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1 / 2}
$$

in accordance with the formula of Ex. 10.3 of Chap. 1. In the special case $\mu=0$, the function $U(\xi, \eta)$ becomes simply $\left(\xi^{2}+\eta^{2}\right)^{-1 / 2}$, which is the same as $q_{1}^{-1}$. This suggests rewriting the Hamiltonian as

$$
H=H_{0}+\left[q_{1}^{-1}-U\right]
$$

where

$$
H_{0}=\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2} \cdot p_{1}^{2}\right)-q_{1}^{-1}-p_{2}
$$

and where the term in brackets drops out when $\mu=0$.

What is the physical meaning of the problem if $\mu=0$ ? The answer is simple: the smaller primary mass disappears and the large one takes on the total mass of unity at the origin. The problem is then that of a mass moving in a fixed plane under the attraction of a central force. Since the mass at $O$ is unity, this is identical with the problem $p=-r^{-2} \mathbf{r}$ treated in Chap. 1. In the current context, the problem takes the form (5.1), with $H$ replaced b: $H_{0}$. Therefore, the central force problem can be put in the form

$$
\dot{q}_{k}=\frac{\partial H_{0}}{\partial p_{k}}, \quad \dot{p}_{k}=-\frac{\partial H_{0}}{\partial q_{k}}
$$

where $H_{0}$ is defined by (5.3). According to the second paragraph of this section, $H_{0}$ can be written $\left(\frac{1}{2} v^{2}-r^{-1}\right)-c$, where $r=q_{1}$. The first term is just the energy $h$ of the moving particle. Therefore $H_{0}=h-c$. This suggests a new canonical transformation to simplify $H_{0}$, and hence the Eqs. (5.4). It is reasonable to let $Q_{1}=h, Q_{2}=c$, so that $H_{0}=Q_{1}-Q_{2}$. If we can find such a transformation, the Eqs. (5.4) will become

$$
\dot{Q}_{k}=\frac{\partial H_{0}}{\partial \dot{P}_{k}}, \quad \dot{P}_{k}=-\frac{\partial H_{0}}{\partial Q_{k}}, \quad k=1,2
$$

so that

$$
\dot{Q}_{1}=0, \quad \dot{Q}_{2}=0, \quad \dot{P}_{1}=-1, \quad \dot{P}_{2}=1
$$

which are easy to solve.
With this in mind, let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& Q_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2} q_{1}^{-2}\right)-q_{1}^{-1} \\
& Q_{2}=p_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

But how are $P_{1}, P_{2}$ to be chosen so that the transformation is canonical? Let us look for a generating function that will furnish the desired transformation. Since it is $P_{1}, P_{2}$ that are missing, we shall try for a function of the form $S\left(q_{1}, q_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)$, for then $-P_{k}=\partial S / \partial Q_{k}$, according to (4.2). Since $p_{2}=\partial S / \partial q_{2}$, the second of Eqs. (5.6) requires that $\partial S / \partial q_{2}=Q_{2}$. Therefore $S=q_{2} Q_{2}+F$, where $F$ cannot depend on $q_{2}$ and must be of the form $F\left(q_{1} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)$. Since $p_{1}=\partial S / \partial q_{1}=\partial F / \partial q_{1}$, the first of Eqs. (5.6) demands that

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial q_{1}}\right)^{2}+Q_{2} q_{1}^{-2}\right]-q_{1}^{-1}=Q_{1}
$$

Since any solution will serve our purpose, let

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial q_{1}}=q_{1}^{-1}\left(-Q_{2}^{2}+2 q_{1}+2 Q_{1} q_{1}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}
$$

Therefore

$$
F=\int_{0}^{q_{1}} x^{-1}\left(-Q_{2}^{2}+2 x+2 Q_{1} x^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} d x
$$

where $G$ depends only on $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$. As we shall see shortly, it is best to

hoose $G$ so that the integrand vanishes when $x=G$; and because $q_{1}>0$, $t$ is best to choose $G$ positive.
If $Q_{1}=h=0$, there is just one choice for $G$, namely $Q=Q_{1}^{2} / 2=c^{2} / 2$. If $Q_{1} \neq 0$, we must choose between

$$
\left[-1 \pm\left(1+2 Q_{1} Q_{2}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}\right]\left(2 Q_{1}\right)^{-1}
$$

The term $1+2 Q_{1} Q_{2}^{2}$ is $1+2 h c^{2}$. According to equation (5.2) of Chap. 1 with $\mu$ as defined there equal to unity), this is the same as $e^{2}$. Therefore $\bar{j}=(-1 \pm e)(2 h)^{-1}$. If $h>0$, we are forced to choose the + sign to make i positive. If $h<0$, either sign makes $G$ positive but we must choose the orger value to keep the integrand real for $x>G$. In either case, then, $G$ $=(-1+e)(2 h)^{-1}$. In summary, we have chosen for $S$ the function $q_{1} Q_{2}+$ $F_{1} \mathrm{cr}$

$$
S\left(q_{1}, q_{2} ; Q_{1}, Q_{2}\right)=q_{1} Q_{2}+\int_{0}^{q_{1}} x^{-1}\left(-Q_{2}^{2}+2 x+2 Q_{1} x^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} d x
$$

The "missing" variables $P_{1}, P_{2}$ are then defined by $-\partial S / \partial Q_{1}$ and $-\partial S / \partial Q_{2}$, respectively. What is their physical interpretation? We start with $P_{2}$. According to (5.7) and Leibniz' rule for differentiation of an integral,

$$
\begin{aligned}
-P_{2} & =q_{2}-Q_{2} \int_{0}^{q_{2}} x^{-1}\left(-Q_{2}^{2}+2 x+2 Q_{1} x^{2}\right)^{-1 / 2} d x \\
& =q_{2}+\arctan \frac{q_{1}-Q_{2}^{2}}{q_{1} e}-\arctan \frac{G-Q_{2}^{2}}{G e}
\end{aligned}
$$

This step uses the fact that the integrand of (5.7) vanishes at $x=G$. Now let $q_{1}=r=c^{2}(1+e \cos f)^{-1}, Q_{2}^{2}=c^{2}$. The second term on the right-hand side of (5.8) becomes arc $\cos (-\cos f)=\pi-f$. Therefore,

$$
-P_{2}=\left(q_{2}-f\right)+\left(\pi-\arctan \frac{G-Q_{2}^{2}}{G e}\right)
$$

By our choice of $G$, the last term vanishes. Therefore $-P_{2}=q_{2}-f$. Recall that $q_{2}$ is the angle made by the radius vector to the particle with the positive $\xi$-axis. It follows that $q_{2}-f$ is the amplitude of pericenter, measured from the $\xi$-axis. As a check, observe that at time $t$ the $\xi$-axis forms an angle of $t$ with the fixed $x$-axis, since the rotation rate is 1 . Therefore $t+$ ( $q_{2}-f$ ) is $\omega$, the (constant) amplitude of pericenter measured from the $x$-axis. We conclude that $-P_{2}=\omega-t, \dot{P}_{2}=1$, which is consistent with (5.5)

It remains to interpret $P_{1}$, which is defined by

$$
-P_{1}=\frac{\partial S}{\partial Q_{1}}=Q_{1} \int_{0}^{q_{1}} x\left(-Q_{2}^{2}+2 x+2 Q_{1} x^{2}\right)^{-1 / 2} d x
$$

The interpretation is left to the exercises which follow.

## 6. EQUILIBRIUM POINTS AND THEIR STABILITY

Let a system be governed by the equations

$$
\dot{q}_{2}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{k}}, \quad \dot{p}_{k}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{k}}, \quad k=1, \ldots, m
$$

with Hamiltonian $H\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}\right)$. Suppose that $p_{1}^{2}, \ldots, p_{m}^{k}$; $q_{1}^{2}, \ldots, q_{m}^{k}$ is a point at which all the first partial derivatives of $H$ vanish; it is called an equilibrium point. Then the set of constant functions $p_{k}=p_{k}^{0}$, $q_{k}=q_{k}^{0}$ satisfy the differential equations; it is called an equilibrium solution.

The major example for our purposes occurs in the restricted three-body problem. Consider the problem in the form (6.1) with $m=2$ and the Hamiltonian given by (2.5), namely,

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2}\right)-\left(q_{1} p_{2}-q_{2} p_{1}\right)-U\left(q_{1}, q_{2}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \mu(1-\mu)
$$

The four partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{1}}=p_{1}+q_{1}, & \frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{1}}=-p_{2}-\frac{\partial U}{\partial q_{1}} \\
\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{2}}=p_{2}-q_{1}, & \frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{2}}=p_{1}-\frac{\partial U}{\partial q_{2}}
\end{array}
$$

Clearly, they all vanish at a point ( $p_{1}, p_{2} ; q_{1}, q_{2}$ ) if and only if $p_{1}=-q_{2}$, $p_{2}=q_{1}, q_{1}+\left(\partial U / \partial q_{1}\right)=0, q_{2}+\left(\partial U / \partial q_{2}\right)=0$. Since $q_{1}=\xi, q_{2}=\eta$, the last two equations are identical with (12.1) of Chap. 2. Hence the equilibrium points for this Hamiltonian system are the five points $\left(-q_{2}^{0}, q_{1}^{0} ; q_{1}^{0}, q_{2}^{0}\right)$, where ( $q_{1}^{0}, q_{2}^{0}$ ) is any one of the five libration points.

We return to the general problem (6.1) and an equilibrium point $\left(p_{1}^{2}, \ldots, p_{m}^{k} ; q_{1}^{2}, \ldots, q_{m}^{k}\right)$. An important question concerning such a point is this: will a "small" disturbance in the coordinates of this point cause the resulting solution of the system to depart considerably from the point? It is customary to call the point stable if the following is true: if a solution of (6.1) starts with initial conditions sufficiently "near" ( $p_{1}^{2}, \ldots, p_{m}^{k} ; q_{1}^{2}, \ldots$, $q_{m}^{k}$ ), it will remain near this position for all time. In the special problem of the libration points we are asking: if a particle is placed near one of the libration points with (relative) velocity near zero, will it remain near this position for all time? Since $\frac{1}{2}\left(\dot{\xi}^{2}+\dot{q}^{2}\right)+\Phi(\xi, \eta)$ is constant, this means that the velocities must also remain small for all time.

The general question can be put in a more precise form in terms of the concept of L-stability.* To explain what this means, let the distance between two points ( $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}$ ) and ( $p_{1}^{2}, \ldots, p_{m}^{k} ; q_{1}^{2}, \ldots, q_{m}^{k}$ ) be measured by

$$
\left[\sum\left(p_{k}-p_{k}^{0}\right)^{2}+\left(q_{k}-q_{k}^{0}\right)^{2}\right]^{1 / 2}
$$

Then a point of equilibrium is called L-stable if, for each positive number
${ }^{*}$ L for Liapounov.
$\epsilon$, there is a positive number $\delta$ such that each solution of (6.1) which starts with initial position within a distance $\delta$ of the point exists for all time thereafter and never departs from this point to a distance exceeding $\epsilon$. Clearly, if there is such a $\delta$, it must satisfy $\delta \leqq \epsilon$.

The problem of L-stability of the libration points is a very difficult one and will be discussed in the sequel. Here we shall describe a simpler example, due to T. Cherry. Let $m=2$ and let $H\left(p_{1}, p_{2} ; q_{1}, q_{2}\right)$ be the Hamiltonian

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left(q_{1}^{2}+p_{1}^{2}\right)-\left(q_{2}^{2}+p_{2}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2} p_{2}-p_{2} q_{1}^{2}-2 q_{1} q_{2} p_{1}\right)
$$

Then the Eqs. (6.1) become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{p}_{1}=-q_{1}+p_{2} q_{1}+q_{2} p_{1} \\
& \dot{p}_{2}=2 q_{2}+p_{1} q_{1} \\
& \dot{q}_{1}=p_{1}+p_{2} p_{2}-q_{1} q_{2} \\
& \dot{q}_{2}=-2 p_{2}+\frac{1}{2} p_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2} q_{1}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Obviously the origin $(0,0 ; 0,0)$ is an equilibrium point. Is it L-stable? To answer the question, observe that for any fixed constant $\tau$ the functions

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{1}=\sqrt{2} \frac{\sin (t-\tau)}{t-\tau}, \quad p_{2}=\frac{\sin 2(t-\tau)}{t-\tau} \\
& q_{1}=-\sqrt{2} \frac{\cos (t-\tau)}{t-\tau}, \quad q_{2}=\frac{\cos 2(t-\tau)}{t-\tau}
\end{aligned}
$$

satisfy the Eqs. (6.5) for all $t \neq \tau$. If $\tau \neq 0$, the initial values of these solutions can be obtained by letting $t=0$ :

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
p_{1}^{\prime}=\sqrt{2} \frac{\sin \tau}{\tau}, & p_{2}^{\prime}=\frac{\sin 2 \tau}{\tau} \\
q_{1}^{\prime}=\sqrt{2} \frac{\cos \tau}{\tau}, & q_{2}^{\prime}=-\frac{\cos 2 \tau}{\tau}
\end{array}
$$

The distance of this point from the origin is $\sqrt{3} \tau^{-1}$. Therefore, by choosing $\tau$ as a sufficiently large positive number, we can find a solution (6.6) which at time $t=0$ starts as close to the origin as we please. What happens to the solution as $t$ increases? At any time $t, 0<t<\tau$, its distance from the origin is $\sqrt{3}(\tau-t)^{-1}$, which becomes infinite as $t \rightarrow \tau$. We conclude that the origin is not L-stable.

## 7. INFINITESIMAL STABILITY

In 1964, Wintner,* writing about the concept of L-stability, said:
This definition of stability seems to be the natural one. Actually, it is not natural at all. In fact everything that is known from Poincare's geometrical theory of real differential equations and from the parallel, though more difficult, theory of surface transformations points in the direction that condition (ii)** cannot be satisfied except in highly exceptional cases. Even in the restricted problem of three bodies, not a single solution is known to be stable.

Writing twenty-five years later, it is easy to be wise. Within the last few years, as a result of the work of Kolmogoroff and his school, it is now established that some of the libration points are indeed L-stable. But their methods are far beyond the scope of this book, and we turn aside to look at an easier question.

Classically it was, and remains, customary to substitute for L-stability another concept of stability which is much easier to handle. The basic idea is this. Consider once again the system (6.1) and an equilibrium point $p_{1}^{x}, \ldots, p_{m}^{x} ; q_{1}^{x}, \ldots, q_{m}^{x}$. Let $p_{k}=p_{k}^{x}+\epsilon_{k}, q_{k}=q_{k}^{x}+\eta_{k}$ represent a solution of the system (6.1) which is "near" the equilibrium solution. Expand each of the derivatives $\partial H / \partial p_{k}, \partial H / \partial q_{k}$ through terms of the first order in $\epsilon_{k}$ and $\eta_{k}$ around the point $p_{1}^{x}, \ldots, p_{m}^{x} ; q_{1}^{x}, \ldots, q_{m}^{x}$. Because the first partial derivatives themselves vanish at the point, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{k}} \int p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m})= & \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial p_{k} \partial p_{i}}\right)_{0} \epsilon_{i}+\left(\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial p_{k} \partial q_{i}}\right)_{0} \eta_{i} \\
& + \text { terms of higher order; }
\end{aligned}
$$

*The Analytical Foundations of Celestial Mechanics, Princeton University Press, 1941, p. 98.

* This is the $\epsilon-\delta$ condition described in Sec. 6.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_{k}}\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m} ; q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}\right)= & \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial q_{k} \partial p_{i}}\right)_{0} \epsilon_{i}+\left(\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial q_{k} \partial q_{i}}\right)_{0} \eta_{i} \\
& + \text { terms of higher order; }
\end{aligned}
$$

the subscript 0 indicates that the second derivatives are to be evaluated at the point. Now let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{k 1}=\left(\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial p_{k} \partial p_{i}}\right)_{0}, \quad b_{k 1}=\left(\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial p_{k} \partial q_{i}}\right)_{0} \\
& c_{k 1}=\left(\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial q_{k} \partial p_{i}}\right)_{0}, \quad d_{k 1}=\left(\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial q_{k} \partial q_{i}}\right)_{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then the Eqs. (6.1) become (we write the equations for $\dot{p}_{k}$ first)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{e}_{k}=-\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} c_{k 1} \epsilon_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} d_{k 1} \eta_{i} \\
& \dot{\eta}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} a_{k 1} \epsilon_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} b_{k 1} \eta_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

provided the terms of higher order can safely be dropped. By this we mean, somewhat optimistically, that a solution of the exact Eqs. (6.1) which starts sufficiently near the equilibrium point will mimic the behavior of that solution of the linear system (7.2) wt ich starts in the same position relative to $(0, \ldots 0 ; 0, \ldots, 0)$. With this in mind, we define the point $\left(p_{1}^{x}, \ldots, p_{m}^{x}\right.$; $\left.q_{1}^{x}, \ldots, q_{m}^{x}\right)$ to be infinitesimally stable for the system (6.1), if the origin is L-stable for the linear system (7.2). The infinitesimal stability of equilibrium solutions is what is studied in classical mechanics under the theory of "small" oscillations.

Is the optimism justified? Is a point which is infinitesimally stable also L-stable? We examine the system (6.5) for which the origin is not L-stable. Let $p_{k}=\epsilon_{k}, q_{k}=\eta_{k}$ and drop the terms which are not linear. The resulting system is simply

$$
\dot{\epsilon}_{1}=-\eta_{1}, \quad \dot{\epsilon}_{2}=2 \eta_{2}, \quad \dot{\eta}_{1}=\epsilon_{1}, \quad \dot{\eta}_{2}=-2 \epsilon_{2}
$$

The solution of this is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \epsilon_{1}=A \cos t-C \sin t \\
& \epsilon_{2}=B \cos 2 t+D \sin 2 t \\
& \eta_{1}=C \cos t+A \sin t \\
& \eta_{2}=D \cos 2 t-B \sin 2 t
\end{aligned}
$$

where $(A, B ; C, D)$ are the initial values of $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \epsilon_{2} ; \eta_{1}, \eta_{2}\right)$. It is easy to check that $\left(\epsilon_{1}^{2}+\epsilon_{2}^{2}+\eta_{1}^{2}+\eta_{2}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}=\left(A^{2}+B^{2}+C^{2}+D^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}$. It follows that if the solution starts within $\epsilon$ of the origin, it remains within $\epsilon$ of the origin. This is more than enough to guarantee L-stability for the linear system.

We have shown that a point which is stable according to the classical theory need not be stable according to the desirable criterion of L-stability.

Nevertheless, the classical method has its uses and we shall discuss it at length.
