## 8. THE CHARACTERISTIC ROOTS

We have seen that the problem of infinitesimal stability of-an equilibrium point leads to the study of linear systems (7.2). The traditional method of solving such systems is to look first for solutions of the form $\epsilon_{k}=A_{k} e^{\lambda I}, \eta_{k}=B_{k} e^{\lambda I}$. Substitution into Eqs. (7.2) leads to the linear system*

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum\left(-c_{k l}-\lambda\right) A_{l}+\sum\left(-d_{k l}\right) B_{l}=0 \\
& \sum a_{k l} A_{l}+\sum\left(b_{k l}-\lambda\right) B_{l}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Denote by $A, B, C, D$, respectively, the $m \times m$ matrices $\left(a_{k l}\right),\left(b_{k l}\right),\left(c_{k l}\right)$, $\left(d_{k l}\right)$ defined by (7.1) and let $I$ denote the $m \times m$ identity matrix. The matrix of coefficients is then

$$
\mathscr{M}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
-C-\lambda I & -D \\
A & B-\lambda I
\end{array}\right)
$$

If the determinant of the coefficients is not zero, then the system (8.1) has only the solution $A_{k}=0, B_{k}=0, k=1, \cdots, n$. A non-trivial solution can be guaranteed if the deterrcinant vanishes. This means that $\lambda$ must satisfy the equation $|\mathscr{M}|=0$. If we multiply each of the first $m$ rows by $(-1)$, we get

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cc}
C+\lambda I & D \\
A & B-\lambda I
\end{array}\right|=0
$$

The left-hand side is a polynomial in $\lambda$ of degree $2 m$. Its roots are called the characteristic roots of the system (7.2). We shall prove that for systems (7.2) whose coefficients originate in a Hamiltonian, as indicated by (7.1), the polynomial is even. This means that if $\lambda$ is a characteristic root, so is $-\lambda$.

Observe first that, according to (7.1), the matrices $B$ and $C$ are transposes of one another, so that (8.2) may be written

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cc}
C+\lambda I & D \\
A & C^{T}-\lambda I
\end{array}\right|=0
$$

Since, by (7.1), $A=A^{T}, D=D^{T}$, we may transpose the determinant on

- In this section $\sum$ means $\sum_{i=1}^{n} n$.
the left to obtain

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cc}
C^{T}+\lambda I & A \\
D & C-\lambda I
\end{array}\right|=0
$$

$\mathrm{N} \backslash \mathrm{w}$ interchange the last $m$ rows with the first to get

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cc}
D & C-\lambda I \\
C^{T}+\lambda I & A
\end{array}\right|=0
$$

Finally, interchange the last $m$ columns with the first. We obtain

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cc}
C-\lambda I & D \\
A & C^{T}+\lambda I
\end{array}\right|=0
$$

This shows that if $\lambda$ satisfies (8.3), so does $-\lambda$, and the proof is complete.

$$
\left|\begin{array}{ll}
A & B \\
C & D
\end{array}\right|=0
$$

## 9. CONDITIONS FOR STABILITY

Suppose we are testing an equilibrium point $\left(p_{1}^{x}, \ldots, p_{m}^{x} ; q_{1}^{x}, \ldots, q_{m}^{x}\right)$ for stability. We start by looking at infinitesimal stability. To avoid complications which arise in the general case, but not in the problems we consider, let it be supposed from now on that the $2 m$ characteristic roots $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{m}$ are distinct. This means, in particular, that none of them can be zero since the associated polynomial is even; if one $\lambda$ were zero, two of them would be.

It is now easy to prove: the origin is L-stable for the system (7.2) or, what is equivalent, the point ( $p_{1}^{x}, \ldots, p_{m}^{x} ; q_{1}^{x}, \ldots, q_{m}^{x}$ ) is infinitesimally stable if and only if all the numbers $\lambda_{n}$ are pure imaginary.

First suppose that some $\lambda_{k}$ has a non-zero real part. Then one of the numbers $\lambda_{k l}-\lambda_{k}$ has a positive real part. The general solution of (7.2) contains terms of the form $e^{\lambda_{k} l}, e^{-\lambda_{k} l}$. One of these becomes infinite in magnitude as $t \rightarrow \infty$. Therefore the origin cannot be infinitesimally stable.

Conversely, if all the $\lambda_{k}$ are pure imaginary, let $\lambda_{k}=i \mu_{k}, \mu_{k}$ be real. The general solution of (7.2) is of the form

$$
\epsilon_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{2 m} A_{k l} e^{i \mu_{k} t}, \quad \eta_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{2 m} B_{k l} e^{i \mu_{k} t}
$$

Therefore $\left|\epsilon_{k}\right| \leqq \sum_{i=1}^{2 m}\left|A_{k l}\right|,\left|\eta_{k}\right| \leqq \sum_{i=1}^{2 m}\left|B_{k l}\right|$ for all time. If we choose the sums

on the right to be small, then the solution remains small for all time. This completes the proof of the theorem stated in the second paragraph.

How does this help with the problem of L-stability? Only to this extent. It was shown* by Liapounov that if the Hamiltonian has continuous partial derivatives of the third order, then a point cannot be L-stable unless it is infinitesimally stable. The condition on the Hamiltonian will be met in our problems. Therefore we can conclude that if any $\lambda_{n}$ has a non-zero real part, the point is not L-stable. On the other hand, if the system is infinitesimally stable, that is, all the $\lambda_{n}$ are pure imaginary, no conclusion about L-stability can be drawn without further investigation. This is demonstrated by the examples given in Sec. 7.

In the next section we shall investigate the stability of the five librat on points. To avoid distracting digressions, we ask the reader to verify some computations in the following exercises. The notation is that of Secs. 12 and 13 in Chap. 2. We let

$$
\begin{aligned}
s & =(1-\mu) \rho_{1}^{-3}+\mu \rho_{2}^{-3} \\
A & =\frac{\partial^{2} \Phi}{\partial \xi^{2}}, \quad B=\frac{\partial^{2} \Phi}{\partial \xi \partial \eta}, \quad C=\frac{\partial^{2} \Phi}{\partial \eta^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 10. THE STABILITY OF THE LIBRATION POINTS

Recall from Sec. 7 that the equilibrium points of the restricted three-body problem are five in number and have coordinates $\left(-q_{1}^{2}, q_{1}^{2} ; q_{2}^{2}, q_{3}^{2}\right)$ where $\left(q_{1}^{2}, q_{2}^{2}\right)$ are the coordinates of the corresponding libration points in the $\xi-\eta$ coordinate system. In order to test these points for stability, we must compute the coefficients defined by (7.1) and the determinant which occurs in (8.3). If we start with the Hamiltonian in the form

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2}\right)-\left(q_{1} p_{2}-q_{2} p_{1}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(q_{1}^{2}+q_{2}^{2}\right)-\Phi\left(q_{1}, q_{2}\right)
$$

it is easily verified that (8.3) becomes

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cccc}
\lambda & -1 & 1-\Phi_{11} & -\Phi_{12} \\
1 & \lambda & -\Phi_{12} & 1-\Phi_{22} \\
1 & 0 & -\lambda & 1 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & -\lambda
\end{array}\right|=0
$$

where the subscripts indicate partial differentiation with respect to the variables $q_{1}$ or $q_{2}$. Since $q_{1}=\xi, q_{2}=\eta$, evaluation of the determinant yields

$$
x^{2}+x(4-A-C)+4 A C-B^{2}=0
$$

where $x=\lambda^{2}$ and $A, B, C$ have the same meaning as in Exs. 9.1-9.6.
Now if the points are to be L-stable, it is necessary that all the $\lambda$ be pure imaginary. Therefore both roots $x$ of (10.2) must be negative. According to Ex. 9.6, this is never possible for $L_{1}, L_{2}, L_{3}$. Hence the points are unstable. The same exercise shows that $L_{4}, L_{5}$ are unstable when $27 \mu(1-$ $\mu) \geqq 1$.

Therefore the only possible cases of stability left are $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ when $27 \mu(1-\mu)<1$, that is, $\mu<.03852$. In the major examples of interest to astronomers, this condition on $\mu$ is satisfied and many years of observation indicate that the points are L-stable. A theoretical proof of stability has appeared only recently, thus settli ig an important question of long standing. The proof is due to the Russian mathematician Leontovich who used advanced methods devised by Kolmogoroff and Arnold.*

## Chapter Four

## PERTURBATION THEORY

## 1. THE VARIATION OF PARAMETERS

The general solution of the equation $\dot{x}=x+t$ is $x=-1-t+c e$ where $c$ is an "arbitrary constant," or parameter. This illustrates the fat that, under the conditions usually met with in practice, a differential equi tion of the first order

$$
\dot{x}=f(x, t)
$$

will have for its solution a function $x=x(c, t)$, where $c$ is a parameter. I other words,

$$
\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}(c, t)=f(x, t)
$$

Now suppose we wish to study a modification of the given Eq. (1.1) namely,

$$
\dot{x}=f(x, t)+g(x, t)
$$

For this purpose it is sometimes useful to employ a technique known a: the variation of parameters. The idea is this. We start with the solutior $x=x(c, t)$ of the original Eq. (1.1), and try to make it fit (1.3) by permit: ing the parameter $c$ to become a function of the independent variable $t$. Then

$$
\dot{x}=\frac{\partial x}{\partial c} c+\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}
$$

so that (1.3) reads

$$
\frac{\partial x}{\partial c} \dot{c}+\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}=f(x, t)+g(x, t)
$$

By virtue of (1.2), the interior terms cancel, leaving us with a new differential equation

$$
\dot{c}=g(x, t)\left(\begin{array}{l}
\partial x \\
\partial c
\end{array}\right)^{-1}
$$

The variable $x$ occurring in $g(x, t)$ is to be replaced by $x(c, t)$. This leaves us with a new differential equation of the form

$$
\dot{c}=h(c, t)
$$

For example, suppose the equation of the opening sentence is modified

$$
\dot{x}=x+t+\alpha x^{2}
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant. Since the original equation (with $\alpha=0$ ) has the solution $x=-1-t+c e^{t}$, it follows that $\partial x / \partial c=e^{t}$. Because $g(x, t)=\alpha x^{2}$, Eq. (1.4) becomes

$$
\dot{c}=\alpha\left(c e^{t}-1-t\right)^{\prime} e^{-t}
$$

which is of the form (1.5).
At this point the reader can, and should, argue that Eq. (1.7) is at least as difficult to solve as the original one (1.6), and that nothing has been gained. In general he would be right; there are very few examples in which the method reduces an equation to one which is easier to "solve." But, as we shall see in the sequel, there are important uses for the technique, and for the present we wish only to give the student some practice in it.

What has been said for a single equation applies equally well to systems of equations. Consider the system

$$
\dot{x}_{k}=f_{k}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, n
$$

and its modification
(1.9) $\quad \dot{x}_{k}=f_{k}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right)+g_{k}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, n$.

The system (1.8), again under suitable restrictions, will have a solution of the form

$$
x_{k}=x_{k}\left(c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} ; t\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, n
$$

where $c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n}$ are parameters. According to (1.8),

$$
\frac{\partial x_{k}}{\partial t}\left(c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} ; t\right)=f_{k}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, n
$$

We shall try to make the functions (1.10) fit the Eqs. (1.9) by permitting the $c_{k}$ to be functions of $t$. Since

$$
\dot{x}_{k}=\sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{\partial x_{k}}{\partial c_{t}} \dot{c}_{t}+\frac{\partial x_{k}}{\partial t}
$$

$$
=\sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{\partial x_{k}}{\partial c} \dot{c}_{t}+f_{k}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right)
$$

according to (1.11), it follows by comparison with (1.9) that

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{\partial x_{k}}{\partial c_{t}} \dot{c}_{t}=g_{k}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, n
$$

It is understood that each $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}$ appearing on the right-hand side is to be replaced accerding to (1.10). If the determinant $\left|\partial x_{k} / \partial c_{t}\right|$ does not vanish, the Eqs. (1.12) may be solved for the "unknowns" $\dot{c}_{k}$ to yield a system

$$
\dot{c}_{k}=h_{k}\left(c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} ; \gamma\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, n
$$

As an example, consider the syst m

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x}_{1}=-x_{2} \\
& \dot{x}_{2}=x_{1}
\end{aligned}
$$

and a modification

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x}_{1}=-x_{2} \\
& \dot{x}_{2}=x_{1}+\alpha \sec t
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant. The system (1.14) has the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}=c_{1} \cos t+c_{2} \sin t \\
& x_{2}=c_{1} \sin t-c_{2} \cos t
\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ are parameters. We now interpret $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ as functions of $t$ and try to fit the functions (1.16) to the Eqs. (1.15). Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{c}_{1} \cos t+\dot{c}_{2} \sin t-c_{1} \sin t+c_{2} \cos t=-c_{1} \sin t+c_{2} \cos t \\
& \dot{c}_{1} \sin t-\dot{c}_{2} \cos t+c_{1} \cos t+c_{2} \sin t=c_{1} \cos t+c_{2} \sin t+\alpha \sec t
\end{aligned}
$$

After an obvious cancellation, the equations can be solved for $\dot{c}_{1}$ and $\dot{c}_{2}$. It turns out that

$$
\dot{c}_{1}=\alpha \tan t, \quad \dot{c}_{2}=-\alpha
$$

Unlike the earlier example, it happens that these can be solved simply. The final result is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& c_{1}=-\alpha \log |\cos t|+k_{1} \\
& c_{2}=-\alpha t+k_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ are constants. With these choices for $c_{1}, c_{2}$, the Eqs. (1.16) give the solution of (1.15).
*exercise 1.1. Show that the original Kepler problem of Chap. 1 can be interpreted as a system of the form (1.8), and a disturbed system, as described in Sec. 16 of that chapter, as a modified system (1.9).

Explain why Eqs. (17.8) and (18.2) of Chap. 1 correspond to (1.13) here.

## 2. THE PERIHELION OF MERCURY

In Sec. 15 of Chap. 1, a very simplified picture of the solar system was presented. The actual motions are considerably more complicated because, for one thing, we do not have nine independent two-body problems. Each planet is disturbed from its elliptic course by attractions from the other planets.

There is one important disturbance from elliptic motion which we shall discuss here. It was found that the disturbed motion of Mercury could not be explained entirely by attractions of the other planets. In particular, it was found that the change in $\omega$ deduced in this way was less than the observed amount by about $43^{\prime \prime}$ per century. No explanation was found until the theory of general relativity was produced by Einstein.

To understand his explanation of the phenomenon, we go back to Sec. 6 of Chap. 1. It is shown there that the determination of a motion under the central force $f(r)$ can be reduced to the equation

$$
\rho^{\prime \prime}+\rho=c^{-5} \rho^{-5} f\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\right)
$$

where $\rho=\rho(\theta)$ and $\theta$ is an angular variable. Now if $f(r)=\mu r^{-5}$ according to Newton's law, the equation takes the form

$$
\rho^{\prime \prime}+\rho=c^{-5} \mu
$$

But it happens that, if we accept the theory of relativity, the particle behaves as if the law of attraction is actually $f(r)=\mu r^{-5} \cdot \epsilon c^{2} r^{-4}$, where $\epsilon$ is "small." Actually $\epsilon=3 \mu V^{-5}$, where $V$ is the velocity of light. With this substitution for Newton's law in (2.1), Eq. (2.2) must be revised as

$$
\rho^{\prime \prime}+\rho=c^{-5} \mu+\epsilon \rho^{5}
$$

This can be written as the system

$$
\rho^{\prime}=s, \quad s^{\prime}=c^{-5} \mu-\rho+\epsilon \rho^{5}
$$

We study the effect of the disturbing term or "relativistic correction" $\epsilon \rho^{5}$ by first supposing that $\epsilon=0$ and solving the undisturbed system

$$
\rho^{\prime}=s, \quad s^{\prime}=c^{-5} \mu-\rho
$$

Observe that the independent variable is $\theta$, not $t$, but this does not affect the applicability of the method of variation of parameters described in Sec. 1. The system (2.4) is equivalent to (2.2), and we know that the solution of (2.2) is

$$
\rho=c^{-5} \mu[1+e \cos (\theta-\omega)]
$$

where $e$ is the eccentricity of the undisturbed orbit and $\omega$ is the amplitude of perihelion. Since $\rho^{\prime}=s$, we have

$$
s=-c^{-5} \mu e \sin (\theta-\omega)
$$

Therefore (2.5) and (2.6) together give the solution of the undisturbed system.

We study the system (2.3) by writing its solution in the form (2.5), (6); but now the "constants" $e$ and $\omega$ are regarded as functions of $\theta$. So differentiate each of (2.5) and (2.6) with respect to $\theta$ and substitute the resulting formulas for $\rho^{\prime}$ and $s^{\prime}$ into (2.3). If we abbreviate $\theta-\omega$ by $f$, the following formulas are found:

$$
\begin{gathered}
e^{\prime} \cos f+e \omega^{\prime} \sin f=0 \\
-e^{\prime} \sin f+e \omega^{\prime} \cos f=\epsilon c^{-5} \mu(1+e \cos f)^{5}
\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore

$$
e^{\prime}=-\epsilon c^{-5} \mu(\sin f)(1+e \cos f)^{5}
$$

and

$$
\omega^{\prime}=\epsilon c^{-5} \mu e^{-1}(\cos f)(1+e \cos f)^{5}
$$

This system is no easier to "solve" than the original one (2.3). But this is not our purpose. We are trying to explain a change in $\omega$ of $43^{\prime \prime}$ per century, and for this purpose rough methods will serve. Due to the presence of the small number $\epsilon$ on the right-hand side of (2.7) and (2.8), we expect that $e$ and $\omega$ change very slowly. Since we are talking about a century and the period of Mercury is only about eighty-eight days, we argue that it is probably safe to take $c$ and $\omega$ as constant on the right-hand side of the equations for a period $0 \leqq \theta \leqq 2 \pi$. Then, according to (2.8),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\omega(2 \pi)-\omega(0) & =\epsilon c^{-5} \mu e^{-1} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} \cos (\theta-\omega)[1+e \cos (\theta-\omega)]^{2} d \theta \\
& =2 \pi \epsilon c^{-5} \mu
\end{aligned}
$$

which is the approximate change in $\omega$ in one period due to the relativistic correction. If we multiply by the number of periods in a century it turns out that the numerical result is the $43^{\prime \prime}$ which needs explaining. Observe that the result is a positive number, which explains the familiar reference to the "advance in the perihelion of Mercury."

EXERCISE 2.1. Equations (2.7) can be derived directly from (17.8) of Chap. 1 by setting $F_{n}=0, F_{e}=0, F_{r}=\epsilon c^{2} r^{-4}$ and eliminating the time by use of $r^{2} \theta=c$. Carry out the details.

## 3. FIRST ORDER PERTURBATION THEORY

The rough method used in the preceding section to study the motion of the perihelion of Mercury has a very general formulation. To explain it we

return to the problem studied in Sec. 1. Suppose the system (1.9) to be of the special form

$$
\dot{x}_{k}=f_{k}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right)+\epsilon F_{r}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right)
$$

where $k=1, \ldots, n$ and $\epsilon$ is a parameter. Then (1.12) becomes

$$
\sum_{1} \frac{\partial x_{k}}{\partial c_{i}} \dot{c}_{i}=\epsilon F_{c}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} ; t\right)
$$

and (1.13) takes the form

$$
\dot{c}_{k}=\epsilon G_{c}\left(c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} ; t\right)
$$

We shall refer to the systems (3.1) or (3.2) as undisturbed if $\epsilon=0$ ald disturbed if $\epsilon \neq 0$.

As we observed earlier, the system (3.2) obtained from (3.1) by the variation of parameters may be no easier to "solve" than (3.1). But, for sufficiently small values of $\epsilon$, it is frequently possible to get a good approximation to the solution over intervals of time that are not "too" long. The main idea is this. Suppose the values of $c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n}$ are known at some instant $t_{0}$; call them $c_{1}^{0}, \ldots, c_{n}^{0}$. Then the solution of the undisturbed system, (3.2) with $\epsilon \approx 0$, is simply $c_{k}=c_{k}^{0}$. The form of (3.2) suggests that if $\epsilon$ is small enough, then $c_{k}$ cannot change rapidly; in other words, for a length of time not too far from $t_{0}$, the solution of (3.2) cannot vary much from $c_{k}^{0}, k=1, \ldots, n$. With this in mind, we suppose that a good approximate solution can be obtained in the form

$$
c_{k}(t)=c_{k}^{0}+\epsilon \eta_{k}(t), \quad k=1, \ldots, n
$$

where the conditions at $t_{0}$ are met by supposing that

$$
\eta_{k}\left(t_{0}\right)=0
$$

Substitution of (3.3) into (3.2) yields these equations for $\eta_{k}$ :

$$
\dot{\eta}_{k}=G_{k}\left(c_{1}^{0}+\epsilon \eta_{1}, \ldots, c_{n}^{0}+\epsilon \eta_{n} ; t\right)
$$

If we suppose further that $G_{k}$ is a sufficiently smooth function, then the right-hand side is well approximated for small $\epsilon$ by letting $\epsilon=0$. We arrive at the approximate equation

$$
\dot{\eta}_{k}=G_{k}\left(c_{1}^{0}, \ldots, c_{n}^{0} ; t\right)
$$

so that, by virtue of (3.4),

$$
c_{k}=c_{k}^{0}+\epsilon \eta_{k}=c_{k}^{0}+\epsilon \int_{t_{0}}^{t} G_{k}\left(c_{1}^{0}, \ldots, c_{n}^{0} ; \tau\right) d \tau
$$

This is the same result produced by integrating (3.2) directly, while supposing that $c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n}$ on the right-hand side remain constant. Observe that the method is precisely that used in Sec. 2, where, however, the variable is $\theta$ rather than $t$. Because only the first power of $\epsilon$ appears in (3.3), the term $\epsilon \eta_{k}$ is called a first order perturbation.

The example of Sec. 2 furnishes a simple example of how the method is applied. We shall now present a more elaborate example. Consider the system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x}_{1}=-x_{2} \\
& \dot{x}_{2}=k^{2} x_{1}+\epsilon\left(x_{2}^{2}+q \cos l t\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $k, \epsilon, q, l$ are constants. We shall begin with the undisturbed system

$$
\dot{x}_{1}=-x_{2}, \quad \dot{x}_{2}=k^{2} x_{1}
$$

and apply the method of variation of parameters. The solution of the undisturbed system is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}=c_{1} \cos k t+c_{2} \sin k t \\
& x_{2}=c_{1} k \sin k t-c_{2} k \cos k t
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these into (3.5), regarding both $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ as functions of $t$. Then solve the resulting equations for $\dot{c}_{1}$ and $\dot{c}_{2}$. We obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{c}_{1}=\epsilon \sin k t\left[k^{2}\left(c_{1} \sin k t-c_{2} \cos k t\right)^{2}+\frac{q}{k} \cos l t\right] \\
& \dot{c}_{2}=-\epsilon \cos k t\left[k^{2}\left(c_{1} \sin k t-c_{2} \cos k t\right)^{2}+\frac{q}{k} \cos l t\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

According to (3.6), the values of $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ at each instant can be found from the values of $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ at the instant. In discussing (3.7), we may therefore suppose $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ known at some time, which we take to be zero for simplicity; let their values be $c_{1}^{0}$ and $c_{2}^{0}$, respectively. According to the rough method described above, we can get a first approximation to the solution of (3.7) from

$$
\begin{aligned}
& c_{1}=c_{1}^{0}+\epsilon \int_{c}^{l} \sin k \tau\left[k^{2}\left(c_{1}^{0} \sin k \tau-c_{2}^{0} \cos k \tau\right)^{2}+\frac{q}{k} \cos l \tau\right] d \tau \\
& c_{2}=c_{2}^{0}-\epsilon \int_{c}^{l} \cos k \tau\left[k^{2}\left(c_{1}^{0} \cos k \tau-c_{2}^{0} \cos k \tau\right)^{2}+\frac{q}{k} \cos l \tau\right] d \tau
\end{aligned}
$$

The precise evaluation of the integrals is of no importance here. What matters is that each integral is of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
A+B t & +(C \cos 2 k t+D \sin 2 k t)+(E \cos 4 k t+F \sin 4 k t) \\
& +G \cos (k+l) t+H \sin (k+l) t
\end{aligned}
$$

if $k=l$, and there are two additional terms

$$
J \frac{\sin (l-k) t}{l-k}+K \frac{1-\cos (l-k) t}{l-k}
$$

if $k \neq l$.
There is a traditional classification of the terms which occur in the sum

above. In addition to the constant terri, there are terms in the sine and cosine of $4 k t, 2 k t$ and (if $k \neq l$ ) of $(k+l) t,(k-l) t$. These are called the periodic terms. The term in $t$ is called secular. In some problems, terms of the form $t \cos p t$ or $t \sin p t$ will occur; these are mixed or Poisson terms. The intended distinction between the periodic and secular terms is clear: the periodic terms indicate a bounded disturbance which recurs regularly; the secular term indicates a steadily increasing disturbance. However, the distinction has little justification rigorously and may be due entirely to the method by which the approximate solution has been obtained. For example, the first term in the power series expansion of

$$
J \frac{\sin (l-k) t}{l-k}
$$

is simply $J t$. If an approximation method is used which happens to give $J t$ rather than (3.8), it will look like a secular term when it may, in fact, be an approximation for small $t$ to a periodic term. There is still another difficulty: the approximation to the solution may be valid for such a short interval of time that the periodic terms do not have time to complete even one period before the approximation fails.

Because of these doubts, we may view with a certain amount of skepticism another distinction that is made. A term of the form $\sin 2 k t$ has a period $\pi / k$; one of the form $\sin (l-k) t$ has the period $2 \pi /(l-k)$. If $l$ is very close to $k$, the latter period will be large compared to the former. Thus we have a distinction between short-period and long-period terms. There is some evidence in the problems of celestial mechanics that secular terms may be approximations to long-period terms, but to date there is only one real justification for the distinctions among terms: it works in practice for the numerical cases familiar to the astronomer or engineer.

## 4. THE ERROR IN FIRST ORDER THEORY

In the last section we used some very rough reasoning to conclude that a good first approximation to the solution of

$$
c_{k}=\epsilon G_{k}\left(c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} ; t\right)
$$

with values $c_{k}^{n}$ at $t=t_{0}$ is

$$
c_{k}^{n}(t)=c_{k}^{0}+\epsilon \int_{t_{0}}^{t} G_{k}\left(c_{1}^{0}, \ldots, c_{n}^{0} ; \tau\right) d \tau
$$

where $k=1, \ldots, n$. We use the small " $a$ " to indicate "approximate" solution because we shall reserve the symbol $c_{1}(t)$ for the true solution.

It is our purpose now to examine the meaning of a "good first approximation."

We content ourselves with the case $n=1$, which is typical of the general case. If we drop the subscripts, then (4.1) becomes

$$
\dot{c}=\epsilon G(c, t)
$$

and (4.3) becomes

$$
c^{n}(t)=c^{0}+\epsilon \int_{t_{0}}^{t} G\left(c^{0}, \tau\right) d \tau
$$

According to (4.3), the true solution must satisfy the equation

$$
c(t)=c^{0}+\epsilon \int_{t_{0}}^{t} G(c(\tau), \tau) d \tau
$$

We ask: how large is the difference $\left|c^{n}(t)-c(t)\right|$ and for how long an interval of $t$ 'me $\left|t-t_{0}\right|$ ? For simplicity, we shall suppose that $G(c, t)$ is continuous and bounded for all $c$ and $t$, and that $\partial G / \partial c$ exists for all $c$ and has the same properties as $G$. Then

$$
|G(c, t)| \leqq A, \quad\left|\frac{\partial G}{\partial c}(c, t)\right| \leqq B
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. According to the mean-value theorem,

$$
G\left(c^{0}, \tau\right)-G(c(\tau), \tau)=\left(c^{0}-c(\tau)\right) \frac{\partial G}{\partial c}(\xi, \tau)
$$

where $\tau$ is fixed and $\xi$ lies between $c^{0}$ and $c(\tau)$. Since $B$ bounds the derivative $\partial G / \partial c$, we conclude that

$$
\left|G\left(c^{0}, \tau\right)-G(c(\tau), \tau)\right| \leqq B\left|c^{0}-c(\tau)\right|
$$

Now, according to (4.5),

$$
c^{0}-c(\tau)=\epsilon \int_{t_{0}}^{t} G(c(\tau), \tau) d \tau
$$

Therefore

$$
\left|c^{0}-c(\tau)\right| \leqq \epsilon\left|\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\right| G(c(\tau), \tau)|d \tau|
$$

Since $A$ bounds the function $G(c, t)$,

$$
\left|c^{0}-c(\tau)\right| \leqq \epsilon\left|\int_{t_{0}}^{t} A d \tau\right|=A \epsilon\left|\tau-t_{0}\right|
$$

From (4.6), we conclude that

$$
\left|G\left(c^{0}, \tau\right)-G(c(\tau), \tau)\right| \leqq A B \epsilon\left|\tau-t_{0}\right|
$$

If we subtract Eq. (4.5) from Eq. (4.4), the result is

$$
c^{n}(t)-c(t)=\epsilon \int_{t_{0}}^{t}\left[G\left(c^{0}, \tau\right)-G(c(\tau), \tau)\right] d \tau
$$

so that, by (4.7),

$$
\left|c^{n}(t)-c(t)\right| \leqq A B \epsilon^{2}\left|\int_{t_{1}}^{t}\left(\tau-t_{0}\right) d \tau\right|
$$

We conclude that

$$
\left|c^{n}(t)-c(t)\right| \leqq K^{2} \epsilon^{2}\left(t-t_{0}\right)^{2}, \quad K^{2}=\frac{1}{2} A B
$$

It follows that if $\left|t-t_{0}\right| \leqq K^{-1} \epsilon^{-1 / 2}$, then $\left|c^{n}(t)-c(t)\right| \leqq \epsilon^{2 / 3}$. This means that $c^{n}$ and $c$ agree within a term of order $\epsilon^{2 / 3}$ over a length of time of the order of $\epsilon^{-1 / 2}$; the smaller the $\epsilon$, the better the approximation and the longer the time over which the approximation is valid.

In practice, these estimates are of little use. First, the equations which actually occur are considerably more complicated, so that the constants like $A$ and $B$ which occur in the practical problems are impossible to determine. Secondly, $\epsilon$ is fixed by the problem and there is no choice in how small it may be taken. Nevertheless, it is satisfactory to have a theoretical justification of the procedure.

exercise 4.2. Find an estimate corresponding to (4.8) in the case $n$ is larger than 1 .

## 5. THE EQUATIONS OF DISTURBED ELLIPTIC MOTION

In Secs. 16-18 of Chap. 1 the method of variation of parameters, in a somewhat disguised form, was applied to obtain equations for the variation of the elements of a disturbed elliptic motion

$$
\ddot{\mathbf{r}}=-\mu r^{-1} \mathbf{r}+\mathbf{F}
$$

in terms of the components $F_{r}, F_{u}, F_{z}$ of $\mathbf{F}$. To make cross-reference unnecessary, we reproduce the equations here in a rearranged form.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\dot{a}=2 a^{2} e c^{-1}(\sin f) F_{r}+2 a^{2} c \mu^{-1} r^{-1} F_{u} \\
\dot{e}=c \mu^{-1}(\sin f) F_{r}+c \mu^{-1}\left(e+2 \cos f+e \cos ^{2} f\right)(1+e \cos f)^{-1} F_{u} \\
\frac{d i}{d t}=r c^{-1} F_{z} \cos (\omega+f) \\
\dot{\omega}=-c \mu^{-1} e^{-1} F_{r} \cos f+(\mu e c)^{-1}\left(c^{2}+r \mu\right) F_{u} \sin f \\
-r c^{-1} F_{z} \cot i \sin (\omega+f) \\
\dot{\Omega}=r c^{-1} F_{z} \csc i \sin (\omega+f)
\end{gathered}
$$

(5.6) $\dot{T}=(\mu e a \sin f)^{-1}[r c-\frac{1}{2} \mu e(t-T) \sin f] \dot{a}-a c(\mu e)^{-1} \dot{e} \cot f$.

In addition, we found equations for related variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{n}=-\frac{3}{2} n a^{-1} \dot{a} \\
& \dot{c}=r F_{u}
\end{aligned}
$$

Moreover, because $\varpi=\omega+\Omega$, we can add Eqs. (5.4) and (5.5) together to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\varpi= & -c \mu^{-1} e^{-1} F_{r} \cos f+(\mu e c)^{-1}\left(c^{2}+r \mu\right) F_{u} \sin f \\
& +r c^{-1} F_{z} \tan \frac{l}{2} \sin (\omega+f)
\end{aligned}
$$

The basic set of equations is formed by (5.1)-(5.6), but it is clear that (5.9) may be substituted for either (5.4) or (5.5). Also, because $c^{2}=$ $\mu a\left(1-e^{2}\right)$, Eq. (5.8) may be substituted for (5.1) or (5.2). Many other combinations are permitted, provided the basic set can be obtained from them. Thus (5.1) may be replaced by an equation for $\dot{b}$, where $h=-\mu / 2 a$. If (5.2) is replaced by (5.8), we may also replace (5.3) by an equation for $\dot{H}$, where $H=c \cos i$. Each of these choices occurs in practice, depending on the nature of the force $\mathbf{F}$ causing the disturbance.

But whichever choice is made, i turns out that (5.6) is a serious source of trouble because of the presence of the term in $t$. One way out is to replace (5.6) by an equation for the mean anomaly $l$. Since $l=n(t-T)$ and $\dot{l}=n(1-\dot{T})+\dot{n}(t-T)$, it follows from (5.6) and (5.7) that

$$
\dot{l}=n-n(\mu e a \sin f)^{-1} r c \dot{a}+n a c(\mu e)^{-1} \dot{e} \cot f
$$

in which $t$ no longer appears explicitly. An alternative which is sometimes used is $\sigma$, defined by

$$
\sigma=l-\rho, \quad \rho=\int^{l} n(\tau) d \tau
$$

From (5.10) we get the equation

$$
\dot{\sigma}=-n(\mu e a \sin f)^{-1} r c \dot{a}+n a c(\mu e)^{-1} \dot{e} \cot f
$$

Two other variables are also used. First is the quantity $\epsilon$. defined by $\epsilon=\omega-n T$ and known by the impressive title the mean longitude at the epoch. It suffers from the same defect as $T$ itself, namely, the presence of $t$ in the equation for $\dot{\epsilon}$. This is circumvented by choosing in place of $\epsilon$ a quantity $\epsilon_{1}$, defined by $\epsilon_{1}=n t+\epsilon-\rho$, or, what is equivalent, $\epsilon_{1}=\omega+$ $l-\rho$.

Whatever six variables are chosen, it is clear that for an analytical study of the differential equations, the quantities $F_{r}, F_{u}, F_{z}$ must be replaced by suitable functions of these variables. The same is true of $r$ and $f$, which do not occur on the left-hand side of our equations. How the replacement is done will be the object of the next section.

$e$ and $\omega$ can be replaced by equations for the variables $e \sin \omega$ and $e \cos \omega$. ## 6. THE PERTURBATION EQUATIONS IN ANALYTIC FORM

If a particle is moving in disturbed elliptic motion, then at each instant $t$ the elements of the osculating ellipse are determined by the values of $\mathbf{r}$ and $\mathbf{v}$. Conversely, it follows that the position and velocity at the instant can be determined from the values of the six elements of the osculating ellipse. As we saw in the preceding section, some of these elements can be replaced by other quantities such as $\sigma, l$ or $c$, provided the totality of them determine the six elements. Whatever choice is made, let us denote the quantities by $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{k}$, or, generically, simply by $q$. Then $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{k} ; t\right)$, and similarly for $\mathbf{v}$.

It is important for us to compute the derivatives $\partial \mathbf{r} / \partial q$ and to find their components in the directions of $\mathbf{r}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}, \mathbf{c}$ described in Sec. 16 of Chap. 1. For definiteness, we choose the quantities to be the standard elements $a, e, i$, $\omega, \Omega$ and the mean anomaly $l$. The symbol $\partial \mathbf{r} / \partial q$ denotes the partial derivative with respect to each one of these six quantities, the other five and the time being held fixed.

As in Fig. 10, p. 33, let $x, y, z$ denote a fixed coor tinate system centered at $O$ and let $\mathbf{n}$ denote a unit vector in the direction of the line of nodes. By $\hat{\mathbf{r}}, \hat{\mathbf{a}}, \hat{\mathbf{c}}$, we mean the unit vectors $r^{-1} \mathbf{r}, \alpha^{-1} \alpha, c^{-1} \mathrm{c}$. Therefore

$$
\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{F}_{r} \hat{\mathbf{r}}+F_{a} \hat{\mathbf{a}}+F_{z} \hat{\mathbf{c}}
$$

By $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$ we mean the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{c}} \times \hat{\mathbf{n}}$; it lies in the orbital plane of the osculating ellipse at time $t$ and is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$. Then

$$
\mathbf{r}=r \cos (\omega+f) \hat{\mathbf{n}}+r \sin (\omega+f) \hat{\mathbf{m}}
$$

It is clear that $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is determined by $\Omega$ alone and $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$ by both $\Omega$ and $i$. We may therefore differentiate $\mathbf{r}$, as given by (6.2), with respect to any of the four remaining quantities $a, e, \omega, l$ by differentiating the coefficients of $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$, and not $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$ themselves. Therefore, provided $q$ is one of these four quantities,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial q}= & \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial q}[\cos (\omega+f) \hat{\mathbf{n}}+\operatorname{sir}(\omega+f) \hat{\mathbf{m}}] \\
& +r \frac{\partial(\omega+f)}{\partial q}[-\sin (\omega+f) \hat{\mathbf{n}}+\cos (\omega+f) \hat{\mathbf{m}}]
\end{aligned}
$$

According to (6.2), the first expression in square brackets is simply $r^{-1} \mathbf{r}$ or $\hat{\mathbf{r}}$. The second lies in the orbital pla te and forms a right-handed system with $\hat{\mathbf{r}}$; it is clearly $\hat{\mathbf{a}}$. It follows that

$$
\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial q}=\frac{\partial r}{\partial q} \hat{\mathbf{r}}+r\left(\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial q}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial q}\right) \hat{\mathbf{a}}, \quad q=a, e, \omega, l
$$

Since $u$ can be eliminated between the equations

$$
r=a(1-e \cos u), \quad l=u-e \sin u
$$

the quantity $r$ depends only on $a, e, l$; it is independent of $\omega, i, \Omega$. Moreover,

$$
1+e \cos f=a\left(1-e^{2}\right) r^{-1}
$$

so that $f$ depends at most on $a, e, l$.
In particular, $\partial r / \partial \omega=0, \partial f / \partial \omega=0$. Therefore Eq. (6.3) for $q=\omega$ becomes simply $\partial \mathbf{r} / \partial \omega=r \hat{\mathbf{a}}$. Hence, by (6.1), $\mathbf{F} \cdot \partial \mathbf{r} / \partial \omega=r F_{a}$. This enables us to rewrite (5.8) as

$$
\dot{c}=\mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \omega}
$$

We turn to the case $q=l$. According to (6.4),

$$
\frac{\partial r}{\partial l}=a e \sin u \frac{\partial u}{\partial l}, \quad l=(1-e \cos u) \frac{\partial u}{\partial l}=\frac{r}{a} \frac{\partial u}{\partial l}
$$

Since $\sin u=\mu^{1 / 2} a^{-1 / 2} c^{-1} r \sin f$, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\partial r}{\partial l}=e \mu^{1 / 2} a^{2 / 2} c^{-1} \sin f
$$

From (6.5) we get $-e \sin f(\partial f / \partial l)=-a\left(1-e^{2}\right) r^{-2}(\partial r / \partial l)$, so that

$$
r \frac{\partial f}{\partial l}=c r^{-1} \mu^{-1 / 2} a^{2 / 2}
$$

Since $\partial \omega / \partial l=0$, Eq. (6.3) becomes

$$
\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial l}=e \mu^{1 / 2} a^{2 / 2} c^{-1} \sin f \hat{\mathbf{r}}+c r^{-1} \mu^{-1 / 2} a^{2 / 2} \hat{\mathbf{a}}
$$

According to (6.1) once again

$$
\mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial l}=e \mu^{1 / 2} a^{2 / 2} c^{-1} \sin f F_{r}+c r^{-1} \mu^{-1 / 2} a^{2 / 2} F_{a}
$$

Clearly, this permits us to write (5.1) as

$$
\dot{a}=2 a^{1 / 2} \mu^{-1 / 2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial l}
$$

Since $c^{2}=\mu a\left(1-e^{2}\right)$, we can compute $\dot{e}$ from $\dot{a}$, as just found, and $\dot{c}$, as given by (6.6). Then

$$
\dot{e}=(a \mu)^{-1 / 2} e^{-1}\left(1-e^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}\left[\left(1-e^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial l}-\mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \omega}\right]
$$

If $q=a$, we get from (6.4) that

$$
\frac{\partial r}{\partial a}=(1-e \cos u)+a e \sin u \frac{\partial u}{\partial a}, \quad 0=(1-e \cos u) \frac{\partial u}{\partial a}
$$

Thercfore $\partial u / \partial a=0$ and $\partial r / \partial a=r / a$. Also, by (6.5),

$$
-a e \sin f \frac{\partial f}{\partial a}=\left(1-e^{2}\right) r^{-1}-\varepsilon\left(1-e^{-2}\right) r^{-1} \frac{\partial r}{\partial a}=0
$$

Hence $\partial f / \partial a=0$. Since $\partial \omega / \partial a=0$, the formula (6.3) says simply that $\therefore \partial a=(r / a) i$. According to (6.1),

$$
\mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial a}=\frac{r}{a} F_{r}
$$

The procedures applied when $q=I$ or $a$ works just as well when $q=c$, .Ithough the computation is a little longer. The result is

$$
\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial c}=-a \cos f \mathbf{i}+a \sin f\left[1+\frac{r}{a\left(1-e^{2}\right)}\right] \hat{\mathbf{a}}
$$

so that

$$
\mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial r}{\partial c}=-a \cos f F_{r}+a \sin f\left[1+\frac{r}{a\left(1-e^{2}\right)}\right] F_{a}
$$

This formula and (6.7) enable us to rewrite (5.10) as

$$
i=n-\left(1-e^{2}\right)(u a)^{-1 / 2} e^{-1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial c}-2 a^{1 / 2} \mu^{-1 / 2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial a}
$$

We have exhausted the cases when (6.3) is applicable. To treat $q=i$, we turn back to (6.2). Of all the quantities which appear on the right-hand side, only $\hat{m}$ depends on $i$. If $\Omega$ is held fixed and $i$ is changed by amount $\Delta i$, this has the effect of rotating $m$ by the amount $\Delta i$ in the plane of $m$ and $\hat{c}$. Since this plane is perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, it remains fixed. Hence, $\partial \hat{\mathbf{n}} / \partial i=\hat{\mathbf{c}}$. Therefore, by (6.2), we have $\partial \mathbf{r} / \partial i=r \sin (\omega+f)(\partial \hat{\mathbf{m}} / \partial i)=$ $r \sin (\omega+f) \mathbf{c}$. From (6.1) we obtain

$$
\mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial i}=r \sin (\omega+f) F_{r}
$$

This enables us to write (5.5) as

$$
\Omega=\left[\mu a\left(1-e^{2}\right)\right]^{-1} \csc i \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial i}
$$

and with the help of (6.8) it converts (5.4) into

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{\omega}= & -\left[\mu a\left(1-e^{2}\right)\right]^{-1} \cot i \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial i} \\
& +(\mu a)^{-1 / 2}\left(1-e^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} e^{-1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial c}
\end{aligned}
$$

To obtain $\partial \mathbf{r} / \partial \Omega$, the last on our list, we start with (6.2), according to which

$$
\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \Omega}=r \cos (\omega+f) \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{m}}}{\partial \Omega}+r \sin (\omega+f) \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{n}}}{\partial \Omega}
$$

From this we can derive (see Ex. 6.1)

$$
\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \Omega}=r\left[\cos i \hat{\mathbf{a}}-\sin i \cos (\omega+f) \hat{\mathbf{c}}\right]
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \Omega}=r\left[\cos i F_{a}-\sin i \cos (\omega+f) F_{c}\right]
$$

and (5.3) becomes
(VI) $\frac{d i}{d t}=\left[\mu a\left(1-e^{2}\right)\right]^{-1} \cot i \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \omega}-\left[\mu a\left(1-e^{2}\right)\right]^{-1} \csc i \mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \Omega}$.

## 7. ALTERNATIVE FORMS OF THE EQUATIONS

In the major applications of perturbation theory, the disturbing force $\mathbf{F}$ originates from a disturbing function $R(\mathbf{r}, t)$, as described in Ex. 6.2, through the relation $\mathbf{F}=\operatorname{grad} R=\partial R / \partial \mathbf{r}$. The most important example is this. We are interested in the motion of a mass $m_{1}$ with respect to mass $m_{2}$ when this motion is disturbed by a mass $m_{3}$ whose motion with respect to $m_{1}$ is known. Some special cases are these: $m_{1}=$ earth, $m_{2}=$ moon, $m_{3}=$ sun; $m_{1}=\operatorname{sun}, m_{2}=$ minor planet, $m_{3}=$ Jupiter.

To obtain the equations of motion we return to Eqs. (7.1) of Chap. 2.

Divide the first by $m_{1}$, the second by $m_{2}$, and subtract the first from the second. We get

$$
\ddot{\mathbf{r}}=-\mu r^{-1} \mathbf{r}+G m_{2}\left[\frac{\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{r}}{r_{21}^{2}}-\frac{\mathbf{s}}{s^{2}}\right]
$$

where $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_{2}-\mathbf{r}_{1}, \mathbf{s}=\mathbf{r}_{3}-\mathbf{r}_{1}, \mu=G\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right), s=|\mathbf{s}|$. The vector $\mathbf{s}$ is known as a function of $t$ and is independent of $\mathbf{r}$. Define the function $R$ by

$$
R(\mathbf{r}, t)=G m_{2}\left(r_{21}^{-1}-s^{-1} \mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{r}\right)
$$

The gradient $\partial R / \partial \mathbf{r}$ can be calculated by using the suggestion to Ex. 7.3 of Chap. 2. As a result, we find that the differential Eq. (7.1) becomes $\ddot{\mathbf{r}}=$ $-\mu r^{-1} \mathbf{r}+\mathbf{F}$, with $\mathbf{F}=\partial R / \partial \mathbf{r}$.

Under the circumstance that $\mathbf{F}$ is of the form described, we have $\partial R / \partial q=\mathbf{F} \cdot \partial \mathbf{r} / \partial q$ for each of the quantities $q$ selected in Sec. 6. Then Eqs. (I)-(VI) of that section take the form
(I)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{a}=2 a^{1 / 2} \mu^{-1 / 2} \frac{\partial R}{\partial l} \\
& \dot{e}=c(a \mu e)^{-1}\left[\left(1-e^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \frac{\partial R}{\partial l}-\frac{\partial R}{\partial \omega}\right] \\
& \dot{i}=n-\left(1-e^{2}\right)(\mu a)^{-1 / 2} e^{-1} \frac{\partial R}{\partial e}-2 a^{1 / 2} \mu^{-1 / 2} \frac{\partial R}{\partial a}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\dot{\Omega} \quad \therefore \therefore c^{i^{\prime} R} \dot{\partial l}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{\omega}=-c^{-1} \cot i \frac{\partial R}{\partial l}+c(\mu a v)^{-1} \frac{\partial R}{\partial e} \\
& \text { (VI) } \quad \frac{d i}{d t}=c^{-1} \cot \frac{\partial R}{\partial \omega}-c^{-1} \csc i \frac{\partial R}{\partial \Omega}
\end{aligned}
$$

It should be remembered that $n$ is an abbreviation for $\mu^{1 / 2} a^{-1 / 2}$ and $c$ for $\left[\mu a\left(1-e^{2}\right)\right]^{1 / 2}$.

A simpler set of equations can be obtained from these by using a somewhat different set of quantities, introduced by Delaunay. Let $L=$ $(\mu a)^{1 / 2}, H=c \cos i$. Then his six quantities are $L, c, H, l, \omega, \Omega$. To transfer the preceding perturbation equations to the new variables, let $R$ denote the disturbing function expressed in terms of the original variables and $\mathscr{R}$ the same function in terms of the new variables.

Clearly, $\partial R / \partial l=\partial \mathscr{R} / \partial l$. Because $L=(\mu a)^{1 / 2}$ Eq. (I) becomes

$$
\dot{L}=\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial l}
$$

Equation (II) is discarded because $e$ is not present in the new list of variables. But in its place we recall [see (6.6)] that $\dot{c}=\partial R / \partial \omega$. But $\partial R / \partial \omega$ $=\partial \mathscr{R} / \partial \omega$. Therefore

$$
\dot{c}=\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial \omega}
$$

As to (III), we observe first that $a$ is implicitly contained in $\mathscr{R}$ through the variables $L, c$ and $H$, and $e$ through the variables $c$ and $H$. Therefore

$$
\frac{\partial R}{\partial a}=\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial L} \frac{\partial L}{\partial a}+\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial c} \frac{\partial c}{\partial a}+\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial H} \frac{\partial H}{\partial a}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\partial R}{\partial e}=\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial c} \frac{\partial c}{\partial e}+\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial H} \frac{\partial H}{\partial e}
$$

If we compute the partial derivatives with respect to $a$ and $e$ and substitute into (III), we get

$$
\dot{i}=n-\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial L}
$$

Now $l$ occurs in $\mathscr{R}$ only through $H$. Therefore

$$
\frac{\partial R}{\partial i}=\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial H} \frac{\partial H}{\partial i}=-c \sin i \frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial H}
$$

and (IV) becomes

$$
\dot{\Omega}=-\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial H}
$$

If we use this computation of $\partial R / \partial$, and $\partial R / \partial e$ as compited from (7.3) I:1 (V) is comected ints
$\left(\mathrm{V}^{\prime}\right)$

$$
\dot{\omega}=-\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial c}
$$

If we start with $H=c \cos i$, then (II') and (VI) together yield

$$
\dot{H}=\frac{\partial \mathscr{R}}{\partial \Omega}
$$

But if the planet has no satellite, as for example Venus, the mass can be determined by comparing the observed and theoretical distur-

bances it produces on some other planet, say the earth. Devise a method for determining such a mass by use of the formulas of this section.
*exercise 7.4. (To be used in Sec. 5.) From the following approximations,

$$
J_{1}(e) \doteq \frac{e}{2}\left(1-\frac{e^{2}}{8}\right), \quad J_{2}(2 e) \doteq \frac{1}{8} e^{2}, \quad J_{3}(3 e) \doteq \frac{1}{16}
$$

and the expansions obtained in Sec. 12 of Chap. 1, obtain the following formulas, valid through terms of order $e^{2}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin u \doteq\left(1-\frac{e^{2}}{8}\right) \sin l+\frac{1}{8} e \sin 2 l+\frac{3}{8} e^{2} \sin 3 l \\
& \frac{a}{r} \cos u \doteq\left(1-\frac{e^{2}}{8}\right) \cos l+\cos 2 l+\frac{3}{8} e^{2} \cos 3 l \\
& \frac{a}{r} \doteq 1+e \cos l+e^{2} \cos 2 l \\
& \frac{r}{a} \doteq 1-e \cos l-e^{2} \cos 2 l+e^{2} \cos ^{2} l \\
& \cos u \doteq-\frac{1}{8} e+\left(1-\frac{3}{8} e^{2}\right) \cos l+\frac{1}{8} e \cos 2 l+\frac{3}{8} e^{2} \cos 3 l
\end{aligned}
$$

From these and from the relations $r \cos f=a(\cos u-e), r \sin f=$ $a\left(1-e^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \sin u \doteq a \sin u$, obtain the approximations

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{r}{a} \cos f \doteq-\frac{3}{8} e+\left(1-\frac{3}{8} e^{2}\right) \cos l+\frac{1}{8} e \cos 2 l+\frac{3}{8} e^{2} \cos 3 l \\
& \frac{r}{a} \sin f \doteq\left(1-\frac{3}{8} e^{2}\right) \sin l+\frac{1}{8} e \sin 2 l+\frac{3}{8} e^{2} \sin 3 l
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the last two formulas to show that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\frac{r}{a}\right)^{2} \cos 2 f \doteq \frac{3}{8} e^{2}-3 e \cos l \\
& \quad+\left(1-\frac{3}{8} e^{2}\right) \cos 2 l+e \cos 3 l+e^{2} \cos 4 l \\
& \left(\frac{r}{a}\right)^{2} \sin 2 f \doteq-3 e \sin l+\left(1-\frac{3}{8} e^{2}\right) \sin 2 l+e \sin 3 l+e^{2} \sin 4 l
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, obtain for an arbitrary angle $\beta$ the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\frac{r}{a}\right)^{2}[3 \cos (2 f+\beta)+1] \doteq\left(1+\frac{3}{8} e^{2}\right)-2 e \cos l-\frac{1}{8} e^{2} \cos 2 l \\
& \quad+\frac{1}{8} e^{2} \cos \beta-9 e \cos (\beta+l)+3\left(1-\frac{3}{8} e^{2}\right) \cos (\beta+2 l) \\
& \quad+3 e \cos (\beta+3 l)+3 e^{2} \cos (\beta+4 l)
\end{aligned}
$$

## 8. AN INTRODUCTION TO LUNAR THEORY

The most highly developed part of celestial mechanics is the theory of our own moon regarded as a satellite of the earth, with the sun as the
disturbing mass. The modern theory is beyond the weapons available in this book and we shall describe a very simplified approximation to the problem. The reader is warned that the approximate problem cannot be trusted to give good results concerning the actual motion of the moon. The main purpose is to provide some experience in the techniques we have developed so far in order to draw a few qualitative conclusions.

The mathematical setting is that described at the beginning of the preceding section with $m_{1}=$ earth, $m_{2}=$ moon, $m_{3}=$ sun. It will be supposed that all motion takes place in the plane of the ecliptic, so that equations involing $\Omega$ and $l$ become irrelevant. Since we are talking about the motion of the moon relative to the earth, we fix a coordinate system in this plane with origin at the earth. Angles will be measured from the $x$ axis, positive in the direction of the moon's motion around the earth. It will be supposed that the motion of the sun around the earth is circular and uniform, and that the origin of time is fixed at an instant when the sun crosses the positive $x$-axis. Then at the instant $t$ the vector $s$ from the earth to the sun forms an angle of $n^{\prime} t$ with the positive $x$-axis, where $n^{\prime}$ is the mean motion of the sun. The length $s$ of $s$ is a constant. The angle from the $x$-axis to the vector $r$ joining the earth to the moon is $\omega+f$, as usual, and the angle $\psi$ between $r$ and $s$ is $\theta+f-n^{\prime} t$. Since $r_{23}$ is the distance from the moon to the sun, the cosinc law gives

$$
r_{23}^{2}=r^{2}+s^{2}-2 r s \cos \psi=s^{2}\left(1-2 p \cos \psi+p^{2}\right)
$$

where $p=r / s$. It will be supposed $t \mathrm{l}$ at $p$ is so small that powers of $p$ above the first can be ignored in the sequel.

According to Kepler's third law (see Sec. 15 of Chap. 1), we have $\left(n^{\prime}\right)^{2}$ $s^{2}=G\left(m_{2}+m_{1} \doteq G m_{2}\right.$. Therefore the disturbing function, as given by (7.2), becomes, on neglecting the mass of the earth,

$$
R=\left(n^{\prime} s\right)^{2}\left[\left(1-2 p \cos \psi+p^{2}\right)^{-1 / 2}-p \cos \psi\right]
$$

If we expand the first term in brackets in powers of $p$ and drop all powers above the second, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}
R & =\left(n^{\prime} s\right)^{2}\left[1-\frac{1}{4} p^{2}\left(1-3 \cos ^{2} \psi\right)\right] \\
& =\left(n^{\prime} s\right)^{2}\left[1+\frac{1}{4} p^{2}(3 \cos 2 \psi+1)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

The first term $\left(n^{\prime} s\right)^{2}$ of $R$ is a constant; we drop it out since only derivatives of $R$ occur in the perturbation equations. Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
R & =\frac{1}{4}\left(n^{\prime} s\right)^{2} p^{2}(3 \cos 2 \psi+1) \\
& =\frac{1}{4} n^{\prime 2} a^{2}\left(\frac{r}{a}\right)^{2}[3 \cos (2 f+\beta)+1]
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\beta=2 \omega-2 n^{\prime} t$. Finally, by the concluding formula of Ex. 7.4, we obtain the (very) approximate disturbing function

$$
\begin{aligned}
R= & \frac{1}{4}\left(n^{\prime} a\right)^{2}\left[\left(1+\frac{3}{8} e^{2}\right)-2 e \cos l-\frac{1}{8} e^{2} \cos 2 l\right. \\
& +\frac{11}{8} e^{2} \cos \beta-9 e \cos (\beta+l)+3\left(1-\frac{5}{8} e^{2}\right) \cos (\beta+2 l) \\
& \left.+3 e \cos (\beta+3 l)+3 e^{2} \cos (\beta+4 l)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

If this expression for $R$ is substituted into the perturbation equations of Sec. 7, we obtain the equations governing our primitive lunar theory. But remember that the conclusions are unreliable because so many assumptions and approximations have been introduced. For example, Eqs. (IV) and (VI) disappear on the assumption of plane motion. In particular, we cannot obtain the well-known fact that the line of nodes regresses (that is, $\hat{\Omega}<0$ ).

There is another familiar phenomenon, however, that can be partly explained on the basis of (8.1). Let us consider the constant part of $R$ alone, namely,

$$
R_{1}=\frac{1}{4}\left(n^{\prime} a\right)^{2}\left(1+\frac{3}{2} e^{2}\right)
$$

and its effect on $\omega$. According to (V) of the preceding section.

$$
\dot{\omega}=c(\mu a e)^{-1} \frac{1}{4}\left(t^{\prime} a\right)^{2} 3 e+\text { non-constant periodic terms. }
$$

To compute the size of the constant term, we write $c=\mu^{1 / 2} a^{1 / 2}\left(1-e^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}$ $\hat{=}(\mu a)^{1 / 2}$ so that the term becomes $\frac{3}{2}\left(n^{\prime 2} / n\right)$.
If we use the fact that the period of the sun is 1 year and of the moon .075 years, we get $n^{\prime}=2 \pi, n=2 \pi / .075$. The constant is therefore about .353 .
Then, according to our theory, the term contributes a positive rotation of .353 radians per year to the major axis of the moon's orbit. Actually this is only about half of the observed motion, which requires a more elaborate theory to explain it.

## 9. THE PERIODIC TERMS IN LUNAR THEORY

According to the calculation made in Sec. 8 of the effect on $\omega$ of the secula term $R_{1}$, we have approximately

$$
\dot{\omega}=\frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{n^{\prime}}{n}\right)^{2} n+\text { periodic terms. }
$$

The corresponding calculation for the mean anomaly (see Ex. 8.2) yields

$$
\dot{I}=n\left[1-\frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{n^{\prime}}{n}\right)^{2}\right]+\text { periodic terms. }
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dot{l}+\dot{\omega}=n\left[1-\left(\frac{n^{\prime}}{n}\right)^{2}\right]+\text { periodic terms. }
$$

The average value of the right-hand side of (9.2) obtained over a long tim interval is denoted by $\bar{n}$ and is called the mean sidereal motion. Consisten with Ex. 8.3, the number $2 \pi / \bar{n}$ is the mean sidereal period. It is the number .075 (years) introduced at the end of Sec. 8, and what we did there amounts to replacing (9.1) by the further approximation

$$
\dot{\omega}=\frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{n^{\prime}}{\bar{n}}\right)^{2} \bar{n}+\text { periodic terms. }
$$

Let $k$ denote the constant $1-\frac{3}{4}\left(n^{\prime} / \bar{n}\right)^{2}$; it is close to 1 . Then

$$
\dot{\omega}=(1-k) \bar{n}+\text { periodic terms. }
$$

If we replace (9.2) by

$$
\dot{I}+\dot{\omega}=\bar{n}+\text { periodic terms }
$$

then

$$
\dot{l}=k \bar{n}+\text { periodic terms. }
$$

Now let $l_{0}, \omega_{0}$ be the values of $l$ and $\omega$ at the instant $t_{0}$ at which we wish to start the integration of the perturbation equations. Define

$$
\dot{I}=l_{0}+k \bar{n}\left(t-t_{0}\right), \quad \dot{\omega}=\omega_{0}+(1-k) \bar{n}\left(t-t_{0}\right)
$$

These are the "main" parts of $l$ and $\omega$ due to the secular part of $R$ and allowing for a general average of the periodic parts.

Recall that in the first-order perturbation theory described in the earlier sections of this chapter, we treat the parameters (or elements) which occur on the right-hand side of the perturbation equations as constants during the integration. In the lunar theory we are now describing, the elements in question are $a, e, \omega, l$. It turns out to be of advantage in integrating the

equations to replace $\omega$ and $l$, not by $\omega_{0}, l$, but by $\bar{\omega}, \bar{j}$ in order to take account of the secular effect. On the other hand, $a$ and $e$ are still treated as constants. Observe that the same effect is achieved by replacing $\omega$ by $e_{1}+(1-k) \bar{n}\left(t-t_{0}\right)$ and $l$ by $l+k \bar{n}\left(t-t_{0}\right)$ in the disturbing function $R$ [see (8.1)], and then treating all four elements as constants during the integration.

So far we have considered only secular effects. In order to illustrate the effect of periodic terms in $R$, we turn our attention to a phenomenon known as the erection. If the motion of the moon were undisturbed, then the polar coordinate $\theta=f+\omega$ would increase by $2 \pi$ during a period. Another way of saying this is that $f+\omega-n t$ returns to its original value when $t=2 \pi / n$. It is reasonable to ask what happens in the case of disturled motion. The question takes the form: what change does $f+\omega-$ it undergo during the motion of the moon; is this change periodic?

In order to answer the question, we start with the approximation $f=$ $1+2 e \sin l$, justified in Ex. 9.1. Then if we write $\xi=f+\omega-\bar{n} t$, we find that

$$
\dot{\xi}=(1+2 e \cos l)(\dot{l}+\dot{\omega})-\bar{n}+2 \dot{e} \sin l-2 e \dot{\omega} \cos l
$$

Now define $\omega_{1}=\omega-\bar{\omega}$. Since $d \bar{\omega} / d t=(1-k) \bar{n}$, we can rewrite this a:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{\xi}= & {[1-2 e \cos l)(\dot{l}+\dot{\omega})-\bar{n}[1+2 e(1-k) \cos l] } \\
& +2 \dot{e} \sin l-2 e \dot{\omega}_{1} \cos l
\end{aligned}
$$

We make some further approximations which can be justified only vaguely here. Because $e$ and $1-k$ are small, replace the brackets on the right by 1. The first line on the right-hand side becomes $\dot{l}+\dot{\omega}-\bar{n}$. It can be shown that the effect of this term is small compared to what remains. So, finally, we get the approximation

$$
\dot{\xi}=2 \dot{e} \sin l-2 e \dot{\omega}_{1} \cos l
$$

According to (9.3) and the definition of $\omega_{1}$, we know that $\dot{\omega}_{1}=$ terms of the periodic part of $R$ effecting $\dot{\omega}$. The periodic part is $R-R_{1}$. Therefore, by Eq. (V) of Sec. 7 and the approximation $c=\sqrt{\mu a}$, we get

$$
\dot{\omega}_{1}=(\mu a)^{-1 / 2} e^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial e}\left(R-R_{1}\right)
$$

Similarly, since $R_{1}$ does not involve $\omega$, Eq. (II) gives us

$$
\dot{e}=-(\mu a)^{-1 / 2} e^{-1}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \omega}\left(R-R_{1}\right)-\frac{\partial R}{\partial l}\right]
$$

It can be shown that of all the periodic terms in $R$, the one that makes the major contribution to the present problem is the erection term $R_{1}=$ $\frac{1}{2}\left(n^{\prime} a r\right)^{2} \cos \beta$. By definition, $\beta=2 \omega-2 n^{\prime} t$. Moreover, by the principle stated earlier, we may replace $\omega$ by $\omega+(1-k) \bar{n}\left(t-t_{0}\right)$ in order to treat all the elements as constants during the integration. Therefore, we replace
$R-R_{1}$ by $\frac{1}{2}\left(n^{\prime} a r\right)^{2} \cos 2 \gamma$, where $\gamma=\omega-(1-k) \bar{n} t_{0}+\left[(1-k) \bar{n}-n^{\prime}\right] t$. From the preceding equations for $\dot{\omega}_{1}$ and $\dot{e}$, it is found that

$$
e \dot{\omega}_{1}=\frac{1}{2} \times\left(\frac{n^{\prime}}{n}\right)^{2} n e \cos 2 \gamma
$$

and

$$
\dot{e}=\frac{1}{2} \times\left(\frac{n^{\prime}}{n}\right)^{2} n e \sin 2 \gamma
$$

These and the replacement of $\xi$ convert (9.5) into

$$
\frac{d}{d t}(f+\omega-\bar{n} t)=-\frac{1}{2} \times\left(\frac{n^{\prime}}{n}\right)^{2} e n \cos (2 \gamma+l)
$$

From this, the desired change in $f+\omega-\bar{n} t$ can be computed by integration. Geometrically, it represents a displacement of position in longitude from the position the moon would have under ordinary Kepler motion. The phenomenon is the evection mentioned above. It was discovered by Hipparchus, a Greek astronomer.
